World.title: No, France is not ‘burning’
World.content:
It is merely witnessing another episode of unrest that – like many others in its history – has a violent element to it.

For the past few weeks, images of burning buildings and devastated shopping streets have dominated international media coverage of France. “France is burning”, “France in turmoil”, “Chaos in France”, the headlines have declared, focusing on the violent element of an otherwise peaceful student movement demanding better conditions for education.

To understand why this has happened in the past and is happening today, let us start by examining the word “violence”. In today’s context, it is used indiscriminately to refer to a broken shop window, a police officer injuring a demonstrator, a car set on fire, or shots fired at an unarmed crowd.

This confusion tends to inaccurately place material damage and attacks on people, revolt and its repression, on the same level.

Brazilian archbishop Dom Helder Camara, an advocate of liberation theology, distinguished between three types of violence: the first, that of injustice that oppresses; the second, that of the revolt it provokes; and the third, that of repression.

I would add one more form of violence: that of inequality, discrimination, social humiliation and precarious life. A social order can be violent even in its apparent tranquillity.

French history reminds us how often revolts, the injustices that fuel them and the repressions that answer them are closely intertwined.

The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, in the lead-up to the outbreak of the French Revolution, is one famous event. It was an act of armed insurrection by revolutionaries who rejected an oppressive absolute monarchy and saw the prison as a symbol of its abuses.



The defenders of the fortress fired on the assailants, killing about 100 people. After their capitulation, the Bastille governor, Bernard-Rene Jourdan de Launay, was killed, and his head impaled on a pike and paraded in the streets.

In the following weeks, peasants started invading properties of the aristocracy, ransacking them and burning property deeds that recorded feudal rights. These documents embodied the feudal domination peasants were subjected to.

Three years later, on August 10, 1792, revolutionaries stormed the royal residenceod the Tuileries Palace, which led to the deaths of hundreds of Swiss Guards. In September, in a climate of panic in the face of foreign invasion, armed groups executed more than 1,000 prisoners, among them Catholic priests and criminals arrested for common crimes.

These outbursts of popular anger were rooted in the systemic violence of the ancien regime: privileges of birth, feudal oppression, tax inequalities, arbitrariness in the use of force and repression. Popular violence cannot be separated from that of a social order founded on domination.

Throughout the 19th century, the same driving forces — fear and anger against those in power — continued to fuel collective violence. In February 1831, an anticlerical crowd sacked the archbishop’s palace in Paris and destroyed its furnishings, thus striking at a Church associated with the deposed monarch.

In 1871, following France’s defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, thousands of disaffected Parisians rebelled and established the Paris Commune. They took hostages in an attempt to persuade the government in Versailles to stop bombarding them. The killing of the hostages ultimately took place during “Bloody Week”, as the Versailles army massacred Parisians by the thousands.

Social violence, however, has not always taken the spectacular form of insurrection and its suppression. It has also been expressed in the form of labour mobilisation and the targeting of factories, machines and representatives of the employers.

On January 26, 1886, in Decazeville, engineer Jules Watrin, deputy director of the local mines, was beaten, thrown from a window, and killed by a crowd of miners angered by bad working conditions. His name gave rise to the neologism “watrinade” – the killing of a manager or a boss.

In Armentieres, in 1903, a textile strike degenerated into the ransacking of shops. In Limoges, three years later, demonstrators forced open the gates of factories and destroyed porcelain in one plant. Two gun shops were looted and an explosive device set off outside a director’s home.



In 1968, a student-led protest for better university conditions triggered a society-wide mobilisation, drawing in millions of workers who went on strike. The barricades in the Latin Quarter of Paris were accompanied by overturned or torched cars, the throwing of cobblestones and the use of Molotov cocktails. In Nantes, the director of Sud Aviation was held captive in his factory for several days.

In the following years, the process of deindustrialisation put workers yet again in a precarious situation and drove yet another wave of labour protests.

In 1979, the steelworkers of Longwy and Denain, faced with massive job cuts, took part in mobilisations that left behind broken doors and scattered files at the subprefecture of Briey, vehicles set on fire and shop windows smashed.

In 2009, after the announcement of the closure of the Continental plant in Clairoix, employees ransacked the subprefecture of Compiegne. In 2015, at Air France, two executives were attacked during a demonstration against job cuts.

In 2016, during the protests against the labour law reforms, which allowed employers to fire workers more easily, storefronts were smashed and police vehicles were attacked. Two years later, the demonstrations of the “yellow vests” over economic grievances brought an unprecedented level of visibility to such actions. In December 2018, the Arc de Triomphe was defaced and shops were looted. Yet, this movement was also notable for the serious injuries inflicted upon many protesters by law enforcement.

Mobilisations by farmers and fishermen have also led to spectacular protest actions, targeting in particular representatives of the state and public buildings. In 1994, a demonstration by fishermen protesting against the crisis in their sector turned into clashes with law enforcement and caused a fire that devastated the Parliament of Brittany. In 1999, farmers ransacked the office of Environment Minister Dominique Voynet.

But not all collective violence falls within organised protest movements. Some erupt in the aftermath of tragic events, crystallising accumulated anger and social tensions. In 2005, after the deaths of Zyed Benna and Bouna Traore, protests in working-class neighbourhoods of Paris resulted in thousands of vehicles being set on fire and attacks on public buildings. In a grim echo, 18 years later, after the death of Nahel Merzouk, killed by a police officer in Nanterre, a suburb of Paris, vehicles and shops were attacked.

This long history teaches us that popular violence is neither new nor uniform. From burning feudal property archives to sabotaging a factory machine, to ransacking a police prefecture, or setting fire to a shop, acts of violence can have different aims. But material destruction often constitutes a political language directed at the symbols of a power deemed deaf or unjust.

The most spectacular acts are often carried out by a minority and cannot by themselves define mobilisations that are largely peaceful. Moreover, the practices of demonstrators should not obscure the violence that runs through society.



Therefore, to claim that violence today suddenly erupted in a formerly peaceful France is to misunderstand an essential part of this political and social history.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Israel’s war on homes: From Hebron to Gaza and southern Lebanon
World.content:
“Around 12:30 at night, the Israeli army vehicles were at al-Jalda Square,” one Hebron resident told Al Jazeera. “They told us to leave our homes. We asked until when, and they said until further notice. We left with the clothes on our backs.”

Hours earlier on October 23, two Israeli soldiers had been killed by armed Palestinian men at a checkpoint near the city. Hebron, the occupied West Bank’s largest city, has been under Israeli siege ever since, with restrictions extending across a governorate of about 800,000 Palestinians.

A black X now marks the homes from which families have been forcibly expelled. Soldiers have moved into others, turning them into military outposts.

In just over a week, nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been displaced, according to UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, which called the measures collective punishment in violation of international law.

The current operation builds on years of demolitions. From 2009 up until the siege began on October 23, Israeli forces demolished 2,491 buildings and displaced 3,534 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Across Area C and occupied East Jerusalem, the monthly average of demolitions since 2024 has been at least double that of the preceding 15 years.

Many demolitions are linked to Israel’s restrictive permit system. Palestinians struggle to obtain Israeli-issued building permits, leaving structures built without them vulnerable to demolition.

In Masafer Yatta, a cluster of 13 communities in the South Hebron Hills, Israeli authorities have demolished about 400 structures in 15 years, displacing 969 Palestinians. Nearly half were demolished since January 2025.

World.title: Gaza doctors struggle with bereavement, overwork, trauma amid genocidal war
World.content:
Doctors and nurses struggle to cope with the horrors they endured during the height of the Gaza war.

Deir el-Balah, Gaza – Manar Fayyad, 29, an anaesthesiologist at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, has suffered severe psychological trauma since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

The turning point came when he discovered that a man lying before him in the operating room was his own brother Shadi, who was killed in an Israeli air strike on December 27, 2023.

He recalled the moment he was summoned into the operating room to administer anaesthesia to a critically injured man before emergency surgery.

“He died before I could reach him,” he said. “When I arrived in the operating room, I recognised the man’s clothes. I had a strange feeling, so I approached him and uncovered his face. To my shock, he was my brother Shadi, who was 34.”

Since then, the hospital has become inseparable from the traumatic memory, and he has been unable to continue to work, ultimately bringing his professional career to a premature end.

He continues to struggle with the psychological effects of the experience, trying to cope with it on his own without professional help. He has withdrawn from social life and avoids people and noise as he searches for peace since his brother died.

Sitting by the sea and writing offers him some solace, helping him express his pain and process what has happened. Yet he remains preoccupied with the idea of leaving Gaza, hoping that distance might free him from the reminders of that day.

Having lost his brother, his profession and much of his social life, Fayyad now faces a different battle: one against trauma that he is trying to confront alone.

Khaled Raafat, 29, a nurse in the emergency department at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, stepped away from work for an extended period after losing his wife, children, mother and several siblings in an Israeli air strike on his family home on October 18, 2023. He was at the hospital at the time, trying to save their lives of others injured that day.



“Learning that I had lost my family marked a painful turning point in my life,” Khaled told Al Jazeera. “I could no longer do my job in the same way. The hospital, once associated in my mind with my humanitarian duty, became a reminder of personal pain that was beyond what I could bear. It deeply affected my ability to continue my professional and social life.”

Raafat said he eventually decided to rebuild his life.

“I realised that life could not stop at the tragedy and that I had to find a way to carry on. I decided to work towards my psychological recovery, got married and started a new family in an attempt to regain stability and hope,” he said. “I then returned to work at the hospital.”

At least 1,700 medical personnel have been killed in Israeli attacks during the war while 83 healthcare workers remain in Israeli detention, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

These figures do not reveal the deep psychological burden borne by medical workers who have lost family, friends and colleagues and witnessed horrific injuries and death on a daily basis. They have also faced continued displacement, relentless pressure and have been overworked for years.

A study found that 41 percent reported losing family members and 46 percent had experienced both personal bereavement and displacement from their workplaces, according to a report on the strain on medical workers in Gaza published in the Public Library of Science.

At least 78 percent of healthcare workers in Gaza lacked access to mental health services, showing the gap between the trauma healthcare workers endure and their access to psychological care. It has meant that Gaza’s health system is struggling to retain its remaining staff and prevent them from leaving the medical field.

Although it is difficult to assess how many doctors, nurses and other medical workers have left Gaza and their jobs, official reports have acknowledged a “loss of human resources” and “diminished capacity in the healthcare system”.

To help halt this brain drain and protect healthcare workers who have experienced psychological trauma – probably most of those in Gaza, they need psychological and social support.

“They are caught between their professional duty to save lives and the pain of losing the people closest to them,” Munir al-Bursh, director general of Gaza’s Ministry of Health, told Al Jazeera. “They find themselves treating others’ wounds while struggling to heal their own.”

Working under constant pressure without adequate support or rest deepens exhaustion and threatens healthcare workers’ ability to continue, he said.



“Protecting medical personnel is not just about securing medicines and equipment. It also means safeguarding their mental health and giving them time to rest and recover. Those who save others also need someone to reach out and help them.”

The acute shortage of medical staff after the killings, detentions and injuries of many healthcare workers makes it difficult to give those who remain enough time to recover, he added. This is compounded by the continuing arrival of patients and wounded people, shortages of equipment and a lack of replacement staff.

The experiences of these doctors and nurses reveal the psychological toll of war on Gaza’s healthcare system. Those accustomed to confronting death and saving the wounded have sometimes found themselves facing it as bereaved family members rather than medical professionals. Caught between their duty to save others and their own grief, some have paid a profound psychological price with consequences for both their professional and personal lives.

Nurse Hiba al-Tawil, 39, witnessed her brother’s death in the intensive care unit at the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, where she worked.

“Losing my brother at my workplace was a difficult experience that had a profound psychological impact on me,” she told Al Jazeera. “Being in the intensive care unit afterwards reminded me of what had happened and made it harder to cope with the loss.”

She later transferred to another department. which helped ease the psychological pressure she was experiencing and allowed her to distance herself from the place where her brother died.

The psychological clinic at the hospital treats doctors and nurses struggling with trauma caused by bereavement and their experiences during the war. In some cases, these experiences can develop into severe psychological disorders that affect their everyday lives and ability to work.

Reham Abu Rokba, a psychologist at the complex, said treatment begins with assessing the patient’s psychological condition, diagnosing symptoms and determining their impact before developing a treatment plan.

For patients with post-traumatic stress disorder, treatment may include cognitive behavioural therapy, which helps them understand their psychological responses to traumatic events and regain their ability to cope.

Depending on the patient’s needs, treatment may involve about 12 individual sessions and, when necessary, medication.

Reham said that continued psychological support, appropriate treatment and adherence to the treatment plan can help ease symptoms and lead to improvements.

“Recovery requires time and ongoing participation in psychological support sessions,” she told Al Jazeera. “Providing the appropriate treatment and ensuring adherence to it can help alleviate symptoms and lead to tangible improvements in an individual’s mental wellbeing.”

World.title: Police storm Portugal housing protest camp
World.content:
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square in Lisbon early on Sunday.

Police have used shields and batons to disperse housing protesters who stormed a tent camp in Portugal’s capital, Lisbon, a week after similar operations drew criticism from protesters and rights groups.

Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square at about 4:30am (04:30 GMT) on Sunday, a day after thousands marched demanding the government withdraw a rental bill they say would deepen the country’s housing crisis.

Protesters had erected more than 50 tents following Saturday’s march through Lisbon. Police commander Iuri Rodrigues issued three warnings to remove the tents, saying they had been erected illegally and that anyone resisting their removal could face disobedience charges.

Hundreds of demonstrators shielding the camp were dispersed, while police also dismantled a smaller encampment in Porto’s Dom Joao I square.

Earlier, lawmaker Pedro Delgado Alves said Rossio Square was peaceful and that nothing justified “a police intervention involving force, physical violence or baton charges, the kind of scenes we witnessed last week”.

The intervention followed operations in the same squares the previous Sunday, when police arrested 25 people in Lisbon and six in Porto. Housing campaign group Casa para Viver said 60 people were injured across those operations, which police described as “proportionate”.

Rising housing costs

The protests reflect growing anger over housing costs across Europe, including demonstrations in Spain and opposition to government economic policies in France, Germany and Albania.



Portugal faces one of Europe’s severest housing affordability crises, with young people among the hardest hit. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents on new leases have almost doubled.

The Bank of Portugal estimates a nationwide shortage of 300,000 homes, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.

Demonstrators want the minority centre-right government to scrap legislation that would make evictions easier and remove rent caps on new leases, saying it would worsen affordability and leave tenants more exposed.

World.title: A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
World.content:
Oman is in a unique position to mediate talks on a security arrangement that could stabilise the region.

Proposing a non-aggression pact amid regional hostilities may seem premature. Yet agreements to stop war matter most when distrust is the deepest. The key question is whether regional governments can agree on rules that make their disagreements less destructive.

In a recent lecture at Cambridge University in the UK, Oman’s Foreign Minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, called for a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf littoral states: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council along with Iraq and Iran. He described it as the essential prerequisite for an inclusive regional security architecture.

Could such a pact work? As Albusaidi conceded, it would be hard to achieve. But as another major escalation looms between Iran and the United States, the region urgently needs a diplomatic path forward.

Indeed, the ongoing conflict has proved so hard to resolve because the region’s security arrangements have remained underdeveloped, relying for too long on external powers. The way forward then can be an inclusive agreement.

Reviving the promise of 1976

The Omani proposal is anchored in a historic precedent. In November 1976, the foreign ministers of all eight Gulf littoral states met in Muscat to pursue collective security after Britain’s withdrawal from the region.

It remains the only time all eight have sat at one table. The Iranian Revolution, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran–Iraq war then pushed the region towards defensive arrangements that later hardened into exclusion.



For decades, Iran, in particular, was seen as a threat to the rest of the region. Yet, given that the country holds roughly half the Gulf coastline, any security architecture without it is structurally unsound.

It was not until 2019 that the idea of a regional security arrangement was revived. In May of that year, then Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif proposed a regional non-aggression pact with Gulf neighbours during a visit to Baghdad, which Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov endorsed.

That September, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani launched the Hormuz Peace Endeavour (HOPE) at the UN General Assembly, envisaging a non-aggression pact among Hormuz states. Gulf reactions were largely dismissive, citing Iranian support for armed groups threatening regional stability.

The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived the idea on the Arab side. In May, the Financial Times reported that Saudi Arabia was discussing a non-aggression framework with Iran, reportedly modelled on the Helsinki process between the US and Russia during the Cold War.

This month, Qatar’s defence minister called for GCC–Iran dialogue, joined by Turkiye and Pakistan, towards a non-aggression agreement.

Oman’s proposal comes as the latest iteration of this regional shift. Muscat is in a unique position to mediate given its history of acting as a mediator and its recent record of hosting US-Iran talks in 2025 and February 2026. It has access that few others have.

Concluding a pact that works

The strongest objection against a Gulf pact with Iran is simple: Why trust a state whose conduct has threatened the region’s security? Gulf concerns about Iranian actions are not misunderstandings. Oman itself formally protested to Iran after drone attacks targeting Musandam and Al Wusta in July.

Reassurance is therefore insufficient. Inclusion must mean obligation. Membership in a regional pact would have to bind Iran as much as any other signatory, providing a means to constrain threatening behaviour and address legitimate grievances.

A pact must rest on observable conduct, reciprocal restraint and consequences for violations. At minimum, it would need commitments against the threat or use of force, interference in internal affairs, attacks on civilian infrastructure and support for armed groups conducting cross-border attacks, alongside protection of navigation.

To reach a workable agreement, negotiations can adopt a gradual approach. Consultations among the eight countries could first identify minimum shared interests: territorial security, functioning ports, reliable energy exports, civilian protection and uninterrupted trade. Oman can facilitate, but each state would represent itself; Muscat’s channel to Tehran confers no mandate to negotiate for its neighbours.



Initial talks should yield limited, reciprocal measures: military hotlines, rules for maritime encounters, notification of exercises and rapid communication after attacks. An understanding about protecting energy facilities, desalination plants and commercial shipping would offer an early test of compliance.

Hormuz is the obvious starting point, though progress could be hard. Oman-Iran talks have already outlined a temporary navigation arrangement. However, as Albusaidi conceded, it cannot be implemented unless Washington and Tehran compromise, including by reversing wartime actions that halted maritime traffic. Any wider framework must respect international navigation rights.

Armed groups would be the hardest issue to resolve. Governments should undertake neither to direct nor materially support cross-border attacks by such actors, and demonstrate compliance through verifiable steps. Where control is contested, the pact would need procedures for establishing evidence and requiring corrective action.

Compliance with initial measures could open cooperation on maritime safety, environmental protection and emergency response. Serious violations should trigger investigation, urgent consultation and agreed diplomatic consequences, while the right of self-defence would remain intact.

A regional pact would not settle every conflict touching the Gulf. The United States and Israel, both parties to this year’s war on Iran, would remain outside it and Yemen’s war involves actors whose agendas a Gulf arrangement could not easily bind. But a framework need not end every war to be worth having. It need only make it harder for any of them to become a war among its signatories.

The pact’s credibility will depend on whether it changes conduct. Fewer or no attacks, functioning crisis channels and demonstrable respect for sovereignty will matter more than signatures.

Present hostilities make the task difficult, but they also expose the cost of postponing it. The first achievement would be modest but consequential: establishing that disagreement entitles no state to endanger another’s security.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Rubio says Trump administration did not help Bolsonaro flee Brazil to US
World.content:
Trump says defeated presidential candidate, who faces investigation in Brazil, can stay in the US ‘as long as he wants’.

Share Rubio says Trump administration did not help Bolsonaro flee Brazil to US on social media

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says President Donald Trump’s administration did not help Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flee the country for the United States after losing a run-off to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

Bolsonaro arrived in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday, a day after the US Department of State said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas after his October 25 election loss, which bucked a trend of conservative electoral wins in Latin America.

Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, and before leaving, he had been ordered to surrender his passport because police deemed him a flight risk.

“We didn’t facilitate anything,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday in Atlanta, Georgia, where diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies were gathered.

“We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country,” Rubio said.

He added that the US government was not “involved directly in any of the moves that were made”.

Rubio also said he had seen Brazil’s foreign minister, Mauro Vieira, in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday and he expected to see Brazilian officials again in November in France during a foreign ministers meeting.

Separately, Trump, who had previously called Brazil’s election “rigged”, voiced sympathy for Bolsonaro and said he could stay in the US indefinitely.

“I think he got treated very shabbily, very shabbily, so he can stay here as long as he wants,” the president told reporters at his Florida residence on Saturday.



The Reuters news agency reported that Bolsonaro was admitted to the US under humanitarian parole, a status that typically lasts for one year.

Trump’s comments suggested relations between the Western Hemisphere’s two largest democracies may remain strained for some time.

After Bolsonaro’s run-off loss, he fled Brazil to the US via Argentina and Ecuador on a journey that some US media outlets reported was partly arranged with the help of Jason Miller, a White House official.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede the Brazilian election and called the results fraudulent without providing evidence.

Since arriving in the US, he has claimed to be the true “leader” of Brazil and said he left the country because he was a victim of “persecution”.

World.title: Canelo Alvarez defeats Christian Mbilli to reclaim WBC title in Riyadh
World.content:
Mexican boxing star wins 12-round decision to defeat the French fighter and regain the super middleweight belt.

Mexican veteran Saul “Canelo” Alvarez has delivered a commanding performance to defeat French fighter Christian Mbilli and regain his WBC super middleweight title in an emotional victory in Saudi Arabia.

Alvarez won a 12-round decision on Sunday in Riyadh after exerting his influence in the second half of a fight that went ahead despite the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.

The 36-year-old Mexican was returning to the ring for the first time since he was beaten by American Terence Crawford in September 2025 in a loss that ended Alvarez’s reign as holder of the division’s four major titles.

He faced Mbilli, 31, who was elevated to titleholder in January, and the fight, which started off as a tight contest, turned into a convincing victory for Alvarez.

The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in Alvarez’s favour.

The Mexican superstar struggled for words after receiving the belt.

“It’s so difficult to explain. It’s so difficult to explain,” Alvarez said in English. “It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title, now, after 20, 21 years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now I won the title again.”

Alvarez added another world title to a haul that stretches from light middleweight to light heavyweight in a 20-year career.

A host of other sporting events has been called off since the Houthis launched drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight against the Houthis.



Alvarez hinted at the security situation when he thanked his family “who are watching me from afar today for the first time”.

He was the more composed boxer in the opening round in Riyadh, but by round three, Mbilli was ripping off combinations and looking the more active of the two fighters.

The Frenchman took the initiative in round five although the bout remained a tactical battle.

Alvarez began showing his class and ringcraft in the sixth, easily winning the round, but it was in the seventh that he really pressed home his advantage, pinning Mbilli to the ropes and delivering a right uppercut that had the Frenchman rocking on his feet.

In the eighth, Mbilli had a point taken away for punching behind the head, and he seemed to lose more momentum from then on, allowing Alvarez to begin dictating the fight in the next round as the wily veteran pulled ahead of his younger opponent.

World.title: French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.
World.content:
Pinned

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Here’s what else to know.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often clash with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

World.title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
World.content:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.

The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.

As night fell, demonstrations turned violent.

A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.

Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.

Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".

She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."

World.title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".

Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."

The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.

Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.

Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.

As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.

Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.

"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.

World.title: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city
World.content:
There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv.

Families cried as they reunited with relatives they had not seen for years, with two sisters running and crying out as they embraced their father.

Some elderly residents were so weak they were carried on stretchers. They had been trapped in the frontline city without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.

Upon their arrival, Dasha and Anya Palii sprinted across the tarmac screaming towards the bus carrying their father Mykhailo.

Their cries and their tears captured the sheer relief of three years of desperate worry, fearing they would never see him again.

Their mother Zhanna clasped Mykhailo's face and stroked his forehead again and again, as if checking he was the same man she had left behind. He promised her, finally, they will now get married.

Tetiana and Volodymyr, an older couple carrying their cat, told the BBC they no longer have a home, after it was burned down in the first year of the war. They have been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour.

They said they instantly took the decision to leave but feared their journey could be disrupted. Now they have to work out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.

World.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
World.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.

All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.

The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.

The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.

North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.

World.title: India's opposition holds mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
World.content:
Tens of thousands of people have gathered in Delhi for a major opposition rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner.

The rally, organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, is taking place at Ramlila Maidan, a large ground in central Delhi known for hosting cultural events and political protests.

Visuals showed Gandhi in an open-top jeep alongside other opposition leaders heading towards the venue. The Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support, though its leaders have yet to be seen.

Security has been tightened, with thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed near the grounds.

Sunday's event is the latest show of opposition anger over a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from draft electoral rolls in India.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.

But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.

The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.

World.title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
World.content:
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.

Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.

A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.

"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - VuÄiÄ supporters - gathering near voting stations," PÃ©ter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."

Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.

OrbÃ¡n in Hungary, VuÄiÄ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.

Orban chose cheese, VuÄiÄ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.

They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.

World.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
World.content:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.

Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.

The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.

Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.

It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.

He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.

Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.

The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.

It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.

Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

World.title: Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.

In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.

More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.

The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.

Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Ebola: 34-year-old pilot, wife identified as suspected cases who tested negative in North-east Nigeria
World.content:
A 34-year-old pilot and his wife, a medical doctor, were the two people investigated for suspected Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) in Adamawa State after developing symptoms including fever, vomiting, fatigue, headache, cough, bleeding gums and nosebleeds.

Although Nigerian officials said two suspected Ebola cases were being investigated in the state and eventually turned negative, their identities were not disclosed. PREMIUM TIMES can now disclose the officials’ identities, though we are redacting their names.

An internal memo from the Adamawa State Ministry of Health and Human Services, obtained exclusively by PREMIUM TIMES, said the couple were admitted to the isolation centre of the Modibbo Adama University Teaching Hospital (MAUTH), Yola, on 29 October.

The memo, dated 30 October 2026 and signed by the State Epidemiologist, Jones Kadabiyu, said the Adamawa State Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC) received the report at 6:45 a.m. following a clinician’s report from MAUTH.

The development came as health authorities intensified surveillance following Nigeria’s confirmation of its first Ebola case in the current outbreak.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) had on Saturday announced that two suspected Ebola cases had been identified in the North-east, but did not initially disclose the state where the cases were detected.

However, the agency later confirmed that the two suspected cases were in Adamawa, noting that the laboratory tests on samples from both individuals were negative for Ebola after two rounds of testing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In a statement signed by its Director-General, Jide Idris, the NCDC said it was working with the Adamawa State government to investigate the suspected cases.

The agency said it isolated the two individuals and immediately activated public health measures while collecting samples for laboratory testing.

“Fortunately, the samples turned out negative for EBV after two rounds of testing,” Mr Idris said.

The NCDC said there is currently no laboratory-confirmed Ebola case in Adamawa State, adding that the previously confirmed case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) remains the only confirmed case in Nigeria.

What PREMIUM TIMES learnt

According to the memo, the pilot developed symptoms on 13 October, while his wife developed similar symptoms on 25 October.

The names of the two patients are contained in the documents seen by PREMIUM TIMES. However, this newspaper is withholding their identities to protect their privacy.

A preliminary report dated 31 October from Yola North Local Government Area (LGA), Adamawa State, said the pilot travelled to Kenya “for personal reasons” on 14 October and returned to Nigeria on 25 October. It said he had developed a fever before his trip and was treated for malaria.

“Prior to his departure, he reportedly developed a fever on 13 October 2026 and was treated for malaria. He reportedly remained well while in Kenya,” it noted.

However, upon returning to Yola, he developed symptoms including fever, nausea and vomiting, fatigue, headache, cough, bleeding gums and nosebleeds. His wife subsequently developed similar symptoms after caring for him at home.

They were both admitted at the MAUTH isolation centre.

The state health authorities collected samples from both patients on 30 October and transported them to the National Reference Laboratory for testing, according to the report.

Contacts traced

The memo report said 18 contacts had been identified, traced and line-listed, while the preliminary report dated 31 October put the number at 17.

The PHEOC also notified the State Rapid Response Team, the State NCDC office, Local Government Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers, the World Health Organisation (WHO) and UNICEF.

The state health authorities recommended continued contact tracing, infection prevention and control measures, enhanced surveillance and coordination with relevant authorities.

The NCDC has urged Nigerians to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information.

It also advised people who develop symptoms such as fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding, particularly after a relevant exposure, to seek immediate medical attention.

Ebola outbreak

Nigeria is one of five countries that have detected Bundibugyo virus disease during the current outbreak, which began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.

The outbreak has remained concentrated in the DRC but has spread beyond the country.

Nigeria’s first confirmed case of Ebola in 2026 was a woman who travelled from Uganda to Abuja and tested positive on 20 October. She was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland for continued treatment.

The NCDC’s latest situation report said 62 contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed case had been identified and were being monitored.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, had said genomic analysis showed that the virus detected in the Nigerian patient was closely related to the strain identified in Kenya’s first imported case. He, however, said the finding did not establish that the Nigerian patient was infected in Kenya.

WHO’s latest update reported 10,274 confirmed cases and 4,992 deaths in the DRC as of 28 October. Kenya had recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths, while Nigeria had one confirmed case at the time of the update.

Ebola is a viral disease that can cause severe illness and spreads mainly through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of an infected person.

World.title: When youths move, society changes: The 2026 barricades, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
The ongoing mass protests in France were ignited and led by students. They are the segment of society to which all shades and classes of society belong. When such a class reaches consensus and hits the streets, as it has done in parts of Europe in the last few weeks, change in society is likely to follow. Otherwise, society itself is endangered and violent change might become inevitable. The situation becomes even more combustible when workers join, waving flags of unity and joining the youths at the barricades.

The situation in France is similar to its 1968 Students Uprising, when the parents and grandparents of today’s protesters seized the country. Over 10 million people took to the streets, and the then French President Charles de Gaulle, on May 29, 1968, fled to Germany. When the famous war general returned, he dissolved the National Assembly and called new elections.

The 1968 French student demands were for more classrooms to reduce university overcrowding, democracy in schools, educational reforms, and a world free from injustice, such as the United States’ genocide in Vietnam. Workers weighed in with strikes and factory occupations. They demanded higher salaries, better work conditions, and social reforms.

Today, 58 years later, the demands are virtually the same, except that high school students have reduced the average age of the protesters. Unfazed by the deployment of over 70,000 police officers, they are protesting against teacher shortages, dilapidated school structures, cuts in school budgets, and inflation. By mid-October 2026, over 6,500 protesters, most of them minors, had been arrested. Over the October 17–18, 2026 weekend clashes alone, at least 2,500 arrests were made, while, in the October 24 protests, 1,435 persons were arrested. Even with the clashes and arrests in cities like Paris, Lyon, Bordeaux, and Marseille, the French government was in dialogue with the protesters, including reaching consensus on routes to take in order to minimize destruction of public property and offering concessions.

However, as the French authorities try to reach understanding with the protesters, there are world leaders who want to divert attention and even escalate the crisis by urging them to clamp down on the protesters, whom they present as enemies. For instance, US President Donald Trump said the causes of the protests were not as stated by the protesters but were actually about immigration and integration. He wrote in his Truth Social post: “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out-of-control mass migration. This isn’t about schools; this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country!”

Trump told Americans: “Just look at France… Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon.” He added: “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country.” He added: “Emmanuel (Macron) should have closed his borders a long time ago. I told him to do it.”

Unstable Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu toed the Trump line, claiming France had “ceded to an invasion by Islamist extremists.” Equally, the Prime Ministers of Poland, Donald Tusk, and Hungary, Peter Magyar, sang the same hymn as Trump. However, the French leadership would not fall for such nonsense. Macron responded: “There has been a foreign manipulation of information since then, and that has led to some unacceptable and stupid comments from many foreign leaders.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Pointing out that some of the international postings on the protests were fake, he said: “We’ve seen AI images that show scenes that never happened in France. There are people who have stated that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.” Macron’s rejection of false imputations is correct, although he does not go as far as admitting that the causes of the protests are mainly due to the economic crises the country is facing. Production has taken a downturn, with manufacturing, agriculture, and the broad industrial sectors contracting.

By the second quarter of 2026, France’s public debt had reached €3.5955 trillion, or 119 percent of GDP. Its deficit is at 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026, in comparison to the European Union’s 3 percent limit.

Since 2002, its debt has doubled as a share of GDP. Its pension deficits are projected to reach €15 billion by 2035. This is one of the grounds on which the trade unions joined the protests. France’s position has worsened in recent years with its increasing loss of the resources it has freely scooped for decades from its former African colonies. It lost its uranium and mining control in the Niger Republic. Its direct exploitation of countries like Burkina Faso, Mali, Guinea, and Senegal is being challenged, with even pliant Gabon giving notice of discontinuation. But France is not the only European country reeling under protests. In Albania, once a social haven, high school fees, corruption allegations, and rising mass unemployment sent the students into the streets. Clashes were recorded in Tirana and a number of cities. Protests rocked Italian cities like Milan, Turin, and Rome over high education costs and rising hardship. The protests in the Spanish cities of Madrid and Barcelona centred around high housing costs and pensions, while those in Portugal were on the cost of living and housing.

In Europe generally, the student-worker alliances centre around a better education and work environment. But the country that has now taken the crown of student action is Serbia. There, rather than simply organize protests, the students decided to take over power by forming an opposition coalition against the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, which has been in power for the last fourteen years. They organized a non-partisan electoral list of professionals and social activists. In the October 25, 2026 parliamentary elections, the student coalition won 52.7 percent of the votes and 140 of 250 seats in the National Assembly. The ruling party secured 39.17 percent of the votes and 104 seats. Voter turnout was 68.78 percent. President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat.

But while the European students are awake to their responsibilities, in many parts of the world, the students are sleeping. In Nigeria, the largest Black population in the world, many students and youths are actually snoring as the struggle for the future of their country in the 2027 general elections gets underway.

More criminally, many of those who are awake are submitting themselves to be used as thugs and hired urchins by politicians whose antecedents are not secret. Apart from politicians and their children imposing leaders on students, there was a time when the president of the central National Association of Nigerian Students, NANS, was not even a student! However, these do not mean that the barricades cannot go up in such countries. When the students and youths move, society changes.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Nigeria vs Venezuela Preview: Flamingos target another U-17 World Cup Semi-Final return
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos will put their growing confidence to the test when they take on Venezuela in the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup on Sunday, with a place in the last four at stake in Morocco.

Akeem Busari’s side have recovered impressively from their opening-day disappointment to win three consecutive matches, eliminating defending champions DPR Korea and Mexico along the way. Venezuela, meanwhile, arrive with renewed belief after producing one of the round of 16’s biggest surprises by knocking out Germany, who had won all three of their group-stage matches.

The encounter will take place at the Mohammed VI Football Academy, Pitch 4, in Salé, Morocco, with kick-off scheduled for 7:00 p.m. Nigerian time (6:00 p.m. local time).

For Nigeria, victory would secure a place in the semi-finals for the first time since their historic third-place finish at the 2022 edition in India. It would also take the Flamingos to fourregular-time victories in a single edition of the competition, setting a new national record.

The winner will face either China PR or Brazil in the semi-finals, meaning another victory would bring Nigeria one step closer to the final.

Flamingos find their rhythm after opening-day setback

Nigeria’s campaign began with a 2-1 defeat to Poland in Group B, leaving the young Nigerians with little room for further mistakes.

Wiktoria Skrzypczak converted a penalty in the 33rd minute before Natalia Skrok extended Poland’s advantage in the 65th minute. Oluebube Umejiaku gave Nigeria hope with a goal in the 79th minute, assisted by Kanyinsola Yusuf, but the Flamingos could not find a late equaliser.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Busari’s team responded with a much-improved performance against Puerto Rico, securing a 2-0 victory to get their campaign back on track. Oluwakemi Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 25th minute following an assist from Queen Joseph. At the same time, Precious Oscar came off the bench to seal the win in stoppage time after being set up by Umejiaku.

However, their next performance announced Nigeria as a serious contender in the competition.

The Flamingos produced an outstanding display to defeat two-time defending champions DPR Korea 3-1, inflicting a first regulation-time defeat on the Asian side at the tournament in 2,900 days and ending their remarkable 18-match unbeaten run.

Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 15th minute, with Mary Dunstan providing the assist. Umejiaku doubled Nigeria’s advantage in the 38th minute after being set up by Tosin Rafiu, while Yusuf added a third in the 56th minute. DPR Korea’s Yu Jong-hyang converted a late penalty in the 82nd minute, but Nigeria held on for a memorable victory.

The result secured Nigeria’s passage from Group B with six points, having scored six goals and conceded four in three matches.

The Flamingos carried that momentum into the round of 16, defeating Mexico 2-1 to book their place in the quarter-finals.

Umejiaku broke the deadlock in the 40th minute after Mexico failed to deal with Esther Stephen’s searching pass. At the same time, Dunstan doubled Nigeria’s lead in the 71st minute, finishing after Kanyinsola Yusuf’s cross was only partially cleared.

Emily Delgado scored a late consolation for Mexico in stoppage time, but Nigeria had done enough to progress.

The victory was significant beyond qualification. It gave the Flamingos their third win at Morocco 2026, matching their best return at a single edition of the competition, previously achieved in 2010, 2014 and 2024.

Now, they have a chance to go one step further and reach the semi-finals for the second time in their history.

Venezuela ride Germany upset into last eight

Venezuela’s journey to the quarter-finals has been less straightforward, but their latest result makes them an opponent Nigeria cannot afford to underestimate.

They finished third in Group D with three points from three matches, recording one victory and two defeats.

Their campaign opened with a 2-0 loss to France before they recovered to defeat Zambia 3-2 in a dramatic encounter.

Zambia took an early lead through Elizabeth Mofya in the fourth minute, but Ariana Ojeda restored parity for Venezuela nine minutes later. Grace Phiri put Zambia back in front in the 54th minute before Orliany Durán levelled the contest in the 63rd minute.

Andrea Suárez then struck deep into stoppage time to secure Venezuela’s only group-stage victory.

Their final group fixture ended in another 2-0 defeat, this time against Japan, leaving them reliant on the third-placed-team qualification route to reach the knockout stage.

However, Venezuela produced their biggest performance of the tournament in the round of 16, defeating Germany 1-0 on 28 October.

Germany entered the knockout stage with a perfect record, having won all three group matches to top Group E with nine points. But Venezuela stunned the European side when Diana Bravo scored in the fifth minute, and they defended their advantage to secure a place in the last eight.

The result underlined their ability to compete against highly rated opposition, even after an inconsistent group campaign.

Nigeria must therefore approach the contest with the same intensity they showed against DPR Korea and Mexico. Venezuela may have finished third in their group, but their elimination of Germany showed they can make life difficult for any opponent.

Venezuela return to the Quarter-Finals with renewed ambition

Venezuela are making another appearance at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after missing several editions, and their progress in Morocco offers a chance to re-establish themselves among the competition’s leading nations.

Their best performance came in 2014, when they reached the semi-finals and eventually finished fourth. They also participated in the 2010 and 2016 editions but failed to qualify for the tournaments in 2018, 2022 and 2024.

Their return to the quarter-finals in Morocco gives them a chance to repeat their 2014 achievement and move closer to a first final appearance.

The victory over Germany will undoubtedly boost their confidence, particularly after the difficulties they faced during the group stage. Nigeria must be ready for a team that has found a way to deliver when the stakes are highest.

First World Cup meeting between the two adds another layer of intrigue

Nigeria and Venezuela have never faced each other at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, making Sunday’s quarter-final their first meeting in the competition.

With no previous World Cup encounter to draw lessons from, both teams will have to rely heavily on their performances in Morocco and their coaches’ tactical preparations.

Nigeria have scored eight goals and conceded five across their four matches, while Venezuela have found the net four times and conceded six.

The numbers suggest that the Flamingos have carried a greater attacking threat. Still, Venezuela’s victory over Germany reminds us that knockout football is not always decided by group-stage statistics.

Attacking quality against improved Venezuelan defensive discipline

One of Nigeria’s biggest challenges will be finding a way through a Venezuelan defence that has already shown it can protect a narrow advantage against strong opposition.

Their 1-0 victory over Germany was built around an early breakthrough and disciplined defending. If Venezuela adopt a similar approach against the Flamingos, Busari’s players will need patience, intelligent movement and better decision-making in the final third.

Nigeria have shown that goals can come from different areas of the team, with Umejiaku, Dunstan, Adegbuyi and Yusuf all making important contributions during the campaign.

Umejiaku, in particular, has been influential in the knockout stages, scoring against both Mexico and Poland, while Dunstan’s goal against Mexico further demonstrated Nigeria’s ability to get contributions from midfield.

The Flamingos must also be careful not to become frustrated if Venezuela defend deep and restrict the space available in attacking areas. Rushing passes or committing too many players forward could leave them vulnerable to the South Americans’ counter-attacking opportunities.

Another important factor will be the opening goal. Venezuela scored early against Germany and held their lead for the rest of the match. If they take the initiative against Nigeria, the Flamingos could struggle to break down a compact defensive structure.

At the other end, Nigeria must remain alert whenever possession is lost. Venezuela have already demonstrated their ability to punish opponents, and the Flamingos cannot afford the defensive lapses that proved costly against Poland.

Goalkeeper Jane Ijirigho will also have an important role to play if the South Americans create clear chances, while Nigeria’s attackers must make theirs count.

Ultimately, the contest could be decided by which team handles the crucial moments better. Nigeria have the momentum, attacking confidence and experience of overcoming the defending champions, but Venezuela have earned their place in the quarter-finals and will not be intimidated.

For Busari and his Flamingos, the mission is clear: overcome Venezuela, secure a place in the final four and keep Nigeria’s dream of winning the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup alive.

World.title: 2027 Politics Watch: From Sokoto ultimatum to conflicting ₦50,000 relief terms, Saturday’s roundup
World.content:
On Saturday, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) gave security authorities in Sokoto 24 hours to act over an alleged attack on its governorship candidate. Meanwhile, police in Ekiti announced the arrest of 11 suspects following a separate incident involving African Action Congress presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore.

ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar condemned both incidents, as his son, Abba, separately pledged 10 buses to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election campaign.

Elsewhere, two official government publications gave conflicting descriptions of a proposed ₦50,000 cash relief programme: one promised monthly payments, while the other described a one-off grant.

The discrepancy emerged as opposition parties questioned the programme’s timing, while the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) outlined preparations for the 2027 elections.

ADC issues Sokoto ultimatum; Ekiti police announce arrests

The ADC Presidential Campaign Council demanded action within 24 hours against Sokoto Marshals personnel accused of attacking the convoy of its governorship candidate, Manir Muhammad Dan’iya.

In Saturday’s statement, signed by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the council alleged that the personnel damaged vehicles, including the candidate’s sport utility vehicle, and detained two Department of State Services (DSS) operatives attached to him.

“This is not governance. It is banditry in uniform, and it must not be tolerated in a democracy,” the council said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ADC alleged that two Department of State Services operatives attached to the candidate were detained during the confrontation. The allegation has not been independently confirmed by the DSS, while Sokoto police say they are investigating the incident.

It demanded the operatives’ release, the arrest of those responsible and an investigation, warning that it would pursue further lawful steps if the authorities failed to act.

Mr Dan’iya said the confrontation occurred near Sokoto Airport at about 9 p.m. on Friday, 30 October, after he accompanied former Governor Aminu Tambuwal to the airport. However, some reports quoting the ADC Presidential Campaign Council’s subsequent statement placed the incident on Thursday. The discrepancy has not been resolved.

He accused personnel of the Sokoto Marshals and the state Community Guard of blocking his convoy and firing shots.

The Sokoto APC rejected the allegations. Its chairman, Haruna Adiya, said the security deployments were linked to preparations for a traditional title conferment ceremony, disputing claims that personnel had been deployed to restrict opposition activities.

Sokoto police spokesperson Ahmed Rufai said the command was investigating the reported confrontation.

Mr Tambuwal called for an impartial inquiry and urged supporters to remain calm. He said the ADC would proceed with its presidential campaign flag-off in Sokoto on 4 November.

Mr Atiku also demanded investigations into the Sokoto incident and Friday’s reported attack on Mr Sowore at a restaurant in Ado-Ekiti.

In Ekiti, police announced the arrest of 11 suspects on Saturday in connection with the incident.

Police spokesperson Abutu Sunday said officers arrested the suspects in Atikankan at about 10 p.m. on Friday and were investigating their individual roles and possible links to the confrontation.

The AAC rejected the police’s earlier description of an altercation, alleged government involvement and demanded an independent inquiry and the release of CCTV footage.

The police statement did not identify a political sponsor or establish the arrested persons’ responsibility.

In Sokoto, the reported detention of DSS operatives remains unconfirmed by the agency. The police investigation has also not established whether security personnel acted unlawfully or on political instructions.

INEC outlines safeguards, maintains election timetable

INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan warned on Saturday that attacks on election officials, including National Youth Service Corps members, would attract legal action.

At a South-South readiness meeting in Port Harcourt, he said the commission was working with security agencies through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security to protect voters, personnel and election materials.

He also warned staff against partisanship, negligence and financial misconduct.

Mr Amupitan said INEC was preparing its Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, including 57,000 newly procured devices, and auditing electronic results management systems.

For riverine communities, he said the commission had finalised an agreement with maritime transporters to move personnel and materials.

He put the South-South’s registered voters at 15,823,550, including 3,736,434 in Rivers State, and warned against disenfranchisement through operational failures.

The chairman said the general elections would hold as scheduled, amid opposition concerns that problems with election preparations could provide grounds for postponement.

Questions about the preliminary voters’ register remain unresolved.

On Friday, INEC ICT Director Lawrence Bayode acknowledged that registration officers had introduced irregular records, prompting demands for an independent forensic audit and identification of those responsible.

As PREMIUM TIMES reported in Friday’s roundup, INEC promised corrections before releasing the final register on 15 December.

The commission’s account of Saturday’s meeting did not announce an independent forensic audit.

Although the reported confrontations involving opposition politicians and INEC’s preparations involve different circumstances, both have highlighted the responsibilities of security agencies during the electoral process.

Abba pledges buses as rival ADC faction names campaign council

Abba Atiku Abubakar, son of ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, unveiled the Haske Bola Tinubu Organisation at a Friday press conference in Abuja, reported on Saturday.

He pledged 10 luxury buses for transport and campaign mobilisation, beginning in the Federal Capital Territory.

Abba also announced plans for a two-million-person mobilisation march across the six geopolitical zones, starting in Abuja.

He cited student loans, infrastructure investments and other government interventions as reasons for supporting President Tinubu.

“Political conviction is a matter of personal judgement, conscience and the freedom of every individual to make independent choices,” he said.

Abba joined the APC and endorsed Mr Tinubu in January.

His latest announcement concerned campaign mobilisation rather than a new defection. The buses were pledged, but reports did not confirm they had been delivered.

Separately, a faction of the ADC led by Nafiu Gombe announced a North-West campaign council following a Friday meeting in Sokoto.

Factional spokesperson Christopher Okechukwu said on Saturday that Nuradeen Lawal Chindo would chair the council, with Bello Shehu as secretary.

Bala Sani Kumo, identified as the faction’s deputy campaign director-general for the North, presided over the inauguration.

The faction said the council would coordinate its activities across the seven North-West states.

The ADC leadership headed by David Mark is campaigning for Mr Atiku. The party’s competing leadership claims have been litigated. before

The faction’s announcement did not establish INEC recognition of the new council or any change to the party’s existing presidential nomination.

Official publications conflict over ₦50,000 relief payments

Two official government publications give different accounts of how frequently eligible Nigerians will receive payments under the National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI). In his 30 October announcement, Humanitarian Affairs Minister Bernard Doro said eligible households would receive ₦50,000 monthly. However, the programme’s official FAQ describes the payment as one-off assistance. The government has not clarified which schedule applies.
