The FAQ says beneficiaries are selected through verified records, including the National Social Register.

The distinction matters for households assessing the support available to them and for determining the government’s total financial commitment.

Against that uncertainty, the ADC and Allied Peoples Movement (APM) separately accused the administration of using the intervention to seek electoral support.

ADC National Publicity Secretary Bolaji Abdullahi described it as an election gimmick, questioned whether the payment was adequate against household expenses, and asked why comparable assistance had not accompanied the administration’s earlier economic reforms.

He also sought accountability for previous interventions, arguing that fresh announcements did not resolve questions about their implementation.

In an interview with LEADERSHIP, APM spokesperson Abubakar Yusuf called the initiative vote-buying and alleged that earlier obligations to N-Power beneficiaries remained unpaid.

He nevertheless advised eligible Nigerians to accept assistance and make independent voting decisions.

The government says the initiative aims to provide immediate support to vulnerable households facing economic hardship. The opposition’s allegations about electoral motives have not been established.

Beyond the conflicting payment descriptions, questions remain about funding, beneficiary verification, and safeguards against political interference.

READ ALSO: Sokoto Assembly okays establishment of state police

Candidate disputes and competing Tinubu endorsements

In Imo State, the Renewed Hope Foot Soldiers for Tinubu warned that the senatorial dispute between Governor Hope Uzodimma and former Governor Rochas Okorocha could weaken APC unity and affect the president’s re-election campaign in the South-east.

The group, led by Gbenga Owojori, also argued that Mr Uzodimma should have a fair opportunity to pursue his Senate ambition.

Its intervention followed a Federal High Court ruling directing the APC to submit Mr Okorocha’s name for Imo West.

Mr Uzodimma’s camp had announced plans to challenge the judgement. The group’s statement did not establish that an appeal had been filed or that the ruling had been stayed.

In Bayelsa, officials of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and APC disagreed over Governor Douye Diri’s support for Mr Tinubu.

PDP Chairman George Turnah questioned Mr Diri’s participation in the president’s campaign activities.

APC Chairman Warman Weri Ogoriba rejected the criticism, saying the governor had demonstrated his support through public engagements.

Mr Turnah had said on Friday that Sandy Onor remained the PDP’s presidential candidate, even as the party backed Mr Tinubu through the Rainbow Coalition.

The competing endorsements have therefore not been accompanied by an announced withdrawal of Mr Onor’s candidacy.

World.title: All you need to know about proposed law to regulate house rent in Abuja
World.content:
For many residents of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), securing a roof over their heads can mean raising hundreds of thousands, and sometimes millions, of naira at once.

Beyond the annual rent itself, prospective tenants often have to contend with agency, agreement and caution fees, while existing tenants face rent increases that can force them to move to less expensive and sometimes more distant communities.

It is against this backdrop that the House of Representatives has begun consideration of a new bill seeking to regulate advance rent payments and protect tenants from what it describes as unlawful rental practices.

The Federal Capital Territory Advance Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Bill, 2026 (HB.2839), jointly sponsored by Paul Nnamchi (APC, Enugu) and Ahmed Doro (PDP, Katsina), passed first reading on Thursday, 22 October.

But the proposal is not simply another attempt to tell landlords how much rent to collect.

A closer look at the 17-page bill obtained by PREMIUM TIMES shows that it seeks to create an entire regulatory framework for tenancy in the FCT, covering advance payments, written agreements, agents, complaints, refunds, eviction practices, penalties and dispute resolution.

What exactly does the bill propose?

The central provision is contained in Section 4 of the bill.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Section 4(1) of the bill provides that a landlord, estate agent or property manager “shall not demand, receive or compel a tenant to pay more than twelve months’ rent in advance” as a condition for granting, renewing or continuing a tenancy.

This simply prohibits the demanding, receiving or compelling of a tenant to pay more than one year’s rent in advance as a condition for obtaining, renewing or continuing a tenancy.

That means the bill does not ban advance rent or make monthly rent compulsory. Instead, it establishes 12 months as the maximum amount that can be compulsorily demanded upfront.

A landlord would still be able to collect one year’s rent in advance if that is the agreed arrangement. But demanding two or three years as a condition for granting or renewing a tenancy would become an offence if the bill becomes law.

The bill also attempts to prevent landlords and agents from simply finding another way around the restriction.

It specifically lists intermediaries, unexplained premiums, compulsory service charges, artificial renewal or re-grant of a tenancy, separate agreements and other arrangements designed to extract more than 12 months’ rent in advance as prohibited means of evasion.

Tenants can still voluntarily pay more than a year

The proposed restriction has an exception. Section 4(4) states that a tenant may voluntarily pay more than 12 months’ rent in advance if “the tenant initiates the offer” and the payment is not imposed by the landlord and the tenant must not have been subjected to coercion, discrimination, threats or retaliation.

The agreement must be recorded in writing, and the person receiving the payment bears the burden of proving compliance.

This could become one of the contentious provisions during the legislative process.

While the bill attempts to distinguish voluntary payments from compulsory demands, proving that a tenant genuinely volunteered to pay several years’ rent could be difficult where the landlord controls access to the property.

The bill goes beyond advance rent

The proposed law also seeks to formalise the relationship between landlords and tenants.

Section 5 requires landlords or their authorised agents to provide written tenancy agreements stating the rent, payment schedule, duration of the tenancy, refundable deposits, fees and other charges, and the rights and obligations of both parties.

“A landlord or agent shall not impose a fee, premium, charge or other compulsory payment unless its nature, amount and lawful basis were disclosed to the tenant before the tenancy agreement was concluded.”

Landlords and agents would also be required to disclose the nature, amount and legal basis of compulsory fees before a tenancy agreement is concluded and issue receipts or verifiable electronic acknowledgements for payments.

The bill also prohibits retaliation against tenants who refuse to make unlawful payments or who complain about violations.

A landlord or agent would not be allowed to threaten or unlawfully evict such a tenant, impose a punitive charge, withdraw a lawful benefit or otherwise retaliate against the tenant.

Tenants could demand refunds

The bill introduces a remedy that could significantly change the balance between tenants and landlords.

Section 7 introduces a mechanism for recovering unlawfully collected rent. A tenant who has paid rent in violation of the proposed 12-month limit could apply to the proposed FCT Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Authority for a refund.

Where the proposed authority determines that a payment contravened the law, it may order the recipient to refund the unlawful amount within 30 days.

The bill also allows an aggrieved party to appeal an order of the authority to the FCT High Court.

“7(1) A tenant who has paid rent in contravention of section 4 may apply to the Authority for a refund order. (2) Where the Authority determines that a payment was received in contravention of section 4, it may order the recipient to refund the unlawful amount within thirty days after service of the order.”

A new bureaucracy for rent regulation

Under Section 8, the bill proposes the establishment of the Federal Capital Territory Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Authority.

The authority would receive and investigate complaints, monitor landlords, estate agents and property managers, issue compliance notices, facilitate mediation, order refunds and refer suspected criminal offences to relevant law-enforcement or prosecuting authorities.

It would also establish complaint offices and electronic reporting channels throughout the FCT, including satellite towns, and publish periodic reports on rental practices and enforcement outcomes.

Its governing board would include representatives of the FCT Administration, the federal ministry responsible for housing, the federal ministry responsible for justice, tenants, landlords or property owners and estate surveyors and valuers.

The president will appoint the chairperson and members of the board, subject to Senate confirmation. The president will also appoint the director-general, subject to Senate confirmation.

What happens when landlords violate the law?

The bill proposes financial penalties.

A person convicted of knowingly demanding or receiving unlawful advance rent would face a fine of between ₦500,000 and ₦5 million.

A corporate body could face a fine of between ₦5 million and ₦20 million.

The court could also order refunds, compensation for proven losses and payment of lawful costs.

Failure to comply with a compliance notice issued by the proposed authority would also constitute an offence punishable by a fine of up to ₦1 million.

Estate agents and property managers are expressly covered. Where an offence is committed through an intermediary, anyone who knowingly authorised, participated in or facilitated the offence could also be liable.

Unlawful eviction also targeted

The bill is not solely about the amount of money tenants pay. It also targets the methods some landlords may use to recover possession.

It prohibits violence or threats, disconnecting essential services, removing or damaging a tenant’s property, changing locks without lawful authority and other forms of unlawful self-help.

At the same time, it makes clear that tenants remain obliged to pay rent lawfully due and that landlords retain the right to recover rent and possession through due process.

This is significant because the bill attempts to protect tenants without removing landlords’ existing property rights.

Will the bill make housing cheaper?

This is perhaps the biggest question the lawmakers will have to confront.

The bill regulates how much rent can be demanded upfront, but it does not regulate the actual amount landlords can charge as rent.

There is no rent ceiling and no limit on how much rent can increase when a tenancy is renewed.

A landlord who cannot demand two years’ rent upfront could still charge a high annual rent.

The bill also does not address the shortage of affordable housing, construction costs, mortgage access or the wider factors driving rent increases.

Its impact will therefore depend heavily on enforcement.

The proposed authority would have to monitor landlords and agents, investigate complaints and enforce its decisions across the FCT.

The bill also provides for the authority to become operational within six months of the law taking effect.

Things missing or not addressed in the bill

Despite its proposed restrictions on advance rent, the bill does not comprehensively regulate other charges tenants face when securing accommodation in Abuja, including agency fees, agreement fees and caution deposits. In Abuja, these charges are random and some tenants pay as high as 40 per cent of their rent for them.

Although Section 5 requires landlords and agents to disclose the nature and amount of charges, it does not prescribe a maximum percentage or amount that can be demanded as agency or agreement fees. Neither does it establish a standard ceiling for caution deposits. The bill requires refundable deposits to be stated in tenancy agreements but does not clearly set out a standard formula for calculating them.

This means tenants could have a clearer right to know what they are paying for without necessarily having protection against excessive charges.

Section 4 prohibits landlords and agents from using charges that are not reasonably related to a service as a means of circumventing the 12-month advance rent restriction. However, this does not amount to a comprehensive regulation of legitimate agency fees or other letting costs.

Consequently, tenants could still face substantial upfront expenses even if the bill becomes law. A landlord may no longer be able to compel a tenant to pay two years’ rent, but the tenant could still be required to pay agency, agreement and other charges, provided those charges comply with the law.

Another major issue left unresolved is the payment arrangement for salary earners.

Many Abuja residents earn monthly salaries but are expected to pay a full year’s rent upfront, with some landlords demanding two years’ rent from new tenants. For workers whose income comes in monthly, raising such a large sum at once can be difficult, even when they can afford the rent over the course of a year.

The proposed law would prohibit landlords from compelling tenants to pay more than 12 months’ rent in advance. However, it does not require landlords to accept monthly or quarterly payments.

A landlord could therefore still insist on a full year’s rent upfront, provided the demand does not exceed the proposed limit.

This means the bill addresses the length of compulsory advance rent but does not fully address the financial difficulty created by the annual payment system.

A tenant who cannot raise 12 months’ rent at once may therefore remain unable to secure accommodation, even if the landlord is no longer demanding two years’ payment.

It’s not the first attempt by lawmakers

The latest proposal is part of a longer-running attempt by lawmakers to address rent practices in Abuja.

In January 2022, the Senate introduced a bill sponsored by Smart Adeyemi, then representing Kogi West, seeking to regulate the payment of rent in the FCT. The bill passed second reading in February 2022.

PREMIUM TIMES reported at the time that the proposal sought to reduce advance rent for new tenants from the prevailing one- or two-year payments to three months, followed by monthly payments.

Mr Adeyemi argued that the existing system placed an excessive burden on low-income residents, particularly salaried workers who could not easily raise one or two years’ rent at once.

While supporters argued that advance rent was placing unbearable pressure on residents, Chimaroke Nnamani, then the senator for Enugu East, opposed the proposal, arguing that rent payment was an economic matter that should be driven by market forces, including the availability of land, construction costs and income.

He argued that the government should instead invest in housing schemes, mortgages and housing credit rather than regulate the business of private landlords.

The Senate nevertheless voted overwhelmingly for the bill at second reading and referred it to the Committee on Housing and Urban Development for further consideration.

However, the bill ultimately lapsed and did not become law before the expiration of the 9th National Assembly in May 2023.

Under Nigerian legislative rules, any bill that does not complete all stages of passage, including matching approval by the House of Representatives and presidential assent, before the end of a four-year parliamentary tenure expires and must be completely reintroduced.

The difference between the two proposals is substantial.

While Mr Adeyemi’s bill sought to replace the annual advance payment system with an initial three-month payment and subsequent monthly payments, the 2026 proposal allows landlords to continue demanding up to 12 months’ rent in advance.

The new bill, therefore, does not go as far as the 2022 proposal in addressing the difficulty faced by salary earners. It seeks to prevent compulsory payments beyond one year but leaves the annual payment arrangement intact.

The distinction matters because limiting advance rent to 12 months does not necessarily make accommodation more accessible to workers who receive their income monthly.

What happens next?

Having passed first reading in the House of Representatives, HB.2839 is still at an early stage of the legislative process.

The next stage is second reading, when lawmakers will debate the general principles and objectives of the proposal and decide whether it should proceed to detailed consideration.

If it passes, the bill will be referred to the relevant House committee for scrutiny. At this stage, lawmakers may examine its provisions clause by clause, invite submissions from government agencies, landlords, tenants, estate agents and housing professionals, and hold a public hearing to obtain views from affected groups.

The committee will subsequently present its report and recommendations to the House at plenary. Lawmakers will consider the report and any proposed amendments before the bill proceeds to third reading, when the House will consider its final version and vote on its passage.

READ ALSO: Lawmakers move to make formal identification compulsory for renting apartments in Abuja

If passed by the House, the bill will be transmitted to the Senate for consideration. Both chambers must pass the same version. Where their versions differ, the disagreements must be reconciled before the harmonised bill is transmitted to the President for assent.

The president’s assent would bring the bill into law, subject to the applicable constitutional process.

If enacted, the proposed legislation will establish the FCT Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Authority. The bill states that the authority should become operational within six months of commencement, while the FCT minister is expected to take steps towards appointing its board and director-general within three months.

The bill also provides that its commencement date will be determined by the president through a notice published in the Federal Gazette.

Until the legislative process is completed and the law comes into force, the proposed restrictions and penalties remain legislative proposals and cannot be enforced against landlords or agents.

World.title: Ebola: No new cases in Nigeria as two suspected cases in North-east test negative
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said two suspected Ebola cases identified in Adamawa State have tested negative for the virus.

The development came hours after the agency announced that two suspected Ebola cases had been identified in Nigeria’s North-east, without disclosing the state where they were found.

In a statement signed by its Director-General, Jide Idris, on Saturday evening, the NCDC said the samples collected from the two individuals tested negative for Ebola virus after two rounds of testing.

The agency said the suspected cases were reported in Yola, Adamawa State, on 30 October after the two individuals presented with symptoms suggestive of Ebola.

“Fortunately, the samples turned out negative for EVD after two rounds of testing,” Mr Idris said.

Mr Idris said there is currently no laboratory-confirmed Ebola case in Adamawa State.

He added that the index case previously confirmed in the Federal Capital Territory remains the only confirmed Ebola case reported in Nigeria to date.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ebola outbreak

The development comes 11 days after Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus.

Nigeria is one of five countries that have detected Bundibugyo virus disease during the current outbreak, which began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.

The outbreak has remained concentrated in the DRC but has spread beyond the country.

Nigeria’s first confirmed case of Ebola in 2026 was a woman who travelled from Uganda to Abuja and tested positive on 20 October. She was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland for continued treatment.

The NCDC’s latest situation report said 62 contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed case had been identified and were being monitored.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, had said genomic analysis showed that the virus detected in the Nigerian patient was closely related to the strain identified in Kenya’s first imported case. He, however, said the finding did not establish that the Nigerian patient was infected in Kenya.

WHO’s latest update reported 10,274 confirmed cases and 4,992 deaths in the DRC as of 28 October. Kenya has recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths, while Nigeria has one confirmed case at the time of the update.

World.title: Ebola: Saudi Arabia suspends travel to Kenya, halts visa issuance
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has suspended travel by its citizens to Kenya and halted the issuance of visas to travellers arriving from the East African country as concerns grow over the spread of the Ebola virus across parts of Africa.

The restrictions also prohibit entry into the Kingdom for travellers arriving directly from Kenya or through third countries if they have stayed in Kenya or any other country experiencing an active Ebola outbreak within the 21 days preceding their arrival.

The Saudi Press Agency (SPA) announced the measures in a statement published on its official X account, saying they followed epidemiological assessments by the country’s health authorities.

According to the agency, the measures are intended to mitigate the risks associated with the Ebola outbreak and protect the health of citizens, residents and visitors.

The restrictions build on preventive protocols introduced by the Kingdom in July 2019 and strengthened in May 2026 for travellers arriving from countries considered at risk of Ebola outbreaks.

In June, Saudi Arabia also suspended travel to and arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and South Sudan, while strengthening surveillance and screening at its entry points for travellers arriving from neighbouring countries.

The Kingdom’s Public Health Authority, known as Weqaya, said the health situation within Saudi Arabia remained reassuring and under constant surveillance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It added that it was monitoring regional and international epidemiological developments in coordination with relevant health agencies and would implement additional preventive measures as necessary.

Spread across Africa

The restrictions come amid the ongoing Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which was first declared in the DRC in May 2026.

The outbreak has since spread beyond the DRC, with imported cases reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, as well as France.

According to the United States Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as of 28 October, the DRC had recorded 10,274 confirmed cases and 4,992 deaths.

Kenya had reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, while Uganda recorded 20 cases and two deaths. Nigeria had one confirmed case, with no deaths recorded.

The spread of the virus beyond the DRC has heightened concerns among health authorities about cross-border transmission and the need to strengthen surveillance and early detection.

Ebola in Nigeria

Nigeria’s Ebola response has also entered a new phase following the identification of two suspected cases in the North-east.

On Saturday, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced that the two individuals had been isolated, while contact identification and listing were ongoing.

The agency said laboratory tests were being conducted to determine whether they had contracted the virus.

However, it cautioned that being classified as suspected cases does not mean the individuals had tested positive for Ebola, stressing that confirmation would depend on laboratory results.

The NCDC did not disclose the states where the suspected cases were identified.

World.title: Group seeks end to health workers’ absenteeism in PHCs
World.content:
The Health Policy Research Group from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka has appealed to the Enugu State Government to intensify action to address health workers’ absenteeism in Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) in Enugu State.

The Coordinator of the group, Obinna Onwujekwe, made the appeal on Thursday during a programme, Stakeholders’ Policy Dialogue on addressing health workers’ absenteeism and strengthening accountability in PHC facilities in Enugu.

Mr Onwujekwe, a professor, also urged the government to strengthen accountability in PHCs across the state.

He said the dialogue provided an opportunity for the representatives of the Enugu State Ministry of Health, Primary Healthcare Agency, National Health Insurance Authority, community leaders and media professionals to brainstorm on addressing health workers’ absenteeism at PHCs.

The coordinator said the dialogue was organised to present research findings and engage policymakers and other stakeholders on practical measures to reduce absenteeism among health workers.

He stressed that the research identified transportation challenges, inadequate workplace support and limited community involvement as some of the issues contributing to absenteeism in PHC facilities.

Mr Onwujekwe explained that the group prioritised three interventions capable of improving health workers’ attendance and service delivery.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He explained that the decision to prioritise the interventions followed extensive consultations with relevant individuals and bodies.

“One of the findings is that providing transportation support to health workers, especially those serving in remote communities, will encourage them to report to work regularly.

“We also discovered that providing support systems within health facilities, where colleagues support one another, can improve attendance.

“Community involvement is equally important because when communities participate in monitoring healthcare services, it helps to strengthen accountability,” he said.

The coordinator said the research demonstrated that combining the three interventions could significantly reduce absenteeism and improve healthcare delivery.

He explained that the policy dialogue was intended to translate research evidence into practical government policies and programmes.

“We have conducted a study and generated evidence. What we are doing today is bringing stakeholders together to discuss how this evidence can be translated into policies and practice.

“We are talking about evidence-based policymaking, where decisions are guided by research findings rather than assumptions.

“Our expectation is that the government and other policymakers will take renewed action to ensure that these interventions are implemented across the state,” he said.

The coordinator expressed optimism that implementing the recommendations would ensure that residents seeking medical attention at PHC facilities would meet health workers on duty.

He acknowledged that although Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State had invested heavily in building of PHCs, the research and policy dialogue would help ensure that health workers were constantly on duty at the facilities.

“Our research is complementary to the efforts of the state government because we want to ensure that the health centres being constructed are not left without health workers.

“We expect the government to utilise this evidence to strengthen its interventions against absenteeism,” he said.

Clock-in system

Mr Onwujekwe praised the state government’s introduction of a clock-in system to monitor health workers’ attendance at PHCs.

The coordinator argued that the introduction of the clock-in system was a recognition of the challenges posed by absenteeism.

He said addressing the problem requires multiple strategies beyond attendance monitoring.

“The evidence we have produced will further help the governor and the state primary health care development agency to reduce absenteeism in PHCs,” he said.

Pamela Ogbozor, a research associate, presented the research findings, explaining that the intervention ran from August 2025 to January 2026 in four PHC facilities in Nsukka, Igbo-Etiti, Enugu North and Nkanu West Local Government Areas.

Ms Ogbozor stressed that eight other facilities served as control locations, where the researchers did not introduce the interventions.

She said 100 per cent of health workers in intervention facilities regularly completed attendance registers, compared with 90 per cent in control facilities.

The research associate said the study also recorded that 15.4 per cent of workers in intervention facilities left before their shifts ended, compared with 48 per cent in control facilities.

ALSO READ: Delta extends retirement age for clinical health workers

She listed types of absenteeism to include workers failing to report for duty, arriving late or leaving before the end of their shifts.

The researcher warned that absenteeism could expose patients to complications, death and workload with few on duty.

A representative of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission in the dialogue, Stephen Obi, said absenteeism and ghost workers were serious challenges to healthcare delivery.

“Absenteeism and ghost workers go together and to the commission, it is a serious challenge,” he said.

Mr Obi said the dialogue had provided valuable information which he would be taken back to the commission.

One of the participants in the dialogue, Alex Ugwu, lauded the programme.

Mr Ugwu, who is the chairman of the Ward Development Committee at Hilltop PHC Ngwo, told reporters after the programme that the initiative had broadened their knowledge about ways of tackling absenteeism at PHCs.

“This programme has helped us to know the places to improve on to address absenteeism in the health sector across Enugu State and beyond,” he said.

He hailed the research group, explaining that the outcome of previous research had resulted in government policies that improved healthcare service delivery in his community’s PHC.

World.title: Binance says resuming withdrawals after major hack
World.content:
Binance said Sunday that it had resumed withdrawals after a major hack that affected more than $6 billion in funds.

Binance, which is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, had suspended user withdrawals after the attack.

“First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals is $BTC bitcoin network,” Binance said on X.

The company said in an earlier update that it was preparing to resume the first phase of withdrawals between 0600 and 0900 GMT on Sunday.

“We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” it said.

Binance said Saturday that it has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist.

“User funds remain safe. Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” it said on X.

The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the attack on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.

The hack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyber thefts linked to North Korea, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons program.

News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.

World.title: Trump says US still has ‘one or two targets’ in Iran
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump. Photo by Kevin Dietsch / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP.

President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.

Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the United States and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable.”

The Republican president said the United States is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran’s military and nuclear program.

“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.

“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.

The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.

Earlier Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump has not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the United States would be open to a diplomatic solution.

Iran’s supreme leader on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.

Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the US midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a “historic, one-time opportunity” to topple the Iranian government.

The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted in a general election on Tuesday but yet to form a new government.

“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response,” Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders, according to a statement.

Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.

This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and military top brass.

The supreme leader has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes.

– Oil price spike –

Rubio warned that “we can achieve military objectives if we seek to”, adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.

Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.

Iran has previously warned it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.

A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported Saturday.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Friday three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.

The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of the upcoming polls.

Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump’s ability to enact policy.

Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu’s political camp with the most seats in parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.

– ‘Flames of war’ –

Fresh diplomatic efforts are underway to avert any resumption of fighting.

Qatari mediators landed in Tehran on Friday, and US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei.

“I read the letter,” said Rezaei, head of Iran’s supreme national security council, in a video broadcast on Iranian television.

“I haven’t yet responded. Their tone has completely changed,” he added, describing that as “a good sign” without going into more detail.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no plans for meetings with US officials.

“Iran’s conditions are clear, and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.

Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.

Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.

Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.

“The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” he said on social media.

Araghchi warned on X that there would no longer be any “red lines”.

World.title: Trump intervenes as Ghana demands justice over killing of 15-year-old boy in US
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump. Photo by Kevin Dietsch / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP.

U.S. President Donald Trump has agreed to facilitate a visa for the Ghanaian mother of Javits Frimpong, a teenager killed while walking to school in New York.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Trump’s intervention on Saturday, as Ghana demanded justice for 15-year-old Frimpong, whose killing has shaken the Bronx.

“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani declared.

The mayor said Trump agreed during their telephone conversation to grant a visa immediately to the teenager’s mother, Doris Gyamfi, who lives in Kumasi, Ghana.

However, the White House had not independently confirmed the arrangement, and it remained unclear whether the visa had been issued by Saturday evening.

Frimpong was shot in the abdomen around in the morning in Bronx’s neighbourhood.

Police officers rushed him to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was pronounced dead while investigators began searching for three suspected teenage assailants.

The teenager had moved from Ghana in October 2025 to reunite with his father, Thomas Frimpong, hoping to pursue his education and build a promising future.

“He was very clever, so he always says he wants to be a physician,” his grieving father told newsmen in New York.

The elder Frimpong said his son had complained of persistent bullying at DreamYard Preparatory School, where two students were reportedly suspended, although police have not established any connection to the killing.

Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, subsequently contacted the bereaved father, conveying condolences from President John Dramani Mahama and promising government support.

“We will pursue justice, and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it,” Ablakwa declared.

Ghanaian diplomats in New York visited the family while the government demanded a thorough investigation and pledged legal and consular assistance to secure accountability.

Following Mamdani’s announcement, Ablakwa welcomed Trump’s intervention and disclosed that Ghana would finance the mother’s travel, assist with visa arrangements and support funeral expenses.

“The Government of Ghana welcomes your intervention and President Trump’s timely decision,” Ablakwa said, acknowledging the cooperation between the American and Ghanaian authorities.

Bronx Congressman Ritchie Torres also expressed grief, saying: “Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him.”

The New York City Department of Education offered counselling and cooperation with investigators, stating: “Our hearts are with this young person’s family and school community during this unimaginably difficult time.”

Meanwhile, vigils brought together Ghanaian residents, religious leaders and neighbours demanding justice on Saturday as police continued investigating the killing without announcing arrests or establishing a motive.

World.title: WARRI DELINEATION: UIY challenges INEC over disputed wards
World.content:
Ugbarajo Itsekiri Youths, UIY, has demanded that the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, provide the legal and geographical basis for the Warri Federal Constituency units and ward delineation data it uploaded.

UIY said the report had potential implications for community identity, representation, political participation and public confidence in democratic institutions, particularly amid allegations of electoral boundary manipulation.

The group’s National Public Relations Officer, Gbubemi Ejesi, said Itsekiri youths regarded the disputed developments as a serious threat to electoral justice, the political representation of indigenous communities and peaceful coexistence in Warri.

According to him, the recently uploaded electoral structure, including the reported inclusion of locations and units whose geographical and administrative assignments are being challenged, had raised disturbing questions about INEC’s methodology, the authenticity of the geographical coordinates used and the extent to which the exercise complied with applicable judicial decisions.

The statement reads: “UIY expresses its strongest condemnation of the alleged irregularities surrounding the recent ward delineation data uploaded by INEC for Warri Federal Constituency, Delta State.

“We regard the disputed developments as a serious threat to electoral justice, the political representation of indigenous communities, and peaceful coexistence in Warri. The recently uploaded electoral structure, including the reported inclusion of locations and units whose geographical and administrative assignments are being challenged, has raised disturbing questions about INEC’s methodology, the authenticity of the geographical coordinates used, and the extent to which the exercise complies with applicable judicial decisions.

“Of particular concern is the allegation that the disputed delineation is being used to establish an electoral and political presence for Ijaw interests in areas of Warri South, where UIY maintains that such a community-based political structure did not previously exist. Warri cannot be subjected to an electoral arrangement that indigenous communities believe disregards their history, established territorial interests, and legitimate political rights for non-indigenous ethnic groups.

“The Ugbarajo Itsekiri Youths reject the disputed Warri Federal Constituency delineation report recently uploaded by INEC. We are particularly concerned about the reported creation of three disputed wards allegedly carved out of ancestral Okere and Pessu lands, which UIY maintains are historic Itsekiri territories.

“We strongly challenge any attempt to alter the electoral structure of these areas without a transparent, lawful, and verifiable process consistent with applicable judicial decisions.

“Our concern is not merely about the names assigned to wards or polling units. It is about the potential consequences of electoral boundary manipulation for community identity, representation, political participation, and public confidence in democratic institutions.

“INEC must explain the legal and geographical basis for the disputed arrangements and demonstrate that its actions are consistent with the relevant court decisions and official records. We will not accept administrative ambiguity as a substitute for electoral justice.

“UIY is deeply concerned by allegations that some geographical coordinates associated with the uploaded delineation may be inaccurate, misplaced, or imported from locations outside their proper administrative areas, including other local government areas and locations outside Delta State.

“If established, such discrepancies would raise serious questions about the reliability of the exercise and the integrity of the resulting electoral structure.

“We are equally concerned about the reported inclusion of the so-called Ewein wards in Warri South Local Government Area, which UIY disputes as lacking a properly established geographical and administrative basis within the relevant electoral structure.

“We therefore challenge INEC to publish the coordinates, maps, ward descriptions, polling-unit registers, and supporting administrative records for independent verification.

“An electoral ward must be supported by verifiable geographical and administrative evidence. No disputed location should be legitimised merely because its name appears on an official portal.

“If the evidence establishes that any ward or polling unit was created, relocated, or assigned through inaccurate data or an unlawful process, INEC must immediately correct the affected records in accordance with the law.

“One of the most troubling aspects of the disputed upload is the reported assignment of areas around Dore Numa Market, Mowoe Primary School, along Robert Road, Delta Boat Yard opposite the NEPA office, and the Naval Base to the electoral structure associated with Ogbe-Ijoh in Warri urban.

“UIY maintains that these locations fall within areas historically recognised by our people as Itsekiri reserve areas and calls for the relevant official records to be examined.

“We question the basis upon which these locations were reportedly assigned and demand that INEC disclose the maps, coordinates, administrative boundaries, and legal instruments supporting the assignments.

“The commission must explain how these locations were assessed and whether the relevant historical, geographical, and judicial records were properly considered.

“We are concerned that the disputed assignments could facilitate the establishment of political structures in areas whose community and territorial status remains contested.

“INEC must not allow electoral administration to become a vehicle for deepening existing disputes. The disputed delineation has heightened concerns about the movement of political interests from outside Warri South into its electoral structure.

“The emergence of political figures with roots in Burutu Local Government Area, including Hon. Ebike Victor Oromoni, whom we understand to be an indigene of Burutu, a former two-term Burutu Local Government PDP chairman, and a former Senior Special Assistant to the immediate past Delta State Governor, has intensified these concerns among our people.

“For the avoidance of doubt, an individual’s origin or political affiliation does not, on its own, establish electoral wrongdoing.

“Our concern is whether the disputed ward arrangements are being used to facilitate political representation through boundaries or polling-unit assignments that lack a lawful and verifiable basis.

“The relevant question is straightforward: What geographical, administrative, and legal evidence supports the disputed electoral structure in Warri South?

“INEC must answer this question with documentary evidence. UIY is further alarmed by the reported inclusion of Bolouama Town Hall, Obokone Town Hall, Orupa Town Hall, Oturubiri, and Ewein as polling units and/or wards within Warri South Local Government Area.

“We strongly challenge the basis for these assignments and call for an immediate, transparent examination of their geographical coordinates, administrative classifications, and legal status.

“Our position is that the inclusion of these locations must not be accepted without evidence demonstrating that the assignments comply with applicable laws, official administrative records, and binding judicial decisions.

“If any of these locations has been wrongly assigned to Warri South, the error must be corrected without delay. The commission must publish the relevant records so that affected communities, electoral stakeholders, and the public can independently examine the disputed claims.

“UIY is also concerned about reports that Ubeji polling units have been mapped into Ugbuwangue Ward and that Orere polling units associated with the Omadino/Obodo axis have been transferred into Bowen Ward.

“These reported changes raise important questions about the methodology used to determine ward boundaries and assign polling units. We demand a detailed explanation of the reasons for these changes, including the coordinates used, the previous and current polling-unit registers, and the administrative records relied upon.

“Where discrepancies are identified, INEC must correct them through a transparent process that complies with the law.

“The commission owes the people of Warri an explanation that can withstand independent scrutiny.

“Okere and Pessu: UIY reaffirms its position on Itsekiri ancestral territory.

“The Ugbarajo Itsekiri Youths reiterates its position that Okere and Pessu are ancestral Itsekiri territories whose historical identity and territorial interests must not be undermined through disputed electoral arrangements.

“We reject any attempt to use electoral delineation to prejudge or alter legitimate territorial claims. We call upon INEC and the relevant authorities to examine the historical records, official maps, applicable judicial decisions, and other admissible evidence relating to the disputed areas.

“Electoral boundaries must be determined through lawful procedures and reliable evidence, not through unilateral administrative decisions that leave affected communities feeling excluded or dispossessed.

“UIY will continue to defend Itsekiri interests through peaceful advocacy, documentary evidence, constitutional processes, and every lawful avenue available to our people.”

World.title: New tax laws outlaw revenue roadblocks, Adesokan says
World.content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

There is no room for agents of state and local governments to mount roadblocks in the name of revenue collection under the new tax laws, the Executive Secretary of the Joint Revenue Board (JRB), Mr Olusegun Adesokan, has said.

Adesokan stated this in Abuja last week while reviewing the implementation of the new tax laws, saying the harmonised legislation was designed to curb multiple taxation and illegal revenue collection across the country.

He said the board was working with the police to tackle illegal revenue collectors who mount roadblocks, harass motorists and impose unauthorised charges on transporters along highways.

According to him, illegal revenue collection has become a major contributor to the high cost of transporting goods across the country and would no longer be tolerated.

The JRB executive secretary acknowledged that multiple taxation and harassment of traders and transporters remained widespread despite the ongoing reforms.

“We know the problem exists, and we are working to fix it. We may not be able to clear everything completely today, but as time goes on, we are working on it,” he said.

Adesokan explained that illegal roadside collections increase transportation costs, with the resulting burden passed on to consumers through higher food prices and the cost of other goods.

He said the reforms were intended to address overlapping taxes and levies that increase the cost of doing business, adding that 21 of the 36 states had passed the relevant laws to facilitate their implementation.

The states, according to him, are Kebbi, Kaduna, Zamfara, Ekiti, Enugu, Abia, Anambra, Gombe, Adamawa, Yobe, Borno, Niger, Plateau, Benue, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Delta and Ondo.

He said the states yet to pass the legislation were at different stages of implementing the reforms, partly because of legislative processes and consultations with stakeholders.

Adesokan said the board, which comprises tax authorities at the federal and state levels, was working to ensure uniform implementation of the new tax laws and eliminate arbitrariness in tax administration across the country.

He stressed the need to support micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), describing them as the foundation of a fast-growing economy and an important part of the country’s business environment.

He urged state tax authorities to respect the tax exemption provisions for small businesses and avoid actions that could undermine the reforms.

Adesokan cited small traders and artisans among categories of taxpayers covered by applicable exemptions, saying tax authorities should focus on those with the capacity to pay rather than burdening low-income earners.

He added that the board had issued guidelines to promote uniform personal income tax administration and harmonised tax practices across the states.

Under the new tax laws, micro and small businesses with an annual turnover of ₦100 million and below are exempt from paying tax.

World.title: Zamfara governor presents staff of office to 19 emirs
World.content:
Governor Dauda Lawal of Zamfara State has presented staff of office and official vehicles to 19 newly coronated emirs in the state.

The ceremony, held at the Trade Fair Complex in Gusau, the state capital, was attended by the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Sa’ad Abubakar; the Etsu Nupe; and the Emir of Gwandu, among other dignitaries.

Following their oaths of office, Lawal presented staff of office to 11 first-class emirs and eight second-class emirs.

Each of the 19 emirs also received three official vehicles: a GAC ULTRA SUV (2025/2026 model), a MIKANO ZNA HILUX vehicle and an EV ANTIQUE MODEL car (DDP).

The vehicles, according to the state government, are intended to facilitate the emirs’ movements within their domains and enable closer engagement with their communities.

Speaking at the ceremony, Lawal said the presentation reflected his administration’s recognition of the traditional institution as an enduring part of society and a key partner in promoting peace, stability and development.

He said the ceremony also reaffirmed his government’s commitment to giving traditional rulers the recognition and institutional support required to discharge their responsibilities effectively.

“The staff of office being presented today signifies the authority entrusted to you by the state. It also represents a responsibility to govern your respective domains with fairness, wisdom, integrity and compassion,” he said.

The governor urged the emirs to discharge their duties without discrimination, uphold justice and ensure that their palaces remained accessible to all members of their communities.

“Our people must find guidance, fairness and reassurance in their traditional rulers,” he said.

Lawal also reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to completing the reconstruction and rehabilitation of the remaining royal palaces, describing them as important centres of traditional authority and community engagement.

On the vehicles presented to the emirs, he urged them to maintain and use them responsibly in the discharge of their official duties.

The governor further called on the traditional rulers to build productive partnerships between their respective emirates and the state government.

Earlier, the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Sa’ad Abubakar, urged the newly coronated emirs to remain loyal to the constituted authority and uphold the dignity of the traditional institution in the discharge of their responsibilities.

World.title: AI-Generated Pregnancy Claims: Nollywood’s Annabel Apara laments price of fame in deepfake era
World.content:
By Prisca Sam-Duru

It started with pictures. Then videos on social media. In both, Nollywood actress Annabel Apara appeared visibly pregnant, smiling, cradling a bump that never existed. She was even seen purportedly sharing announcements and clips documenting a pregnancy journey.

Within hours, the images were everywhere – shared on WhatsApp groups, reposted on blogs, debated in comment sections. The only problem? It was all fake. That’s what an AI deepfake can do.

“I’ve been seeing a lot of AI-generated pictures and videos of me being supposedly ‘pregnant,’ and that isn’t true,” Apara said, breaking her silence on the viral fabrication.

For the fast-rising actress, who broke into Nollywood in 2024 and has been steadily building a name for herself, the experience was both bewildering and worrying. How quickly people believed it. How fast they shared it.

She is not alone. Across the world, actors, musicians and public figures are waking up to find their faces, voices and bodies cloned by artificial intelligence – used to sell products, endorse politicians, or, as in Apara’s case, manufacture a pregnancy announcement.

But for young female celebrities in Nollywood, the violation feels more personal. It is not just an image; it is their body, their privacy, their story being rewritten without consent.

Apara’s response was measured but firm: disregard it, and verify.

The actress, a content creator as well as an actor, urged fans to stop the cycle of “see it, believe it, share it” and instead check her verified handles before accepting any news about her as truth.

“Verify claims about me through my official, verified social media accounts,” she said. The message is simple, but in an age of hyper-realistic AI, it is increasingly urgent.

If the incident revealed the dark side of technology, it also revealed Apara’s focus.

At a time when many would be drawn into an online war of words with bloggers, the actress has chosen to keep her eyes on the work.

Currently studying English Arts at the University of Lagos, Apara is part of a new generation of Nollywood talents who refuse to be boxed in. She acts, she creates content, she writes, she produces. For her, storytelling does not end when the director shouts “cut.”

Her credits already include “After School”, “One Night Guests”, “Walls Apart”, “Along Came Love”, “Danfo Dreams”, “Campus Chronicles”, “Campus Queen” and “Love Denied” – a growing list that has earned her attention since she came under the mentorship of actress and producer Ruth Kadiri.

“I am committed to growing across multiple areas of the entertainment industry,” she says, describing a career ambition that lives both in front of and behind the camera.

And to the fans who reached out, who asked rather than assumed, she is grateful.

For Annabel Apara, the fake baby bump will fade from timelines in a few days. Another AI scandal will take its place. But the lesson remains, and it is bigger than one actress.

In an era where AI can create a pregnancy with a single prompt, the responsibility to ask, “Is this real?” no longer belongs to celebrities alone. It belongs to fans and lovers of dignity.

World.title: Cost of UK study rises as govt reviews living costs, POF
World.content:
By Vera Anyagafu

For thousands of Nigerian students dreaming of a UK degree, the goalpost has shifted again, not placed out of reach, but set a little higher than before.

On or after November 30, 2026, Nigerians applying for a UK student visa will be required to show slightly more money for living costs.

The adjustment was contained in the Home Office Statement of Changes to the Immigration Rules, HC 584, laid before Parliament on 3 September 2026.

WHAT WAS REVIEWED AND WHAT IT MEANS

The review is not about tuition, visa fees or health surcharge.

It is about the maintenance requirement, the proof-of-funds (POF) for living costs that every Student visa applicant must demonstrate.

The Home Office said the increase is part of its annual alignment of the Student route with support available to home students.

In its explanatory memorandum, it stated that, “There is a maintenance requirement for student applicants to demonstrate they have funds to support themselves for each month of their course (up to 9 months). This level of funds is aligned with the maintenance loans available for home students, which is reviewed every year by the Department for Education.”

It added that, “This change increases the maintenance requirement to match the maintenance loans available for home students for the 2026/2027 academic year,” noting that the maximum accommodation offset has also been updated in line with the new threshold.

Since last year, the threshold has been reviewed annually as part of wider reforms to keep the student route credible and sustainable, it also stated.

WHAT IT WAS BEFORE VS WHAT IT IS NOW

The new rates apply based on the date you submit your application online.

Before the cut-off date in late November, applicants were assessed under the current maintenance threshold, but from the end of November 2026, all new applications will be assessed under a slightly higher threshold. The increase applies both to those studying in London and those outside London, with London retaining a higher requirement to reflect higher living costs. The message is that for courses of nine months or more, applicants will now have to show a slightly higher total for living costs.

And, while the uplift is small in percentage terms, it means a bank balance that was exactly sufficient under the old rules may no longer be sufficient under the new ones. These amounts cover living costs only, as applicants must still show any outstanding first-year tuition as stated on their Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS), plus visa and Immigration Health Surcharge costs.

The statement also makes clear this is not a ban, saying that the UK continues to host hundreds of thousands of international students yearly, about a quarter of its total higher education population. It added that the intent is not to suggest students are unwelcome, but to ensure they are better equipped to sustain themselves after arrival.

WHAT NIGERIAN APPLICANTS MUST KNOW

For Nigerian applicants, the naira equivalent is now higher at a time when exchange rates are already stretching family budgets.

Timing is also critical.

Those targeting the January 2027 intake who submit on or after November 30, 2026, will be assessed under the higher threshold.

Applications submitted before November 30, 2026, will still be decided under the rules in force on November 29, 2026.

The other detail that continues to cause refusals is the 28-day rule on funds.

Funds must remain in an acceptable account for 28 continuous days, and the end of that period must be within 31 days of the application date.

Any dip below the required total, even for a day, can lead to refusal.

Using a personal account, or a parent/guardian account with proper consent and proof of relationship, remains essential.

There is also some relief that many applicants overlook.

Where a student has already paid accommodation deposit directly to the university, that amount can be deducted from the living cost funds they need to evidence, reducing the total funds to be shown.

In the end, the fundamentals have not changed, as the UK continues to offer quality education and post-study work opportunities that attract Nigerians.

What has changed is the need for more deliberate financial planning.

Those who prepare early, maintain the required balance without interruption and keep their documents in order will still be able to make the move, albeit at a slightly higher cost of proof.

World.title: NCDC Confirms Negative Ebola Tests in 2 Suspected Adamawa Cases
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) says two suspected Ebola Virus Disease cases identified in Yola, Adamawa, have tested negative following two rounds of laboratory testing.

Dr Jide ​‌⁠⁠​‍⁠⁠‍‌‍‍‍‌​⁠⁠‌​Idris, NCDC Director-General, disclosed this in a statement on Saturday, saying the agency was working with the Adamawa Government to investigate the reported cases.

Idris said the report was received by the Adamawa Public Health Emergency Operations Centre in the early hours of Oct. 30, following the identification of two individuals with symptoms suggestive of Ebola.

He explained that the individuals were immediately isolated, while samples were collected and appropriate public health measures initiated to determine the cause of their illnesses.

The NCDC director-general said laboratory results from two rounds of testing were negative for Ebola, confirming that there was currently no laboratory-confirmed case in Adamawa.

He commended the Adamawa Commissioner for Health and his team for their proactive response, assuring that the NCDC would continue to provide technical support to strengthen the state’s response operations.

Idris also clarified that the previously confirmed case in the Federal Capital Territory, remained Nigeria’s only laboratory-confirmed Ebola case.

He urged Nigerians to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information or speculation, advising the public to rely on official government and public health communication channels.

The NCDC boss described Ebola as a serious infectious disease requiring prompt detection, appropriate clinical management and effective infection prevention and control measures.

He advised anyone experiencing symptoms such as fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding to seek immediate medical attention.

Idris stressed that people experiencing such symptoms, particularly after possible exposure, should inform healthcare workers about relevant travel or contact history.

He also cautioned against self-medication, urging individuals to follow professional medical advice and guidance from public health authorities.

According to him, the NCDC, Adamawa Government and other relevant stakeholders will continue to monitore the situation and provide updates as verified information becomes available.

He reaffirmed the commitment of public health authorities to protecting Nigerians through early detection, evidence-based interventions, transparent communication and coordinated national response efforts. (NAN)

World.title: INEC Forecloses Changing 2027 Election Timetable, Says Polls Can’t Be Shifted
World.content:
*To release final voters’ register December 15*Warns against attacks on officials, corps members

Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash Amupitan, has ruled out any adjustment to the timetable for the 2027 general election without lawful justification, declaring that the polls must hold as scheduled.

This comes as he warned against attacks on electoral officials, including National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members, during next year’s elections, saying perpetrators would face the full weight of the law.



Speaking yesterday in Port Harcourt, Rivers State capital, during an interactive meeting with INEC staff from the six South-south states to assess the commission’s preparedness for the forthcoming elections, Amupitan maintained that the commission would adhere strictly to its statutory obligations, stressing that the election timetable was fixed and would not be altered without lawful justification.

Amupitan also said the commission was addressing submissions of claims for corrections to the voters’ register ahead of the release of the final voters’ register scheduled for December 15.



“Our statutory timeline is fixed. We will not change anything. The election must be held as scheduled,” he said.

The INEC chairman also announced that Rivers State would receive particular attention in the commission’s preparations, given its position as the state with the highest number of registered voters in the South-south.



According to figures released by the commission, Rivers has 3,736,434 registered voters, followed by Delta with 3,525,988; Edo, 2,865,263; Akwa Ibom, 2,566,198; Cross River, 1,928,978; and Bayelsa, 1,200,691.

The six states have a combined 15,823,550 registered voters.

Amupitan said Rivers’ electoral significance placed additional responsibility on INEC officials to ensure no eligible voter would be denied the opportunity to exercise their franchise.



“With the 3,736,434 registered voters for Rivers State, the state leads the South-south. As a result, the commission will pay closer attention to what happens in Rivers State. It is your duty to ensure that no voter is disenfranchised because of operational failures,” he said.

On the voters’ register, Amupitan disclosed that INEC had published the register online and at designated locations for public scrutiny, adding that the commission had received more than 5,000 claims for corrections, including names and dates of birth, as well as over 600 objections.



He said the commission was addressing the submissions ahead of the release of the final voters’ register scheduled for December 15.

The INEC chairman explained that although he had initially considered revalidating the entire voters’ register after assuming office, he abandoned the proposal because he feared the exercise would come too close to the general election.



Amupitan expressed confidence in INEC’s capacity to deliver peaceful, transparent and credible elections, citing lessons from recent off-cycle governorship elections, particularly the Osun State governorship poll.

He described the Osun election as encouraging, noting that it recorded the highest voter turnout in the history of off-cycle elections in the state and earned positive assessments despite earlier security concerns.



“Osun State elections gave us the confidence that we can achieve this despite the noise. It is good that we had a series of those elections before the general elections because we learn lessons from every election,” he said.

He added that the commission would build on the experiences gained from the off-cycle elections to strengthen its preparations for 2027.

“We will conduct elections that will move the nation forward and not an election that will bring it down,” he assured.



On security, Amupitan said INEC was collaborating with relevant security agencies, including the Nigeria Police Force and the Department of State Services (DSS), to guarantee the safety of voters, electoral personnel, ad hoc staff and election materials.

He stressed that Nigerians must be able to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and exercise their franchise without fear of intimidation or violence.



“We want every part of Nigeria to be calm during the elections so that people can come out to vote. We will not tell them to take their PVCs and then will not guarantee their safety,” he said.

The INEC chairman also dismissed suggestions that Artificial Intelligence (AI) or computer algorithms could determine the outcome of the 2027 elections, insisting that Nigerian voters would remain in charge of electoral decisions.



“It is the people of Nigeria that will decide the outcome of the elections and not AI or any algorithms,” he declared.

He, however, acknowledged the growing cybersecurity threats associated with emerging technologies, saying the commission was exploring ways to deploy technology to better protect its digital infrastructure against possible attacks.



Amupitan urged INEC personnel across the South-South to remain professional and committed, emphasising that the credibility of the 2027 elections would ultimately depend on the conduct of officials at polling units and other field locations.

He warned against attacks on electoral officials, including NYSC members, during next year’s elections, stressing that perpetrators will face the full weight of the law.



Amupitan said the commission was strengthening its operational plans to ensure the safety of election personnel, voters and materials, particularly in areas exposed to security threats.

“Anyone who threatens or harms INEC officials, including National Youth Service Corps members deployed for election duties, will face the full weight of the law,” he warned.



The INEC chairman also cautioned electoral officers against partisanship, negligence, absenteeism and financial misconduct, stressing that such violations would attract disciplinary action.

Amupitan said the readiness assessment was designed to identify operational weaknesses and address logistical challenges before the elections.

World.title: Two New Suspected Ebola Cases in North East Test Negative, Says NCDC
World.content:
Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

Barely five days after the first imported case of Ebola virus disease was evacuated to Switzerland, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has confirmed that two new suspected cases of the disease tested negative in the North East state of Adamawa.

The NCDC had earlier yesterday reported that two suspected cases were identified in the North-east, and that they were isolated, with contact identification and laboratory testing ongoing.



However, in an update released last night, NCDC Director-General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the cases, which were identified in Yola, Adamawa State, had returned negative after two rounds of testing.

“Samples were collected for laboratory testing to establish the cause of the illness. Fortunately, the samples turned out negative for EBV after two rounds of testing,” Idris said.



He clarified that there was no laboratory-confirmed EVD case in Adamawa State, adding that the index case previously confirmed in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) remained the only confirmed case in Nigeria.

While commending the Adamawa State Government for its proactive response, Idris urged the public to remain calm, avoid sharing unverified information and continue to practise good hand hygiene and enhanced sanitation.



He assured that NCDC would continue to monitor the situation and provide updates as verified information becomes available.

NCDC had initially said it identified two suspected cases of the disease in the North-east geopolitical zone.

The agency, which did not disclose the particular state, added that laboratory testing was being conducted to determine whether the individuals had contracted the disease.



“Two suspected cases of Ebola disease have been identified in Nigeria’s North-east region. Both individuals have been isolated, contact identification and listing are ongoing, and laboratory testing is being conducted.

“Being classified as suspected cases does not mean they are confirmed Ebola cases; confirmation is subject to laboratory results,” the statement read.



The NCDC, however, cautioned that being classified as suspected cases did not mean the individuals had tested positive for Ebola, stressing that confirmation would depend on laboratory results.

The agency urged Nigerians to maintain good hand hygiene, practise enhanced sanitation, and follow guidance from public health authorities.



It said it would provide further updates as verified information became available.

The development came less than two weeks after the federal government confirmed Nigeria’s first imported case of the virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, on October 20, 2026.

The patient, a woman who had travelled from Uganda to Nigeria, tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain and was subsequently isolated and treated by Nigerian health workers.



Announcing the first case of the disease, the Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Ali Pate, had stated that the infected woman had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda and developed symptoms on October 7 before seeking medical attention at a private hospital in Abuja on October 11.



After confirmation, health authorities initially identified 44 contacts of the patient, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers, and people who might have travelled with her.

The number later rose to 53, and health authorities placed the contacts under surveillance.

The patient was subsequently evacuated to Switzerland on October 26 alongside her husband, who had remained asymptomatic.



The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Nigeria would need to complete a 42-day monitoring period before it could be declared free of Ebola, comprising 21 days of monitoring for identified contacts and another 21 days in line with established protocols.

The federal government had announced a payment of N100,000 weekly to each contact of the confirmed case to encourage compliance with quarantine directives and prevent possible community transmission.

World.title: Don’t Be Deceived, Vote for Tinubu in 2027, South East Govs Tell Igbo
World.content:
*Mbah: Ndigbo are strategic people, relationship builders

*Kalu: Igbo leaders not part of one-term presidency arrangement

Governors Peter Mbah of Enugu State; Hope Uzodimma of Imo State; Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State; and Charles Soludo of Anambra State have called on the people of the South East region to vote massively for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election and ignore every form of deception and political distractions.



The governors made the call during the All Progressives Congress (APC) Women Mega Rally and Empowerment Programme for the South East flagged off by the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu at Okpara Square, Enugu yesterday.

Speaking, the host governor, Dr. Mbah, urged the people of the region to support Tinubu’s re-election bid to enable him to consolidate the gains of his administration’s economic reforms.



He attributed ongoing development projects, including the construction of primary healthcare centres, to the federal government’s economic reforms.

“If I ask what future you want for your children, I’m sure you are seeing that future unfold gradually through the bold and courageous reforms of Mr. President.



“It is through those reforms that enough money has been made available to all the states. Which is why in Enugu, when you look around you, you will see the Smart Green Schools, Type 2 Primary Healthcare Centres, and numerous other projects and initiatives we have undertaken in just three years.



“This is happening because of the bold and courageous reforms of Mr. President and we know the job is not finished yet. A good sailor does not abandon his ship mid-sea because of challenges.

“So, we must finish the journey we all started together. We must come out on January 16 with our PVC and ensure that the good work Mr. President is doing will continue.



“Don’t listen to any voice. Those voices telling us a different thing. We, the Igbos have gone to communities outside our zone to build businesses. And we also know how to build relationships. And that is being put to test. We are not a people that are ethnic bigots. We are a people that are strategic.



“And that is why we must all come out in our numbers and support Mr. President to continue the good work. Support all our APC candidates to ensure that they are returned come January and February,” he emphasised.

Speaking on the empowerment programme targeting 5,000 women across the South-east, Mbah said the initiative followed the empowerment of more than 2,000 women, including payment of hospital bills, in Enugu by the First Lady, within 48 hours.



“When you empower a woman, you strengthen the family. When you empower a woman, you build a strong community,” he said.

Also speaking, Governor Uzodimma reiterated the commitment of the region to supporting Tinubu’s re-election in 2027.

He explained that Igbos had experienced marginalisation for over 60 years, but were beginning to witness a new era of political inclusion and development under Tinubu.



He commended the president for expanding the scope of infrastructure and economic development in the South-east region.

“We are now seeing good roads, electricity, health reforms as well as educational reforms in the country. A winning team must not be changed,” he said.
