Earlier this month, President Donald Trump announced a deal to allow Russian diesel exports to global energy markets and waived a further slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales that had only just been signed into law.

Trump also threatened to withhold intelligence from Kyiv over its strikes on Russian refineries, and Ukraine’s access to the crucial Starshield satellite system was throttled for a period before it was restored last week.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday that Ukrainian drones had attacked three Russian oil refineries and a gas-chemical complex, according to Russian state news agency TASS,

The same day, Zelensky accused Moscow of continuing to target Ukraine’s infrastructure, saying Russian ballistic missiles had struck oil refining infrastructure in Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region.

“The Russians have not taken a single step toward energy de-escalation,” he said in a Telegram post. “We will also act accordingly and entirely justly.”

Friday’s sale announcement also left open whether any missile components would be produced in Ukraine as part of a so-called “offset agreement.”

The State Department said that it was “not aware” of any such arrangement between Ukraine and Lockheed Martin, the defense firm that produces the Patriot, but noted that the matter could be directly negotiated between Kyiv and Lockheed.

Trump had shocked many by announcing in July at the NATO summit in Turkey that Ukraine would receive a license to produce its own Patriot missiles, a move that could eventually alleviate pressure on US production lines amid a munitions shortage linked to the Iran war and growing international demand. But any Ukrainian interceptor factory could take years to build, and the president has seemingly backed off from the move.

This story has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

World.title: What are the possible scenarios after Israel’s elections?
World.content:
With most votes counted, Israel’s election has produced no clear winner, setting up weeks – and possibly months – of political uncertainty. Several outcomes and scenarios may come into play.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc has lost the majority it held in the outgoing parliament. With about 53 seats projected, it falls short of the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government in the 120-seat Knesset.

Netanyahu could try to recruit one of the opposition parties to join his government, but they all ruled out cooperation with him during campaigning. Politicians who have joined him in recent years have often found themselves significantly weakened with little substantive influence over policy. Netanyahu could also try to seek individual opposition defectors, but that would require several defections to close the gap.

The opposition, on the other hand, has won a majority in the parliament, but their path to power is crossed by ideological, national and personal divisions.

Netanyahu’s main rival Gadi Eisenkot is projected to win 21 seats, but he cannot reach the 61-seat majority without the two Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint list, who are projected to win a record 19 seats. On Wednesday, Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called on his partners to count the Arab parties as part of the bloc, rejecting what he called Netanyahu’s “racist division between Jewish and Arab votes.”

But two of Eisenkot’s right-wing allies oppose forming a government that includes the Arab parties or a minority government that relies on their outside support.

Given the apparent deadlock, another scenario is a national unity government pairing Netanyahu’s Likud and one or more parties from the opposition, an option that would replace his current hardliner government. Both Netanyahu and the opposition leaders have ruled this out during the campaign, but it may be one of the only ways to avoid another election.

World.title: Oleshky evacuees return to Ukraine under Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire
World.content:
Dmytro had not seen his wife Larisa for 1,711 days.

Waiting near the border between Ukraine and Belarus, his nervous eyes were on the horizon, looking for the bus carrying Larisa and others fleeing the occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky.

Hundreds of people – and many pets – arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday afternoon after being evacuated from the frontline city under a ceasefire that Pope Leo XIV called for and first lady Melania Trump helped to negotiate.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the arrival of the evacuees on Telegram, thanking Trump for the mediation.

“And I thank everyone in the world—all journalists, all political and civic leaders, and all concerned people—who drew global attention to the situation in Oleshky and the genuine humanitarian catastrophe in the territory of Ukraine temporarily occupied by Russia. When the world pays attention, people are saved,” he said.

Dmytro, whose last name cannot be published for security reasons, is a soldier in the Ukrainian military which made Larisa vulnerable when Russia took over Oleshky, their southern Ukrainian hometown.

The couple managed to get their daughter out, but Larisa was worried that if she tried to leave, she’d be picked up at a Russian military checkpoint during filtration – the humiliating and often violent questioning Ukrainians who found themselves under Russian occupation had to undergo before being allowed to leave for areas still under Ukrainian control.

So she stayed, hoping for a miracle. Instead, her life became a nightmare.

The town was hit by a major flood in 2023 after the nearby Nova Kakhovka Dam collapsed – most likely because of a Russian explosion. Several hundred people were reported to have died in the flooding and the town suffered major damage. The Russian-installed authorities were unable, or unwilling, to invest into repairs.

More destruction came in the subsequent years of heavy fighting in the area and the humanitarian situation has deteriorated in recent months. The town was reported by Ukrainian authorities to have ran out of food and other supplies in September, with no access to electricity, gas, medicine and other essentials. Reports from that time said people were surviving on grass and weeds.

The director of the Chernihiv Regional Hospital Andriy Zhydenko was waiting at the border with his staff to provide medical assistance to the evacuees. He told CNN the the effects of prolonged malnutrition will be a key concern, explaining that the evacuees will need to be fed carefully because they have been starving for so long that consuming too much food too quickly could be dangerous.

“There are people with injuries, stroke survivors, and those with limited mobility,” he said, adding that everyone at the hospital was overjoyed to be welcoming Ukrainian citizens home. “All of my staff wanted to come here. People have suffered greatly there. There is no humanity.”

Long way home

Some 40% of Oleshky’s prewar population of around 24,000 managed to flee to Ukraine-controlled territory when it was still possible early in the fighting, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a US-based conflict observer. Thousands of others have escaped since then, but many remained, either unable or unwilling to leave.

Zhanna Ptakhova and her daughers Elizaveta and Daria Paliy were among those who made it out when it was still possible.

But Ptakhova’s husband, and Elizaveta’s and Daria’s father, stayed in Oleshky. He was going to taking care of their home until they could safely return.

But that has not happened. “The conditions were terrible. No electricity, no gas, no heat – but he’s a man with golden hands,” Ptakhova told CNN.

“He took a house that had been adapted for modern civilian life and turned it into a home suited for a primitive lifestyle; he built a stove, raised chickens to feed himself, planted a garden, and through his own hard work, he survived there,” she said.

The family was going to be reunited after three years apart.

Access routes to Oleshky have been heavily mined and littered with drone and vehicle debris and evacuation across the Dnipro River directly into Ukraine-controlled territory is not possible.

That made the journey out long and scary. Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets traveled to Oleshky to personally escort the evacuees into Ukraine-controlled territory, becoming the first high-profile Ukrainian official to openly travel to occupied areas under Russian control and Russia since the start of the war.

Once a two-day demining operation was completed on Thurday, people who wanted to leave gathered on Friday and traveled through the occupied Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea to Anapa in Russia’s Krasnodar region.

The evacuees then flew from Anapa airport to Gomel, Belarus, according to the Russian Defense Ministry and Ukrainian officials.

World.title: The real question we should all be asking about AI
World.content:
The stock market is turning its back on Big Tech.

Google just had its worst day ever. Intel tumbled more than any day since the Nixon administration. Amazon and Meta both had significant declines this week, too. The Nasdaq tumbled and is just over a percentage point away from a correction (a 10 percent decline from its all-time high).

The common thread: Building the infrastructure to power AI is really, really expensive – and Big Tech profits aren’t yet justifying that massive expense. AI companies are increasingly doling out more cash for data centers than their businesses are able to generate.

But if the stock market is supposed be to delivering some kind of message, Big Tech isn’t hearing it.

Spending on AI has reached $1.6 trillion since 2023 and is expected to hit $1 trillion every single year for the next decade or so, according to JPMorgan. None of that changed this week.

That’s because the market that’s financing all of this – the bond market – is mostly shrugging its shoulders while the stock market is in the midst of a mild freakout. Lenders have been lining up to take on Big Tech’s debt to pay for the technology that’s reshaping the global economy.

That means the questions the market seems to be asking about AI – will Big Tech keep growing its spending? (it most certainly will) and will AI will turn a profit anytime soon? (doesn’t look like it) – are the wrong ones.

The real question we should be asking about AI is: How much longer will the bond market sustain the nonstop spending spree?

That will ultimately dictate whether AI turns into a success or a bust.

AI math

The way AI math works is like this: Spend a lot of money upfront on the infrastructure needed to support AI (data centers, servers, chips, power, labor, building materials, etc.). Then, once the data center is switched on, AI companies can monetize that investment … somewhere between three months to two years later, according to Goldman Sachs.

With profit arriving that far down the road, hyperscalers (the Big Tech guys like Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta) need to borrow a ton of money upfront and pay back investors down the road.

“A ton” doesn’t really do it justice. Those four hyperscalers alone have been collectively responsible for more than a third of all capital expenditures from the S&P 500 over the past 12 months, notes John Higgins, chief economic adviser at Capital Economics.

That’s why a third of Big Tech’s capital expenditures this year are expected to be financed with debt – something like $250 billion worth of bonds from hyperscalers alone, according to Goldman Sachs. That’s expected to peak next year at around 35 percent of hyperscalers’ spending.

Wires in a Trainium2 UltraServer at an Amazon Web Services lab in Austin, Texas, on February 3, 2026. Amazon had a significant decline in the stock market this week. Mark Felix/AFP/Getty Images

But bond market investors don’t have infinite money to spend. And there’s a ton of competition for lending right now – especially from US Treasuries as the government is trying to pay for Social Security, Medicare and an expensive war, all at the same time.

That raises an obvious question: Exactly how much money are investors willing to lend AI companies?

It’s more than you might think.

The hypothetical maximum amount of debt the market can absorb is unknowable, but Goldman Sachs did the math anyway and came up with $510 billion of available investment-grade (top-tier) debt for the biggest hyperscalers. That’s more than double what they’re currently expected to be borrowing by the end of the year.

In other words: The biggest AI companies have a lot of runway left to borrow.

Who’s lending to whom?

The question isn’t how much; the question is how much longer.

The answer depends on two parts: Who is paying and who is receiving.

“We are not concerned about access to capital,” said Amanda Lynam, chief credit strategist for Goldman Sachs on a recent company podcast. “We are just expecting there to be a more nuanced conversation about where to issue and at what price.”

Private investment funds, venture funds and private equity are ready to do the heavy lifting to support the AI buildout, Lynam said, with trillions more dollars of “dry powder” to finance it.

But hyperscalers aren’t the only game in town. Other companies, including neoclouds, are playing in the space too. They’re highly indebted companies that rent out computing to other businesses, and their credit situation is starting to look iffy. Their non-investment-grade bonds deliver high yields that investors willing to take on more risk are willing to gamble on, in exchange for potentially massive rewards..

That’s the market in which CoreWeave plays, with its bond yields surging to 15 percent this month as losses piled up. Elon Musk said the neocloud industry, which includes CoreWeave, is due for a massive shakeout (he called it “guppy-level death.”)

The CoreWeave AI data center is under construction on October 21, 2026, in Kenilworth, New Jersey. The company’s bond yields surged to 15 percent this month as losses piled up. Stephanie Keith/Getty Images

Every new technology has winners and losers, and Musk may be right about neoclouds. We’ll see.

Hyperscalers, by contrast, look like winners. Their cloud revenue (a stat Wall Street uses to measure AI demand) grew 50 percent in the second quarter. They have huge contract backlogs and the capacity to absorb higher borrowing costs.

Those bottlenecks can support high prices, which helped hyperscaler revenue surge 19 percent over the past 12 months, according to Higgins.

And the advent of agentic AI has sent demand exploding: requests from agents consume 15 times as many tokens as human-initiated requests, according to OpenRouter.

“The outlook for these things doesn’t look obviously bleak, given that AI is gradually being used more and more in the economy,” Higgins said.

So what’s the problem?

The concern is that the cost of borrowing could get unwieldy. And that could change the economics that are still working for AI.

Negative sentiment that’s pervasive in the stock market could start to bleed out into the bond market, sending bond yields higher and raising borrowing costs for AI companies.

The bond market works best when there’s an end in sight, Lyman noted. Every AI investor believes there’s a light at the end of the tunnel. We just have no idea how long this tunnel is.

The uncertainty about when companies will ultimately start turning a profit and making money off all their massive AI investments could give the bond market pause, she said.

In the meantime, the outlook for the technology and the big companies’ finances looks quite strong, said Stephanie Aliaga, a global market strategist with JPMorgan, in a recent note to investors.

Warning signs would include a downshift in businesses’ AI usage, cheaper pricing or fewer customer commitments.

We’re not seeing any of those yet.

World.title: Irrigation Minister: Cairo Water Week a key platform for global dialogue
World.content:
Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation Hani Sewilam said Cairo Water Week has become a key international platform for dialogue, exchanging expertise and building partnerships to address water challenges.

In a statement on Friday, October 30, 2026, Sewilam thanked the international organizations, national institutions and companies that supported the ninth edition, held from October 25 to 29 under the auspices of President Abdel Fattah El Sisi and themed “Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity and a Sustainable Planet.”

He said the event’s success and broad international participation highlighted the importance of partnerships in achieving sustainable water development.

He stressed the Ministry’s commitment to strengthening cooperation with international organizations, research institutions and the private sector to implement the second-generation water system (2.0), support the National Water Resources and Irrigation Strategy 2050, and promote regional and international cooperation.

Sewilam praised the European Union and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), which co-organized the event, as well as UNESCO, the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA) and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) for their contributions.

He also commended the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), alongside other partners, including GIZ, the German Development Bank (KFW), the Dutch and British embassies, IHE Delft and the American University in Cairo.

The Minister thanked Germany’s RWTH Aachen University for supporting AI-based training and developing a presentation for the Irrigation Museum in the New Administrative Capital.

He also praised national sponsors, including the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority, the Agricultural Bank of Egypt, Gennat Agricultural Company and PepsiCo Egypt, for supporting efforts to strengthen water and food security.

The five-day event concluded on Thursday, featuring 137 technical and scientific sessions and competitions, with the participation of ministers, governors, ambassadors and international and regional organizations, including FAO, the EU, UNESCO, IWMI and the WWC.

World.title: Egyptian, Hungarian FMs discuss bilateral ties, regional developments
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty held talks in Budapest on Friday, October 30, 2026, with Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán on bilateral relations and the latest regional developments.

Abdelatty stressed the importance of building on the Strategic Partnership Declaration signed by the two countries in 2023, describing it as an important framework for promoting bilateral relations and expanding cooperation across various fields.

In this regard, he expressed Egypt’s keenness to translate this partnership into practical projects and programs that deliver tangible benefits to the two countries’ peoples.

The top Egyptian diplomat also underscored the significance of holding regular meetings of the joint higher committee as a key mechanism for advancing bilateral collaboration.

He stressed the need for increasing trade exchange, boosting tourism cooperation, while capitalizing on promising opportunities to expand economic and investment partnerships.

The two ministers reviewed ongoing joint projects between Egypt and Hungary in a number of areas, especially in the railway.

Abdelatty emphasized the need to build on the results of cooperation achieved in this area and explore new prospects for expanding the partnership in infrastructure and transport projects, while benefiting from Hungary’s expertise and capabilities in supporting Egypt’s development efforts.

The pair also exchanged views on a number of regional and international issues of mutual concern, particularly the latest regional developments and efforts to contain ongoing crises and prevent further escalation.

In this respect, Abdelatty called for prioritizing political and diplomatic solutions, resorting to dialogue, intensifying de-escalation efforts and preserving regional stability.

World.title: Egypt, Morocco discuss expanding cooperation in ports, industry, logistics
World.content:
Egyptian Ambassador to Morocco Ahmed Nihad Abdel Latif discussed ways to expand cooperation in ports, industrial zones and logistics with Mehdi Tazi-Riffi, CEO and Chairman of Tanger Med Group, during a meeting at the group’s headquarters in Tangier city, Morocco.

The meeting, attended by Egyptian Commercial Counselor in Morocco Moataz Bellah Ali, focused on strengthening economic relations and advancing the two countries’ shared goal of building a comprehensive economic partnership.

Abdel Latif said the outcomes of the first session of the Joint Coordination and Follow-up Committee, held in Cairo on April 6 under the co-chairmanship of the two countries’ prime ministers, reflected a shared commitment to deepening economic ties through increased trade, joint investment, industrial integration and closer cooperation in transport and logistics.

He also highlighted Egypt’s industrial, production and logistical capabilities, pointing to the significant progress made in infrastructure and transport development in recent years.

For his part, Tazi-Riffi outlined Tanger Med’s experience, particularly its integrated model linking port operations with surrounding industrial zones and its role in facilitating international trade and the movement of goods across global markets.

The discussions explored prospects for cooperation between Tanger Med and Egyptian ports, as well as the Suez Canal Authority and the Suez Canal Economic Zone.

Both sides stressed the importance of strengthening links between ports, industrial zones and logistics hubs in the two countries to enhance their international competitiveness and expand their role in global trade and investment.

They also discussed exchanging expertise in port management and operations, developing industrial zones, leveraging the two countries’ transport and logistics networks, and encouraging partnerships between Egyptian and Moroccan private-sector companies.

The proposed cooperation is expected to create new opportunities in manufacturing, exports and investment, while expanding access for Egyptian and Moroccan products to African and European markets.

World.title: Industrial strategy targets supply chains, local manufacturing
World.content:
Egypt’s Industrial Strategy 2030 seeks to establish a more competitive industrial base integrated into global supply chains by promoting industrial localization, deepening domestic manufacturing and increasing local value added, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said.

Speaking at a ceremony hosted by the Egyptian-British Business Association (EBBA) to mark the 30th anniversary of the Egyptian-British partnership, Hashem outlined the strategy’s main pillars and explored opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the ministry and the association.

The event was attended by EBBA Chairman Khaled Nosseir, former Electricity Minister Mohamed Shaker, Tareq El-Molla, Chairman of the House of Representatives’ Energy and Environment Committee, and a number of business leaders, lawmakers, ambassadors and representatives of government bodies and organizations.

Hashem explained that the strategy focuses on five main industrial groups: industries integrated into global supply chains, including automotive and ready-made garments; strategic industries, such as iron and steel, aluminum, chemicals and fertilizers; supporting and feeder industries, including metalworking, food processing and textiles, enabling industries, covering solar energy equipment, water-saving technologies, precision molds and tools, and printed circuit boards; and circular economy and recycling industries.

He said the Ministry is working to establish an integrated support framework for investors and manufacturers through the provision of industrial land, streamlined licensing procedures, financing facilities and technical assistance, as well as stronger links between small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and major industrial companies.

The measures are intended to strengthen integration across production chains and enhance the sector’s efficiency.

Technology is another key pillar of the strategy, Hashem said, highlighting efforts to align scientific research with the actual needs of factories and channel research outcomes into developing industrial products and processes.

He stressed the importance of balancing the transfer of international technologies with the development of domestic technological capabilities to meet local market needs.

The Minister also underscored the importance of developing industries based on locally available resources and maximizing the use of Egypt’s mineral wealth to increase value added and reduce import dependence.

He pointed in particular to the development of feeder industries, including refractory materials, alloys and castings used in iron and steel production, as well as industries based on phosphate rock.

On the regional front, Hashem said the ministry seeks to deepen industrial integration with African countries and explore opportunities to establish Egyptian industrial projects across the continent, opening new avenues for investment and cooperation and expanding the reach of Egyptian products in regional markets.

Addressing workforce development, he described human capital as a key ministry priority, revealing plans to introduce a vocational education program aimed at improving the quality of technical and vocational education graduates and equipping them to compete in domestic and international labor markets.

The program will cover basic and specialized skills, training in modern technologies and expanded practical instruction inside factories.

It will also seek accreditation from reputable international educational institutions and establish links between graduates and local and international companies to bridge the gap between industrial labor requirements and the availability of qualified workers.

Hashem also reviewed the ministry’s manufacturer support system, which aims to strengthen communication among industrial establishments, expand commercial and production partnerships, and develop local suppliers and feeder industries to increase domestic content and reduce reliance on imported production inputs.

The system also provides a mechanism for addressing manufacturers’ complaints in coordination with relevant ministries and authorities. Linking smaller factories with the production requirements of major industrial companies, he noted, would help them integrate into supply chains, expand their operations and strengthen productive capacities.

“The Ministry is also working to support innovative industrial ventures and help them move toward large-scale production, transforming technological ideas and applications into commercially viable products,” Hashem said.

He added that Egypt is seeking to attract European small and medium-sized enterprises facing difficulties adapting to economic challenges and encourage them to establish industrial partnerships with Egyptian private-sector companies.

Such partnerships would provide European firms with access to growing markets in the Middle East and Africa while facilitating the transfer of technology and expertise to Egypt.

On investment facilitation, Hashem highlighted measures to ease access to industrial land, including the introduction of a lease-to-own system, simplifying industrial licensing procedures and reducing associated financial burdens.

He also announced plans to launch an industrial advisory service through the Industrial Modernization Center to provide investors and manufacturers with technical and procedural assistance, information on investment opportunities and guidance on establishing and expanding industrial projects.

Turning to rural industrial development, Hashem said the ministry is implementing the “Productive Village” initiative to establish industrial activities in rural communities based on the competitive advantages of each area, particularly in food processing and textiles.

The initiative seeks to generate employment, particularly for women, reduce post-harvest losses during the transportation of agricultural products, and curb migration from villages to cities and abroad by creating local economic and production opportunities.

Hashem further stressed the importance of maintaining regular communication with the industrial community, including local manufacturers and foreign investors, through periodic meetings with embassies and representatives of foreign companies operating in Egypt.

These meetings aim to identify challenges facing industrial investments and develop solutions to overcome them, he noted.

He added that the ministry had organized several roundtable meetings with foreign companies, beginning with British businesses operating in automotive manufacturing and components, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, water treatment technologies and technical training.

The discussions focused on identifying operational challenges and exploring appropriate solutions.

The minister also highlighted efforts to integrate informal factories into the formal economy, helping address unfair competition between licensed manufacturers operating under official regulations and establishments outside the formal framework.

The ministry is also working to help existing factories access export markets and accelerate procedures for establishing new industrial projects, he added.

Meanwhile, the manufacturer support system provides comprehensive assistance to distressed factories, including connecting them with potential investors, facilitating financing through the Distressed Factories Restructuring Fund, and providing the technical and operational solutions needed to resume production.

These measures aim to preserve existing industrial capacity, restore struggling factories to operation and ensure the sustainability of domestic production.

World.title: Final Verdict: Swiss Supreme Court Upholds Alieu Kosiah’s 20-Year Sentence for Lofa War Crimes
World.content:
Court clears ex-ULIMO commander of crimes against humanity but leaves sentence intact

Monrovia – Former ULIMO commander Alieu Kosiah will serve the full 20 years in prison for atrocities committed in Lofa County during Liberia’s civil war, after Switzerland’s Federal Supreme Court upheld his war crimes conviction in a ruling made public Friday.

By Rodney Sieh



The decision makes final the first war crimes conviction ever handed down by a Swiss civilian court. It is also the first conviction anywhere of a Liberian for war crimes committed during the country’s two civil wars, which ran from 1989 to 2003 and killed an estimated 250,000 people.

Kosiah was found guilty of crimes committed in Lofa between 1993 and 1995, including killing civilians and ordering their killing, rape, using a child soldier, ordering pillage, cruel treatment of civilians, and desecrating the body of a dead civilian through an act of cannibalism.

The Appeals Chamber of Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court had found that those crimes alone would justify 150 years in prison. The sentence was reduced to 20 years, the maximum allowed under Swiss law.

Crimes Against Humanity Charge Thrown Out

In a partial win for the defense, the Supreme Court acquitted Kosiah of crimes against humanity, a conviction the Appeals Chamber added in 2023. The court ruled that the crimes against humanity provision, which entered Swiss law in 2011, cannot be applied to acts committed between 1993 and 1995.

The acquittal does not affect his 20-year sentence or his expulsion from Switzerland once he has served it.

Lawyers for the victims welcomed the final conviction but criticized the acquittal.

“Today the survivors of Alieu Kosiah’s crimes have final justice, more than 30 years after they suffered and twelve years after his arrest,” said Alain Werner, Director of Civitas Maxima, the Geneva-based group that represents victims in the case. “When this case began, it was often their word against his, about events during a brutal and traumatic civil war. Today Switzerland’s highest court has confirmed that they were believed.”

Werner said his team was “deeply disappointed” by the acquittal, arguing that civilians in Lofa were deliberately targeted — killed, raped, looted and forced to carry loads for fighters — in a widespread and systematic attack.

“What happened in Lofa between 1993 and 1995 is the very definition of a crime against humanity,” he said.

Twelve Years in Detention

Kosiah settled in Switzerland in the late 1990s and was arrested in November 2014 after Liberian victims filed a criminal complaint through their lawyers. He has been in detention ever since.

Survivors traveled from Liberia to testify against him during the investigation and at both of his trials.

The case was built with the help of the Global Justice and Research Project (GJRP), a Liberian organization that has documented civil war crimes for more than a decade. Together, Civitas Maxima and GJRP have contributed to six criminal trials in four countries linked to Liberia’s civil wars, resulting in five convictions.

‘Our People Should Not Have to Keep Looking to Europe’

The ruling once again throws a spotlight on Liberia’s failure to try its own war criminals. More than two decades after the war ended, no war crimes trial has been held on Liberian soil. Armed groups recruited more than 21,000 children during the conflict.

Liberia has committed to establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court, but the court has yet to hear a case.

GJRP Director Hassan Bility thanked Swiss authorities for more than ten years of commitment that allowed Liberian survivors to take part directly in the trials, but said justice should be delivered at home.

“These crimes were committed in Liberia by a Liberian against Liberians, and the judgment was delivered thousands of miles away,” Bility said. “Our people should not have to keep looking to Europe or the United States for justice. It is more than time for these trials to take place in Liberia, and for the War and Economic Crimes Court to start its work.”

[OPTIONAL: Reaction from the War and Economic Crimes Court office, the Ministry of Justice, or Lofa County residents/lawmakers.]

World.title: Liberia: Bong County’s New Road Machines Could Open the Way from Farm to Market, Says EPA Boss Yarkpawolo
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County – The arrival of 30 pieces of heavy earthmoving equipment in Bong County is being greeted as a turning point for the county’s farmers, traders and rural families. The head of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says the machines could turn isolation into opportunity.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo, the EPA Executive Director and a son of Zota District, said the yellow machines carry meaning far beyond the construction work they are expected to do. In his view, passable roads sit at the heart of food security, farm income and the daily survival of rural households.



In a statement marking the arrival, Dr. Yarkpawolo commended President Joseph Nyuma Boakai for placing roads at the center of his administration’s agenda. He argued that the initiative could begin to ease transportation problems that have long held back farming and trade in Bong, one of the country’s most important agricultural counties.

He leaned on a saying the President is known for: that people cannot eat a road, yet a road is what allows people to eat. “People do not eat road, but it is road that can make people eat,” he recalled. According to the EPA chief, the line captures what farmers across rural Liberia live with every season.

Farmers in Bong, he explained, put months of labor and money into growing rice, cassava, vegetables and plantains. But the work does not end at harvest. Getting crops out of the village and into a market is often the harder part, and where roads have deteriorated, that journey can fail altogether.

The rainy season makes matters worse. Mud, washed-out surfaces and damaged crossings can cut off whole farming settlements, leaving vehicles unable to reach them. Produce waiting by the roadside may rot before a buyer ever sees it, and the farmer absorbs the loss. “A farmer can grow rice, cassava, vegetables, and plantains, but without a reliable road to the market, that harvest may spoil before it can be sold,” he said.

The damage, Dr. Yarkpawolo noted, does not stop with the farmer. Market women struggle to get supplies, traders lose business, and families in towns and cities pay more because the cost of hauling food over bad roads gets passed along at the market stall.

That is why, he said, agriculture and infrastructure should not be treated as two separate items on the government’s to-do list. “A road connects the hands that grow our food to the households that need it,” he stated. He added that it also lets farmers earn the money to feed, educate and uplift their children.

Roads, he stressed, are also lifelines to schools and clinics. Children in remote communities can find it hard to reach the classroom, and patients needing urgent care may not reach a hospital in time when the only route is barely passable. More dependable roads throughout the year, he said, would ease those burdens. “Beyond food, better roads can help children reach school, patients reach hospitals, and businesses reach new customers,” he said.

His comments come amid an ongoing national conversation about road development and economic recovery, especially in rural counties where farming remains a main source of work and income. In Bong, many households rely on farming and small-scale trading to get by, and weak road links have historically made it harder to move goods and reach basic services.

Dr. Yarkpawolo believes sustained rehabilitation of rural roads could open doors for residents who have waited years. Farmers who can move crops quickly and cheaply stand a better chance of earning enough to enlarge their farms, buy inputs and improve conditions at home.

Traders would gain too. With better roads, he said, they could reach more villages, buy directly from producers and carry goods to bigger markets. Stronger ties between farmers and city consumers could also help bring down some of the transport costs that keep market prices high.

For Zota District and other rural parts of Bong, the stakes are personal.

“Today, as Bong County’s yellow machines arrive home, I welcome them with pride as a son of Bong,” he declared. He said the machines offer farmers, market women and cut-off communities a chance to turn isolation into access and hard work into income.

Yet the EPA chief was clear that delivery is not the same as results. He warned that the arrival of equipment does not fulfill the government’s responsibility, and called for practical steps to keep the machines running and ensure they produce measurable benefits.

Maintenance, he said, must be a priority. Without disciplined management and steady attention to servicing and operating needs, the machines’ usefulness will fade.

He also urged fairness in deployment, insisting that communities facing the toughest travel problems should get a real share of the benefit.

“Their arrival must now translate into results. We must maintain the machines, deploy them fairly, and ensure they serve the communities that need them,” he said.

Dr. Yarkpawolo said the program should not be judged by the number of machines parked in Bong, but by what changes on the ground. “Their true value will be measured in roads made passable, travel made easier, and livelihoods improved,” he said. Road work, in his words, must deliver tangible gains: easier movement, better market access and more earning opportunities for rural households.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Mayor Jefferson Koijee Hands Over Disputed Sinkor Property to VP Koung, Vows Political Fight Continues
World.content:
The former mayor, who served under the administration of ex-President George Manneh Weah, used the statement to renew allegations of political persecution against the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Koung.

Former Monrovia City Mayor Jefferson T. Koijee says handing over the 19th Street premises does not amount to surrender or an admission of guilt, accusing the Boakai-Koung administration of political persecution while declaring 2029 as his political destination.

Former Monrovia City Mayor Jefferson T. Koijee says he has officially handed over a disputed property on 19th Street, Coleman Avenue, in Sinkor, to Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung following an intervention by his spiritual adviser, Pastor Philemon A. Tarpeh.

In a public statement, Koijee said the decision was driven by his faith and commitment to peace, insisting that relinquishing the premises should not be interpreted as an admission of wrongdoing or a retreat from his political struggle.



“I have chosen peace. My faith remains unshaken. 2029 is our destination,” Koijee declared, signaling his intention to remain politically active ahead of the next presidential election.

The former mayor, who served under the administration of ex-President George Manneh Weah, used the statement to renew allegations of political persecution against the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Koung.

At the center of his argument is the ownership dispute surrounding the Sinkor property.

Koijee recalled that on September 18, 2018, then Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, Mo Ali, publicly alleged that he had acquired a house valued at US$250,000 in less than nine months.

According to Koijee, the allegation followed him for years and was repeatedly used to portray him as corrupt.

However, he said a writ of summons issued by the Monrovia City Magisterial Court on October 13, 2026, identifies Vice President Koung as claiming the same property.

He questioned how the property could have been attributed to him in 2018 but is now being claimed by the Vice President.

“So which lie were they telling then, and which lie are they telling now?” Koijee asked, challenging the government to explain the circumstances surrounding the competing claims.

He said the Boakai-Koung administration owes the Liberian public an explanation, although the competing ownership claims and the legal status of the property remain matters requiring clarification through the appropriate legal process.

Koijee also revisited the international sanctions announced against him on December 8, 2023, saying his political opponents celebrated the development as the end of his political career.

He claimed that the sanctions resulted in repeated visa denials and other restrictions but credited Pastor Tarpeh’s prayers and spiritual support for helping him overcome the difficulties.

“The man they buried is still standing,” he said, invoking biblical passages to reinforce his message of resilience and faith.

The former mayor further rejected allegations linking him to criminal activities, including murder, accusing the current administration of using state institutions and public platforms to tarnish his reputation.

Koijee argued that despite nearly three years of accusations, authorities had failed to prove the allegations against him in court.

“They called me a criminal. They called me a murderer,” he said. “For almost three years the Boakai-Koung regime has controlled the police, the prosecutors, and the microphones, and not one case has been proven against me.”

He challenged the government to produce evidence supporting the allegations, including financial records and properties allegedly linked to him.

However, his claims about the absence of proven cases do not, on their own, establish that all allegations against him are unfounded. The specific status of any investigations or proceedings would need to be established through official records.

In defending his public service record, Koijee cited his tenure as Monrovia City Mayor, arguing that he prioritized public service over personal comfort.

He said he continued using an official vehicle purchased by his predecessor rather than requesting a new one, adding that he nearly lost his life in an accident involving the same vehicle on June 16, 2018.

Koijee maintained that throughout his six years as mayor, he never purchased a new official vehicle for himself and challenged critics to verify the claim through records at City Hall.

He also directed questions at Chairman George Sylvester Mulbah, demanding clarification over his alleged relationship with the Office of the Vice President.

“Seven statements, and still no answer. Are you employed in the Office of Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung? Yes or no?” Koijee asked.

He did not provide further details about the seven statements referenced in his challenge.

Despite handing over the disputed premises, Koijee said he would continue advocating for what he described as constitutional governance, independent courts and equal justice.

He framed the property handover as a decision to avoid confrontation rather than a withdrawal from the political arena.

“They can take a property, but they cannot take my voice, my faith, or the people’s hunger for change,” he declared.

Koijee concluded by reaffirming his political ambition ahead of the 2029 elections, describing the next presidential contest as the destination of his ongoing political struggle.

“I have handed over the premises. I have not handed over the truth,” he said.

The property dispute, the circumstances surrounding its handover and the competing claims of ownership are likely to remain subjects of public interest as the political exchanges between the former mayor and the current administration continue.

World.title: Liberia: STAND Slams Boakai-Koung Over Poverty, CBL Pay Disparities; Demands Probe Into President’s Son
World.content:
MONROVIA-The Solidarity & Trust for a New Day (STAND) has accused the Boakai-Koung administration of failing ordinary Liberians while allowing wide salary disparities within government, and reiterated call for an independent investigation into drug trafficking allegations involving Joseph Boakai Jr.

By Jaheim T. Tumu – [email protected]

STAND said the government’s billion-dollar budget has not translated into meaningful relief for citizens struggling with poverty, poor public services and economic hardship.



It also questioned why senior Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) officials reportedly receive substantial salaries and allowances while some lower-paid public workers face salary reductions.

In a statement issued, STAND Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu Jr. said the government’s approach to public spending and accountability reflects what the group described as a growing gap between the privileges enjoyed by senior officials and the difficulties facing ordinary citizens.

“Despite boasting of a billion-dollar budget, the government has failed to translate increased public spending into meaningful relief for ordinary Liberians,” STAND said.

STAND argued that nearly three years into the Boakai-Koung administration, many Liberians continue to struggle to meet their basic needs, while public schools and healthcare services remain inadequate.

STAND Questions CBL Pay Packages

STAND cited reported compensation packages at the Central Bank of Liberia as an example of what it considers unequal treatment within the public sector.

According to the group, some senior CBL officials reportedly receive monthly salaries of US$14,000, along with US$15,000 in housing allowances.

The statement also cited a reported compensation package of approximately US$29,000 per month disclosed by a nominee for CBL deputy governor, Euphemia G.T. Swen-Monmia

STAND contrasted those figures with the case of a Governance Commission employee who, it said, faces demotion and a salary reduction from approximately US$1,281.91 to US$900 per month.

The group argued that the contrast raises questions about the government’s commitment to shared sacrifice at a time when many workers are struggling financially.

“This situation is neither a shared sacrifice nor a genuine Rescue Mission; it’s a two-tier system that punishes the underprivileged while shielding privilege,” STAND stated.

The group called on the Civil Service Agency, Governance Commission, Central Bank and Legislature to explain the reported disparities and subject public-sector salaries, allowances and benefits to an independent review.

It also demanded that any decisions found to be unlawful or improperly authorized be corrected and those responsible held accountable.

The compensation figures and employment decision cited by STAND were not independently verified in its statement.

Demands Drug Investigation Into President’s Son

Beyond economic concerns, STAND reiterated its call for an independent investigation into drug trafficking allegations involving Boakai Jr. arguing that political and family connections should not determine how the law is applied.

The group questioned what it described as the government’s failure to demonstrate the same urgency in addressing allegations against the President’s son as it has shown in pursuing drug-related charges against former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor.

“If one witness’s testimony provides probable cause to prosecute Mrs. Taylor, why should Jojo Boakai be above arrest and prosecution when a drug cartel has publicly accused him?” STAND asked.

Morlu, STAND Chairman asserted that substantial evidence exists against Jojo Boakai and challenged the government to demonstrate that justice is being applied equally.

STAND also called on President Boakai to justify Taylor’s continued detention and show that family connections do not exempt anyone from the law.

The allegations against Jojo Boakai have not been independently established by the statement. STAND’s claims do not, by themselves, establish criminal wrongdoing, and any investigation or prosecution must be based on evidence and due process.

STAND Calls SPARK Foundation a ‘Humanitarian Fraud’

STAND also criticized the launch of Jojo Boakai’s SPARK Foundation, describing it as a “Humanitarian Fraud” and arguing that philanthropy should not replace accountability.

“Philanthropy cannot replace accountability, and a foundation cannot serve as a shield against scrutiny,” the group said.

The organization alleged that the foundation could be used to create a humanitarian image for the President’s son while questions surrounding the reported US$317 million drug case remain unresolved.

It further raised questions about whether the foundation could be financed with drug proceeds or taxpayers’ funds. However, the statement provided no independently verified evidence establishing that either source was used.

STAND called for the allegations to be investigated independently, insisting that no charitable initiative should place anyone beyond legitimate scrutiny.

The group said it condemns crime and does not seek to protect anyone accused of wrongdoing, but wants the law applied equally to all Liberians.

Group Warns of Civil Disobedience

STAND warned that the government’s response to allegations of corruption, selective justice and economic exclusion could determine its next course of action.

The group said the administration’s continued failure to address allegations involving powerful officials and the President’s son could become grounds for targeted civil disobedience conducted within the confines of the law.

It announced plans to make a broader declaration in the coming days, promising to challenge what it described as the administration’s “Rich Family-First” approach to governance.

STAND also criticized the Legislature, accusing lawmakers of failing to exercise effective constitutional oversight and neglecting the economic struggles of ordinary Liberians.

The group said it intends to confront lawmakers over alleged corruption and political patronage, arguing that the Legislature must hold public officials accountable rather than allow alleged abuses of power to go unchecked.

STAND called on reform-minded groups to unite and pursue lawful means of demanding greater transparency, accountability and fairness in government.

The group warned that corruption, economic exclusion and declining public confidence could threaten Liberia’s stability and democracy.

World.title: Liberia: As Boakai Launches Clean Cities Campaign, Whein Town Residents Renew Demand for Landfill Closure Amid Health Warnings from Experts
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE, Montserrado County — After sunset, when mosquitoes descend on homes in Whein Town, residents say spending time outdoors becomes almost unbearable. During the day, swarms of flies hover around food and businesses, while foul-smelling water and the presence of rodents and snakes fuel fears about what living beside a massive garbage dump may be doing to their health.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

For families in this community outside Monrovia, the struggle is not simply about living near garbage. It is about the growing cost of securing clean water, protecting children from insects and trying to maintain a livelihood in an environment they say has become increasingly difficult to endure.



The source of much of their frustration is the Whein Town Landfill, a facility established as a temporary solution to Liberia’s urban waste problem but still receiving garbage years beyond its intended lifespan.

Residents say the continued dumping has left them feeling abandoned by authorities responsible for managing the waste generated by Monrovia and Paynesville.

“We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” said Amos Moore, a resident who accused the government of failing to honour its commitment to close the landfill after its original five-year lifespan expired.

“It is a shame that the government will unleash such suffering on a large group of its people.”

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, said residents have complained about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to their community.

For residents such as Moore, the central question is why a facility intended to provide a temporary answer to an urgent sanitation problem has become a seemingly permanent feature of their community, while promises of relief remain unfulfilled.

Their concerns have drawn renewed attention from public health and environmental experts, who warn that poorly managed landfills can expose nearby populations to serious risks, particularly when waste exceeds a facility’s intended capacity.

The Monrovia City Corporation, which manages the facility, acknowledges that the landfill has outlived its usefulness. However, it says it is taking what it describes as “immediate, aggressive action” to address the situation.

For residents, those interventions have yet to resolve their most pressing concern: ending the dumping.

The Cost of Living Beside the Dump

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, said residents have complained about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to their community.

Residents say the continued dumping has left them feeling abandoned by authorities responsible for managing the waste generated by Monrovia and Paynesville. MCC truck being loaded with garbage for Whein Town Landfill.

Jones recalled an incident around 2012 or 2013 when authorities allegedly brought seized drugs to the area and burned them near the landfill. He said fumes spread into the community, prompting residents to protest and demand greater oversight of activities at the facility.

Following the incident, he said, a community monitoring team was established to observe activities at the landfill.

The team initially comprised eight residents who worked in shifts, including overnight, to monitor what was happening at the site.

But financial constraints eventually reduced the number of monitors to four, Jones said, adding that their stipends have not been paid consistently.

Two groups of community monitors have completed their assignments, while the latest group had worked for about two months awaiting payment, he said.

The monitoring arrangement, intended to give residents a measure of oversight, has not addressed their broader concerns about the continued operation of the facility.

“If you ask me what I want them to do, I would tell you to close the dumpsite,” Jones said.

He maintained that residents remain willing to engage the government but believe authorities have repeatedly failed to follow through on commitments made to the community.

The landfill was established in 2011 under the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation Project as a temporary, five-year emergency waste-disposal facility managed by the MCC. It was intended to improve the collection and disposal of solid waste in Monrovia and Paynesville.

Firefighter battling a firebreak at the When Town Landfill in February, 2026.

Although accounts of the facility’s development cite both 2011 and 2012, residents agree that its continued operation has far exceeded the original period they understood it would serve.

Fifteen years later, they say, the consequences have become part of everyday life.

When Clean Water Becomes an Added Expense

For Leon Miaway, one of the most persistent problems is the mosquito population.

He said residents struggle to remain outdoors after 5 or 6 p.m., when mosquitoes become particularly troublesome, forcing many families to rely on mosquito nets to protect themselves at night.

Flies create a different problem during the day, especially in the rainy season, when Miaway said they frequently come into contact with food.

For households already struggling with daily expenses, the concerns extend to water.

Miaway said changes to the area where garbage is deposited have raised fears that liquid leaking from waste may be reaching nearby water sources. He believes the absence of adequate containment measures at the newer dumping area has worsened the situation.

The extent of any contamination has not been independently established, but residents say the uncertainty has forced some households to spend additional money on water for drinking and cooking.

“Before you prepare any good food now, it means you have to spend more, even to buy water,” Miaway said.

For families with limited incomes, the added expense can mean making difficult choices between buying water they consider safer and meeting other household needs.

Miaway also said malaria is common in the community and expressed concern about children walking barefoot around areas where stagnant water collects.

He complained that residents had not seen regular visits by government agencies or humanitarian organizations to collect household data or distribute mosquito nets and other supplies.

“It has been a long while, like, over two, three years now,” he said.

The absence of consistent assistance, residents say, has reinforced their belief that they are being left to manage the consequences of the landfill largely on their own.

Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, former Director of the National Public Institute of Liberia, warned that the landfill could also be contributing to greenhouse gas emissions as organic waste decomposes, adding to the broader environmental consequences of poorly managed waste. (Fire outbreak at the landfill in February, 2026).

The residents’ renewed complaints come as President Joseph Nyuma Boakai launches the Presidential Clean Cities Initiative, a nationwide sanitation programme intended to support urban cleanliness, improve environmental health and create employment opportunities for young Liberians.

For residents of Whein Town, however, the campaign presents a troubling contradiction: while the government is mobilizing young people to clean cities and communities, their own neighbourhood continues to receive mountains of garbage from Monrovia and Paynesville, despite longstanding concerns about the landfill’s capacity and environmental condition.

They fear that unless the government addresses the continued operation of the Whein Town landfill, the clean cities campaign will fail to achieve its intended purpose for communities bearing the greatest burden of urban waste disposal.

Without addressing the conditions in Whein Town, residents fear the Clean Cities Initiative could improve the appearance of urban centres while leaving an already burdened community to continue paying the environmental price

“As long as the landfill is not closed, this cannot be a clean cities’ campaign. This is more pollution, more suffering and more sickness,” said Elijah Johnson, a student of the University of Liberia. We have complained for years that this is a death trap, yet still no solution.

‘They Are Still Dumping Every Day’

Princess Dennis, another resident, said families living near the landfill are increasingly worried about illnesses they associate with the surrounding conditions.

She cited malaria and other infections as concerns, particularly for children, and said previous mosquito-net distributions did not reach everyone.

Dennis alleged that some distributions stopped around a telecommunications junction, leaving residents in other parts of the community without nets.

But she stressed that receiving mosquito nets or other relief items would not resolve what residents consider the underlying problem.

“I’m upset about the dumpsite here,” she said, appealing to the authorities to stop the continued dumping of waste.

Dennis said garbage trucks continue to bring waste to the facility every day despite the community’s complaints.

She also operates a business along the road near the landfill, where she said flies affect customers and force her to cover her goods.

For a small business owner, the problem is both a public health concern and an economic burden: maintaining basic hygiene becomes more difficult when flies are constantly present.

Water insecurity compounds the difficulty.

Dennis said some residents sometimes consume water they consider unsafe because they cannot afford alternatives.

“When we don’t get money, we can drink the water,” she said.

Her account illustrates the difficult choices confronting households that cannot consistently pay for alternative water supplies but fear the possible consequences of using nearby sources.

Residents have raised concerns about illnesses ranging from malaria and diarrhoeal diseases to more serious conditions they believe may be associated with environmental pollution. However, establishing whether the landfill is responsible for particular illnesses requires clinical evidence and independent environmental testing.

For residents, the lack of clear information about water quality and potential exposure remains a source of anxiety.

Residents Fear Another Confrontation

Despite their frustration, some residents are reluctant to organize direct action against the landfill.

Miaway recalled previous protests during which residents blocked roads and some participants were arrested. He said the community does not want a repeat of those incidents and prefers its leadership to negotiate with authorities on its behalf.

The hesitation reflects a difficult position: residents want the dumping to stop but fear that confrontations could lead to arrests without delivering a lasting solution.

They have instead continued to press their case through community meetings, local leaders and calls for government intervention.

Their demand is not limited to mosquito control, water provision or occasional medical outreach. They want the landfill closed or relocated.

That demand has also been reflected in previous petitions to the Legislature, in which residents sought intervention over the facility’s continued operation and the lack of basic services in the community.

For them, years of complaints and temporary interventions have not delivered the change they seek.

Experts Warn of Environmental and Public Health Risks

Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, a former Director General of the National Public Health Institute of Liberia and an infectious disease expert, said landfills can become serious environmental and public health hazards when they are overfilled and inadequately managed.

Dr. Nyan said the Whein Town facility has affected wildlife, may have contributed to rodent infestation and has reduced available living space in the surrounding area, contributing to community congestion.

He warned that congestion can facilitate the spread of infectious diseases, particularly when sanitation and other basic services are inadequate.

Dr. Nyan also cited findings from empirical studies conducted around 2022–2023 by public health students at the African Methodist Episcopal University. He said the studies indicated contamination of soil, streams, wells and other groundwater sources around the area.

Those findings, he said, raise concerns about possible exposure to gastrointestinal infections and other illnesses.

FrontPage Africa has not independently reviewed the studies’ methodology or results. Further investigation would be needed to establish the extent of any contamination and determine its sources.

Dr. Nyan said residents have also reported respiratory symptoms that warrant clinical documentation and investigation to determine whether exposure to polluted air is contributing to their health problems.

He warned that the landfill could also be contributing to greenhouse gas emissions as organic waste decomposes, adding to the broader environmental consequences of poorly managed waste.

His most serious concern is the possibility of a landslide or collapse at the site, which he said could result in loss of life and property.

Dr. Nyan called on the government to enforce the landfill’s closure and invest in recycling, reuse and waste-reduction programmes.

He also urged Liberia to consider stronger restrictions on plastic use as part of a broader effort to reduce the volume of waste reaching disposal sites.

For Dr. Nyan, continued dumping at a facility believed to have reached its capacity raises questions about how long the government can delay a more sustainable solution without exposing communities to additional risks.

‘The Environmental Burden Is Borne by Nearby Communities’

Mohammed W. Bah, a Liberian researcher and PhD student in Urban and Environmental Planning and Policy at the University of California, Irvine, said a landfill that exceeds its intended capacity can create serious environmental and public health problems when waste is no longer properly contained.

Bah, whose research focuses on climate adaptation, coastal vulnerability, climate-related displacement and relocation, said exposed garbage can attract flies, rodents and other disease vectors. Mohammed W. Bah, a Liberian researcher and PhD student in Urban and Environmental Planning and Policy at the University of California, Irvine, said a landfill that exceeds its intended capacity can create serious environmental and public health problems when waste is no longer properly contained.

Poorly controlled waste and leachate—the liquid that drains from decomposing garbage—can contaminate soil and surface or groundwater, while open burning and landfill fires can worsen air quality.

“These risks are particularly concerning when residential communities are located close to the site, as in Whein Town,” he said.

Bah also described the situation as an environmental justice issue, noting that communities located near waste facilities often bear disproportionate environmental and health burdens associated with services used by larger populations.

He said residents should have access to information about the landfill’s condition, environmental monitoring results, closure plans and measures being taken to protect them.

As an immediate response, Bah called for uncontrolled dumping to stop, exposed waste to be properly contained and covered, and disease vectors such as mosquitoes, flies and rodents to be controlled.

He also recommended assessments of water and soil contamination, improved drainage and leachate management, and access to safe drinking water for surrounding communities.

Given reports that the facility has exceeded its intended capacity and design life, Bah said an independent assessment should determine whether it can continue operating safely.

“If the site has exceeded its designed lifespan and can no longer be safely operated, the solution cannot merely be to continue adding waste indefinitely,” he said.

He called for a planned transition to an alternative disposal facility, accompanied by the proper closure and environmental remediation of Whein Town.

But Bah cautioned that moving the landfill would not, on its own, resolve Liberia’s wider waste-management problems.

The government, he said, must improve garbage collection, promote waste separation and recycling, encourage reuse and strengthen enforcement against illegal dumping.

“Whein Town demonstrates why environmental planning has to be proactive rather than reactive,” Bah said.

“Once a temporary solution becomes permanent without necessary infrastructure, monitoring and long-term planning, the environmental burden is often borne by nearby communities.”

MCC Acknowledges Landfill Has ‘Outlived Its Usefulness’

The Monrovia City Corporation says it recognizes the challenges at Whein Town and is pursuing measures to address them.

In a statement to FrontPage Africa, the MCC said it was taking “immediate, aggressive action” to tackle technical challenges at the facility, acknowledging that the landfill “has outlived its usefulness” and that the rainy season has compounded the situation.

“The MCC considers the health concerns of the residents as a top priority; as such, we are constantly fumigating the facility and providing routine health care interventions to the residents,” the corporation said.

The MCC also said mosquito nets had been distributed in the community and that it conducted a free medical outreach between March and April 2026. Whein Town Landfill, a facility established as a temporary solution to Liberia’s urban waste problem but still receiving garbage years beyond its intended lifespan.

Addressing allegations that garbage was being dumped directly on the ground, the corporation said it remained committed to responsible waste disposal and “would do nothing to endanger the health of the people of Whein Town.”

The corporation further disclosed that it was at an advanced stage of concluding a public-private partnership framework with a private-sector company for the joint management of the sanitary landfill.

However, the statement did not specify when the proposed partnership would be finalized, what immediate changes it would bring to waste disposal practices, or whether the arrangement would lead to the landfill’s closure.

The MCC’s acknowledgment that the site has outlived its usefulness is significant, but residents remain concerned about the continued arrival of garbage and the absence of a publicly established closure timetable.

Its claims of fumigation, medical outreach and mosquito-net distribution also contrast with residents’ accounts of inconsistent assistance and the persistence of mosquitoes, flies and concerns about water quality.

The different accounts underscore the need for transparent information about the frequency and coverage of the corporation’s interventions, alongside independent monitoring of environmental conditions.

Beyond Fumigation: A Lasting Solution

The MCC’s proposed partnership could offer a route toward improved management, but experts say the long-term solution must address the landfill’s capacity, environmental condition and eventual closure if it can no longer be operated safely.

A credible response would also require reliable access to safe drinking water, independent testing of nearby wells and other water sources, and public disclosure of the results.

For residents, such steps would provide more than reassurance. They would help establish whether the water they use is safe, clarify the health risks they face and identify which interventions are urgently needed.

The government must also explain the status of alternative waste-disposal arrangements and how it intends to prevent an indefinite continuation of the current situation.

Liberia’s growing urban population requires an effective waste-management system. But residents of Whein Town argue that the need to dispose of garbage from Monrovia and Paynesville cannot justify leaving one community to shoulder the risks without adequate safeguards.

Their experience highlights a broader challenge: waste infrastructure cannot be considered successful if the environmental costs are transferred to the people living closest to it.

For Jones, Miaway, Dennis and Moore, the immediate issue remains personal. It is about whether families can eat without flies hovering over their food, obtain water without worrying about contamination and allow children to move around their neighbourhood without fearing the conditions surrounding them.

The MCC says it is taking action. Experts say the risks warrant urgent assessment and intervention. Residents, however, say they have heard promises before.

“We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” Moore said.

For Whein Town, the test of the government’s response will not be another promise or a temporary distribution of supplies. It will be whether the dumping ends, the environmental risks are properly assessed and the community finally receives the protection and basic services its residents say they have been denied for years.
