World.title: Nashville chef's date night with football scout turns deadly
World.content:
On the night of Feb. 25, 2023, outside Vanderbilt Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, Blaise Taylor was answering police questions about how a date turned into a medical emergency.

BLAISE TAYLOR (police bodycam): We were together having a date night.

Authorities wanted to know what happened to 24-year-old Jade Benning, who had been rushed to the hospital, arriving unresponsive.

BLAISE TAYLOR (police bodycam): She started not to feel well.

A selfie taken the night of Jade Benning and Blaise Taylor's date. Evidence

Jade Benning started that night with the hope of strengthening her relationship with Blaise Taylor, then a 26-year-old assistant football scout for the Tennessee Titans. Jade, a professional chef, was planning a special night at her apartment — cooking dinner, to be followed by painting pictures. But as the evening progressed, just minutes after taking selfies, Jade fell ill. Blaise said she was spitting up and shaking — unsure what to do, he first called his father.

Evi Taylor, Blaise's mother, said their children would often contact their father, a college football coach, with medical questions.

Evi Taylor: Being in sports and things, a lot of times, you know, they would go to their dad. … He would be on the field. Like if somebody got hurt, he would be the first one there.

Blaise Taylor calls 911

Blaise's call with his dad lasted 30 seconds. He told his son to immediately call 911, which Blaise did.

BLAISE TAYLOR (911 call): I don't know what's happening … She's got spit coming out of her mouth and she's shaking.

EMT responders found Jade lying face down on her bed, with no pulse. She was taken by ambulance to a hospital. By then, Jade's best friend, Nijaiha Jackson, had returned to Jade's apartment, only to learn Jade was unresponsive.

Nijaiha Jackson: She has to be OK. I just saw her an hour ago. (cries)

Just an hour earlier, Jade was her usual lively self. She was known, says her family and friends, for being spirited — traits on display in cheerleading. She was captain of the squad at her high school in Little Rock, Arkansas, and cheered in competitions.

Dennis Browning: Jade was very much a bridge builder.

Dennis Browning, Jade's dad, says she has always been about bringing people together — even her own parents — after her mom, Bridget Benning Burks, and her dad divorced.

Dennis Browning: She was always putting out the fire.

Jade Benning Bridget Benning Burks

She moved from Little Rock to Nashville, to pursue her career, and her dream of owning a restaurant.

Dennis Browning: She was close to doing it.

Natalie Morales: When did you start to hear the name Blaise Taylor?

Bridget Benning Burks: It wasn't long after she moved there, she told that she had met this person … And my husband's big into sports so he knew exactly who he was.

Blaise Taylor was well known to people in Arkansas who followed college football. A former standout defensive back and top student, who had earned a scholarship to Arkansas State University.

Evi Taylor: You know, when he got to college … he got his bachelor's and his master's in business in three-and-a-half years while playing football and starting his own nonprofit.

Blaise Taylor Taylor Family

Blaise was all about helping people, not hurting them, says his family. He and his sister, Starr, while students at Arkansas State, started a foundation, providing educational opportunities for children.

Starr Taylor: He's always been really passionate about community service and giving back

After college, Blaise went on to an assistant coaching job at Duke. Blaise then moved to Nashville for that scouting job with the Tennessee Titans, where he was working when he met Jade.

Evi Taylor: He mentioned her name once … maybe going on a date or something. … And he just said that she was a chef. And that's all I knew about her.

Jade and Blaise's relationship had been a casual one, with each seeing other people. Then, in November 2022, about three months into dating, Jade called her mom with surprising news.

Bridget Benning Burks: She said, hold on, I got to send you a picture to look at. And so, she texted a picture and it was a pregnancy test — positive.

Dennis Browning: And she goes, "you're going to be a grandpa." … And that's when I asked her, I said, well, "who's the father?"

She told her parents it was Blaise. Jade learned she was having a girl and chose the name Ivy for the baby. By the time of that date night, Jade was nearly six months pregnant. Those paintings Jade planned for that night were meant for Ivy's room. Jade's creation included the words, love, and hope. But hope turned to horror when Nijaiha received that call from Jade, where she says Jade was accusing Blaise of putting something into her drink.

Nijaiha Jackson: It just sounded like something I never heard before. She just sounded scared.

The call lasted a little more than six minutes. Nijaiha says Jade's voice faded at the end and then, the call was disconnected. As Nijaiha raced to Jade's apartment to figure out what was going on, she called Bridget.

Nijaiha Jackson: To have this responsibility to tell my best friend's mom that something is wrong … having to explain to her mom, police, the doctors, all these things that I, only I heard, and needing them to believe me because I knew that my friend was, needed help.

Nijaiha and Blaise separately followed the ambulance to the hospital. Once there, Nijaiha repeated what she heard on that call from Jade to anyone who would listen, including law enforcement and medical staff. Meanwhile, Bridget traveled all night to Nashville to be her daughter. Bridget says she kept calling Jade's phone.

Bridget Benning Burks: Finally, after probably the third time I'm calling, he answered. And I was like … "What have you done to my child?"

Searching for answers

Bridget knew her daughter Jade Benning was in critical condition, but when she arrived at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, she realized just how dire the situation had become.

Bridget Benning Burks: They told me that, um, she had gone approximately 45 minutes without oxygen. I knew.

Jade was brain dead. She was hooked up to life support, put in ICU, and any hope of even communicating with her daughter to learn what happened was gone.

Natalie Morales: And what about the baby? What were the doctors saying?

Bridget Benning Burks: Well, the baby at this time was 24 weeks … and if Jade went an extended time without oxygen, the baby went the same. … and a baby at 24 weeks wouldn't have a chance.

Amid their sorrow, Jade's family and friends were searching for answers as to how a healthy 24 year-old could now be in this state. Still, there was that phone call Jade made, where Nijaiha Jackson said she heard Jade accuse Blaise of putting something in her drink.

Natalie Morales: Is Blaise at the hospital too with you, are you seeing him?

Bridget Benning Burks: No. Actually, when they moved her to ICU, he was told that he needed to leave. And at that time, they placed her under an alias name for her protection. … The only people that had access to her were her parents.

Police had spoken to Blaise, who cooperated several times earlier that night at the hospital. Aside from what Nijaiha said she heard on that call, which was not recorded, there was no proof that Blaise harmed Jade. And, it was Blaise, remember, who had contacted 911. Blaise's parents were concerned and traveled from Texas to Nashville to be with him.

Evi Taylor: And of course, you know, worried about her and, you know, she's pregnant and, is she going to be OK? Is the baby gonna be OK?

In the days that followed, Blaise and his family say they were cut off from receiving updates about Jade's condition. Jade's family says they also were not receiving information they wanted from police about next steps into the investigation.

Dennis Browning: As a parent, you know, you want answers like right now — you know, what happened … what are you gonna do?

They thought authorities weren't moving fast enough. It wasn't just the phone call their daughter had made. There were also conversations months earlier, where Jade had told them Blaise was unhappy at the prospect of becoming a dad.

Dennis Browning: She told me that he didn't want to have anything to do with the baby.

Nijaiha and others say that Blaise, at one point, even suggested to Jade she terminate the pregnancy.

Nijaiha Jackson: Kinda giving her an ultimatum on either get an abortion or you're risking this being over between you and I.

Jade made it clear to Blaise she wanted the baby and was fine to do it without him. For a while, their relationship cooled off. Jade's family, though, was more than ready to help out.

Lyn Burks, Jade's stepdad, had been looking forward to having a grandchild, no matter the circumstance.

Lyn Burks: We was very excited. If he didn't want anything to do with it, we was OK with that. … we wasn't gonna ask for one thing from him.

Her family says Jade told them to keep the pregnancy quiet, per Blaise's instructions. But Evi Taylor says Blaise did tell people, including his family, in December 2022.

Evi Taylor: He just told us that, um, that she was pregnant. … So I think it was a difficult conversation because obviously they had a casual relationship.

Evi said they discussed a paternity test, to be performed after the baby was born, to confirm that Blaise was the father. Still, his family was supportive.

Starr Taylor: My dad immediately like grabbed all of our hands and we just prayed … for Jade, for Blaise, um, for the child.

Then, on New Year's Eve 2022, Blaise reached out to Jade. They started dating again. Now, with Jade on life support, her family and Nijaiha questioned Blaise's motives for reconnecting back then — wondering if he had been planning something nefarious. Despite expressing their concerns about Blaise to police, Jade's apartment had yet to be sealed off as a potential crime scene.

Nijaiha Jackson: I was just like, "I know what I heard, and something needs to be done. Like, we need to go to her apartment."

So, just one day after Jade was admitted to the hospital, Nijaiha and three friends decided to investigate on their own. They went to Jade's apartment and recorded video.

Nijaiha Jackson: I got some gloves from the hospital, and I told everybody to put them on. … and we went into the apartment, and we started recording upon entry.

Natalie Morales: Did you … worry at all that, "I could be hindering the police investigation. I might be contaminating the scene?"

Nijaiha Jackson: Honestly, at that time, no.

When the group entered Jade's bedroom, Nijaiha said she noticed something out of place.

Nijaiha Jackson: I see that the camera is in the corner. … and the camera was never there.

Nijaiha said she had seen the Blink security camera in the kitchen when she left the apartment earlier the night Jade became ill. She wondered if Blaise moved the camera, so it would not record him putting something in Jade's drink.

Nijaiha Jackson: So I moved the camera back to the kitchen. … I wanted it back where it was in case he came back for whatever reason.

While in the apartment, they noticed vomit on Jade's comforter. Thinking it might be important, they put it in a garbage bag to bring to Bridget. The next day, police did secure the scene and did their own search, collecting drinks and other items to be tested. Bridget also gave police the comforter. At the hospital, now two days after being admitted, results from Jade's lab work were coming back.

Dennis Browning: That's when the positive results came back in her blood and in her urine.

Natalie Morales: Positive results for?

Dennis Browning: Cocaine.

Cocaine — something doctors said might explain Jade's condition.

Natalie Morales: Was cocaine ever something that she had tried as far as —

Dennis Browning: No.

Bridget Benning Burks: Never.

Dennis Browning: Never.

Jade Benning Bridget Benning Burks

Jade's parents and friends knew she sometimes used marijuana and would drink. But, they say, once Jade learned she was pregnant, that stopped. For days, Jade had been kept on life support. Now, the family had a heartbreaking decision to make: when to remove the equipment.

Bridget Benning Burks: We talked, and with it being so close to her birthday, we were like, our wishes are to wait until her birthday.

On March 6, 2023, on what would have been Jade's 25th birthday, life support was stopped.

Dennis Browning: When she died, a part of me did too.

Five months later, Jade's autopsy was completed, finding she died from acute cocaine toxicity, with the cocaine having been ingested. While cocaine had been identified in her system in the hospital, the levels revealed in the autopsy were extraordinarily high, and according to the medical examiner, rarely seen — more than seven times what is typically found in fatal cocaine overdoses.

Dennis Browning: Which is like off the chart.

Natalie Morales: What did that tell you, Bridget, in that moment?

Bridget Benning Burks: That he did something. He didn't want the baby, so … he ultimately put something in her drink that took her life.

The manner of death, though, was listed as could not be determined, not as homicide. There was no evidence Blaise bought any drugs, and no drugs were found in the drinks police took from Jade's apartment. The one place cocaine was identified was in the vomit stain on that comforter. Still, Jade's family and friends were convinced Blaise poisoned Jade, putting cocaine into her drink.

Dennis Browning: I think … he had an image he wanted to uphold, you know, being this picture-perfect person … I guess he felt like, you know, having a child would somehow tarnish that.

After Jade died, Blaise was offered a college football analyst job in Utah and decided to move.

Evi Taylor: It's kind of like a coaching assistant … And that was like a step up in his career, you know, where he'd actually be on the field with the players.

To Jade's family, the man responsible for killing their daughter and her unborn baby was living his life, while they were waiting for him to be held responsible.

OFFICER (bodycam): How are you doing?

BLAISE TAYLOR: Good.

OFFICER: Can I ask your name?

BLAISE TAYLOR: Blaise.

OFFICER: Blaise?

Then, after a year of investigating Jade's death, on March 14, 2024, in a store parking lot in Utah —

Police bodycam video of Blaise Taylor before his arrest in Utah for the murder of Jade Benning and their unborn child. North Park Police Department

OFFICER (bodycam): What's your last name?

BLAISE TAYLOR: Taylor.

OFFICER: Put your hands behind your back for me, OK?

BLAISE TAYLOR: What's going on?

OFFICER: We have a warrant out of Tennessee for homicide.

Blaise Taylor was arrested, facing murder charges for killing Jade and her unborn child. He was brought back to Nashville, and the Taylor family worked to have him released, a month later, on a $2.5 million bond.

Natalie Morales: Did he have any reason … to try to hurt Jade or the unborn child because he did not want to become a father?

Evi Taylor: Absolutely not. I mean, we already knew, um that she was pregnant. … he has a job … So there's no reason.

And there's no evidence, says Blaise Taylor's defense attorney.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: There was absolutely nothing that tied Blaise Taylor to the drugs that caused the death of Ms. Benning and her unborn child. Nothing.

Best friend on Jade Benning's phone call

For two families, who define justice differently, the stakes were high as Blaise Taylor, in June of 2026, went on trial for the murders of Jade Benning and her unborn child.

Davidson County prosecutors Jan Norman, Roger Moore and Kendall Ponchillia needed to convince the jury that Blaise Taylor intentionally poisoned Jade Benning. And that he thought he could get away with it, but his plan was foiled by that call Jade made to Nijaiha.

Prosecutor Jan Norman: We all agree that his plan was to poison her with the liquid cocaine and then to leave her there.

Prosecutor Roger Moore: And that phone call totally disrupted … what could theoretically have been the perfect murder.

And so, Nijaiha Jackson was the key witness for the prosecution — describing to the jury what she says she heard on that call from Jade.

Nijaiha Jackson, a key prosecution witness, testifies about the phone call she received from Jade Benning. Pool

NIJAIHA JACKSON (in court): She immediately started saying, "What did you do? What did you put in my drink?" And then I heard her say, "Blaise, you're scaring me" and he was like "You're scaring me." And then she was asking him to empty his pockets and ... he was like, "I don't have anything."

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN: Can you repeat the last thing that you heard Jade say?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: She said that "you did this so something could happen to the baby."

Natalie Morales: What do you make of that call?

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: I can't make heads or tails of it.

Letitia Quinones-Hollins, one of Blaise Taylor's defense attorneys, has doubts about that call, since it was not recorded and only relies on what Nijaiha says she heard.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: Think about your very best friend and you hear that she is in danger. … Do you call 911 to get her help?

That was a question she asked Nijaiha during cross-examination.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): You could have reported to 911, correct?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: And if they would have asked me questions about her physical state I would have not been able to provide those answers.

Nijaiha also testified about that visit to Jade's apartment with friends to undertake their own investigation, before police secured the scene. She spoke about taking those precautions: wearing gloves, videotaping the process, and about moving the camera from the bedroom to its usual spot in the kitchen, and taking the comforter.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): Were you there when that comforter was bagged up?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Yes.

JAN NORMAN: Did anybody touch it with anything other than gloved hands to put it in that bag?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: No.

For the defense, the fact that the friends moved the camera and took the comforter raised questions about the integrity of the scene and evidence.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): Why were you so careful about not touching anything, but you weren't careful enough to preserve the scene? What was the difference?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: I'm not sure.

Nothing usable was recovered from the camera. Because Jade's death involved a drug, prosecutors knew this was something they would have to address.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): Prior to Jade learning that she was pregnant … did Ms. Benning, did she drink alcohol?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Yes.

JAN NORMAN: And did she use any other substances?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Um, she smoked marijuana.

But the state argued that when Jade learned she was pregnant, her drinking and marijuana use stopped — and that she was not known to use cocaine.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): Have you ever heard of her using cocaine or even talking about it?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: No.

The defense also questioned Nijaiha about this.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): Would you smoke marijuana together?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Yes.

LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS: Would you drink together?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Yes.

LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS: Did she ask you to do mushrooms with her?

NIJAIHA JACKSON: Um, maybe. I don't recall.

Best friends Nijaiha Jackson, left, and Jade Benning. Nijaiha Jackson

Nijaiha Jackson: It felt like they were tainting Jade's character and her image as well as mine. … have to defend myself and her, was, like, very jarring.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: Nobody, including myself, wants the victim blame … But at the same time … what we are talking about here is a drug overdose. Whether it was accidental, whether it was intentional, that's what we were there to determine.

Throughout the trial, the defense contrasted Jade's history with drugs to that of Blaise.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: The only person that had experience and connection with drugs between the two of them was Ms. Benning. And it wasn't just her past.

Evidence was presented that earlier the same day Jade collapsed, she had a text conversation with someone identified in her phone as Danny Weed Guy, a drug dealer, asking: "Heyy, my coworker wants to get a half from you."

Prosecutor Jan Norman: Every single text message to Danny Weed after she found out she was pregnant … there's a corresponding text message every single time that it was not for Jade's use.

There was no evidence that the request was for Jade, nor that they ever met that day —only the message, with Danny Weed responding, "bet I gotchu when I get back."

Natalie Morales: Was Danny Weed called as a witness at all just to clear any of this up or to testify?

Prosecutor Jan Norman: No, because Jade did not die from marijuana use. Jade died from acute cocaine toxicity.

But for the defense, any interaction between Jade and a drug dealer should have been investigated more thoroughly.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: He was not considered a witness for the prosecution and … he did not want to talk with us … But he was never spoken to by the police.

The state argued this was all about liquid cocaine as a murder weapon — nothing else. Dr. Erin Carney, a medical examiner for Davidson County, testified that the levels of cocaine found in Jade's system were rarely seen.

DR. ERIN CARNEY (in court): Based on the high level of cocaine … I actually signed her death certificate to say ingested cocaine.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN: And what was the manner of death?

DR. ERIN CARNEY: It could not be determined ... It was much more suspicious that someone gave it to her without her knowledge, but it didn't have enough to get to that, you know, homicide determination.

To try to help the jury get to that homicide determination, the prosecution was going to call a witness from Blaise Taylor's past.

Jan Norman: We were going to ask her to do something that in our opinion was a very big deal … to testify about things about herself that were so incredibly personal.

Former girlfriend of Blaise Taylor shares her story in court

Apple Dennie: When I first met Blaise Taylor … he seemed very smart. … And he just was really charming.

Apple Dennie and Blaise Taylor Apple Dennie

Apple Dennie met Blaise Taylor at Arkansas State in 2016, when she was a freshman and he was an upperclassman. They dated on and off for a few years. Apple says she eventually saw a different side of Blaise.

Apple Dennie: Calculated … and controlling, and willing to do whatever it takes to maintain an image.

That Blaise Taylor was the one Apple Dennie would testify about as a crucial prosecution witness. She told the jury that Jade Benning was not the first woman Blaise got pregnant. She said that while she was dating Blaise in 2017, he admitted to reconnecting with a former girlfriend, when he thought he and Apple were on a break. And there was more.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): What was it that he came to tell you about?

APPLE DENNIE: That, uh, he got her pregnant.

JAN NORMAN: And what was his demeanor like when he came to you to tell you about this?

APPLE DENNIE: Very erratic. He was upset. Um, didn't want to have a baby with her.

Blaise, says Apple, was seeking her help. Apple had been in the same situation with him a few months earlier when she became pregnant with Blaise's baby.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): What were your feelings when you learned that you were pregnant?

APPLE DENNIE: I was really scared and confused. I knew I wasn't ready to have a kid.

JAN NORMAN: What did you ultimately end up doing?

APPLE DENNIE: I had an abortion.

Apple says that decision was solely her own, and that Blaise was supportive, going with her to appointments. But this other woman told Blaise she might want the baby.

Natalie Morales: What did Blaise ask you to do when he came forward and told you that he had gotten another woman pregnant?

Apple Dennie: He was … asking if I could get the abortion pills and give them to him so he could give them to her without her knowing.

Apple testified about that conversation.

Apple Dennie testifies for the prosecution about her former relationship with Blaise Taylor.

APPLE DENNIE (in court): So he was looking stuff up to figure out how she like if there was something he could do to make her have an abortion, um, and asked me if I could get the abortion pills, and he could make her take them or put it in her drink.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN: Did you do that?

APPLE DENNIE: Did I get the pill? No.

No evidence was presented that Blaise got a pill. Ultimately, the other woman terminated her pregnancy. Apple and Blaise stayed together on and off, until 2019, when the relationship ended. She says she hadn't given Blaise much thought until years later, when she heard about what happened to Jade Benning. Apple and Jade's mom, Bridget, connected. Apple was then put in touch with authorities.

Natalie Morales: So when you hear the circumstances surrounding Jade Benning's death … what do you think happened to Jade?

Apple Dennie: I think that he carried out a plan that he had thought about years ago.

Defense attorney Jim Sanders: Her testimony to me came across as a woman spurned.

Jim Sanders, one of Blaise Taylor's defense lawyers, questions Apple's motivation to testify. The defense says Apple's own words about her past with Blaise paint a different story.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: There were actual journals and things of that nature where she talked about what an amazing individual, he was … what a positive impact he made on her life.

Apple doesn't deny she once viewed Blaise fondly but says she had no motive to reveal details of her personal life on the stand.

Apple Dennie: I'm telling everyone that I had abortion … And that was probably one of the worst parts about it is having to deal with people thinking these things about me and having to revisit all of that.

The defense contends Apple's testimony should never have been allowed by the court.

Defense attorney Jim Sanders: That testimony from Apple Dennie was more than highly prejudicial. … and it was clearly inadmissible. … you cannot use character evidence or evidence of a bad act to prove the case.

Natalie Morales: Would it show, though … a certain pattern of behavior?

Defense attorney Jim Sanders: Well … where's the pattern here? …

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: We're talking about, according to Ms. Dennie, what he said, not what he did, what he said.

Apple Dennie was one of the last witnesses for the state. The defense's focus turned to the reliability of Jade's lab results, and questions about what actually caused her death.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): Are you familiar with cocaethylene or the metabolite cocaethylene?

MELISSA GIGUERE Ph.D.: Yes.

The defense presented medical experts who testified about a substance called cocaethylene, formed when cocaine and alcohol are combined. It was found in Jade's lab results.

JANCI CHUNN LINDSAY Ph.D. (in court) So, if cocaethylene is there, that indicates that a person has ingested ethanol and cocaine at the same time.

Ethanol is alcohol. The defense argued it only would have been present if Jade was drinking alcohol when she ingested cocaine, and perhaps that combination — not cocaine alone — killed her.

Prosecutor Kendall Ponchillia: The defense made a real big deal … about that Jade could have been using alcohol, that Jade mixed these two together. And there was absolutely no proof … that Jade had a sip of alcohol once she found out she was pregnant.

The state contends that the level of cocaethylene was so small, it was below a reportable unit. And it offered another explanation for its presence —- one involving Blaise.

Prosecutor Kendall Ponchillia: He could have very easily have dissolved the cocaine in a small amount of alcohol.

Fentanyl was found on the comforter in Jade Bennings' bedroom. Evidence

But there was another drug, known to be deadly, found on her comforter: fentanyl. The defense suggested that Jade had to be using fentanyl, or taken something laced with fentanyl, for it to be there.

Defense attorney Letitia Quinones-Hollins: How is that not considered when we're talking about the causation of death?

Natalie Morales: How could that even be explained … this finding of fentanyl on a comforter if she never used fentanyl?

Prosecutor Jan Norman: Because that comforter got put in a bag, it got put in the back of someone's car, then it gets given to the police … everyone makes every precaution about not contaminating evidence, but things happen. We also have the medics that were in there. … It's a trace amount which is consistent with it just touching something that it shouldn't have.

But according to the defense, there is simply not enough evidence to prove what killed Jade. And, it says, whatever killed her did not involve Blaise Taylor.

Defense attorney Jim Sanders: He called 911. He followed the ambulance to the hospital. … talked to the police whenever they ask him a question … Not the act of a guilty guy.

To the prosecution, those are the acts of someone guilty trying to look innocent.

Prosecutor Jan Norman: Jade Benning absolutely named Blaise Taylor as the person who put something in her drink … And her words are direct evidence that he did it.

And that would be up to the jury to decide.

A jury decides

After seven days of testimony in Blaise Taylor's murder trial, attorneys presented their closing arguments. For the state, it ended much the way it began — referencing that call Jade Benning made to her friend Nijaiha Jackson.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): Jade Benning called the one person who knew where she was, knew who she was with, would know that she was calling scared. ... She made sure that you heard her last words. … "I know you put something in my drink."

The prosecution dismissed the defense theories that other drugs were involved, saying this was solely about cocaine.

PROSECUTOR JAN NORMAN (in court): Blaise Taylor intentionally put that cocaine in Jade's drink to kill the baby.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS: We dealt with an official finding of undetermined, the manner of death in this case.

The defense argued that the state did not have enough evidence to even classify Jade's death a homicide, let alone point to Blaise as her killer. And as for Jade's final phone call, jurors were reminded those details relied solely on Nijaiha's recollection.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): Remember, nobody else heard exactly what was going on on that phone call, nobody but Nijaiha.

In terms of a motive, the defense insisted there was none.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY LETITIA QUINONES-HOLLINS (in court): I guarantee you he is not the first human being that in his 20s, had a unexpected pregnancy pop up and he's not happy … And they want you to believe … that would give him motive to kill her and the baby.

Evi Taylor: I thought that we were gonna be OK. … But it's always scary, when your life is in the hands of 12 people that don't know you.

As the case went to the jury, each family held onto hope.

Dennis Browning: We've prepared ourselves to be there for a while … You're sitting on pins and needles.

The wait would not be long. After about two hours of deliberating, there was a verdict.

Blaise Taylor listens as the guilty verdict is read aloud in court. Pool

JURY FOREPERSON: We the jury find the defendant Blaise Allen Taylor for Count 1, guilty for second-degree murder …

Blaise Taylor was found guilty of four counts: second-degree murder of Jade Benning, first-degree premeditated murder of an unborn child, and two counts of felony murder. He received two life sentences, to be served consecutively.

Natalie Morales: Hearing that verdict, take me back to that moment for you.

Bridget Benning Burks: Relief. Like a weight lifted that this would never be done to anybody else by him.

Evi Taylor: I heard guilty and then I don't I think I was just like everything just kind of like blacked out after that. … And that feeling as a parent … that you thought there's no hope. … It's the worst feeling when you can't — when you can't help your son.

Defense attorney Jim Sanders: They didn't prove he was guilty. An innocent man got convicted.

Blaise Taylor's defense team and family are working on an appeal.

Starr Taylor: I want to make sure … that we, as well as the attorneys, continue to fight for his innocence because he didn't do this.

Jade Benning Bridget Benning Burks

For Jade's family, the verdict did bring justice, but the void left in their lives by Jade's death and that of Ivy, her unborn child, will never be filled. They try to celebrate Jade in big and small ways. Their arms have tattoos of butterflies, which Jade loved.

And at what would have been Jade's 10-year high school reunion, Jade's classmates, including her best friend Nijaiha, remembered the special life lost.

Bridget Benning Burks (at the class reunion): I feel the love — I definitely feel the love that they had for her.

Nijaiha Jackson (at the class reunion): There's like a hole … knowing that she isn't here.

Jade's family brought balloons for the class to release as a way to honor their daughter.

Dennis Browning: She touched so many people. … you know I think about her daily.

Bridget Benning Burks: She's always with me. … I always wonder … just what life would have been like … to become a grandma … The rest of life will be what would have been.

Produced by Ruth Chenetz. Jenna Jackson and Ryan Smith are the development producers. Alicia Tejada is the coordinating producer. Jane Shevlin is the associate producer. Marlon Disla, Richard Barber and Diana DeCilio are the editors. Patti Aronofsky is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.

World.title: Rioters loot stores in Germany amid cost of living protests
World.content:
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.

The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.

Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.

31 October 2026, Hesse, Frankfurt am Main: A protester throws a rock at a store window in Frankfurt, Germany on October 31, 2026. Boris Roessler/Getty

in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.

Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.

In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.

Riot police storming past a burning trashcan during riots that erupted after a GenZ demonstration was disbanded in Frankfurt, Germany on October 31, 2026. Stien Hohn / Hans Lucas /AFP via Getty Images

Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

World.title: This week on "Sunday Morning" (Nov. 1)
World.content:
The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET. "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. (Download it here.)

Hosted by Jane Pauley



POLITICS: Midterm elections preview: How might this year's vote change Washington?

Voters in this year's elections will choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives, a third of our Senators, and 36 races for governor. Correspondent David Pogue looks at what midterm election results typically represent, and why – with inflation a key topic on voters' minds, and a historically unpopular president – this year's midterms may upend expectations.

For more info:

See more:



ALMANAC: November 1

"Sunday Morning" looks back at historical events on this date.



COVER STORY: Is the truth really out there? Studying UAP sightings

It's been some 75 years since the term Unidentified Flying Object (or UFO) was coined to describe the mysterious airborne phenomena witnessed by pilots and the public. Now, Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs) are the focus of a new Scientific Advisory Council, led by Avi Loeb of Harvard, which is investigating the staggering number of first-person accounts, video and documents recently released by the government. Correspondent Luke Burbank looks at how scientists hope to study these sightings, to possibly answer the question: Are we alone?

For more info:

For more info:



POLITICS: The issue that could tip the scales in the Texas Senate race

All eyes are on the Senate race in Texas, the outcome of which may determine control of the Senate in Washington; and with more than half a billion dollars spent so far, the contest between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic State Representative James Talarico is the most expensive non-presidential race in U.S. history. "Sunday Morning" national correspondent Robert Costa talks with the candidates' supporters, and with local observers, about a race that has drawn interest from around the country, and how the rising cost of food, gas and housing could prove a tipping point for voters.

For more info:

See more:



BROADWAY: "The Lost Boys": How a vampire musical brings the undead to life

In movies and TV, vampires – the blood-sucking undead – have held a firm grip on the public's imagination. That popularity has now extended to Broadway. Correspondent Tracy Smith talks with actors L.J. Benet and Ali Louis Bourgzui, and director Michael Arden, of "The Lost Boys," which has avoided the stake in the heart that befell other Broadway vampire musicals. Smith also talks with film professor Rebekah McKendry about vampire lore in the media.

Watch L.J. Benet perform "Belong to Someone" from "The Lost Boys":

For more info:



PASSAGE: In memoriam

"Sunday Morning" remembers some of the notable figures who left us this week, including actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known as Captain Jean Luc Godard in the "Star Trek" franchise.



U.S.: The legacy of Milwaukee's Socialist mayors

Beginning in 1910, Milwaukee—a city long associated with beer and bratwurst—elected three Socialist mayors who made parks, public housing and sanitation priorities of city government. Correspondent Mo Rocca examines the origins and record of Milwaukee's "sewer socialism," and what the city's experience reveals about a political label that still provokes debate.

For more info:





GALLERY: The week in photos



MOVIES: "Jimmy": How movie star James Stewart became a war hero

During the Second World War, Academy Award-winning actor James Stewart answered his nation's call, serving as a pilot in the Army Air Corps. He flew 20 successful missions, and came home from WWII a different man. Stewart's fight to be able to fight despite his celebrity, and his emotional post-war return to the screen in "It's a Wonderful Life," are the subjects of the film "Jimmy." Lee Cowan talks with actors K.J. Apa (who plays Stewart), and Max Casella (who plays director Frank Capra), and Stewart's daughter, Kelly Stewart Hardcourt, about what the actor's service did to his soul.

READ AN EXCERPT: "Frank Capra: A Life" by Sam Wasson

Returning to movie screens after his service in World War II, Jimmy Stewart was nervous about appearing in Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life" – a film now acknowledged as one of his very best. Hollywood historian Sam Wasson writes of how Capra helped shepherd Stewart back into the public limelight in a role that was perfectly suited to Stewart's talents – and in the process created a timeless classic.

ARTS: A new Georgia O'Keeffe exhibit opens a window to unfamiliar works

An exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts is building a different picture of Georgia O'Keeffe, best known for her depictions of flowers and desert landscapes. "Georgia O'Keeffe: Architecture" explores the artist's paintings of buildings, from cityscapes to rural settings, and how O'Keeffe captured qualities of light, atmosphere and texture found in man-made structures. Jane Pauley reports.

One of the most famous addresses in the world, 10 Downing Street in London, is home not just to prime ministers, but also to a 19-year-old tabby cat named Larry. World.title: Golden State wins first WNBA title in franchise history
World.content:
The Golden State Valkyries brought to a conclusion a WNBA season that shattered viewership and attendance records with their first WNBA championship Saturday in a thrilling 68-63 victory over the Atlanta Dream in Game 7.

Golden State star Gabby Williams paced the Valkyries with 30 points, 4 blocks and 3 steals in 38 minutes.

The Golden State Valkyries huddle after defeating the Atlanta Dream in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals at Chase Center on Oct. 31, 2026, in San Francisco, California. Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images

"All we heard last year: We don't have no stars, we don't have no talent," Williams said after the game. "Yeah right. We got good people. We got winners."

Jordin Canada led the Atlanta Dream in scoring with 18 points, adding 5 assists and 4 rebounds. Atlanta superstar Angel Reese struggled throughout the game, finishing with 8 points on 3-of-7 shooting in 33 minutes.

The victory was the first for a team in a Game 7. The league transitioned from a five-game series to a seven-game series starting last year.

This is the first title for the Valkyries in just their second season as a team. And the Dream are now winless in four WNBA Finals appearances.

The 2026 season was an unqualified success for the WNBA. The league set a new attendance record with 3.8 million fans attending 330 regular season games, according to the WNBA. The league said average attendance was up 21% from last year's record high.

ESPN, ABC and CBS all delivered their most-watched seasons in history, according to the WNBA. The league had three times as many games averaging at least 1 million viewers as the previous record set last year.

Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries attempts a 3-pointer in front of Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream Game 7 of the WNBA Finals at Chase Center on Oct. 31, 2026, in San Francisco, California. Ezra Shaw / Getty Images

How they got here

The Valkyries, despite having just one All-Star, took a major leap in just their second year in the league.

The team is owned by Joe Lacob and Peter Guber, who also own the Golden State Warriors. The team quickly became relevant, going 23-21 in their first year in existence before losing in the first round of the playoffs.

The signing of Gabby Williams in the offseason propelled the team to even greater success. The Valkyries went 32-12 in the regular season and beat the Paige Bueckers-led Dallas Wings and A'ja Wilson-led Las Vegas Aces to advance to the title series.

The Dream didn't lose a game on its path to the title series, defeating the Kiki Iriafen-led Washington Mystics and the Breanna Stewart-led New York Liberty in sweeps.

The Valkyries won Game 1 at home, 68-64, behind 26 points from Williams. Atlanta dominated the next two games behind all-time great performances from star Angel Reese. The Dream star posted 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2 and 21 points and 12 rebounds in Game 3.

Reese struggled to score in Games 4 and 5, shooting just 4-of-20 with 15 points combined, as the Valkyries wrestled control of the series away from the Dream.

Game 6 controversy

Game 6 started at 12:30 p.m. since the Atlanta Hawks were scheduled to play at the State Farm Arena on Thursday night. The Dream plays its regular season games at Gateway Center Arena, but its capacity is just 3,500 compared to about 17,000 at State Farm Arena.

"This incredible run by our players has also made something else abundantly clear: the Atlanta Dream has earned the right to be taken seriously," the team's ownership, husband and wife Larry Gottesdiener and Robyn Gottesdiener, Suzanne Abair and Renee Montgomery, said in a statement.

"Two months ago, when the WNBA finalized playoff dates and times, we raised concerns that the W Finals schedule conflicted with NBA games at State Farm Arena," the statement continued. "As we moved through the playoffs, we reiterated those concerns. Our concerns did not receive the attention, nor the urgency that they deserved."

Despite the early start time, the Dream still sold out the arena.

In a statement, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said the league preferred to play the game at State Farm Arena.

"The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere at State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success, and we're excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line," said Engelbert. "We thank the NBA, Dream, Valkyries, Hawks, State Farm Arena and USA Network for the collaboration and flexibility that made this move possible. We look forward to delivering another unforgettable Finals experience in Atlanta."

World.title: Inside the U.K. movement to pardon women executed for witchcraft centuries ago
World.content:
Just outside of London sits Maidstone, a quiet country town in a peaceful corner of southern England.

But around 400 years ago, Maidstone was the scene of witch hunts in the literal sense of the phrase.

Records show that more than 20 women convicted of witchcraft were hanged in Maidstone. Witch hunts reached their peak in England in the 1600s.

In total across England and Scotland, around 5,000 women convicted of witchcraft were executed, some by hanging and some by burning.

"They were usually single women, spinsters, or widows, usually without a man to stick up for them," Claire Kehily, a member of the Maidstone Borough Council, told CBS News. "... They were easier to target."



Inside Maidstone's town hall, Kehily showed CBS News a prison cell, reconstructed from an earlier medieval building where accused witches were held before trial.

Now Kehily and her fellow councilors are lobbying the U.K. government and planning to petition King Charles III for an official pardon for all of Maidstone's convicted witches.

"It matters because it was a miscarriage of justice," Kehily said. "The crimes they were accused of they couldn't have been guilty of. And they had no way of being found innocent in many of the cases. This is 400 years ago. But there are still miscarriages of justice. There are still, to these days, people being scapegoated for things."

America's most famous witch trials were in the 1690s in Salem, Massachusetts. Their memory was revived by Arthur Miller's play "The Crucible," an allegory for the political witch hunts led by Sen. Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s.

All of the falsely accused witches in Salem have since been pardoned. But in the U.K., not a single convicted witch has been exonerated.

Samantha Harris, the collections manager at Maidstone Museum, showed CBS News the official record of a witch trial in the town in 1652.

"There had to always be someone to blame," Harris explained, saying that natural disasters or illnesses were often blamed on these women.

"Death of pigs, cattle," Harris said. "... We were scapegoating and blaming people that were often quite vulnerable."

Harris said that for her, getting the women pardoned is personal.

"Being single, being independent, these are things that would have been seen as threatening," Harris said. "I probably would've been targeted absolutely as a witch at the time … If we don't learn from the past, what's to say things won't be recurring again in the future? There's a lot to learn from history."

World.title: Residents evacuated from Russia-occupied city back in Ukraine
World.content:
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.

The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.

Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war. It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.

The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.

Residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky during a humanitarian mission react upon arriving at an undisclosed location in Ukraine on Oct. 31, 2026. Genya SAVILOV /AFP via Getty Images

The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.

Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.

Residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky during a humanitarian mission disembark from a bus upon arriving at an undisclosed location in Ukraine on Oct. 31, 2026. Genya SAVILOV /AFP via Getty Images

Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.

Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.

"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.

Residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky during a humanitarian mission disembark from a bus upon arriving at an undisclosed location in Ukraine on Oct. 31, 2026. Genya SAVILOV /AFP via Getty Images

Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.

He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.

"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.

She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.

Ukrainian serviceman Dmytro, center, hugs his family after they were evacuated from their Russian-occupied hometown as they cross the Belarus-Ukraine border in Chernihiv region, Ukraine, Saturday, on Oct. 31, 2026. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.

Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.

A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

World.title: Virginia and D.C. sue to block construction of Trump arch
World.content:
Virginia and D.C. sue to block construction of Trump arch

toggle caption i Jen Golbeck/AP

The commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit on Saturday to block construction on President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch.

The 45-page lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia called the project "flagrantly unlawful," attorneys general Jay Jones of Virginia and Brian Schwalb of the District of Columbia wrote.

The lawsuit is the latest legal attempt to stop construction of the 250-foot tall arch whose plans were unveiled by the Trump administration in Oct. 2025.

The attorneys general also allege that construction on the arch, which could begin as soon as next week, will "inflict irreparable harm" on the District and Virginia, including snarling traffic between both areas. The arch would be located between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. It would stand twice the height of the monument honoring America's 16th president.

Sponsor Message

"Both jurisdictions will need to take immediate and costly steps to assess, respond to, and mitigate these harmful effects," they wrote in the lawsuit. "These costs are severe and unrecoverable—particularly because Defendants have refused to take them into account or adequately consult with either jurisdiction during their hurried and preordained process to approve the Arch and start construction."

NPR reached out to both the White House and the Interior Department for comment on the lawsuit on Saturday but has not received a response.

Trump has previously defended plans to build the arch and said it would be a "military complex" to hold weapons and snipers. The most recent plans for the arch, which will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission, do not include military elements.

U.S. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkin ordered both sides to talk and to agree on a proposed briefing schedule on the motion for a temporary restraining order by Saturday evening.

World.title: Mixed economic forecast weighs heavy ahead of midterms
World.content:
Mixed economic forecast weighs heavy ahead of midterms

There was a mixed Halloween bag of economic news this week. GDP growth is up, but so are prices. For now at least, interest rates are staying the same. What does that mean for the midterm elections?

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

As we just heard, many midterm races are extremely tight. And for voters, the economy has consistently ranked as a top issue driving them to the polls. This week, just days away from Election Day, we got some key economic news. New GDP numbers show the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy clip, but inflation remains stubbornly high. The Federal Reserve met and decided not to raise interest rates, but higher borrowing costs could still be in store by the end of the year. So what does that mean for the midterms? NPR's Scott Horsley is with us to explain.

SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: Hi. Good to be with you.

PFEIFFER: So affordability, that word we hear over and over and over again. It's at the top of mind of so many voters. What is the new economic data tell us about that?

HORSLEY: Well, it tells us affordability is still a challenge. You know, the cost of living keeps going up, and people's paychecks are not keeping pace. This week, the Commerce Department clocked inflation in September at 3.6%. That's higher than the month before. And significantly, it's higher than it was when President Trump returned to the White House. That's a big reason nearly two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the president's economic stewardship. Voters punished Democrats for inflation back in 2024, and they may decide to punish Republicans this time around.

PFEIFFER: Yet we have the seeming contradiction, which is that the latest numbers show the economy is growing. So why isn't that registering or paying off for ordinary voters?

HORSLEY: Yeah. The economy did perk up a bit in late summer and early fall. GDP, which is the broadest measure of economic activity, grew at an annual rate of 3.4% in July, August and September. That's up from 2.2% the previous quarter. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said this past week, that's a good sign.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KEVIN WARSH: The economy is strong. The economy is pointing in the right direction.

HORSLEY: But a lot of that GDP growth is being driven by the huge investment in artificial intelligence. And, you know, if you build data centers for a living, you're pretty busy these days. But otherwise, this burst of economic growth has not been accompanied by a burst of new jobs.

PFEIFFER: And, Scott, what about the job market? What about unemployment numbers?

HORSLEY: Yeah, the job market is still really sluggish. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September. We're going to get the October numbers this coming week. Even though unemployment is low, just 4.2%, most people don't feel confident that if they quit their job, they can find another one. So they're just staying put. And Chief Economist Mark Zandi of Moody's Analytics, says that means there's not much pressure on employers to raise wages.

MARK ZANDI: There's no hiring. Hiring rates are extraordinarily low, and that's just not consistent with a healthy labor market.

HORSLEY: Wages are growing more slowly than they used to. New figures for September show spending rose 2.5 times as fast as wages did. So it's no wonder people feel concerned about affordability.

PFEIFFER: And we know that many people are aggravated about everyday purchases, like gasoline and groceries. But then there are the major purchases, like a house, which is usually what makes people feel economically secure. How is the housing market look in terms of the ability to buy one?

HORSLEY: I'm afraid the housing market is still haunted by high mortgage rates. Even though the Fed did not raise short-term borrowing costs this week, longer term rates are still high. The average cost of a 30 year home loan is around 7.25%. And Zandi says that's keeping a lot of would-be buyers on the sidelines.

ZANDI: I had been hopeful before this run up in rates that mortgage rates would hang around 6%. And if that were the case, then the housing market would start to fall. We get more home sales. But no, we're now well north of 7% on a fixed rate mortgage. Housing is the most interest rate sensitive sector of the economy, and it is taking it on the chin.

HORSLEY: The housing component of GDP has actually been negative in 8 of the last 10 quarters. But if the cobwebs on the for sale signs get too spooky, at least I can treat myself with one of those Reese's peanut butter cups from the $19 bag I bought to hand out this Halloween.

PFEIFFER: That is NPR Scott Horsley. Scott, thank you.

HORSLEY: You're welcome.

World.title: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
World.content:
France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe

toggle caption i Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.

Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

Sponsor Message

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

The marchers' grievances are diverse.

Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Sponsor Message

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.

Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.

Police impose curfew and other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.

Sponsor Message

In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.

Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

World.title: Key takeaways from this week's political meeting in Beijing
World.content:
Key takeaways from this week's political meeting in Beijing

toggle caption i Ng Han Guan/AP

BEIJING— China's ruling Communist Party concluded its most important meeting of the year, confirming the expulsion of 33 senior party members, as leader Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign continues to widen.

The political meeting, known as the fifth plenum, began on Monday and wrapped up on Thursday.

Of the 376 full and alternate central committee members originally named in 2022, only 279 attended – more than a quarter absent. Many of them are believed to be under investigation.

The focus of the meeting was on anti-corruption and discipline, but Joseph Torigian, a professor of Chinese studies at American University in Washington D.C., says the meeting sends another signal amid wide speculation that he will seek a fourth term in office next year.

"This is Xi Jinping setting up for the next party congress next year by ensuring that everybody is on the same page as him," he says.

The meeting reveals how much work Xi thinks his party still has to do to become a more effective, loyal governing institution, according to Neil Thomas, senior fellow on Chinese politics at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Sponsor Message

That is something he said Americans should also pay attention to, because it impacts the U.S. calculus on how willing China would be to use force over Taiwan, the South China Sea and disputes with the U.S.

"The focus of this fifth plenum suggests to me that Xi is unlikely to take that risk until he feels more comfortable with the party that he leads," Thomas says.

Here are other major takeaways from the meeting:

Who's in and who's out

Among the 33 expelled party members are Zhang Youxia, formerly China's most senior military general and Liu Jianchao, a senior Chinese diplomat previously tipped to be the next foreign minister.

China's military leadership ranks has "almost completely been purged in the last three or four years," according to Thomas.

However, one man not only survived the purges, but has been elevated – general Zhang Shengmin. He has been a key player in Xi's anti-corruption campaign. At the meeting he was promoted to the Politburo, which consists of more than 20 of the party's top officials. His promotion, according to Thomas, reinforces the importance of anti-corruption work in the military.

"There's a lot of churn going on," Torigian says. "That raises questions about just who [Xi's] going to look to to fill in the ranks when there's a big succession coming up at the next Party congress next year."

Sponsor Message

Instilling party discipline

One of the key themes out of the meeting was strengthening party governance.

Xi is looking to maintain the party's conviction from one generation to the next by convincing people to "put the Chinese Communist Party at the center of their lives and not their own selfish interests," according to Torigian.

He adds that this is a topic close to Xi's heart on how a communist regime can "maintain its purity and not degrade and collapse" like many other communist parties have in other countries.

Tackling corruption to "pointless formalities"

Xi's anti-corruption campaign started when he came into power in late 2012.

Since then, 7.9 million individuals have been punished, including over 960 senior officials, Zhang Fuhai, Deputy Secretary of the Communist party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, told reporters on Friday.

"The fight against corruption remains serious, complicated, and eradicating the breeding ground for corruption remains a formidable task," he said.

Xi has also complained about excessive formalities and bureaucracy, which according to Torigian is party language for going through the motions, having lots of meetings "but never actually achieving anything."

At the same time, there will be more regular reporting from discipline inspectors to central authorities to add scrutiny on local officials.

But to avoid attracting the attention of the discipline system, local officials may play things really safe, leading to more inertia, less experimentation, and "may end up having the opposite effect to what Xi intended," Thomas said.

No insight gleaned at the plenum on Xi's successor

Few political watchers believe Xi will pick a successor at the next party congress, and nobody knows exactly what he will do when he is ready to step down, according to Torigian.

Full decisions from the meeting, and perhaps deliverables, are expected to be published in the coming days.

Additional research by Jasmine Ling in Beijing.

World.title: A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance
World.content:
A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

It was the biggest cyber heist in history.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, was hacked this week, with cybercriminals plundering more than $6 billion. Experts widely believe the hackers were a sophisticated unit within the North Korean military that has a track record of committing cyber heists. The FBI on Saturday confirmed that North Korea was behind the hack.

The theft stunned the crypto industry and set off new fears about a sector that many critics deride as the "Wild West" of finance.

Here are 5 things to know about the spectacular heist.

So first, what are crypto exchanges?

They are akin to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or the Nasdaq, but instead of trading stocks, investors turn to Binance and other crypto exchanges to trade digital assets such as Bitcoin.

Sponsor Message

A wide range of investors trade cryptocurrencies at these exchanges, from financial institutions and sophisticated traders, all the way to regular investors looking to make some money.

OK, so what happened this week?

At 4:05 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, hackers were able to access the accounts of investors who trade cryptocurrencies at Binance. It took only about 20 minutes for these hackers to make off off with just over $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies.

Ari Redbord, the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a crypto research firm that has helped Binance trace and recover some of the stolen funds, calls it "the largest bank robbery in human history."

"Imagine a world where someone could walk into a bank and walk out with $6.36 billion in stolen funds and then move those funds at the speed of the internet," he says. "This is bank robbery in the age of technology."

But a lot of details about the heist are still unclear, including how exactly the hackers were able to hack their way into the trading accounts of investors at Binance.

Binance, working with other exchanges and partners, has been able to freeze about $3 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies, effectively preventing hackers from taking full possession of its digital assets.

Sponsor Message

The exchange has also said it will pay back any customers who were victims of the cyber heist — though it's not clear exactly how it will do that.

Why do experts believe it's North Korea?

The level of sophistication and speed of the hack all point to a North Korean military hacking unit widely known as TraderTraitor. The unit was also responsible for what was the previous biggest-ever cyber heist, the theft of $1.5 billion from crypto exchange Bybit last year.

"North Korea has built the most sophisticated cyber capabilities in the world. They have a cadre of teams of professional hackers who are part of their military," says TRM's Redbord.

"This isn't just a commercial hacker who's looking to make some money," he adds. "This is going to be used for weapons proliferation and other destabilizing activity."

The FBI said in a statement that the hack was conducted by Trader Traitor.

"The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH)," the agency said. "It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages."

toggle caption i Kim Won Jin/AFP via Getty Images

What does this heist tell us about the safety of crypto exchanges?

Researchers say it's too early to determine whether there were any major flaws with Binance's security systems. But they say the heist is a clear sign of just how sophisticated North Korean hackers are.

Meanwhile, crypto critics say the way Binance and other crypto exchanges are set up deserve scrutiny.

A unique feature of crypto exchanges is that people can buy and sell digital currencies such as bitcoin — and leave them with the exchanges for safekeeping.

This dual trust in the exchange makes them mighty tempting targets for hackers. And what's more concerning for critics, crypto exchanges also don't have to follow the same strict regulations that govern established Wall Street firm.

"You may trade on the New York Stock Exchange, but you don't keep your funds with the New York Stock Exchange. You keep it with your broker — and your broker is audited and regulated by the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)," says Amanda Fischer, policy director and chief operating officer at financial consumer advocacy group Better Markets. "And your broker has to pay for insurance that will make customers whole in the event that there's a cyber attack."

Sponsor Message

"So the regulatory framework for crypto is much weaker than what investors in the US enjoy in other markets," says Fischer.

Though Binance has promised to pay back customers who lost funds, it is not necessarily bound to do so according to current regulations. And many critics worry that smaller exchanges could struggle to pay back their investors in case of a hack, leaving these traders to suffer the consequences.

Doesn't this reinforce the crypto sector's Wild West reputation?

For many crypto critics, it does. They warn the lack of clear regulations for crypto executives could lead to perverse incentives at these exchanges.

In 2022, FTX — then the biggest crypto exchange — got into financial trouble after a period of intense volatility in the crypto markets, and the exchange dipped into their own customers' funds as it desperately tried to rescue itself. The company collapsed, and its CEO and founder Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud among other charges.

"If a trade goes bad, it can become almost irresistible to dip into those client funds. Just this one time is what they say, to cover their losses," says Fischer at Better Markets. "But we know that that can cascade into catastrophe for investors."

It's another reason why the massive cyber heist of Binance is raising so many alarms.

NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.

World.title: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate
World.content:
Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate

toggle caption i Chloe Anderson/AP

ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.

The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
