According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina
World.content:
From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina

31st Saturday, October 2026 - 01:14 UTC Full article

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru

Pope Leo XIV will begin a tour of South America in Montevideo on November 6 that will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, with open-air Masses, meetings with Presidents Yamandú Orsi and Javier Milei, and events with young people, workers and prisoners. His stop in Argentina, from November 8 to 11, will be the first papal visit to the country since John Paul II’s in April 1987.

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru. “May this journey be an opportunity to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy.” Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13; last week he cancelled a helicopter trip to Assisi as a medical precaution, but the Vatican has announced no changes to the tour.

Uruguay, November 6-8

The Pope will leave Rome on Friday 6 and land at Carrasco airport about eight and a half hours later. That afternoon, Montevideo’s Plaza Independencia will host the official welcome ceremony; he will meet Orsi and celebrate vespers at 7.05 p.m. in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Saturday 7 he will fly to Paysandú, on the border with Argentina, to celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. in Parque París Londres. Back in the capital, he will visit the parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe in the Casavalle neighbourhood, meet the education community at the Catholic University of Uruguay and lead a prayer vigil at 7 p.m. at the Centenario Stadium.

On Sunday 8 he will celebrate Mass at 10.30 a.m. in the city of Florida, in front of the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, Uruguay’s patron saint, on her feast day, a coincidence that was decisive in starting the tour there. At 3.10 p.m. he will leave for Buenos Aires.

Argentina, November 8-11

The Pope will land at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery on Sunday 8 at 4.30 p.m. After paying tribute at the monument to General San Martín, he will meet Milei at the Casa Rosada and, at 6.30 p.m., address authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad.

On Monday 9 he will visit the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole and celebrate Mass at 11.30 a.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards in Palermo. In the afternoon he will meet trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina, work being one of the themes of his pontificate, and leaders of other faiths at the Palacio San Martín, before celebrating vespers with the bishops at the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Tuesday 10 he will travel to Córdoba, where he will celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Military Aviation School and meet clergy at the cathedral. Back in Buenos Aires, he will lead a youth vigil at 8.15 p.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards.

On Wednesday 11 he will visit the Devoto prison complex and celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján, the country’s main shrine. The farewell is scheduled for 1.30 p.m. at Ezeiza, from where he will fly to Lima.

Argentina’s government declared the visit of national interest and set three public holidays: Monday 9 nationwide, Tuesday 10 in the city of Buenos Aires and Córdoba province, and Wednesday 11 in Buenos Aires province. Francis, the first Argentine pope, never returned to his country during his pontificate.

World.title: Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it
World.content:
Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:21 UTC Full article

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted

Argentina’s Office of Administrative Investigations, a specialised prosecution service for crimes committed by public officials, has appealed the dismissal of charges against President Javier Milei, his sister and presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, and nine other defendants in the case over the $LIBRA cryptocurrency, and asked for the investigation to be reopened, arguing that key evidence is still missing.

The office, headed by prosecutor Sergio Rodríguez, joined the case and took over the criminal prosecution, which had been dropped by prosecutor Eduardo Taiano when he requested the dismissals later granted by federal judge Marcelo Martínez De Giorgi. Besides seeking to reopen the case, it filed a subsidiary appeal so that, if the request is rejected, the Federal Appeals Court can review the decision.

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted. Pending steps include tracing the funds, recovering and analysing communications, investigating possible commercial agreements and examining the money movements linked to the case. They also question that the evidence was assessed piece by piece rather than as a whole, and argue that technical difficulties or incomplete responses cannot justify closing the case. They also propose examining whether the president’s conduct could amount to the crime of conflicts of interest in the exercise of public office.

The filing responds to a request from two organisations acting in the case as friends of the court, the Centre for the Investigation and Prevention of Economic Crime and the Institute of Comparative Studies in Criminal and Social Sciences, which had criticised Taiano’s handling of the case, including his refusal to summon Milei for questioning. The decision now rests with Federal Court No. 8, temporarily headed by Judge Daniel Rafecas while Martínez De Giorgi is on leave. The investors who lost money, removed from their role as plaintiffs, have also appealed and are awaiting a ruling from the Federal Court of Criminal Cassation.

In February 2025, Milei shared the $LIBRA cryptocurrency on X; its value soared and collapsed within hours, causing losses for thousands of investors. The president deleted the post, denied promoting the project and has rejected any wrongdoing.

World.title: Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist
World.content:
Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:18 UTC Full article

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds

Hackers stole about US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest digital asset exchange, in the biggest theft in the sector’s history, which the US Secret Service is investigating with other agencies. Blockchain analytics firms point to a hacking group linked to North Korea, though there has been no official attribution.

Most of the theft took place in about 20 minutes from 20:05 GMT on Thursday, from the wallets Binance uses to process transactions, according to TRM Labs. Its chief policy officer, Ari Redbord, told the BBC that such speed “is the product of long preparation”: the attackers had funded an operator wallet 36 hours earlier and prepared in advance the signatures to authorise the transfers. According to TRM, they compromised the platform’s “signing infrastructure”.

Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said the attack “was not carried out by one person”. The initial investigation pointed to an engineer’s laptop, but “additional points of breach” were later uncovered. The attackers exploited an Ethereum network mechanism known as EIP-7702 to gain control of a wallet without passing through normal approval controls, and used a “self-destruct mechanism” to erase their traces, according to Teng, who said customer losses would be covered by the company’s protection fund, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve, and its own resources. Binance says it has begun recovering some funds. Withdrawals remain suspended and the company expects to resume them within about 40 hours; it will publish a full proof-of-reserves report on Monday.

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds, in coordination with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident”.

About half of the stolen assets were stablecoins that their issuers — Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture — have frozen. TRM estimates that about US$2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether is beyond reach, as no company can block them.

TRM Labs and Chainalysis said they had “high confidence” that the culprit is TraderTraitor, also known as Lazarus, a North Korea-linked group the FBI blamed for the theft of about US$1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange in 2025, until now the sector’s largest. Chainalysis detected Binance funds commingling with those from another recent attack attributed to North Korean actors. Pyongyang routinely denies involvement in such thefts. Bitcoin fell about 4% after news of the attack.

World.title: Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election
World.content:
Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election

30th Friday, October 2026 - 17:17 UTC Full article

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office

Pope Leo XIV has voted by mail in the US midterm elections to be held on November 3, making him the first pontiff to take part in an election in that country, the Vatican said on Friday.

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office. “In keeping with this well-established practice of civic participation, he sent his ballot by mail to Chicago,” the statement said, without indicating whom he voted for.

Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his election as pope in May 2025, spent almost two decades in Peru as a missionary and later as a bishop, and holds US and Peruvian citizenship. “The Holy Father also confirmed that during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he met the requirements to do so,” the Vatican said.

Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13. He is due to begin a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on November 6, running until November 17.

World.title: Venezuela names Oliver Blanco, a former opposition aide, as foreign minister
World.content:
Venezuela names Oliver Blanco, a former opposition aide, as foreign minister

30th Friday, October 2026 - 17:00 UTC Full article

A graduate in International Studies, Blanco was an aide to Henry Ramos Allup, a leader of the opposition Democratic Action party, when he presided over the National Assembly elected in 2015

Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez has appointed Oliver Blanco, a 35-year-old diplomat who began his political career alongside a veteran opposition leader, as foreign minister in a reshuffle of her government’s international team. Blanco replaces Félix Plasencia, whom Rodríguez has tasked with moving to the United Kingdom to recover Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England.

“I will defend our sovereignty and the national interest, always working to achieve concrete benefits for the people,” Blanco said on taking office, adding that the moment requires “building from our differences” a country where “everyone has a place”. Rodríguez said she hoped “this strengthened team will keep advancing the changes and Venezuela’s geopolitical recovery, in areas of cooperation and friendship with all countries”.

A graduate in International Studies, Blanco was an aide to Henry Ramos Allup, a leader of the opposition Democratic Action party, when he presided over the National Assembly elected in 2015, the first controlled by the opposition. After stepping back from party politics, he joined Rodríguez’s government following the US military operation in January that removed Nicolás Maduro from power: he was appointed deputy minister for Europe and North America on February 23 and, in July, first deputy foreign minister. Since then he has been involved in restoring relations with countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Chile and Israel.

Plasencia, an associate of Rodríguez since the 1990s, becomes head of International Affairs at the Presidency with a specific task. “He must settle in the United Kingdom until we recover the gold that belongs to Venezuelans,” Rodríguez said. The gold, some 31 tonnes of bars from the Central Bank of Venezuela’s reserves worth about US$4 billion, has been frozen at the Bank of England since 2019, when London recognised Juan Guaidó as interim president. Its recovery is one of the government’s main demands in its negotiations with the opposition led by Dinorah Figuera.

Rodríguez also appointed Marynna Saatdjian as deputy minister for North America and Europe, Saúl Ameliach as deputy minister for International Trade and Yuri Pimentel, a former communications minister under Hugo Chávez, as first deputy foreign minister. The changes come a day after the acting president promised elections under a “renewed” electoral authority, without setting a date.

World.title: Brazil to spend nearly three-quarters of its 2027 defence budget on personnel and pensions
World.content:
Brazil to spend nearly three-quarters of its 2027 defence budget on personnel and pensions

30th Friday, October 2026 - 01:09 UTC Full article

Of the total, about 12.7 billion reais is for investment and 21.7 billion for operating costs. The proposal must be approved by Congress

Brazil plans to allocate 147.68 billion reais to defence in 2027, about US$27 billion at current exchange rates, but 73% of that will go on salaries, retirement benefits and pensions, according to the budget bill sent to Congress. With only 8.6% set aside for investment, the country will have to decide the pace of programmes that include fighter jets, frigates, armoured vehicles and a nuclear-powered submarine.

Of the total, about 12.7 billion reais is for investment and 21.7 billion for operating costs. The proposal must be approved by Congress. The recent depreciation of the real, which lost more than 8% against the dollar after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election, also makes imported components more expensive.

According to defence analyst Andrei Serbin Pont, who reviewed the programmes in an analysis for the Infobae website, the Brazilian Air Force expressed interest in June in buying another 20 Gripen E/F fighters from Sweden’s Saab, in addition to the 36 already contracted, with possible production at Embraer’s plant in Gavião Peixoto, São Paulo state; the order has not been confirmed. The Navy signed a memorandum of understanding on April 24 with Embraer and Germany’s TKMS to build four more Tamandaré-class frigates, and is considering larger ships from France, Italy, South Korea or the United Kingdom, including the possible purchase of second-hand British Type 31 frigates.

The programme hardest hit is the nuclear-powered submarine, whose launch has reportedly slipped from 2034 to 2038 due to funding difficulties, according to the analyst. The Army, for its part, has again postponed the selection of new armoured vehicles and a medium tank, and is negotiating the purchase of ATMOS 155 self-propelled howitzers through a consortium with Brazilian company Avibras. Brazil is also seeking a government-to-government agreement with Italy for its air defence programme, with the participation of European consortium MBDA.

“There is no weapons system Brazil is acquiring today that really alters the balance of power at regional level,” Serbin Pont said. The analyst highlighted continued defence cooperation with Argentina, including joint exercises such as Arandú, and noted that Embraer’s KC-390 transport aircraft is an option to replace the Argentine Air Force’s C-130s; Argentina has also evaluated the ATMOS howitzers. Decisions will depend on the new leadership of the Defence Ministry, which will change with the start of Lula’s fourth term on January 5.

World.title: Shell and TotalEnergies double profits on a refining boom
World.content:
Shell and TotalEnergies double profits on a refining boom

30th Friday, October 2026 - 01:00 UTC Full article

France’s TotalEnergies posted adjusted net income of US$9.1 billion, against US$4 billion a year earlier and above the US$8.3 billion forecast

European oil majors Shell and TotalEnergies doubled their profits in the third quarter of 2026 and posted their best quarterly results since 2022, driven by refining margins almost four times higher than a year earlier amid tensions in the Middle East, according to results published on Thursday. Both expanded their share buyback programmes.

Britain’s Shell reported adjusted earnings of US$10.81 billion for July to September, almost double the US$5.43 billion of the same period in 2025 and above the US$10.33 billion analysts had expected, according to Reuters. Its refining margin reached US$42 per barrel. The company raised its quarterly share buyback from US$3 billion to US$5 billion, one of the largest in its history.

France’s TotalEnergies posted adjusted net income of US$9.1 billion, against US$4 billion a year earlier and above the US$8.3 billion forecast. Its refining and chemicals division earned a record US$3.6 billion, more than five times the previous year’s figure, with a refining margin of US$33.2 per barrel. Chief executive Patrick Pouyanné attributed the result to a near-10% increase in refined volumes and market conditions. The company confirmed a US$2.5 billion buyback for the fourth quarter and signalled another of the same size for the first quarter of 2027.

The results also had weak spots. Shell’s oil and gas production fell 17% in the first nine months of the year, mainly due to disruptions in Qatar linked to the Middle East conflict, although its liquefied natural gas volumes rose 12% thanks to the LNG Canada plant. The company cut its 2026 capital spending forecast to between US$23 billion and US$25 billion. TotalEnergies produced 2.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, 4% below expectations, and booked a US$1.9 billion impairment, mainly linked to offshore wind.

Both companies operate in Argentina, in the Vaca Muerta formation, and TotalEnergies also in the Austral basin off Tierra del Fuego. ExxonMobil and Chevron report their results on Friday.

World.title: “I am the right person”: Delcy Rodríguez casts herself as guarantor of Venezuela’s transition
World.content:
“I am the right person”: Delcy Rodríguez casts herself as guarantor of Venezuela’s transition

29th Thursday, October 2026 - 17:42 UTC Full article

“There will be elections, all those our Constitution requires, organised by a renewed electoral authority and with the world as witness,” Rodríguez said in an address to the nation

Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez on Thursday presented herself as the guarantor of democratic change in the country and promised elections organised by a “renewed” electoral authority, though she set no date. “This process can only be led by someone who knows the inner workings of the Venezuelan state deeply. I know this state and I am the right person to carry this process forward,” she said.

“There will be elections, all those our Constitution requires, organised by a renewed electoral authority and with the world as witness,” Rodríguez said in an address to the nation, recalling that she has served as deputy foreign minister, foreign minister, minister and vice-president. She championed a “political, economic, cultural, spiritual, democratic, orderly and verifiable” transformation and said her government has a roadmap. “Venezuela’s political horizon is not measured by a date on the calendar but by a sequence of objectives we must achieve,” including legal reform, guarantees of participation for all political forces and “elections that are a solution and not a source of irreconcilable conflict”. “An announcement like this is worth not what it promises but what it delivers,” she added.

Rodríguez also announced a national consultation to reform criminal justice, with technical assistance from the European Union, and said she had requested the cooperation of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. The National Assembly last week presented a reform that the Supreme Court declared constitutional, and Rodríguez called for it to be debated in a broad consultation with all sectors.

The address came four days after opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela after nearly ten months abroad, and shortly before her first press conference since her return. Rodríguez had called her arrival a “show”. Rodríguez has governed as acting president since January, after Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power in a US military operation. Her government has been negotiating with the opposition since August a roadmap that includes renewing the Supreme Court and the National Electoral Council and holding regional elections before the presidential vote, a sequence Machado rejects. The US State Department has said that under that roadmap Rodríguez should leave the presidency vacant in 2027.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump suggested that Venezuela become the “51st state” of the United States and elect a governor instead of a president, an idea Rodríguez has rejected in the past.

World.title: From the archive: How Mexico’s Day of the Dead helps us remember the people we’ve lost
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in October 2019 — shows us how remembering lost loved ones can be a colorful celebration of life, love and the memories that keep them with us.

Day of the Dead is by far my favorite holiday in Mexico. My first experience with it was in 2002, when I was here as a university student.

The director of my study abroad program here in Xalapa piled a few of us into his pickup truck and we drove to Naolinco, a picturesque mountain town known for its leather products.

I was immediately enchanted. Altars were all over the place — in people’s homes, in public spaces, in restaurants and stores. As we walked along the street, people invited us into their homes for tamales, bread and homemade wine.

There were carolers at the cemetery. Carolers! With guitars! The brightly colored petals and exquisite smell of cempasúchil, “marigolds,” were everywhere.

Since then, Day of the Dead has caught on north of the border as well. Even before the popular movie “Coco” came out, the southern Texas city I return home to was starting to embrace its Mexican heritage in more expansive ways than it ever had before, with altars, decorated skulls and papel picado, “colorful tissue paper with designs,” suddenly appearing alongside Halloween decorations.

Who knew that the dead could bring us together?

Each year in my home we set up our altar with the same enthusiasm with which we decorate the Christmas tree. As the years pass and more people we know and love die, we’ve had to switch to a bigger table, as our collection of dead has grown.

My grandmother is there, as is my mother. Traditionally, the flower petals are to be sprinkled from the altar to the front door so that the dead can find their way back home from the other side to enjoy the offerings laid out for them.

My grandmother, in life, would not have appreciated her place on the altar. Like many Protestants of a certain age, she was suspicious of the “magical” elements mixed in with modern Catholicism.

Day of the Dead is, of course, a mixture of Catholic and Indigenous tradition, one that the Spaniards were only partially successful at co-opting. At least they got to move the dates to the ones they wanted. (I like to think that my grandmother, now on the other side, would be totally cool with it.)

Death is a universal reality, and all cultures have different ways of dealing with it. When I was growing up in central Texas, death was taboo, something no one wanted to talk about; it was sad at best and terrifying at worst.

Halloween was a time not to think about the dead we knew, but to have fun dressing up and getting candy (and subsequent cavities). When I learned later of the history of Halloween from pagan tradition to Catholicism’s version, All Saints’ Day, I felt decidedly more creeped out.

Why should we spend any time at all thinking about death? How uncomfortable!

How to confront death

My attitude since has evolved considerably. Now that I’m an adult, death has moved closer and closer to me in the form of the passing of actual people I’ve known and loved, and in the reality and certainty of my own mortality as the years go by.

I’m hopefully still a long way from it, but none of us really knows, do we? For something that’s such a firm fact of life, we sure do avoid thinking about it a lot.

Mexicans don’t (as much), and I think there’s something to be learned from that. We can accept that we’re going to die. We can paint skulls on our faces to remind all of us that life is for the living — that we won’t be around forever, so we’d better get to it!

What does Day of the Dead do for us? It keeps the memories of our loved ones alive. It keeps this culture alive and reminds us of the people we came from. Feel guilty about not thinking enough of your loved ones that have already passed on? Don’t: remembering to do that is built into an annual holiday here.

I am not religious myself. I don’t pretend to know what happens after death, though as an agnostic I fully expect that we simply cease to exist in the way a flame from a candle goes out. As Richard Dawkins has said, we know that consciousness is wrapped up in the brain, and we know that the brain rots, so I have no illusions.

To me, this news is not too disappointing, as I’m fairly certain that, as a dead person, I would not have the consciousness to care. Disappointing would be getting to that point of not existing and not having done anything worthwhile.

That said, I do believe that there is a way to keep our dead alive, and Day of the Dead helps us to do that. Because while they might not still be around, they live on in us, and this holiday helps us remember that in an active way. The ways they shaped us, influenced us, taught us and loved us live on.

Death is sad. We don’t usually wish for it, but learning to accept it and not fear it (at least not too much) is a worthy exercise. Celebrate, remember and love your dead. Sit and chat with them a while.

Share some hot chocolate, some tamales, some pan de muerto, play their favorite music, decorate your face the way their faces look now.

Welcome them back, at least for a couple of days, and celebrate your own beating heart.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Farewell to Cárdenas, a resignation at the INE and a record-breaking Catrina
World.content:
Listen to this article

The headlines of the week in Mexico began with news of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil, which left President Claudia Sheinbaum “very happy” and, in her words, was “a breath of fresh air” for Latin America and the Caribbean.

But at home, Mexico’s governing political movement Morena suffered another setback as the resignation of National Electoral Institute (INE) president Guadalupe Taddei raised fresh doubts about the integrity of figures tied to the government, even as Sheinbaum insisted Morena is not to blame. Meanwhile, the opposition National Action Party (PAN) announced six presumptive gubernatorial candidates for the 2027 elections.

This week also brought the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a towering figure of Mexico’s democratic transition. And as the country heads into Day of the Dead (and Formula 1 Grand Prix) weekend, Sheinbaum called on new generations to preserve the holiday’s traditions.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Oct. 26? Here’s what you missed.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas dies at 92

Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and the son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. A member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) for more than 30 years, he left the party in 1987 and ran in 1988 as the candidate of a left-wing coalition. He is widely believed to have won that election, but Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner. Cárdenas went on to co-found the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), contested the 1994 and 2000 elections, and served as Mexico City’s first elected mayor from 1997 to 1999.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles,” and Thursday’s mañanera centered on a tribute to him. Asked what he leaves the Mexican left, she answered: “Honesty and democracy.” A public tribute with his coffin present was set for Friday at the Palacio de Bellas Artes. His son Lázaro Cárdenas Batel is Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

INE president resigns; Sheinbaum weighs in

Guadalupe Taddei announced her resignation as INE president on Sunday after media outlets, including Reforma, reported that companies tied to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, with whom she reportedly has a close personal relationship, won lucrative INE contracts. She is the first head of the INE or its predecessor, the IFE, to resign since 1990. The Federal Auditor’s Office has opened an investigation, and Taddei said: “Each allegation must be examined with evidence.”

On Monday, Sheinbaum called the resignation “good” and said an audit was needed. On Tuesday, she pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” noting that the Chamber of Deputies, not the president, chose Taddei, who was picked by lottery in 2023. By Thursday, Sheinbaum went further, saying she believes Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico.” She also said her government will propose turning the state-run printer Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company to supply most electoral materials. The INE’s focus remains the June 6, 2027, elections.

IMSS workers promised 8% raise

After weeks of protests, Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of 12 actions in 120 days. It includes an 8% salary increase, permanent positions for almost 11,000 temporary workers, 2,500 new specialist doctors, more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys, and a push to guarantee medicines and clear the surgical backlog. Whether it satisfies workers, and ends shortages that have outlasted earlier government efforts, remains to be seen.

Dog poisonings rattle Condesa

Poison hidden in sausage left in and around Mexico City’s centrally located Parque España killed at least three dogs Tuesday, prompting an animal cruelty investigation. The toll later reached four. Attorney General Bertha Alcalde Luján said tests found methomyl, a highly toxic insecticide, in capsules placed inside the meat, and authorities recovered 14 suspect pieces.

On Friday, police arrested a 58-year-old man, identified as Salvador “N,” a block from the park after he resembled a person in images circulating on social media. He was detained for resisting arrest, and prosecutors cautioned that they had not yet established whether he was responsible. Residents are avoiding the park, and Cuauhtémoc borough Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega urged pet owners not to let animals eat anything off the ground.

Guadalajara water plan and allegations of torture

On Wednesday, Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus announced a “historic agreement” with the federal government to invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure. The plan centers on two new aqueducts, from Lake Chapala and from the Calderón Reservoir, due by the end of 2028. The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion, and Lemus promised no new debt, privatization or rate increases. The announcement followed large protests demanding clean tap water.

The Oct. 11 protest in particular remains contentious. Two women, among around 10 people who have filed complaints with the Federal Attorney General’s Office, allege they were tortured by Jalisco state police. At least 39 people were arrested and dozens hurt. Lemus has conceded “serious mistakes” were made, Security Minister Juan Pablo Hernández denied ordering force and Sheinbaum has repeatedly denounced the alleged torture.

Citizen scientists make their mark

In Michoacán, residents who spotted unusual marks in a streambed led researchers to at least 50 dinosaur footprints near Apatzingán. The National Institute of Anthropology and History believes the Late Cretaceous tracks were left by three types of dinosaurs and says further study is needed to pin down species.

In Tabasco, residents of Barra de Santa Ana are working to restore coastal dunes. A 30-member community brigade trained by Eni Mexico and UNESCO will replant vegetation and install sand catchers. Erosion has hit 85% of the 30-kilometer coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones, and up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year.

Sheinbaum moves to keep Mexico’s masterpieces at home

Following the Gelman Collection controversy, Sheinbaum plans to strengthen the Monuments Law to prohibit the permanent export of privately owned works declared artistic or historical monuments. A preliminary draft was published Oct. 15. The change would reconcile the law with 10 presidential decrees protecting works by artists including Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo and David Alfaro Siqueiros. The timing matters, as the Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the 1984 Kahlo decree.

Day of the Dead highlights

Mexico City’s cempasúchil production hit a record 10 million plants, up 53.8% from last year, grown mainly on Xochimilco’s chinampas.

The capital unveiled the world’s tallest Catrina in the Zócalo. At 33.4 meters, the papier-mâché figure tops Puerto Vallarta’s 2023 record holder and is the city’s fifth Guinness record this year. The offering is on display through Nov. 3.

At Friday’s mañanera, held amid marigolds and Catrina figures, Sheinbaum described the Mexican view of “death as part of life” and said the holiday has “recovered” from Halloween’s influence, partly thanks to films like “Coco.”

Economy: Exports surge, growth slows and India talks begin

Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% in the third quarter from the previous quarter, down from 1.4% but above the 0.7% economists expected. Year over year, growth of 3.2% was the largest in 12 quarters, helped by a weak third quarter in 2025.

Exports, meanwhile, reached US $77.79 billion in September, up 37.9% and the third-highest monthly total on record. Over the first nine months, exports rose 30.4% to $627.19 billion, driven by computer and electronic equipment sold to the United States amid an AI data center boom. Mexico posted a $9.25 billion trade surplus, but its oil deficit of $25.68 billion already exceeds the 2025 total.

On the trade front, Mexico and India signed terms of reference on Monday for negotiations on a preferential trade agreement. Merchandise trade between the two totaled $8.74 billion in 2024, and a Mexican business mission to India is under discussion for early 2027.

Charlyn Corral makes history at the Ballon d’Or

Pachuca forward Charlyn Corral, 35, won the Gerd Müller trophy for Best Striker of the Year at Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, becoming the first Mexican woman to earn the distinction. She scored 49 goals in 49 matches for club and country and shared the honor with Harry Kane.

In her acceptance speech, she also asked the audience to recognize compatriot Scarlett Camberos, who was among the 30 nominees for the main award.

Looking ahead

Whether Jalisco’s 25 billion-peso water plan will be enough to keep Guadalajara’s streets calm is an open question. The two aqueducts are not due until the end of 2028, work “could” start next year, and the Oct. 11 allegations of police abuse remain under investigation, so residents may be left with promises rather than clean tap water for some time. On trade, Sheinbaum agreed with Donald Trump that a deal with the United States is “very close”, and on Wednesday she said talks were advancing as both sides weigh whether an interim agreement is possible before U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, Reuters reported. Mexico is still seeking a “significant reduction” in U.S. tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, while Washington is pressing concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

Even a pre-election deal would leave questions for the next Congress, according to an opinion piece in The Hill by Duncan Wood and Ivan Zapien. They argue that a change in control of Congress would not end U.S. pressure on Mexico over trade, migration and security, but a Democratic House could summon officials, scrutinize the USMCA talks and push for tougher labor and environmental enforcement, while Republicans keep pressing on energy and China. Either way, they write, Mexico should expect to answer to more of Washington, more often, after the U.S. declined in July to extend the USMCA for another 16 years.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Why I’m grateful my son is getting the Halloween-Día de Muertos experience I never had
World.content:
The funny thing about growing up in California with Mexican immigrant parents is that you are perpetually intimate with, and distant from, your Mexican roots. Every holiday season, therefore, becomes a delightfully unique interpretation of both cultures mashed together.

Tamales wrapped in banana leaves and filled with turkey for Thanksgiving? Opening gifts at midnight for Noche Buena, and then again on Christmas morning? Getting your face smashed into a birthday cake?

These are all welcome in my life as a Mexican-American who must constantly toggle between my two identities on both soils.

Sometimes, though, one cultural norm or ideology can overtake the other, leaving one half egregiously overlooked, if not completely erased. For me, that has always been the case with Día de Muertos.

Halloween was the festive U.S. tradition my household embraced in its most suburbanized form: dressing up as Ninja Turtles, trick-or-treating with pumpkin-shaped buckets, and devouring pounds of Jolly Ranchers, fun-sized Snickers and M&Ms for weeks after.

I’ve never been the king of spooky season, but I’ve also never avoided it. As I grew older and met my wife, our family Halloween tradition became dressing up in custom-made outfits that reflected our personalities or the region we lived: two high school teachers dressed as our favorite punctuation marks; two Boston post-grads dressed as the local subway trains. (Spoiler: this year we are dressing up as Chedraui employees.)

And yet, despite traveling to Mexico regularly throughout my life, and having immigrant parents who spoke Spanish and were connected to their roots in Veracruz in different ways, I don’t have any real Día de Muertos memories from my childhood.

Finding the tradition

It wasn’t until the 2010s that I recall the concept entering mainstream culture in California and elsewhere beyond Mexico. For my wife and me — both as a couple, but also in our respective Mexican-American upbringings throughout the 1990s and 2000s — we never experienced our parents or family members building altars in our California homes. Not until maybe around Pixar’s “Coco” (2017), that is.

That tradition has quickly spread. Within the past decade, it has become more commonplace to see altares, ofrendas and Día de Muertos-themed households worldwide. Of course, it existed long before “Coco,” but it wasn’t as ubiquitous as it is today.

When my son was born in 2023, my wife and I had already spent significant time in Mexico, including traveling to Oaxaca for a month during Día de Muertos season and fully immersing ourselves in its wondrous spirit of parades, parties and gravesite visits.

We had learned, while exploring Mexico’s vast regional scenes and lodging with family members in various states across the span of multiple summers, about the importance of Día de Muertos as a form of intimate ancestral remembrance. In contrast to the candy-collecting rampage we’d always known the end of October to be, we’ve been able to incorporate those important elements of Día de Muertos into our lives — and in our son’s understanding of this time of the year.

Now, having fully transplanted our lives to Veracruz, we get to experience the best of both worlds as a young family: the playful, goofy costumery and decorations of Halloween, combined with the artisanal charms and spiritual connectivity of Día de Muertos.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Building core memories

Undoubtedly, our son’s autumnal memories will be completely different than ours: Instead of knocking on doors in a cul-de-sac with a group of neighborhood kids, he’s going to a field of cempasúchiles in a mountainous pueblo to get his photo taken on a horse that is whimsically painted like a calavera. Instead of visiting the pumpkin patch and riding a train through cornstalks and bales of hay, his abuela and bisabuelo are coming over to our house to eat pan de muerto and build a collective family altar with photos of family members that he, or even I, will never meet.

Each has their own joys and core-memory-building functions, and I enjoy them both. I hope he does, too.

It’s true that our current community doesn’t offer much traditional Halloween vibes, in the Americanized sense. You may see a decorative witch or black cat dangling from a window, here and there. Earlier this week, I walked past a large inflatable ghost on someone’s balcony, but it was awkwardly angled to avoid the mess of wires that complicate our narrow, colonial streets.

It’s just a different atmosphere in these smaller Mexican cities and towns, and the sidewalks don’t really allow for large groups of children to roam around without parents losing their minds over incessant traffic safety.

Trick-or-treating vs. Día de Muertos parades

In 2024, we flew to Mexico City for Halloween and Día de Muertos. It was noticeably different from our experience in Veracruz. A local group of parents organized families online for a neighborhood walk, with designated homes that had registered in advance, so we knew who would be giving out candy.

Similarly, we went to a mercado in Mexico City that weekend for a “calaverita” — a Mexican version of trick-or-treating, where kids dress up and go stall to stall asking for treats.

In those instances, my son, wife and I got to experience some of that old-school Americana by walking around Mexico City with strangers — some, but not all of them, international — and knocking on doors (or wandering shop aisles) together. That version of Halloween offers a communal, neighborly bonding that isn’t always seen during other holidays, which more often than not take place inside homes with close family members, rather than out in public and in the streets. We certainly could use more of it.

Then, there’s the other side of it all: attending a Día de Muertos parade and being part of a collective throng of spectators, while ceremoniously dressed performers and various forms of alebrijes dance, flutter and chant around you. (It’s worth noting that Día de Muertos parades, like the one in Mexico’s capital, are relatively new traditions in many areas; they weren’t commonplace when I was growing up, but are a part of Día de Muertos’ increasing popularity.)

I’m glad my son will get to be immersed in those cultural experiences in ways my wife and I weren’t for Halloween.

Fusing traditions in an ever-connected world

Having access to those dual experiences is a life hack, really. That’s not to say that Halloween has never existed in Mexico, or that Día de Muertos is nonexistent in California. In each case, the cultural traditions are becoming more fused than ever before, largely thanks to social media, travel access and other global factors.

You no longer have to be in Oaxaca’s Centro to experience Día de Muertos, nor do you have to reside in a U.S. suburb to appreciate Halloween. Depending on where you are, you may not be able to fully replicate the magic of the other — but you learn to salvage whatever aspects you can.

By being in Mexico, we are reminded that we will always have generous access to, and understanding of, both celebratory worlds. That’s ultimately the beauty of being a Mexican-American binational family, no matter the seasonal holiday or time of year.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? It’s not what you’d expect
World.content:
I have to be honest here. Growing up, I did get excited about Halloween parties at school.

Although some colleagues might be flabbergasted by this, as a kid, my friends in elementary school did organize trick-or-treat evenings — which were mostly about the treats, honestly — and children invited each other to their houses to play dress-up and paint their faces as pumpkins and skeletons.

However, for the November festivities, my family always made a point to put a special emphasis on building our Día de Muertos altar at home. It kind of felt more important, in a way, than just getting your pumpkin or vampire disguise. Still, as the air grows colder and the moons appear larger at night, the question arises: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? Well, it’s a bit more complicated than you might expect.

When the barrier between the two worlds grows thin

As the November festivities draw closer, you might come across the debate on social media. More nationalist and opinionated Mexicans will defend our millennia-old traditions over the hyper-Americanization of our fall festivals. Incidentally, there is a similar debate among our fellow countrymen regarding why pan de muerto should only be eaten during this time of year, and we have discussed it at length on MND before.

And the people who share this point of view do have a point. Setting up the altar for the dead, waiting for our deceased relatives to return and share a meal at home once more, is something we inherited from our parents, who in turn inherited it from their grandparents, and so on.

The pre-Hispanic roots of this ritual are enough to warrant an article in their own right — covering the spiritual light of the cempasúchil flower and the way the barrier between the two worlds seems to grow thin at this time of year. But that is not all. Although it is a custom with distinctly Mexica origins, it manifests in widely diverse cultural ways across the country: The massive ofrenda created annually at UNAM is vastly different from the long nights people spend in Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, awaiting the return of their departed loved ones.

We even have a word for them: nuestros muertitos, our beloved deceased. The suffix -ito or -ita in Mexican Spanish implies not only a diminutive form, but also a relationship of affection and respect inherited from Nahuatl -tzin, the honorific suffix used for high-ranking officials as well as for our mothers and fathers.

In preparation for their return, we prepare the favorite foods of our dearly departed — like mole de olla for a dear auntie, or the Diet Coke my grandma used to enjoy so much. Some people leave cigarettes for a brother who has passed away, or even traditional candies like Pulparindo or Pelón Pelo Rico.

So, yeah, you can see how these festivities might weigh a lot more on us than simply going trick-or-treating. Why then, why do we see children running around dressed as skeletons, ghosts and pumpkins as Oct. 31 approaches?

Día de Muertos vs. Halloween: Is there a disagreement about this in Mexico?

First of all, it is worth emphasizing that Mexico is an incredibly culturally diverse country. Even taking into account the legacy of the Mexica Empire — which spread many Day of the Dead practices across the nation — and the overwhelming influence of contemporary globalization, one cannot truly generalize about how the tradition is observed throughout the country. To do so would almost be disrespectful to the 68 official Indigenous languages (with their 364 linguistic variants) and the unique ways in which each culture shows respect and affection for its departed loved ones.

What I mean by this is that there is no single way to celebrate Day of the Dead in Mexico — or Halloween, for that matter.

That said, how right Porfirio Díaz was when he said that Mexico was very far from God, but very close to the United States. Given the geographic, commercial and political proximity we share with our northern neighbors — who are increasingly coming to share our country with us — it is only natural that Mexicans also join in the Halloween festivities.

We love dressing up, eating candy until we’re stuffed and having an excuse to run through the streets dressed as pumpkins. Who doesn’t, right?

Why the answer is complex

We could easily say, however, that both celebrations coexist today — and even engage in a dialogue. On more than one occasion, I have seen jack-o’-lanterns on Día de los Muertos altars. You can even hear children on Oct. 31 asking, “¿Me da mi calaverita?” — the hyper-Mexican version of “Trick or treat!”

Now, while all this is true, it would be somewhat simplistic to say, “Yes, in Mexico we celebrate everything.” Although it is true that we never lack reasons to throw a party here, the reality is that Halloween celebrations are more of a recreational activity than a cultural one. Day of the Dead is something we collectively look forward to and honor with greater solemnity — ranging from our intimate family traditions at home to the grand public displays we see in the streets year after year.

So yeah, if you ask a Mexican if they celebrate Halloween, they’ll probably say they do — but that they observe Día de Muertos.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to set out a Coke for my grandma; she’s on her way back from the other side.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the Mexico News Daily Features desk. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams anthropology. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Last week, 56-year-old Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a Dallas resident of decades and lawful green card holder, died at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas. His daughter says staff at the center would not give him his heart, diabetes and blood pressure medications, and that he told her they ignored him when he reported trouble breathing and tightness in his chest. The Webb County Medical Examiner is performing his autopsy, and no cause of death has been released. He is the 18th Mexican national to die in U.S. immigration custody or during enforcement operations since January 20, 2025.

For those of you keeping track, that is 15 deaths of Mexican nationals in custody and 3 during enforcement operations — 18 in total since Trump took office for a second time. Human Rights Watch counted 52 deaths of people of all nationalities in ICE custody in the 500 days between January 20, 2025, and June 4, 2026, roughly three a month. AFP reports that at least 30 people died in U.S. migrant detention centers last year, the most since ICE was created.

It’s easy to write off the 18 deaths as statistics or soundbites in the daily news cycle. It’s easy to say they were “criminals that shouldn’t have been here in the first place.” So let’s look at the facts, drawing on a recent profile conducted by CNN.

All 18 were men. The youngest was 19, the oldest was 68.

Some had spent decades in the U.S. ICE says one entered in 1976, and another had lived here about 35 years, worked in construction and had three U.S. citizen children. Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades. Others arrived recently: ICE says one entered in 2022 and another in December 2023.

ICE’s own descriptions of their records vary widely. One was sentenced in 2005 to 20 years for attempted sexual contact with a minor. Others were detained for driving without a valid license, littering or public intoxication. For several, CNN’s profiles cite no criminal charges or record.

The 17 deaths CNN profiled occurred in at least 8 states. This suggests a pattern rather than a single “bad cop” or rogue department. The Department of Homeland Security denies that deaths in its facilities have increased and says detainees receive proper medical treatment.

There are an estimated 38 million people of Mexican origin living in the U.S. today. Given the current environment in the country, many in this community have a relative, friend or neighbor who is living in fear or has been mistreated.

Latino voters also helped elect the current administration. Trump won 46% of the Latino vote in 2024, according to exit polls, up from 32% in 2020. Pew research finds that approval among Latino voters who backed him has since fallen 27 points, to 66%. These figures cover Latino voters broadly, not Mexican-Americans specifically.

The key issue I am raising here is about how people should be treated.

This is not about whether one belongs to the left or right political party, or about opposing border control. I am not suggesting that a country shouldn’t enforce its borders. Of course it should. The border has not always been secure, and immigration policy has often been applied inconsistently or unfairly, if at all. Those convicted of crimes should be punished. Overstaying a visa is a violation of federal immigration law and should have consequences.

The issue is how people are treated once the government has them in its custody. Many Americans who agreed that “something needed to be done” have been repulsed by ICE tactics in their communities. U.S. politicians have not agreed on updated, sensible immigration policy in decades. But whatever the policy, a person in federal custody is the government’s responsibility. We have all read about ICE signing bonuses, hiring sprees, pressure to meet arrest quotas, the lack of collaboration with local authorities and expedited, insufficient training.

Consider the reverse. If one American were dying in a foreign government’s custody nearly every month, we would expect State Department warnings, a drop in tourism and a damaged reputation for that country. The comparison is not about crime or illegal migration. It is about deaths in the custody of a state. That is why Mexico’s government has demanded investigations and filed criminal complaints with U.S. prosecutors.

Many readers will hear “Americans killed in Mexico” and think of drug violence. That is a different matter. These deaths happened in government custody, under government responsibility. That is the standard we would demand for our own citizens abroad.

Neighbors, not enemies

Many Americans have Mexican neighbors and workers they value and live alongside. Many of those same Americans now feel anger over rising costs and failing institutions and leadership, on both the left and the right. In recent polling, nearly eight in 10 Latino voters said they were “very concerned” about the cost of food and consumer goods, above the roughly two-thirds of Americans overall.

Directing that anger at each other is a mistake. Americans can be forgiven for being overwhelmed by inflation, gas prices, interest rates, midterms, job-loss fears and AI risks. But whatever our views on immigration, we should not lose sight of how people are treated while they are in the government’s care.

What you can do

If you are an American living in Mexico, try to understand the anger that locals might have towards the United States. Mexicans are watching their citizens die in U.S. custody, and their government has condemned the deaths and begun filing complaints with U.S. prosecutors. That anger is aimed at a policy and likely at government officials, not at you. It’s important to listen and acknowledge their frustrations. Write to your senators and congresspeople. Tell them the “how” of enforcement matters: medical care, transparency and accountability for deaths in custody are minimum expectations. Our immigration policy needed to change. Most people accept that now, but roughly three people dying in federal custody each month should make us all ask what is going on. Write to MND. We invite you to write us about how you see this issue where you live, or experiences you have had talking to locals in Mexico about this issue.

I sincerely hope that this will be seen not as a Republican or Democrat issue but one of basic human rights and decency, and as a result, be acted on quickly before there are more tragic incidents.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: New episode: The real story behind Mexico’s record exports
World.content:
Mexico’s exports are booming. In fact, in July they increased by 44% compared to last year, and are up almost 28% year to date. Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, ahead of Canada and China.

One would think that kind of growth would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy. But is it really as good as it sounds?

A few reasons for caution:

The growth is concentrated. Electrical and electronic equipment, including AI servers, jumped 134% in July and overtook autos for the first time. Auto exports are roughly flat this year, and oil exports are down.

Imports are booming too. They are up about 26% year to date and grew 45.7% in July, producing a rare monthly trade deficit. Imports from Taiwan have more than tripled. If imports are up as much as exports, what is Mexico adding?

Value added is thin. An estimated 3 cents of every dollar of electronics exports is Mexican added value, roughly a tenth of what Mexico adds in the vehicle segment.

The economy isn’t keeping pace. Mexican GDP is generally expected to grow only 1.2%-1.5% this year, well below the U.S. growth rate.

So what is really going on, and what does it mean for Mexico?

Check out this week’s “Confidently Wrong” podcast as we dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding of the real implications.

Latin American investors face a week of two central banks and one US election. Brazil’s central bank decides on Wednesday and Mexico’s on Thursday, while the US votes on Tuesday and publishes its jobs report on Friday.

Stock markets in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia are closed on Monday 2 November for holidays, so Tuesday is their first trading day. Country choice matters more than a regional trend, because Brazil is cutting interest rates while Mexico has held its rate at 6.50%.

Three Things to Watch

Brazil’s rate cut. Copom has cut five times in 2026 and the rate stands at 13.75%. The central bank’s weekly Focus survey of economists showed a median of 13.50% for this meeting on 23 October.

Mexico’s pause. Banxico held its rate at 6.50% on 24 September, its third hold in a row. Polymarket traders price another hold on Thursday at 90.0%.

Brazil’s central bank decides on interest rates on Wednesday 4 November at 9.30 pm UTC. The central bank’s Focus survey median expects a cut to 13.50% from 13.75%.

Why does the US jobs report matter for Latin America?

A strong jobs report would lift the dollar and US bond yields, which makes dollar borrowing costlier and can weigh on Latin American currencies. The report is due on Friday 6 November.

Peru’s inflation and Chile’s economic activity on Monday, Brazil’s factory survey on Tuesday and Chile’s inflation on Friday. Each can shift expectations for local interest rates.

No. Brazil’s B3 and Mexico’s BMV stock exchanges are closed, Colombia has a public holiday, and trading resumes on Tuesday 3 November.

World.title: Turkey’s UN Climate Talks Start in 8 Days
World.content:
Türkiye’s UN climate summit, COP31, opens in the Mediterranean city of Antalya in eight days. It is the 31st annual “Conference of the Parties” under the UN climate convention,.

Türkiye is the official name of Turkey.The official calendar is now set, and Türkiye’s environment minister said on Oct. 22 that 85 world leaders have confirmed they will attend.

No names have been published.Published Sunday, Nov. 1, 2:40 a.m. EST (10:40 a.m. in Antalya) · Source: UNFCCC (the UN climate secretariat), COP31 Türkiye presidency

Key Facts When: COP31 runs Nov. 9-20, 2026 at the Antalya EXPO Center, Türkiye.

Leaders: The Antalya Leaders Summit is Wednesday Nov. 11 and Thursday Nov. 12; 85 leaders are said to be coming.

Time: Antalya is 8 hours ahead of US Eastern Time; 10 a.m. there is 2 a.m. EST.

Unknown: Which leaders come, and whether a joint declaration emerges.

What The Calendar Now Shows

COP31 runs alongside CMP21, the meeting of Kyoto Protocol members, and CMA8, the meeting of Paris Agreement members. Two technical bodies, the Subsidiary Bodies for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA65) and for Implementation (SBI65), meet Nov. 9-14.

The UN climate secretariat (UNFCCC) lists preparatory meetings before the summit: least-developed countries on Nov. 3-4, small island states and an African Group meeting on Nov. 5-6, and the Group of 77 and China, the large developing-country bloc, on Nov. 7-8. The venue, including registration, closes on Sunday, Nov. 15.

File photo from COP28 in Dubai, 2023. COP31 in Antalya brings the same UN process to Türkiye.

Which Day Covers What

Türkiye’s programme gives each day a theme. Nov. 9 covers food, agriculture and health; Nov. 10 energy and transport; Nov. 11 zero waste and the circular economy; and Nov. 12 resilient cities.

Later days focus on oceans and nature, human and social development, and implementation. Final negotiations are set for Nov. 20.

Leaders On Nov. 11-12

Heads of state and government deliver national statements at the leaders’ summit on Nov. 11-12. A resumed high-level segment on Nov. 17-18 hears ministers and senior officials of countries whose leader did not speak.

The 85-leader figure comes from the host government, and no names are public yet. Whether the summit produces a joint declaration is also unknown.

What It Means for US Readers

Antalya runs on UTC+3, three hours ahead of Greenwich time and eight hours ahead of US Eastern Time once US clocks fall back on Nov. 1. A 10 a.m. session in Antalya starts at 2 a.m. EST.

The key window for US watchers is Nov. 11-12, when energy, transport and circular-economy days could produce pledges that touch US companies. The official schedule is marked indicative, so check the COP31 pages from Nov. 9 for broadcast times.

What Is Not Known

The official schedule carries no clock time for the opening sessions, and some items are still marked to be confirmed. We found no new agreement, emissions pledge or finance package announced so far.

It is also unclear which countries will announce new commitments. Türkiye’s presidency says the summit should give political momentum to its priority themes.

When and where is COP31?

COP31 runs from Monday, Nov. 9 to Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 at the Antalya EXPO Center in Aksu, Antalya, Türkiye. The Antalya Leaders Summit is Nov. 11-12.

How does the time difference affect US viewers?

Antalya is 8 hours ahead of US Eastern Time after US daylight saving ends on Nov. 1. A 10 a.m. Antalya session is 2 a.m. EST.

Has a list of attending leaders been released?

Türkiye’s environment minister said on Oct. 22 that 85 leaders have confirmed. No names have been published.

World.title: China Readies Shenzhen Asia-Pacific Summit
World.content:
Shenzhen, China’s southern tech hub, is in the last stretch before the APEC leaders’ meeting: organisers of the summit’s business forum said on Oct. 31 that preparations have entered their final stage. APEC, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, is a club of 21 Pacific-rim economies that includes the United States and China.

The leaders gather on Nov. 18-19, 17 days from now. This weekend, the top US diplomat floated a possible leaders’ encounter there.

Published Sunday, Nov. 1, 2:40 a.m. EST (3:40 p.m. in Shenzhen) · Source: Shenzhen municipal government, China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, US Secretary of State

Key Facts When: Leaders meet Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen; a business forum, the CEO Summit, runs Nov. 17-18.

Host: China hosts APEC for the third time, after 2001 and 2014.

Time: Shenzhen is 13 hours ahead of US Eastern Time on Nov. 18.

Unknown: Whether US and Russian leaders will meet; Rubio called it only an opportunity.

Final Preparations Are Under Way

The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, which hosts the CEO Summit, said on Oct. 31 that its preparations have entered the final stage. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting takes place in Shenzhen, in Guangdong, China’s southern manufacturing province, under the theme “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.”

The official APEC calendar lists the Concluding Senior Officials’ Meeting, the working-level gathering that settles the paperwork, on Nov. 14-15. The CEO Summit follows on Nov. 17-18, then the leaders’ meeting on Nov. 18-19.

Who Hosts The Business Summit

The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, a state-backed trade promotion body, hosts the CEO Summit. It expects about 1,000 government and business representatives from APEC economies.

Planned topics include the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, a long-discussed regional trade-pact idea, connectivity, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and sustainable development. The CEO Summit’s own theme is “Promoting Prosperity Together for a Win-Win Future.”

Will Washington And Moscow Meet?

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday, Oct. 31, that he briefly discussed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov “the opportunity for our leaders to potentially interact at APEC next month.” The talk took place on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta and was not a formal meeting.

The possibility is all it is: a bilateral meeting has not been scheduled or confirmed.

What To Watch

The next fixed dates are Nov. 14-15, Nov. 17-18 and Nov. 18-19. Any formal confirmation of a US-Russian leaders’ encounter would be the first real signal of how the summit is shaping up.

Trade, tariffs and regional supply chains are the usual business at APEC, so US companies should watch for a leaders’ declaration at the close.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors and companies with China exposure, APEC is where trade and supply-chain signals from 21 economies appear in one place. Each economy’s leaders’ attendance is still to be confirmed.

Shenzhen is on China Standard Time, UTC+8, which is 13 hours ahead of US Eastern Time on Nov. 18. A morning session there on Nov. 18 begins on the evening of Nov. 17 in New York.

What Is Not Known

We found no official opening time or daily agenda for the leaders’ meeting. No joint statement or other outcome has been announced.

Whether a US-Russian leaders’ encounter happens remains unconfirmed. Rubio’s remarks establish only that officials discussed the idea.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the 2026 APEC leaders’ meeting?

It takes place in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China, on Nov. 18-19, 2026. China hosts APEC for the third time.

What events surround the leaders’ meeting?

The Concluding Senior Officials’ Meeting runs Nov. 14-15 and the CEO Summit Nov. 17-18, both in Shenzhen. About 1,000 government and business representatives are expected at the CEO Summit.

Has any world leader confirmed attendance?

Rubio said he and Lavrov briefly discussed a possible US-Russian leaders’ interaction at APEC, but nothing is confirmed. Attendance by individual leaders is still to be announced.

World.title: North Macedonia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
NORTH MACEDONIA · POLITICS

Key Facts The system North Macedonia is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister runs the government and the president is largely ceremonial.

Who leads Hristijan Mickoski, leader of the conservative VMRO-DPMNE party, has been prime minister since 24 June 2024.

The majority 77 of 120 lawmakers voted for his cabinet in June 2024. The next election is due in 2028.

The EU stall Brussels wants a constitutional change that names Bulgarians as a people of the country. Mickoski says he wants guarantees first.

For US readers North Macedonia has been a NATO ally since 27 March 2020, in a region where Washington watches Russian influence.

North Macedonia is a small Balkan country of about 1.8 million people, and its government holds a firm majority. Since mid-2024 a conservative-led coalition has run it, while a dispute with neighbouring Bulgaria keeps its European Union bid on hold.

This guide, part of the Rio Times Europe politics coverage, explains who holds power in October 2026 and why it matters to US readers. A neighbour in the same fight is Bulgaria, covered in our Bulgaria guide.

Published Sunday, 1 November 2026, ET · Primary sources: North Macedonia’s State Election Commission, the Assembly, the State Statistical Office, the Council of the EU and NATO.

How North Macedonia’s System Works

North Macedonia has a single-chamber parliament called the Assembly, with 120 seats. A party or coalition needs 61 seats to hold a majority.

The prime minister, chosen by the Assembly, directs the cabinet and sets policy. The president is elected by voters for five years and mainly represents the state.

Ethnic Albanians make up about a quarter of the population, according to the 2021 census. A 2001 peace deal, the Ohrid Framework Agreement, ended a short conflict and guarantees them a share of power, which is why Albanian parties sit in most governments.

Who Holds Power Now

Hristijan Mickoski leads VMRO-DPMNE (the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organisation, Democratic Party for Macedonian National Unity), a conservative nationalist party. He became prime minister on 24 June 2024, when 77 of the 120 lawmakers voted for his cabinet and 22 voted against.

His government rests on three groups. VMRO-DPMNE and its allies won 58 seats in the 8 May 2024 election, and they govern with VLEN, a coalition of ethnic Albanian parties, and For Our Macedonia (ZNAM), a small movement that took 6 seats.

Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, a law professor backed by VMRO-DPMNE, was elected president in May 2024. She is the first woman to hold the office.

Afrim Gashi, of the ethnic Albanian party Alternativa, has chaired the Assembly since 28 May 2024. Timčo Mucunski is foreign minister and handles the talks with Bulgaria and Brussels.

File photo: North Macedonian and EU flags above central Skopje. (Photo: Julian Lupyan, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Opposition Camp

The Social Democratic Union of Macedonia (SDSM), the centre-left party that was the main governing party from 2017 until 2024, fell to 18 seats in 2024. Venko Filipče leads it.

The Democratic Union for Integration (DUI), an ethnic Albanian party that was a partner in the previous government, won 18 seats as part of the European Front, a DUI-led alliance. The Left (Levica), a leftist party, won 6 seats.

The governing parties also swept the local elections of autumn 2025.

The 2025 Local Elections

VMRO-DPMNE won most mayoral posts in the local elections, which ended with a second round on 2 November 2025. Orce Gjorgjievski of VMRO-DPMNE won the race for mayor of the capital, Skopje.

Four municipalities, among them Gostivar, had to repeat their votes because turnout fell below the legal threshold of one third. Exact mayor counts changed after those repeat votes, so we do not give a final tally.

Why the EU Bid Is Stuck

North Macedonia has been an EU candidate since 2005, and accession talks opened in July 2022 after Bulgaria’s parliament lifted its veto in June 2022. That deal requires Skopje to amend its constitution so that Bulgarians are named as one of the country’s peoples.

Mickoski says no government can make that change without guarantees. He says he wants Bulgaria to confirm that the amendment is the last condition, and he wants rights for the Macedonian minority in Bulgaria.

Bulgaria holds a presidential runoff on 1 November 2026 between President Iliana Iotova and Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister.

The Name, NATO and the West

The country was called Macedonia until 2019. Under the 2018 Prespa Agreement with Greece it took its present name, which took effect on 12 February 2019, and that deal cleared the way for NATO membership.

North Macedonia became NATO’s 30th member on 27 March 2020.

What It Means for US Readers

North Macedonia is a NATO ally in the Western Balkans, a region where Washington has long tried to limit Russian influence. A stalled EU path can weaken pro-Western voices there, so each step in the Bulgaria dispute is worth watching.

For investors and travellers, the government’s solid majority points to stable policy rather than early elections. The main risk is slow progress toward EU rules, which would shape trade and investment conditions.

For deeper reading, see Greece Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026.

What Is Not Known

We could not verify a recent independent poll, so current party support is unclear. The exact seat count in the Assembly today may differ slightly from the 2024 result because lawmakers can switch groups.

It is not known whether Bulgaria will accept the guarantees Skopje wants. Nor is it clear when the government will bring the constitutional change to a vote.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the prime minister of North Macedonia?

Hristijan Mickoski of VMRO-DPMNE has been prime minister since 24 June 2024. He leads a coalition with VLEN, a bloc of ethnic Albanian parties, and the ZNAM movement.

Who is the president of North Macedonia?

Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, elected in May 2024, is president. The role is mostly ceremonial.

When is the next election in North Macedonia?

The next parliamentary election is due in 2028 and the next presidential election in 2029, based on four- and five-year terms.

Why is North Macedonia’s EU accession stalled?

Bulgaria wants the constitution to name Bulgarians as one of the country’s peoples. Skopje wants guarantees that no new conditions will follow.

Is North Macedonia in NATO?

Yes. It became NATO’s 30th member on 27 March 2020, after settling its name dispute with Greece.
