World.title: Trump Says Flávio Bolsonaro Can Stay in US
World.content:
Photo: Agência Senado / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

A defeated Brazilian presidential candidate is now living in the United States, and the US president says he is welcome to stay. Donald Trump said he has no plans to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, a conservative senator, but that Flávio can remain as long as he wants.

The remarks, made on Saturday 31 October 2026, follow a visa approval already granted by the Trump administration. They matter to US readers because they touch visa policy and relations with Brazil’s government.

Trump has no plans to meet Flávio Bolsonaro but says he is welcome to stay in the US.

Flávio lost the 25 October runoff to Brazil’s President Lula (Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva), 51.79% to 48.21%.

He landed in Miami on 28 October with his family after leaving Brazil by land to Argentina.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a crypto-based market, gives 22.5% to a Trump-Flávio meeting in 2026 (as of 10:08 p.m. ET, 31 October 2026).

As of 1 November 2026, 02:00 GMT

What We Know

Trump said at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida club, on Saturday 31 October that he has no plans to meet Flávio. He added that Flávio can stay in the US as long as he wants.

Flávio is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. He lost the 25 October 2026 runoff to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who won 51.79% of the vote to Flávio’s 48.21%.

Brazil’s electoral court has declared Lula the winner. Trump has called the election “very strange”, “terrible” and a disgrace, and alleged, without evidence, that it was “rigged”.

Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered Flávio to hand in his passports by noon on Tuesday 27 October. He left Brazil late that day by land to Argentina and boarded a private charter.

The plane stopped in Guayaquil, Ecuador, then landed at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport around 9:30 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday 28 October. His family travelled with him, and the Trump administration approved US visas for them that week.

Trump called the family “fine people”. He has not said whether he will receive Flávio in person.

File photo: the Praça dos Três Poderes (Three Powers Plaza) in Brasília, home of Brazil’s Supreme Court, Congress and presidency.

The Case Waiting at Home

In Brazil, Flávio is under investigation in a Federal Police probe into alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The case concerns a sports-betting company and money he allegedly accepted from Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker whose Banco Master failed.

Flávio denies wrongdoing. An investigation is not a conviction, and we report his denial alongside the allegations.

Flávio and Trump met in the Oval Office of the White House on 26 May 2026, during Flávio’s campaign. Trump praised him afterwards as a smart young man who loves Brazil.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, lists a market titled “Will Trump meet with Flávio Bolsonaro in 2026?” It priced a meeting at 22.5% as of 10:08 p.m. ET on 31 October 2026, with about US$77,000 traded.

That price is the market’s implied probability of a meeting, so traders rate it as unlikely but possible. It is a bet, not a poll.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how long Flávio plans to stay or where he lives in the United States. Nor is it clear whether Trump will receive him.

It is also unknown whether Brazil will seek his return or extradition. We will update this report when any of those points is confirmed.

What It Means for US Readers

The case shows how a visa decision can carry political weight between two governments. Washington approved visas for Flávio and his family that week, while Trump questions an election whose result Brazil’s electoral court has declared.

Watch for any move by Brazil’s Supreme Court on his passports or the investigation, and for any sign that Trump will receive him. Our earlier reports, Trump Courts Brazil’s Winner and Loser and On the Run, Flávio Bolsonaro Lands in Miami, give more background.

More coverage is on our Brazil hub. For now the facts are modest: an open door in Washington and no scheduled meeting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will Trump meet Flávio Bolsonaro?

Trump said he has no plans to meet him. Polymarket, a prediction market, priced a meeting in 2026 at 22.5% as of 10:08 p.m. ET on 31 October 2026.

Can Flávio Bolsonaro stay in the US?

Trump said he can stay as long as he wants. The Trump administration approved US visas for him and his family during the week after the 25 October runoff.

How did Flávio Bolsonaro reach Miami?

He left Brazil late on 27 October by land to Argentina, boarded a private charter, stopped in Guayaquil, Ecuador, and landed at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport around 9:30 a.m. Eastern on 28 October.

Is Flávio Bolsonaro under investigation?

Yes, in a Federal Police probe into alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, tied to a sports-betting company and to money allegedly accepted from banker Daniel Vorcaro. He denies wrongdoing, and an investigation is not a conviction.

World.title: New Zealand Advance Voting Passes 500,000
World.content:
File photo: advance voting from a camper van in Christchurch, 2011. Photo: Schwede66, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Key Facts Turnout: More than 500,000 New Zealanders have already voted, a week before election day.

Polls: Reid Research has Labour ahead by 5.8 points; Verian has National ahead by 2.

Results: Election day is Saturday, November 7; polls close at 1 a.m. Eastern (7 p.m. in New Zealand).

Prediction markets: Polymarket gives National 72.0% and Labour 27.5% to win most seats (Oct 31, 7:23 p.m. ET).

New Zealand is voting early, and in large numbers. More than 500,000 ballots have been cast since advance voting opened on October 26, a week before the New Zealand general election on November 7.

The Electoral Commission, the independent body that runs the vote, has opened advance polling places across the country, and plans more than 2,300 on election day itself.

A Heavy Early Vote, and a Quick Start

Advance voting, meaning voting before election day, opened on Monday, October 26. The Commission counted 175,748 votes in the first two days, so the pace has held up since.

New Zealanders abroad began voting on October 21. Enrolment, the deadline to be on the voting list, closed on Sunday, October 25.

Nobody can say yet who benefits from the early rush. The Commission does not publish how early voters lean.

File photo: the debating chamber of New Zealand’s House of Representatives in Wellington.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Two Polls, Two Different Leaders

The newest poll comes from Reid Research, a New Zealand polling firm. Taken on October 20–26 among 1,000 people, it has Labour at 30.6% and National at 24.8%.

In that poll the Greens stand at 14.5%, ACT (a free-market party) at 10.1% and New Zealand First (a populist party) at 9.9%. Opportunity, a small newer party, is at 7.2%, and Te Pāti Māori, the Māori Party, at 1.9%.

A Verian poll, published on October 27 by another New Zealand polling firm, tells the opposite story. It puts National at 29% and Labour at 27%, with the Greens at 15%, ACT at 12% and New Zealand First at 10%.

Verian has Opportunity at 6%. Both polls therefore place it above the 5% party-vote line that normally decides whether a party wins seats.

Why the Smaller Parties Decide This

New Zealand uses mixed-member proportional voting, which gives each party seats roughly in line with its share of the party vote. No party usually wins a majority alone, so coalitions decide who governs.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon leads a National-led government. Chris Hipkins, the Labour leader, heads the main opposition bloc.

A party that clears 5% enters Parliament and can tip a close contest. That is why Opportunity matters far more than its single-digit poll numbers suggest.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction platform, favour National. On October 31 at 7:23 p.m. ET they priced National at 72.0% and Labour at 27.5% to win the most seats, with about US$141,000 traded.

The same platform gives a National, ACT and New Zealand First coalition 59.0% to form the next government. A Labour, Green and Māori Party coalition is at 23.0%.

Prediction-market prices are bets, not polls. Here they lean toward National while the newest poll leans toward Labour.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Polls close at 7 p.m. in New Zealand on Saturday, November 7, and first results follow soon after. That is 1 a.m. Eastern the same day and 10 p.m. Pacific on Friday, November 6, once US daylight saving time ends on Sunday, November 1.

New Zealand is a close US security and trade partner, so a change of government matters to investors and diplomats. A coalition deal could take days after the vote to settle.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the early voters lean to Labour, National or the smaller parties. It is also not known whether Opportunity will clear the 5% line.

Police say they are making inquiries into claims by two people that they voted more than once. The claims have not been verified as accurate.

Official results are due on November 27, after special votes (ballots cast outside a voter’s home area) are counted.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is New Zealand’s election day?

It is Saturday, November 7, 2026, with voting from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. New Zealand time. First results follow soon after polls close.

Who is ahead in the polls?

It depends on the poll. Reid Research has Labour on 30.6% against National’s 24.8%, while Verian has National on 29% against Labour’s 27%.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Blue Zone Seal and Wellness Tourism Push for Nicoya
World.content:
Costa Rica has laid out a timeline to develop the Nicoya Peninsula’s Blue Zone as a wellness tourism destination, with an official Blue Zone seal, three new tourism products by 2028 and national and international promotion campaigns. The plan runs alongside expanded care for the region’s oldest residents.

The measures are part of the Costa Rica Centenaria strategy, which President Laura Fernández Delgado announced on July 24 during a tour of Guanacaste. According to the Ministry of National Planning and Economic Policy (MIDEPLAN), the National Council for Older Persons (CONAPAM) will lead the strategy, which is still going through the administrative process to make it official.

The Nicoya Peninsula is one of a handful of regions worldwide known as Blue Zones, where an unusually high share of residents live into their 90s and past 100. Researchers have long debated whether that longevity advantage can survive among younger generations of Nicoyans.

The strategy covers health, social protection, tourism, infrastructure and local economic development. The announcement does not include budget figures for any of its components. On the tourism side, the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) plans to develop experiences tied to wellness, nature, culture and local traditions.

In 2026, the work centers on forming an interinstitutional team and carrying out a tourism carrying-capacity study, an assessment of how many visitors the area can absorb without damaging it. An inventory of the region’s existing wellness tourism offerings is due in 2027. A national promotion campaign is planned for 2027 and an international one for 2028, the same year three new tourism products are to be launched. The plan also calls for an official Blue Zone seal.

The push builds on the country’s broader effort to market itself as a wellness destination, including a national wellness route launched last December and growing demand from older travelers seeking health-focused trips. The care measures center on the people behind the Blue Zone’s reputation. CONAPAM is to create a National Registry of Centenarians between 2027 and 2030 to keep updated information on Costa Ricans aged 100 and older.

A national support program delivered through the National Care Network aims to reach 100% of the country’s centenarians and to strengthen daytime care services. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS) plans to give each identified centenarian a comprehensive geriatric assessment and an individual care plan covering medical follow-up, home visits and disease prevention.

The Ministry of Health intends to bring the municipalities in the high-longevity area into its age-friendly cities and communities program, with a target of 80% participation in 2027 and 100% in 2028. The strategy also includes two community economic projects in rural Guanacaste.

In Pozo de Agua de Nicoya, a rural agritourism and agroecology project with technical support from the National Training Institute (INA) involves 22 women livestock producers and 16 women entrepreneurs in traditional cooking, with about 152 direct beneficiaries. In Pochote de Quebrada Honda, a project to strengthen artisanal fishing and community development involves 36 organized fishers and shellfish harvesters, with an estimated 140 direct beneficiaries.

The Social Protection Board (JPS), which runs the national lottery, has registered two projects to buy medical equipment for La Anexión Hospital in Nicoya, both still in the pre-execution stage. The plan also includes a four-wheel-drive vehicle for the Nandayure Pain Clinic and Palliative Care Association.

According to MIDEPLAN, the strategy is meant to help preserve the region’s longevity, strengthen public services and create sustainable development opportunities for the communities of the peninsula.

World.title: Chaves Calls TEC Rector a Terrorist as 417 Limón Students Face Campus Closure
World.content:
Former president Rodrigo Chaves, who now serves as minister of the Presidency and of Finance, called Costa Rica Institute of Technology (TEC) rector María Estrada a terrorist after she warned that a budget cut could force the immediate closure of the institute’s Limón campus, where 417 students are enrolled.

Chaves made the remark on the program No Mientas Show and, when asked, confirmed that he was referring to Estrada. He accused the rector of holding the Limón campus hostage over a reduction he put at roughly 0.4% of the institute’s budget. He also said university authorities were unwilling to give up their privileges.

The Limón Academic Center offers degrees in business administration, computer engineering and industrial production engineering. Estrada has said the campus would have to close at once if a ₡491 million ($1.08 million) reduction in the second extraordinary budget for 2026 takes effect.

Jorge Herrera, president of the National Council of Rectors (Conare), has linked the funds at stake to Law 9635, the 2018 public finance law that helps finance the universities’ regional campuses. Those campuses allow students outside the Central Valley to earn a degree without moving away from home.

The remark escalates a dispute that has been building for weeks. Earlier this month, Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez accused Estrada of political extortion over the same closure warning and pointed to a TEC surplus of more than ₡20 billion ($43.9 million). Estrada has said the law does not allow those funds to be used for the campus’s operating costs.

TEC said on Oct. 15 that it had not received that month’s funding transfer and had used its own resources to pay salaries and scholarships. The institute asked the Finance Ministry, the Presidency and the Legislative Assembly to reject the cut.

TEC’s communications department said the rector had not yet seen Chaves’s comments and would not respond for now. María José Zamora, president of the TEC student federation, rejected the label. She said Estrada was defending a regional campus and has faced attacks because she is a woman.

The Limón dispute sits inside a broader fight over public university funding. Late on Oct. 20, the legislative budget committee approved an ₡8.05 billion ($17.7 million) reduction to deferred funds owed to the public universities in the 2027 budget, through a motion filed by the ruling Pueblo Soberano party (PPSO). About ₡1.9 billion ($4.17 million) of that amount corresponds to TEC.

The cuts drew thousands of students and staff into the streets of San José on Oct. 20, in a march led by the rectors of all five public universities. They come as the government faces a widening revenue shortfall that has also squeezed the courts, police and schools. The full Legislative Assembly must vote on the 2027 budget before the end of November, while the second extraordinary budget for 2026 remains under debate. Those two votes will determine whether the Limón campus keeps its doors open.

World.title: Two of Every Three Dairy Imports in Costa Rica Now Come From the US
World.content:
Costa Rica imported $66.4 million in dairy products from the United States in the first eight months of 2026, nearly four times the $17.5 million recorded in the same period of 2020, according to figures from the foreign trade promotion agency Procomer. US products accounted for 65.2% of the country’s $101.8 million in dairy imports through August, which arrived from 37 countries.

In the same period of 2020, total dairy imports came to $36.6 million. Imports from the European Union reached $14.9 million this year, up 15.4% from the same period of 2025. Two changes opened the door. Since Jan. 1, 2025, US dairy products have entered Costa Rica duty-free, after the tariff phase-out under the Dominican Republic-Central America Free Trade Agreement (CAFTA-DR) concluded.

Beginning in May 2025, the government also sped up the approval of US dairy plants at Washington’s request, once sanitary requirements were met, under a resolution issued by the National Animal Health Service (Senasa) on April 10, 2025. The effect on approvals has been steep. Senasa’s registry listed 259 authorized US dairy plants as of Oct. 21, up from 43 in January.

The shift is also visible in product registrations. Between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, the Ministry of Health’s Regístrelo platform listed 208 cheese products of US origin, compared with 178 from Costa Rica, 49 from Italy and seven from France. Byron Gurdian, head of epidemiological surveillance and animal health at Senasa, said every foreign establishment that exports animal products to Costa Rica must be controlled by the agency.

He said how long an approval remains valid depends on whether the exporting country has a free trade agreement with Costa Rica. Plants from countries without one must renew their approval every three years. Foreign trade specialist Álvaro Monge said the United States, the United Kingdom and European Union members have equivalence agreements under which Costa Rica recognizes their health inspection systems.

Plants from other countries must complete questionnaires reviewed by Senasa and may face on-site visits, a process that can take months or years. Monge said the agency gives priority to scientific criteria over commercial ones. Local producers see the trend differently. Ivannia Quesada, president of the National Chamber of Milk Producers, said the rise in plant authorizations coincided with the rise in imports.

She said foreign plants are subject to different controls than Costa Rica’s own dairy industry, and that the government has known about the producers’ concerns since 2025 but gave the chamber an unsatisfactory response. Quesada also attributed the growth in imports to the strength of the colón against the dollar, which has squeezed local producers and made foreign goods cheaper, and to the displacement of dairy-farming families from the business.

According to Quesada, authorities told the chamber that the approvals met international standards. Cooperativa Dos Pinos is itself among the importers. Marina Rodríguez, the cooperative’s corporate director of sustainability and corporate relations, said Dos Pinos brings in US mozzarella and parmesan under its own brand and distributes them in Central America and the Dominican Republic.

Rodríguez said more competition is a normal result of globalization and trade agreements, and that the cooperative sees it as a challenge. She said Dos Pinos processes 1.4 million liters (370,000 gallons) of Costa Rican milk a day and pays out nearly ₡500 million ($1.1 million) daily to about 1,300 member producers.

Consumer advocates welcomed the change. Erick Ulate, executive director of the Free Consumers Association, said the plant approvals are routine work by Senasa and its foreign counterparts and ensure that imports meet quality and safety standards. He said the result is a wider variety of products at better prices.

The figures come days after the government dropped its bid to join a Pacific trade pact. Washington has also pressed for wider access to the Costa Rican market for US farm products. With the tariff phase-out complete, each of the 259 approved US plants can now ship dairy products to Costa Rica duty-free.

World.title: American Pilot Overturns Mother’s Costa Rica Will Over Missing Interpreters
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Supreme Court has upheld the annulment of an American woman’s will because she signed a Spanish-language document without the two interpreters the law requires. The decision reopens an estate that includes a 55% stake in a dairy farm that sells its milk to Dos Pinos.

The ruling by the court’s Second Chamber, issued in March 2026, sides with the woman’s son, a pilot who lives in Ohio. The will had left him nothing and named his brother sole and universal heir. Besides the dairy stake, the estate includes several agricultural properties, personal property and investments, according to the facts set out in the ruling.

The woman, a U.S. citizen living in Guanacaste, signed an open will before a notary public in October 2014. She died in February 2019. Three months later, her other son, who also lived in Costa Rica, was appointed executor as the only person apparently named in the will. After learning of his mother’s death, the pilot traveled to Costa Rica in June 2019 with his legal representatives. He sought to establish his standing as a legal heir and to object to the will.

His legal team argued the document lacked the translation required by Article 584 of the Civil Code. Because no record showed that at least two interpreters had taken part, they said, the will was absolutely null. Despite the objection, the notary handling the probate declared the brother sole and universal heir in September 2019. That notary considered it enough that the notary who drew up the will had recorded that she translated it into English herself.

The pilot then sued the estate and his brother directly. Besides the language issue, he alleged that no meeting of interested parties had been called. He also said other assets had been left out of the probate, including household goods, bank accounts, cooperative shares, vehicles and investments of significant value.

He asked the court to declare the will absolutely null and end his brother’s administration of the estate. He also sought an accounting, the return of assets his brother had disposed of, and recognition of both brothers as equal heirs. The brother rejected the claims and raised several defenses, including lack of standing.

In June 2022, the Guanacaste Collegiate Civil Trial Court partially upheld the lawsuit and annulled the will. The court also voided every act that flowed from it, including the executor’s appointment and the sole-heir declaration. It ordered the brother to pay legal costs, with attorney fees set at ¢54.9 million (about $122,000).

The brother appealed to the Second Chamber. He argued that his mother understood Spanish after years in Costa Rica and had signed other documents in the language. In his view, the notary’s English translation was a professional courtesy, not a legal requirement, and the trial court had imposed conditions the law does not contain.

The magistrates disagreed. They concluded it had not been proven that the woman understood Spanish well enough to grasp the legal scope of her own will. A key piece of evidence was the will itself, in which the notary recorded that she had translated it into English because the woman did not understand Spanish well.

The court also weighed testimony from that notary and from a second notary who took part in the signing and later handled the probate. The court treated both statements with caution because both notaries had taken part in the acts under challenge. Their testimony also contradicted what the will itself recorded about the woman’s difficulty with Spanish.

According to the ruling, getting by in Spanish, living in Costa Rica for years or signing documents in the language does not show that a person understands the legal implications of a last will. The justices found that the notary’s own translation could not take the place of the two interpreters required by Article 584. They called that omission an essential defect, rejected the appeal and left the annulment in place.

Article 584 states that anyone making a will in a foreign language before a notary must do so in the presence of two interpreters of their choosing. Those interpreters translate the testator’s instructions into Spanish.

The formality carries particular weight because Costa Rican law gives testators broad control over their estates. Under Article 595 of the Civil Code, a person may leave property to whomever they choose, provided they secure financial support for certain dependents. A will that excludes an adult child can therefore stand if it meets every legal requirement.

André Cappella, an associate attorney at the firm Quatro Legal, said everyday conversation in Spanish or a history of signing documents in the language does not prove that someone understands a will’s implications. He added that it is not enough for a notary who speaks the testator’s language to translate the document. When there is doubt, he said, the prudent course is to use the two interpreters the law requires. A version of the will in the testator’s own language can also be prepared, but it does not replace the legal formalities.

Cappella said many defects in a will cannot be corrected after the testator dies. Other common grounds for annulment include a missing date, time or signature. Others are failing to read the document, using witnesses who have an interest in the estate, and failing to complete every formality in a single sitting.

Unless another valid will exists, the estate now falls under the rules for succession without a will. Under Article 572 of the Civil Code, the first order of heirs is a person’s children, parents and surviving spouse or partner. The case shows that the validity of a will in Costa Rica can depend as much on how it was signed as on what it says.

World.title: Scarlet Macaws Start Nesting in Costa Rica, and You Can Watch Live
World.content:
Scarlet macaws (Ara macao) on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast have begun pairing off for a new breeding season, and anyone with a phone or computer can watch part of it unfold from inside the nest. Punta Leona Beach Club & Nature Resort, in Garabito near Tárcoles, has added three camera-equipped artificial nests to its scarlet macaw conservation program, bringing the total to 11 for the 2026 season. The new nests were installed with support from Grupo INS, the state-owned insurance group.

The cameras stream live on the program’s website, lapasrojaspuntaleona.com, which also has an English-language version. The birds are wild, not captive or handled, and the cameras let researchers follow them without disturbing the nests. According to the program, courtship runs from October through December, when pairs form, search for cavities and prepare nest sites. Egg-laying and incubation follow, with the first eggs and chicks expected between December and January 2027. The nesting period runs through June.

The cameras will record how many eggs are laid in each nest, how many hatch and how many chicks survive to leave it, along with the toll taken by natural predators. Figures the program released in February show that eggs take 23 to 28 days to hatch and chicks spend 78 to 90 days in the nest before their first flight.

Across the 2017 to 2025 seasons, the program recorded 98 scarlet macaw eggs in its monitored nests. Of those, 69 hatched and 46 chicks fledged, according to the same February figures. The 11 artificial nests are named Guanacaste, Guayabón, Wisconsin, Ceibo Bajo, Ceibo Alto, Pochote, Panamá, Camíbar, Espavel, Guayacán and Alfa. In February, the program reported monitoring 17 nests, 10 natural and seven artificial. The new announcement does not say how many natural nests are being followed this season.

Each fiberglass nest stands about 1 meter (3.3 feet) tall and 50 centimeters (20 inches) across, with a cavity designed to mimic a tree hollow. The nests are mounted in trees 15 to 20 meters (49 to 66 feet) tall and lined with a layer of wood chips. Biologist Christopher Vaughan, who coordinates the project, said the program began 36 years ago and that early studies of natural nesting cavities shaped the design of the artificial ones. The first nests were built from wood, plastic and other materials in a workshop at Punta Leona, he said.

Vaughan said some of the residents who joined the nest-building effort had been poachers known as laperos, who took macaw chicks from the wild. Today they are the ones who build the artificial nests, he said, calling it an excellent example of habitat management. That history still matters. In other parts of the country, poachers continue to target macaw chicks in the Osa region during breeding season.

The program says about 215 scarlet macaws were counted in the area in the early 1990s and that current monitoring puts the number near 800, a nearly fourfold increase. Earlier program materials put the 1992 baseline at 226 birds. In April, Vaughan estimated that about 70 of the roughly 800 wild scarlet macaws in the Central Pacific live at Punta Leona itself.

Alongside the nests, the program has protected habitat and set up nurseries of native trees to reforest the region, providing future nesting trees and food sources. According to the program, the macaws nest in trees such as ceiba, gallinazo and javillo, and feed on seeds from species including royal palm, ojoche, espavel, teak and beach almond.

Scarlet macaws are now also recorded in communities including Esparza, Orotina, San Mateo, Acosta and Parrita, and around La Cangreja National Park, the program says. Nearby Carara National Park remains one of the most reliable places in the country to see them in flight. Gerald Jiménez, Punta Leona’s corporate relations manager, said the resort aims to go beyond sustainability and leave its surroundings better than it found them. The resort also called on other companies to join conservation efforts, as Grupo INS has done.

Punta Leona has also spoken out on the keeping of wild birds. In April, it opposed a draft revision of Costa Rica’s wildlife regulations that critics said could open the door to keeping macaws and parrots in captivity. The program’s long-running work with scarlet macaws rests on the opposite idea, that the birds breed and fly free.

The nest streams run around the clock, and activity inside the nests is expected to pick up from December, when the first eggs are due.

World.title: Expect Gusts Up to 85 km/h and Rain in Costa Rica This Weekend
World.content:
If you’re heading into the mountains or to northern Guanacaste today, expect strong, gusty winds. Gusts could reach 85 km/h (53 mph) in those areas on Saturday, Oct. 31, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). In the Central Valley and the North Pacific, gusts should run between 30 and 60 km/h (19 to 37 mph). That’s enough to rattle loose roofing, bring down branches and push high-sided vehicles around on exposed stretches of road.

The cause is rising atmospheric pressure over the northern Caribbean, which is driving the trade winds across Costa Rica harder than usual. The IMN expects moderate to strong winds to continue through the rest of the weekend, not just today. Rain is also in the forecast. Extra moisture is bringing showers to the Caribbean and the Northern Zone from early in the day, and that rain is expected to spread into the mountains of the Central Valley and areas to the east.

In the afternoon, the IMN expects isolated downpours in the mountains of the Central Pacific and scattered downpours with thunderstorms in the South Pacific. Along the South Pacific coast, the rain could last into the early evening, while the Central Valley may see occasional showers.

If you have a volcano hike, a canopy tour or a high-elevation park on your schedule, wind is the main thing to watch. Ridgelines and open travetake the strongest gusts, so check with your tour operator before you drive out, since wind can affect zip lines and hanging bridges.

On the road, give yourself extra time on mountain routes and across Guanacaste’s open lowlands, where crosswinds hit hardest. Watch for fallen branches and debris after strong gusts, and keep both hands on the wheel. At home, bring in or tie down anything loose on patios and balconies, from chairs to potted plants. Gusts this strong can damage roofs, snap tree limbs and bring down power lines, so outages are possible in the windiest areas.

In the South Pacific, get off the beach and out of the water at the first sound of thunder, because lightning often strikes ahead of the rain. The wind and showers also arrive as the Pacific coast wraps up its highest tides of the season, which run through today. Going out tonight for Halloween? A light jacket is a good idea in the Central Valley, where occasional showers and gusty winds could linger into the evening.

Conditions can change quickly when the trade winds pick up. Check the IMN’s latest update before heading out, and plan for a breezy, unsettled weekend across much of Costa Rica.

World.title: Grynspan Holds Lead as New Emirati Candidate Disappoints in Race to Lead UN
World.content:
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan again finished first on Friday in the UN Security Council’s seventh informal vote in the race for secretary-general, while the new Emirati candidate delivered a disappointing showing. In a closed-door vote, the Security Council’s 15 members anonymously marked each candidate as “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.”

Grynspan, who took leave from her position at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to campaign, received 11 “encourage” votes and four “discourage” votes, according to a diplomatic source. Diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who recently entered the race and was appearing on the ballot for the first time, received seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes.

Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, received nine “encourage” votes, four “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes. Former Guyanese Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett received eight, six and one, respectively. Both finished ahead of the Emirati candidate.

Unlike the previous round, this vote did not use different-colored ballots to distinguish the votes of the Security Council’s five permanent members. In that previous round, none of the seven candidates avoided a negative vote from at least one of the countries with veto power: the United Kingdom, France, the United States, China and Russia.

Former Senegalese President Macky Sall subsequently withdrew, and Nusseibeh, 48, entered the race. Candidates may join at any point until a selection is made. Until then, she had served as minister of state at the UAE’s Foreign Ministry and as special envoy to the United Nations and the European Union. She previously served as the UAE’s ambassador to the UN from 2013 to 2024. Several human rights organizations have opposed her candidacy, accusing her country of financing paramilitary forces in Sudan.

To succeed Portugal’s António Guterres, whose second term ends at the close of this year, a candidate must secure nine votes and avoid a veto. Once a consensus is reached, the candidate’s name will be submitted to the General Assembly, which in practice follows the Security Council’s recommendation.

Under a tradition of geographic rotation that is not always observed, Latin America is laying claim to the position. Meanwhile, numerous countries are pushing for a woman to lead the UN for the first time.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Creepiest Ghost Stories and Mysterious Legends
World.content:
Every society has tales of terror that challenge our imaginations and our courage. Costa Rica has folk tales that include a priest who lost his head over a woman and now walks the land without a head, a wrastle son who was changed into a devil dog named Cadejos that roams at night, snarling and rattling his chain, and a cart that rolls through the rural areas without oxen to pull it, all because its owner built it with lumber meant for the church. These are stories that go way back in time. Some say they are superstitions. Others swear they are true.

There are also some more recent creepy stories that have gained believers because they have been repeated so many times, and they just could, maybe, possibly be true. Back in the 1900’s, cries and screams coming from a newly filled cemetery plot were reported in Heredia but by the time the bureaucracy got around to investigating and opened the casket, it was all scratched and ripped inside.

In Atenas a blond, naked ghost called Macho Chingo was reported walking along the hills. Macho is a common word for someone blond and chingo is used for someone in the buff. Some reports said he was wearing a necktie and that he’s German. In Alajuela everyone knows about the nun that haunts the old hospital building.

But there is one story from more modern times that occurred in Rio Segundo, an eastern suburb of Alajuela that just, possibly, could be true because some people swear to it. Not too long ago Rio Segundo was a decidedly rural area with big coffee haciendas and whole families lived on the land to help with the coffee work.

Among them a young man and his sweetheart. As they planned their wedding the owner of the hacienda offered the couple a vacant house on the property for them to spend their wedding night. According to custom , the groom wore white pants and a white shirt and a red cummerbund embroidered by the bride.

After the ceremony the pair took off for the vacant house located in a far corner of the farm where nobody would dare to bother them. The house was large, with multiple nooks, crannies, closets and cubbords and to the young couple, from humble backgrounds, it was a palace. Never again would they find themselves in such a spacious home. It prompted them to challenge each other in a game of hide and seek. There were so many great places to hide!

When it was the groom’s turn he hid so well that his new wife wandered from room to room in the dim light trying to find him. At first it was a game, a thrilling game, in anticipation of the night to come. But as minutes passed and then hours, she became weary and worried. Where could he be?

She wandered all through the house several times but she never found him? Did he repent getting married and fled? Or did he fall and lose consciousness? After much time searching she gave up, tired and depressed and heart broken. The love of her life was gone. As time went by she accepted the fact and returned to her parent’s home to get on with her life.

Years went by and the property was sold along with the house. The new owners took their time clearing out all the old furniture left inside including several trunks and barrels, opening them up to see if there was anything left of value inside. And there, in one of the trunks, they found a skeleton dressed in white with a red embroidered cummerbund.

There is no conclusion for this story. Did the bride weep over her lost sweetheart Or was she angry at the skeleton for messing up her life? Did she want the cummebund back? And more curious, how come the guy didn’t figure out how to escape, or was he still waiting all that time for her to find him? Will we ever know the truth behind this story?

World.title: Colin Leslie charged after woman allegedly loses $300 attempting to buy iPhone from Facebook Marketplace being sold by ‘El Chapo’
World.content:
Colin Leslie charged after woman allegedly loses $300 attempting to buy iPhone from Facebook Marketplace being sold by ‘El Chapo’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 33-year-old Belize City technician has been charged after a woman allegedly lost $300 while attempting to purchase an iPhone advertised on Facebook Marketplace by a seller using the name “El Chapo.”

Colin Leslie, a resident of Far West Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, charged with obtaining money by deception following a complaint from a woman.

According to court reports, the woman was browsing Facebook Marketplace on October 11 when she came across a white iPhone advertised for $400. After agreeing to purchase the phone, she was allegedly instructed to transfer $300 to an Atlantic Bank account registered in Leslie’s name.

The woman reportedly made the transfer on October 12 but never received the phone. When she attempted to contact the seller, who operated under the name “El Chapo,” she discovered that she had been blocked.

She reported the matter to police on October 13.

Investigators subsequently interviewed Leslie, who reportedly consented to a search of his phone in the presence of a Justice of the Peace. Police allegedly discovered evidence of the $300 transfer from the woman’s account to Leslie’s account, with investigators claiming the money was later withdrawn.

During his court appearance, Leslie initially indicated that he was guilty and told the magistrate he had discussed reimbursing the woman, claiming she had agreed to accept repayment.

However, the prosecutor explained that the offense could be tried in the High Court and that directions were needed from the Director of Public Prosecutions to determine how the case should proceed.

The magistrate therefore informed Leslie that his guilty plea could not be formally accepted at that stage.

Leslie was granted bail of $4,000 with one surety of the same amount or two sureties of $2,000 each, which he reportedly met.

He must report to the Precinct One Police Station every Tuesday and Friday and is scheduled to return to court on November 30, 2026.

World.title: Romero brothers walk free after man and mother drop charges for pulling gun on them
World.content:
Romero brothers walk free after man and mother drop charges for pulling gun on them

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City brothers accused of threatening a man and his mother with firearms have walked free after both complainants appeared in court and requested that the charges against them be withdrawn.

Lyndon and Jayden Romero were released on Wednesday, October 28, after spending two nights on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

The brothers had been arraigned before the Chief Magistrate on Tuesday, October 27, on two counts each of aggravated assault with a firearm upon a man and his mother. Both pleaded not guilty.

According to police reports, the allegations stemmed from an incident on October 18, when the man and his mother heard a commotion outside their home on Estrella Metzgen Street in Belize City.

The complainant reported that when they went outside, they observed the Romero brothers allegedly holding firearms while arguing with his younger brother, who was seated inside a vehicle.

As the man approached, the brothers allegedly pointed their weapons toward him and his mother and threatened to shoot them.

Fearing for their lives, the man reportedly retreated into his home and contacted police. The brothers allegedly fled in a black Nissan Rogue toward Mahogany Street.

Police subsequently launched an investigation and issued wanted notices. Breaking Belize News reported on October 19 that Lyndon Romero Jr. was wanted for questioning.

On October 26, attorney Ian Grey reportedly informed police that the brothers would surrender themselves. They were subsequently charged and remanded.

However, when they returned to the Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, both the complainant and his mother took the stand and indicated that they no longer wished to pursue the matter.

The two aggravated assault counts against each brother were subsequently withdrawn, resulting in their release from custody.

World.title: ‘Gramps’ sentenced to three months in prison after sixth drug conviction
World.content:
‘Gramps’ sentenced to three months in prison after sixth drug conviction

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 65-year-old Belize City man has been sentenced to three months in prison after pleading guilty to a drug trafficking charge, adding another conviction to a criminal record that already included five previous drug offenses.

Orlando Anthony Fisher, an unemployed resident of Kelly Street, appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, October 26, charged with possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply after police allegedly found him carrying 61 grams of marijuana.

According to court reports, Fisher was detained around midday on Friday, October 23, while police officers were conducting patrols in the Back-A-Town area of Belize City.

Police were patrolling near Lindos Alley when they reportedly observed Fisher walking along East Collet Canal. Police claimed he appeared uneasy upon noticing their presence.

Officers conducted a search and allegedly discovered a transparent green plastic bag containing suspected cannabis concealed in the front of his pants. The substance was subsequently weighed and reportedly amounted to 61 grams.

Under Belize’s Misuse of Drugs Act, possession of more than 60 grams of cannabis carries a legal presumption of intent to supply, unless the contrary is proven.

Fisher pleaded guilty to the charge. However, the court considered his extensive history of drug-related offenses, including five previous convictions, before imposing a custodial sentence of three months.

He was subsequently sent to prison to begin serving his sentence.

World.title: Kenyon Dominguez walks free after admitting he gave police a false name
World.content:
Kenyon Dominguez walks free after admitting he gave police a false name

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who admitted giving police a false name walked out of court a free man this week after a magistrate cautioned him and dismissed the charge against him.

Kenyon Kareem Dominguez appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a charge of committing a mischievous act after allegedly identifying himself as Kareem Young instead of Kenyon Dominguez when questioned by police on Tuesday, October 27.

Dominguez pleaded guilty but explained that his actions were simply a lapse in judgment.

“It was just wah foolish act. Something I will never try again,” he told the court.

He also claimed that he had been detained by police since Thursday, October 22, spending approximately four to five days in custody.

After considering his explanation, the magistrate cautioned Dominguez and dismissed the charge, allowing him to leave court without further penalty.

Dominguez is no stranger to the court system. In August, Breaking Belize News reported that he was fined $150 after admitting to throwing stones at a neighbour’s house. He claimed he was attempting to alert the occupants to a possible intruder in their yard.

World.title: Emerson West and 16-year-old boy jointly charged with murder of Dodrick Madrill
World.content:
Emerson West and 16-year-old boy jointly charged with murder of Dodrick Madrill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged two persons, including a 16-year-old minor, in connection with the murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Salvador Miguel Madrill, who was gunned down in Belize City on Thursday morning.

The accused have been identified as 31-year-old Emerson West, a Belizean boat captain of Belize City, and a 16-year-old boy. Both have been jointly charged with murder.

Madrill was fatally shot on October 29 while walking along Freedom Street shortly after 7:20 a.m. According to police, a vehicle approached him before a gunman exited and fired several shots, killing him.

During Thursday’s police briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed that investigators had identified a vehicle believed to have been involved in the murder and were seeking two persons of interest.

The arrests represent a significant development in the investigation, which comes amid a series of deadly shootings across Belize.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Madrill’s murder preceded Friday’s quadruple homicide along the Coastal Plain Highway, where four men, including two who had previously faced firearm charges alongside Madrill, were killed.

Police have been investigating possible connections between the killings, although no definitive link or motive has been established.

West and the minor are expected to face court proceedings in connection with the murder charge.

World.title: Theft charge dropped against Belize City man accused of stealing uncle’s wires, threatening him with machete
World.content:
Theft charge dropped against Belize City man accused of stealing uncle’s wires, threatening him with machete

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of stealing a sack of electrical wires from his uncle and threatening him with a machete has had the theft charge withdrawn after a magistrate found insufficient evidence to support it.

Fitzroy Elijah Brown appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, charged with theft and aggravated assault upon his uncle, 45-year-old mechanic Egbert Brown.

According to court reports, the incident occurred on October 24, when Egbert received information that his nephew was allegedly cutting wires at his garage on Fabers Road.

Egbert told police that when he arrived, he spotted Fitzroy riding away on a bicycle carrying a white sack. Upon noticing his uncle, Fitzroy allegedly abandoned the sack and fled.

Egbert reportedly pursued his nephew, who allegedly pulled out a machete and pointed it at him twice.

In court, Fitzroy initially pleaded guilty to theft but explained that he had collected the wires and other discarded materials from a bushy, vacant lot, insisting he did not know they belonged to his uncle.

“I never knew it was for him,” Brown reportedly told the court.

The magistrate entered an equivocal plea on his behalf after his explanation contradicted an admission of theft.

After reviewing the prosecution’s facts, the magistrate pointed out that the evidence did not establish the elements of theft and suggested that attempted theft would have been the more appropriate charge.

The police prosecutor subsequently withdrew the theft charge, leaving only the aggravated assault allegation.

Fitzroy pleaded not guilty to aggravated assault, claiming it was his uncle who had pulled a machete from his bicycle during their confrontation.

With no objection from the prosecution, Brown was granted bail of $2,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

His bail conditions prohibit him from contacting or interfering with his uncle, require him to remain at least 100 yards away, and mandate that he report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Wednesday.

However, before processing bail, Brown was required to settle an outstanding $430 court debt stemming from a previous conviction for threatening words.

He is scheduled to return to court on November 30, 2026.

World.title: 16-year-old boy remanded after being charged with unlawful sexual intercourse with 14-year-old girlfriend
World.content:
16-year-old boy remanded after being charged with unlawful sexual intercourse with 14-year-old girlfriend

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 16-year-old boy has been remanded after being charged with unlawful sexual intercourse involving his 14-year-old girlfriend.

The teenager appeared before the Belize Family Court on Tuesday, October 27, where he was arraigned on a single count of unlawful sexual intercourse.

According to court reports, the boy and the 14-year-old girl were reportedly involved in a romantic relationship.

Despite their reported relationship and the two-year age difference, the teenager was criminally charged. Under Belizean law, the age of sexual consent is 16.

Bail was denied, and the boy was remanded to the New Beginnings Youth Development Center at Mile 21 on the George Price Highway.

He is scheduled to return to court in December 2026.

The identities of both minors are being withheld for their protection.

World.title: US investor presses High Court for hearing date in US$295,000 lawsuit against Belize Strategic Fund and Glen Brayshaw
World.content:
US investor presses High Court for hearing date in US$295,000 lawsuit against Belize Strategic Fund and Glen Brayshaw

By Breaking Belize News Staff: American investor Christopher Day is pressing ahead with his US$295,000 lawsuit against Belize Strategic Fund Limited and businessman Glen Brayshaw, with his attorneys making a renewed request to the High Court to schedule a hearing that would move the disputed villa investment case closer to trial.

In correspondence dated October 28, 2026, attorney Immanuel Williams of Glenn D. Godfrey & Company LLP wrote to the Registrar of the High Court, requesting that the matter be brought to the attention of Justice Nadine Nabie.

The letter, concerning High Court Claim No. 244 of 2026, follows an earlier request submitted on August 31, when Day’s attorneys first sought a date for a Case Management Conference (CMC).

Despite the passage of nearly two months, the latest correspondence indicates that a date has still not been scheduled.

The attorneys informed the court that the defendants filed their defence on July 28, while the claimants subsequently filed a formal Request for Information seeking further particulars concerning several assertions made in that defence.

With the pleadings substantially complete, the attorneys are now requesting that the court move the proceedings forward.

“Accordingly, we request that a CMC be fixed with a view to prepare the matter for trial,” the October 28 letter states.

In voice messages shared with Breaking Belize News, Day confirmed that a response had been received in the matter and that they were now awaiting a court date. However, he did not provide details of the response.

Breaking Belize News understands that Day remains determined to pursue the litigation and is prepared to utilize every possible resource at his disposal in his effort to secure justice.

The lawsuit stems from a disputed US$295,000 investment in the proposed 52/13 Villas development at Naia Resort and Spa in Placencia.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News in August, Day and his company, CDAY Properties LLC, allege that the investment was made after representations that the development would provide an income-generating rental opportunity and would be completed by March 2024.

However, Day alleges that when he visited the property in August 2024, construction remained substantially incomplete. He subsequently sought to withdraw from the investment and recover his money.

The claimants have raised allegations including fraudulent misrepresentation, negligent misrepresentation, breach of contract, failure of consideration and conspiracy.

Belize Strategic Fund and Brayshaw have denied the allegations of fraud, maintaining that the development experienced delays rather than being abandoned and that Day acquired a legitimate participation interest in the project.

A central issue in the dispute concerns the legal status of a property identified as Lot 113, against which Day’s investment was purportedly secured.

Day’s attorneys allege that the property does not exist under that designation as a formally registered parcel, while the defendants maintain that Lot 113 is a development designation associated with property owned by Belize Strategic Fund.

In August, the claimants requested documentation supporting the defendants’ assertions, including land ownership records, development maps and correspondence concerning the property’s transfer.

The defendants were requested to provide the information by August 25. While Day has indicated that a response was received, the contents and adequacy of that response have not been independently established.

The next anticipated stage is a Case Management Conference, during which the court would establish a timetable for the exchange of documents, filing of witness statements and other procedural requirements necessary to prepare the matter for trial.

No date has yet been confirmed for that conference, and no trial date has been fixed.

The allegations remain before the High Court and have not been judicially determined.

World.title: ‘Kicking and screaming!’
World.content:
GONSALVES... it’s a positive move, but we have to understand that this is only the commencement of the journey, and that they are coming kicking and screaming

THE 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) opens in St John’s, Antigua, today amid a deepening rift over slavery and reparation, with Caribbean leaders welcoming British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s openness to a formal apology for chattel slavery but firmly rejecting his dismissal of reparation as “not the right answer”, insisting that reparatory justice must remain at the heart of the talks.

Burnham’s position in an op-ed for The Guardian newspaper in England, days before his arrival in Antigua and Barbuda for the summit, was immediately seen by Dr Ralph Gonsalves, senior advisor and elder for The Repair Campaign, as Britain yielding to mounting international pressure to negotiate.

“They coming to the table, but they coming kicking and screaming,” Gonsalves, who served as prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines for 24 years, told the Jamaica Observer on Saturday.

“It’s a positive move, but we have to understand that this is only the commencement of the journey, and that they are coming kicking and screaming,” Gonsalves said.

At the same time, he said he expects that the tone of the discussions at the summit would be “respectful, frank, honest, and at times robust”.

Gonsalves said that while slavery and reparation were not formally on the CHOGM agenda, there is no doubt that the issues will be raised by Caribbean Community (Caricom) leaders, as well as their counterparts from Africa and India.

He pointed to the United Nations General Assembly adoption of a resolution on March 25, 2026, declaring the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as “the gravest crime against humanity”, arguing that the matter had assumed global significance.

“This matter has gone beyond us. It is central to us, but it has gone beyond us. It’s the same way that there’s a tribal war between two sets of Slavic peoples

— Russians and Ukrainians

— but it has global implications,” Gonsalves told the Sunday Observer.

On Saturday, Caricom Chairman Prime Minister Philip J Pierre outlined in a statement that the regional bloc was ready to engage with the United Kingdom, but rejected Burnham’s position that reparation was not “the right answer”.

Burnham, who will attend the November 1-4 CHOGM, has said he is “open” to listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of Britain for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparation.

“I do not believe that is the right answer,” he wrote in The Guardian. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Burnham instead offered a “structured dialogue” with those affected by the slave trade, saying, “Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent, and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery

— and we can show leadership again today.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he added.

In his response, Pierre, the prime minister of St Lucia, said Burnham’s expression of personal sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by slavery and its continuing effects, together with his willingness to consider a formal apology on behalf of the British State, represented a significant development.

“No British prime minister has gone this far before. It would be wrong of us not to say so, and we welcome it in the spirit in which it appears to be offered,” Pierre said. “For more than a decade, this community has asked for exactly such a dialogue. We are ready to engage.”

However, the Caricom chair said the community did not accept the argument that reparations were inappropriate or that Britain’s responsibility had ended because present-day citizens had not personally participated in slavery.

“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions

— and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said.

Pierre pointed to Britain’s role in legislating for, protecting, and profiting from slavery, as well as its decision to compensate enslavers at Emancipation while formerly enslaved people received no land, wealth, or compensation.

He noted that the loan raised to compensate enslavers was still being repaid by British taxpayers until February 2015.

The consequences of slavery, he said, continue to be felt across the Caribbean through chronic disease, inequalities in education and opportunity, economies shaped by extraction, national debt, and vulnerability to economic and climate shocks.

Pierre said a formal apology would be an important first step, but argued that it must be accompanied by practical measures to address the lasting effects of slavery.

He pointed to Caricom’s 10-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, which includes a formal apology, public health, education and training, cultural heritage restitution and reconnection, psychological rehabilitation, technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, debt cancellation, monetary compensation, and decolonisation.

He said the proposed dialogue must allow for discussion of every element of the plan, as well as reparation for the genocide of Indigenous Peoples and the harm caused to people brought from India and China to sustain colonial systems.

“A dialogue that begins by placing reparations outside the room cannot be a complete dialogue,” Pierre said.

The Caricom chair also acknowledged the United Kingdom’s initiative, to be led by former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.

He said the community would examine the proposal seriously but cautioned that most Caricom member states were classified as middle- or high-income economies and were routinely excluded from concessional relief despite their vulnerability to climate and economic shocks.

“Any initiative that is to be meaningful for our region must measure vulnerability, not income alone,” he said, adding that debt relief could not be used as a substitute for reparatory justice.

Pierre said the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, and the Caricom Reparations Commission, chaired by Sir Hilary Beckles, were prepared to work with the British Government on the terms, agenda, and timetable for structured dialogue.

He said he looked forward to meeting Burnham in Antigua and Barbuda.

“Our ancestors did not receive justice in their lifetime. We owe it to them, and to the generations who will come after us, to see this work through

— with dignity, with patience, and with resolve,” Pierre said.

Jamaica’s Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Barbados’s head of Government Mottley also responded to Burnham’s comments.

“Jamaica takes note of news that the United Kingdom is now willing to engage meaningfully on the matter of reparatory justice,” Holness said in a statement.

“We are encouraged to learn that Prime Minister Burnham and his Government are open to listening to calls for a formal apology for chattel enslavement. We have always been open to having full and meaningful dialogue on this important issue. We welcome this development, coming in the wake of our legal petition which is now before the Privy Council. We look forward to the discussions and actions that will follow,” Holness said.

Mottley said her Government, “recognises and appreciates Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s acknowledgement that the transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of human beings, and his offer of a structured dialogue, including his openness to a formal apology”.

She said Barbados is committed to that dialogue and will take part in good faith as a member of Caricom.

“We also thank former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer who, in Samoa in 2024, joined fellow Commonwealth leaders in agreeing that the time had come for a meaningful conversation on reparatory justice. That decision opened the door to the process now before us,” Mottley said.

Stating that her country speaks on this matter with a particular memory, Mottley said that in 1661, under English colonial authority, the first comprehensive slave code in the English-speaking world was regrettably passed in Barbados.

“It defined African men, women, and children as non-human property and became the model for codes across the region and beyond. That system was built by law and enforced by the State,” she said.

“Dialogue matters because we are not yet on the same page on every element. On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree,” Mottley added.

She thanked Burnham and his Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband “for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing and the moral thing to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue”.

Gonsalves, too, pointed to the importance of dialogue as he recalled that in 2013 when he took the matter of reparation to Caricom all his colleagues were supportive.

“We set up the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, we set up the Caricom Reparations Commission. We asked that national reparations commissions be set up in every country; we had the 10 Point Plan being devised and approved in 2014, and the show was on the road, so to speak. But some people said, ‘Man, this thing is a mirage, this is a fool’s errand,’ and so forth. But those of us who understood this issue, we knew,” Gonsalves said.

“Now Britain is saying they want to have a structured conversation and in that structured conversation, he’s open to the question of the apology, and to deal with matters looking forward in a number of areas

— debt relief, appropriate funding for this, that, and the other; and he recognised the horrors of slavery, and all the rest of it. So the British Government has come from a position of no apology to one where we will have this structured conversation,” Gonsalves told the Sunday Observer, adding that he expects “other things will emerge in the structured conversation”.

“So, they’re coming to the table kicking and screaming, but coming nevertheless,” he emphasised.

On Friday Britain’s King Charles III, who is on a Caribbean tour, arrived in Antigua where, as the head of the Commonwealth family of nations, he will preside over the four-day summit.

World.title: ‘Not an undercover PNP front’
World.content:
Fi We Children Foundation (FWCF) Youth Policy Committee members Jordaina Denton (left) and Antonio Davis at a Jamaica Observer Press Club meeting at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew last Thursday.Photos: Garfield Robinson

DETERMINED to shake off accusations of political bias and being an organisation that exists mainly to criticise the Government, Fi We Children Foundation is insisting that its criticism of government decisions is driven by its commitment to protecting children’s rights and holding those in power accountable.

The foundation, which describes itself as a non-profit, non-partisan and youth-led organisation, says its public statements are only part of its work, which includes efforts to reduce violence in schools, improve children’s access to proper nutrition and give young people a greater role in decisions affecting their lives.

During a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Thursday, members of its Youth Policy Committee firmly rejected suggestions that the organisation is operating as an undercover political group, with attorney-at-law Antonio Davis saying its purpose is to give children and young people a voice in matters that directly affect them.

“So we would categorically state that we’re not a psyop [psychological operation]. We would categorically state that we’re not an undercover basis for the PNP [People’s National Party], or any party, really. But what it is really, is that I think this foundation gives children the platform.

“Many times, as young people, we’re in the driver’s seat and we’re just passengers watching life go by, and so this platform gives us an opportunity now to kind of hold on to the reins a little bit, hold on to the driving wheel a little bit, and have a voice… So I wouldn’t really say it’s just bashing the Government, but if we see something, then we say something,” Davis said.

The foundation’s members argued that its willingness to highlight shortcomings in government policies should not be taken as evidence of political allegiance. They said the organisation also recognises positive action by the Andrew Holness-led Administration and wants improvements to continue.

Youth Policy Committee member Darrell Scott said the foundation is not opposed to acknowledging government initiatives that benefit children, but believes there is a responsibility to identify areas requiring attention.

“So it’s not that we won’t applaud the Government…but I think what we want is the continuation of the good work that the Government has done while also highlighting areas that they may have missed,” he said.

Founded in 2019, Fi We Children Foundation emerged from discussions about what its members saw as a gap between policymakers and the issues that matter to children. Scott said the organisation was established to give young people a greater role in representing children’s interests, rather than leaving decisions entirely in the hands of adults.

He said its work began before it became more visible in public discussions, with an earlier focus on children in rural Jamaica, who the foundation believes are often overlooked in national conversations.

Scott attributed some of the disruption to its activities to the COVID-19 pandemic, while also pointing to the expansion of its team and the increased attention being paid to children’s issues as reasons for its more recent public presence.

The organisation now has an online membership of about 215 people and an executive board of four, according to Youth Policy Committee member and law student Jordaina Denton.

She explained that it has two main membership categories: General membership is open throughout the year, while applications for the Youth Policy Committee are opened once annually. Denton said applicants to the committee are shortlisted and interviewed, with members expected to take a more direct role in leading advocacy on youth issues.

The foundation also runs a programme called Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) in Schools, which seeks to equip students with alternative ways of resolving conflicts without resorting to violence.

Denton said the initiative was developed against the background of violent incidents involving students, including stabbings and physical confrontations in schools.

The foundation also conducts forums involving schools and said it had encountered approximately 10 to 15 schools through its ADR work, although Scott cautioned that the figure was not exact because some schools were reached through forums rather than direct programme activities.

Beyond school violence, the organisation has been working on issues surrounding the National School Nutrition Policy. Scott said it had collaborated with the Jamaica Youth Advocacy Network, UNICEF Jamaica and Heart Foundation to advance discussions about children’s nutrition.

Another initiative, called Eyes on the Budget, focuses on helping young people understand how public money is allocated and spent. The foundation also appeared before Parliament’s joint select committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act, during which members contributed to the discussions.

For the foundation, these projects form part of a wider commitment to children’s rights rather than a series of unrelated activities. Scott said its work is guided by that broad purpose, with particular projects developed to address specific concerns as they arise.

However, while the committee members acknowledged that the organisation’s public image has been shaped heavily by its statements criticising government decisions, Denton disagreed that the foundation is failing to promote its other work

“We do promote that information, so we have it on our Instagram page. And even when we went to Parliament for the joint select committee, we had done a press release on that. So I think that it is not necessarily that Fi We Children is simply opposing, I think people take it that way because…people are drawn to see a more negative view of things rather than to see the work that we do that does commend people and promote our work,” she said.

World.title: Patra: Far from finished
World.content:
Patra ...honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award by the organisers of the recently concluded Caribbean Music Awards.

Constantly busying herself with ideas of reinvention, Patra was deep in preparations for upcoming interviews when she first received word that she would be honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award by the organisers of the Caribbean Music Awards (CMA).

In fact, the Queen of the Pack artiste didn’t open the message until days after it was first sent. Still, the delay did little to diminish the emotional impact of the gesture. The news stopped her in her tracks, causing her to reflect on the journey that had brought her to that moment.

“I got very emotional and it put me in a sense of realisation and meditation,” Patra recalled. “I looked back at where I used to be as an artiste and it was very humbling. To be acknowledged by the CMA, it was a beautiful experience for me. I could barely contain myself.”

For an artiste who has spent decades navigating the shifting currents of the music business, the honour represented more than another accolade to add to an already notable résumé. It was a moment to pause and acknowledge the work.

“Going there to pick up the award, healthy, and still being able to do something that I love, was a feeling I still can’t put into words,” she said. “The highlight was when I realised that I really did do a lot to receive this acknowledgement and the moment allowed me to go back and honour that journey.”

Sometimes, she admits, artistes become so consumed with the next show, the next song, and the next move that they fail to fully appreciate what they have already accomplished.

“Sometimes as artistes, we know what we’ve done, the work we’ve put in but sometimes, the reflection really drives that home,” she said.

For Patra, that reflection is particularly powerful because her story is not simply one of success. It is also one of endurance. The little girl from the country who entered contests from school stages to major competitions already had an instinct for performance. But talent alone, she soon learned, would not be enough.

Having entered an industry in which men significantly outnumbered women, Patra was prepared to face anything thrown her way, including pushback. What she experienced, however, was an environment that allowed her to thrive.

“When I started out there were far more males in the industry than there were females. But the way they treated me when I got into the business was remarkable,” she said. “I always wanted to be a superstar and take my country to the world, and they really facilitated my growth. It made me excited getting into this business and I knew it was meant to be,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

That sense of purpose steered her career. Understanding from very early in her journey that surviving in music required more than knowing how to command a stage, the fiery deejay made a deliberate effort to learn the business, including that the often unseen army of people are responsible for bringing music to audiences.

“I made sure to educate myself on the business, and through that process I learnt to care for and appreciate the works of those behind the scenes,” she said.

That education, coupled with guidance from people who genuinely cared about her development, became part of the foundation on which she built her career. And the lessons continued even when she took a hiatus from the active music scene.

Now, Patra says she is ready for a resurgence marked by renewed energy and a different sense of creative possibility.

“I took a break and now I’m ready to get back out there with a new distribution deal through J House and Sony Orchard,” she said. “People haven’t seen anything yet. Patra is warming up, because there are a lot of good things going on.”

The next chapter is already taking shape, with Patra planning to release two albums in the first quarter of 2027, each exploring a different musical direction. One will deliver what she calls her personal “Patra vibes”, while the other will venture into house music.

The sounds may differ, but she insists the woman at the centre of both projects will remain unmistakably Patra.

“It’s going to be two different vibes, but it will still represent me; my image, my sensuality, my attitude, everything,” she said. The projects will also be message-driven and designed to make people feel good, reflecting an artiste who appears increasingly comfortable with the freedom to explore rather than remain confined by the expectations attached to her past.
