“I am happy that with these two projects. I get to present myself to the world in the way I see myself with a sense of freedom. Now, I can do more than one genre of music,” she said, teasing that there will also be surprises on both projects.

In the meantime, she is giving fans a taste of the direction ahead with her latest singles, Me So Sexy and No Threat. The latter, she explained, is about reclaiming her individuality while acknowledging those who came before her, while Me So Sexy serves as the single from the J House Vol 1 project. Its accompanying video is also on the way.

There are performances ahead as well, including an appearance on the Rock The Bells Cruise, keeping Patra firmly connected to the live stage that helped establish her reputation in the first place.

World.title: Six-star Excelsior thrash Mona in Manning Cup
World.content:
Christopher McDonald of Excelsior High School rises above Nathaniel McCarthy of Mona High School while Habbie Mohammed of Excelsior looks on during their ISSA Manning Cup match played at Jamaica College on Saturday October 31, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Defending champions Excelsior High threw down the gauntlet Saturday, dismantling Mona High 6-1 in Group 1 of the ISSA Manning Cup round of 32, while Jamaica College (JC) scored a stoppage time goal to earn a 2-2 draw against Tivoli Gardens High at the Ashenheim Stadium.

It was a statement win by Excelsior as coach Keon Broderick had promised to use their recent expulsion from the Champions Cup by ISSA as motivation in the Manning Cup.

Kevin Deacon opened the floodgates in the 13th minute before Carleon Cavalier doubled the lead in minute 25.

Damarley Williams netted a brace in the 30th and 54th minutes, while Habbie Mohammed (39th) and Christopher McDonald (45+1) completed the rout.

The talented Sean Leighton scored a consolation goal for Mona in the 87th minute.

Excelsior’s coach Keon Broderick said it was a good statement win.

“One of the things that we want to show is that we have a complete programme,” said Broderick, as he made reference to two players that were ruled out as ineligible.

“So even if we are down one or two persons, we still have quality on the field to display in such a good way that we can score six goals and win a game against a quality team like Mona,” he pointed out.

However, Broderick admitted that he didn’t expect to brush aside the Craig Butler-coached Walker Cup finalist that easily.

“Really and truly, I was telling the boys that it was going to be a competitive game. I did not know that Mona High after concealing a couple goals would have dropped. But credit must be given to us as well because the type of football we played to score the third, the fourth, the fifth goal in the first half was really good quality,” said Broderick.

He continued: “And so I’m not going to take anything away from the boys in how they played. But I really believe that it was going to be one of the more challenging games in the round. But our quality would have shown today and we are absolutely relieved that we were able to play”.

Excelsior jumped to the top of Zone 1 with three points as St Catherine High and St George’s College played to a 1-1 draw for one point each.

In Zone 4, JC battled to a disappointing 2-2 draw Tivoli Gardens in a game they looked down and out while trailing 1-2 heading into stoppage time.

The other Zone 4 encounter between home team Eltham High and Norman Manley High was not played because of heavy rains.

Meanwhile, in Zone 2, Walker Cup champions Kingston College beat Vauxhall High 3-1 behind two goals from top marksman Deshawn Byfield and one from Ryland Fray-Campbell. KC lead the zone ahead of Calabar High which edged Camperdown High 2-1.

In Zone 3, Wolmer’s Boys turned up the heat, thrashing St Jago High 4-1 as did St Andrew High School who clobbered Hillel Academy 6-0 to go top of the zone on goal difference.

World.title: ‘An Abominable Betrayal’: Patterson blasts Jamaica’s abstention on Cuba
World.content:
PJ Patterson (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Former Prime Minister PJ Patterson has slammed the Holness administration’s decision to abstain from voting on the United Nations resolution calling for an end to the embargo against Cuba as “an abominable betrayal which history will never forget”.

The vote marked a shift in policy by Jamaica as historically the island has voted “yes” in favour of ending the United States economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba for over 30 years since the annual UN resolution began.

In a scathing rebuke of the decision by Jamaica, Patterson said “It was a day of shame for the land of Marcus Garvey, and a stain on the record of a nation which, before we had even raised our own flag, closed its ports to trade with apartheid South Africa.”

Patterson recalled that in December 1972, he accompanied then Prime Minister Michael Manley to the meeting at which four newly independent Caribbean states resolved to establish diplomatic relations with Cuba, “defying the isolation others sought to impose.”

He said, “We took that decision not because it was easy, but because it was right, and because we understood that the sovereignty we had so recently won would mean little if we allowed others to choose our friends, least of all a friend that is our closest neighbour.”

Noting that he is the last surviving participant in that decision, Patterson said: “I write with a sense of agony and seething outrage that Jamaica could so suddenly abandon the fundamental tenets on which it rested: the sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their domestic jurisdiction, and the right of every people to self-determination free from external threat or coercion.”

Patterson was among 11 former Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community who, four days before the UN vote, issued statements urging global support for an end to the US embargo against Cuba.

“We said then, and I repeat now, that the embargo is contrary to international law, that it violates Cuba’s sovereignty and the most elemental rights of its people, and that the pressures being deployed to defeat the resolution must be resisted,” Patterson said. “Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding signed that letter alongside me. On this crucial matter, Jamaica’s former leaders spoke with one voice. The present Government has chosen silence.”

Patterson challenged Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith’s explanation that the “Government had been reflecting on the matter for some time, that the abstention represents a shift in policy, and that the resolution left no scope to reflect the broader context the Government wished to see.”

READ: Shift in policy

According to the former prime minister, “That explanation does not withstand scrutiny.

“If there was no external pressure, as the Government insists, then it must explain how a fundamental reversal of a policy pursued by every Administration since 1992 serves Jamaica’s best interest. It must also explain why it was never brought to parliament if this reflection had been under way for some time,” he said.

Patterson also accused the government of flouting Parliament’s constitutional authority, noting that the vote came less than 24 hours after the House of Representatives passed, without dissent, a resolution on the economic and humanitarian situation in Cuba.

“It was the Government’s own resolution, brought to the House by the minister of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Patterson said. “In moving it, he declared that Jamaica could not support a unilaterally imposed blockade against Cuba. The resolution called for efforts to reduce the economic restrictions on Cuba and to facilitate its progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under a blockade.”

Patterson argued, “Our abstention violated the unanimous decision of the Legislature. It was a deplorable flouting of Parliament’s constitutional authority, the highest expression of the will of the people in our democracy.

“Members on both sides of the House were led to believe one thing on Tuesday and confronted with its opposite on Wednesday. This is no mere discourtesy. It was an act of deception and a grave parliamentary offence,” the former prime minister continued in his rebuke. “In any Parliament modelled on Westminster, what took place between Tuesday and Wednesday would have resulted in censure and ministerial resignations. The Parliament of Jamaica is entitled to no less. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.”

See full statement by PJ Patterson below.

On Wednesday, 28 October 2026, Jamaica abstained when the United Nations General Assembly voted on the resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States against Cuba. For more than three decades, under every Administration since the resolution was first tabled in 1992, Jamaica voted yes. We did so under governments of both parties, because the yes vote was never partisan. It was a matter of principle.

It was a day of shame for the land of Marcus Garvey, and a stain on the record of a nation which, before we had even raised our own flag, closed its ports to trade with apartheid South Africa. That was an unequivocal declaration that the Jamaican people, though a small nation, would not support the oppression of others. On Wednesday, Jamaica’s Government trampled that tradition. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.

In December 1972, I accompanied Prime Minister Michael Manley to the meeting at which four newly independent Caribbean states resolved to establish diplomatic relations with Cuba, defying the isolation others sought to impose. We took that decision not because it was easy, but because it was right, and because we understood that the sovereignty we had so recently won would mean little if we allowed others to choose our friends, least of all a friend that is our closest neighbour.

I am the last surviving participant in that decision, and I write with a sense of agony and seething outrage that Jamaica could so suddenly abandon the fundamental tenets on which it rested: the sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their domestic jurisdiction, and the right of every people to self-determination free from external threat or coercion.

Four days before the UN vote, eleven of my fellow former Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community and I wrote to all the nations of the world urging support for the resolution. We said then, and I repeat now, that the embargo is contrary to international law, that it violates Cuba’s sovereignty and the most elemental rights of its people, and that the pressures being deployed to defeat the resolution must be resisted. Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding signed that letter alongside me. On this crucial matter, Jamaica’s former leaders spoke with one voice. The present Government has chosen silence.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs tells us that the Government had been reflecting on this matter for some time, that the abstention represents a shift in policy, and that the resolution left no scope to reflect the broader context the Government wished to see. That explanation does not withstand scrutiny.

If there was no external pressure, as the Government insists, then it must explain how a fundamental reversal of a policy pursued by every Administration since 1992 serves Jamaica’s best interest. It must also explain why it was never brought to parliament if this reflection had been under way for some time.

On Tuesday, 27 October, the House of Representatives passed, without dissent, a resolution on the economic and humanitarian situation in Cuba. It was the Government’s own resolution, brought to the House by the Minister of State in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In moving it, he declared that Jamaica could not support a unilaterally imposed blockade against Cuba. The resolution called for efforts to reduce the economic restrictions on Cuba and to facilitate its progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under a blockade.

Within twenty-four hours, Jamaica abstained. Our abstention violated the unanimous decision of the Legislature. It was a deplorable flouting of Parliament’s constitutional authority, the highest expression of the will of the people in our democracy.

Members on both sides of the House were led to believe one thing on Tuesday and confronted with its opposite on Wednesday. This is no mere discourtesy. It was an act of deception and a grave parliamentary offence. In any Parliament modelled on Westminster, what took place between Tuesday and Wednesday would have resulted in censure and ministerial resignations. The Parliament of Jamaica is entitled to no less. It was an abominable betrayal which history will never forget.

The Minister of State’s own words explain precisely why we should have voted yes. Small states have no mighty army to defend us, and insufficient economic weight to shield us against the exercise of military might and power. Our security rests on the international rule of law and on a credible multilateral system with the Charter of the United Nations at its centre. When a powerful nation imposes its will unilaterally on a small neighbour, and we do not object, we weaken the very shield on which our own sovereignty depends.

Foreign policy must rest on each nation’s enlightened determination of its own sovereign interests. It is a considered judgment, drawn from a nation’s history, its values and the commitments it has freely made to others. It must be guided by principle, not expediency.

If ever Cuba needed our support, it is now. Our Caribbean neighbour faces the threat of extinction from a hegemon that denies energy, food, medicine, water and sanitation to human beings whose only sin is to be Cuban.

International law cannot be selectively applied. Inhumane measures of this kind are not imposed upon great powers whose political systems differ from that of the United States. They are imposed upon Cuba because Cuba is small and adjacent. Jamaica cannot afford to look away.

The Government speaks of encouraging dialogue between Washington and Havana and reform within Cuba, and the Minister reminds us that the Prime Minister raised these matters with his CARICOM colleagues in St Kitts and Nevis. If dialogue between Washington and Havana is indeed the Government’s objective, the Jamaican people are entitled to know what initiatives have been taken since the St Kitts and Nevis meeting, and what role CARICOM has been invited to play. Absent such an account, the language of dialogue cannot justify a drastic change of policy.

The people of Cuba stood with us whenever we needed support, and asked nothing in return. Their doctors and nurses served in our rural clinics and hospitals. Through Operation Miracle, nearly 25,000 Jamaicans have had their sight restored or improved, free of charge. Cuba’s scholarships trained our young people. Cuba donated and built schools that have benefited generations of teachers and students. That solidarity was freely given.

And how have we repaid it? By sending the Cuban doctors and nurses home, terminating a medical cooperation programme that had served our people for half a century. By concluding an arrangement to receive from the United States deportees who have no connection to Jamaica, the so-called third-country nationals (TCN) deal, entered into without consultation with Parliament or the people, and still kept secret. And now, by this abstention.

Nor is Cuba the only cause on which this Government has lost its voice. Last year, on a crucial vote pertaining to Palestine and its people, Jamaica chose to be absent from the chamber. That was not neutrality. It was cowardice. One hundred and forty-five countries voted in favour.

Taken together, these egregious errors form a pattern: absence from the vote in support of the Palestinian people; the sending home of the Cubans; the secret TCN deal; and now the UN vote on Cuba. Each step has been taken quietly; each has been explained away; and each carries Jamaica further from the principled ground on which we have always stood.

Jamaica has a long and honourable record in the councils of the world. That record was not built by abstaining when principle was on the line. It was built by a small nation that proved, time and again, what it means to say: we likkle but we tallawah. On apartheid, and in the struggles of the developing world for a just international order, our voice carried a weight far beyond our size, because the world knew we could not be bought or bent. We are now in mortal danger of losing the universal respect we once enjoyed, and respect squandered is not easily regained.

The harm is not confined to our internal reputation and standing abroad. It is felt in every Jamaican household, at home and across the Diaspora. Jamaicans in Toronto and London, in New York and Miami, who have carried our name with pride and defended our nation wherever they have gone, are offended, hurt, angry and ashamed that their Government has chosen to shatter our nation’s reputation in this way. They did not help to build that reputation so that it could be traded away in a single vote.

The entire nation and the Diaspora are entitled to a full and truthful account of how this decision was taken, by whom, and on whose advice. They are entitled to know whether pressure was applied, from what quarter, and what, if anything, was promised or threatened. They are entitled to a Parliament whose unanimous resolutions are honoured, not set aside overnight in New York. And they are entitled to see Jamaica restored to the position which successive Administrations of both parties have proudly held.

We are a people who came through the holds of slave ships, the brutality of the plantation and the long humiliation of colonial rule. We did not win our freedom in order to bend the knee. Our good name was earned after centuries of profound oppression, and a proud people is rightly jealous of it.

Those who lead such a people act in its name. They must never mortgage its good name for favour, nor trade its principles for the promise of reward or the avoidance of displeasure. They must never mistake silence for prudence, or submission for statecraft. What they must do is speak, as Jamaica has always spoken, for the right of the small to stand unafraid before the strong.

The time has come to repudiate, once and for all, the habits of genuflection. We live in no one’s backyard. Jamaica must never accept the doctrine that might makes right.

When the annals of this era are written, they will record that on 28 October 2026 a Government of Jamaica resiled from our finest traditions of standing for law, justice, and sovereign equality but that the people of Jamaica did not.

World.title: Caricom: UK apology for slavery would be welcomed, but reparations must remain on the table
World.content:
GEORGETOWN, Guyana (CMC) – The Caribbean Community (Caricom) has welcomed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s openness to a formal apology for slavery and structured dialogue with affected countries, but insists that reparatory justice must remain central to any discussions.

In a statement issued on Saturday, Caricom Chair and Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister, Philip J Pierre, said the Community was ready to engage with the United Kingdom but rejected Burnham’s position that reparations were not “the right answer”.

Burnham, who is due to attend the November 1-4 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, has said he is “open” to listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of Britain for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparations.

READ: UK PM ‘open’ to slavery apology but not reparations

“I do not believe that is the right answer,” he wrote in the Guardian. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Burnham instead offered a “structured dialogue” with those affected by the slave trade: “Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he added.

Pierre said Burnham’s expression of personal sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by slavery and its continuing effects, together with his willingness to consider a formal apology on behalf of the British state, represented a significant development.

“No British Prime Minister has gone this far before. It would be wrong of us not to say so, and we welcome it in the spirit in which it appears to be offered,” Pierre said. “For more than a decade, this Community has asked for exactly such a dialogue. We are ready to engage.”

However, the Caricom Chair said the Community did not accept the argument that reparations were inappropriate or that Britain’s responsibility had ended because present-day citizens had not personally participated in slavery.

“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions – and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said.

Pierre pointed to Britain’s role in legislating for, protecting and profiting from slavery, as well as its decision to compensate enslavers at Emancipation while formerly enslaved people received no land, wealth or compensation.

He noted that the loan raised to compensate enslavers was still being repaid by British taxpayers until February 2015.

The consequences of slavery, he said, continue to be felt across the Caribbean through chronic disease, inequalities in education and opportunity, economies shaped by extraction, national debt and vulnerability to economic and climate shocks.

Pierre said a formal apology would be an important first step, but argued that it must be accompanied by practical measures to address the lasting effects of slavery.

He pointed to Caricom’s Ten-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, which includes a formal apology, public health, education and training, cultural heritage restitution and reconnection, psychological rehabilitation, technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, debt cancellation, monetary compensation and decolonisation.

He said the proposed dialogue must allow for discussion of every element of the plan, as well as reparations for the genocide of Indigenous Peoples and the harm caused to people brought from India and China to sustain colonial systems.

“A dialogue that begins by placing reparations outside the room cannot be a complete dialogue,” Pierre said.

The Caricom Chair also acknowledged the United Kingdom’s initiative, to be led by former British prime minister Gordon Brown, to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.

He said the Community would examine the proposal seriously but cautioned that most Caricom member states were classified as middle- or high-income economies and were routinely excluded from concessional relief despite their vulnerability to climate and economic shocks.

“Any initiative that is to be meaningful for our region must measure vulnerability, not income alone,” he said, adding that debt relief could not be used as a substitute for reparatory justice.

Pierre said the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, and the Caricom Reparations Commission, chaired by Sir Hilary Beckles, were prepared to work with the British Government on the terms, agenda and timetable for structured dialogue.

He said he looked forward to meeting Burnham in Antigua and Barbuda in the coming days, as the country prepares to host the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

“Our ancestors did not receive justice in their lifetime. We owe it to them, and to the generations who will come after us, to see this work through – with dignity, with patience, and with resolve,” Pierre said.

World.title: UK PM ‘open’ to slavery apology but not reparations
World.content:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham chairs a meeting of the National Economic Council in Glasgow on October 30, 2026, that focuses on driving growth in every region of the United Kingdom. (Photo: AFP)

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday he was “open” to the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.

Writing in The Guardian days before attending a Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean, and as King Charles III tours the region, the British premier argued that “we need to face up to the past”.

With London under pressure to formally apologise for its pivotal part in the trade and compensate Caribbean nations, he pledged to have “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future”.

Burnham said he wanted to “express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today”, but insisted reparations were not “the right answer”.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he wrote in the op-ed.

The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of enslaved people’s rights, the UK leader added, offering a “structured dialogue with those affected”.

“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”

Burnham also revealed he planned to launch a new debt restructuring drive for the poorest Commonwealth countries, led by former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown.

He vowed to work with “global partners” to help those countries repay “over a longer time period and with better rates”.

– ‘Suffering’ –

The issues around slavery have loomed large over King Charles’s ongoing nine-day visit to three Caribbean countries, which will include an address to the Commonwealth summit.

Burnham is also set to attend the gathering that runs from Sunday to Wednesday in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.

The 56-member Commonwealth — which Charles, 77, helms — is mainly composed of British ex-colonies, with the UK’s central role in slavery and the treatment of its former subjects long a contentious issue within the organisation.

In the Bahamas on Tuesday, the monarch acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit.

Meanwhile in Guyana on Friday he visited an execution site of local people during British colonial rule, pausing to reflect in a gesture seen as indicating his awareness of that past injustice.

Britain has never formally apologised for slavery or agreed to pay reparations.

The country profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade, but argues it also led the way in the latter’s abolition.

In 1833, the UK parliament passed a law to abolish slavery in most of the British Empire.

Denis O’Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, which advocates for reparations for slavery for Caribbean nations, said London “must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now”.

“This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice,” he added.

However UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Saturday there was “no need” to revisit the issue of formally saying sorry, while reiterating her firm opposition to reparations.

She urged the Commonwealth to “look forward” and “not endlessly backwards”.

“Slavery was an evil in which people from every continent and region participated,” she wrote on X.

“We should be honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today.”

World.title: Udinese striker Davis eyeing Reggae Boyz spot
World.content:
Udinese's British forward #09 Keinan Davis celebrates after scoring a penalty kick during the Italian Serie A football match between Inter Milan and Udinese at San Siro stadium in Milan on August 31, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

Udinese striker Keinan Davis says discussions have taken place about representing Jamaica, but the England-born forward is still awaiting the completion of his Jamaican passport application before making the next step towards international football.

Davis, who has been enjoying an encouraging spell with Italian Serie A club Udinese, provided an update on his international future during an interview with CBS Sports Golazo, revealing that conversations have already taken place about the possibility of wearing the Reggae Boyz colours.

“I’ve had some conversations,” Davis said, while explaining that sorting out his Jamaican passport remains a major priority.

The 28-year-old 6ft 3 inches striker, born in England of Jamaican descent, said the administrative process was taking some time but expressed hope that the matter would be resolved.

“The procedure takes a little time, but we’ll see what happens in the future. I’m sorting out the passport,” he explained.

He also admitted that his injury history had previously influenced discussions about committing to international football, particularly given the demands of travelling between Europe and the Caribbean.

Davis, who represented England at the Under 20 level, said that when he spoke with Udinese last year, consideration was given to whether the additional travelling associated with international duty would be the best option for him as he sought to establish himself and remain available for club football.

However, the striker indicated that his current physical condition has improved and that he is determined to maintain his fitness.

“But now I’m well and I want to continue to be well,” he said.

The latest comments will provide encouragement for Jamaica, which has been keen to strengthen its attacking options.

His potential involvement would be a significant addition to the Reggae Boyz’ attacking department, given his physical presence, pace and experience in European football.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Hundreds of thousands of protesters march across France for third week in a row
World.content:
Arrests were significantly lower than during previous demonstrations, although tensions and clashes emerged in Marseille, Paris and Lyon as marches dispersed.

French authorities described the situation nationwide as “generally calm” in the early afternoon. France deployed 70,000 police officers to contain what it feared would be another day of unrest.

Many protesters wore Halloween costumes despite French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warning that face coverings could result in fines of €150.

Other European cities including Rome, Milan, Berlin and Frankfurt also experienced a day of youth-led protests against the cost of living and, in Germany, military spending.

The protests in over 30 German cities were ignited by a youth-led initiative called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z gets things done) and remained largely peaceful despite the police cancelling a planned march in Cologne after some participants wore face coverings and set off smoke bombs.

In Italy, the police carried out 60 searches across 23 cities targeting people suspected of inciting violence a mass demonstrations on Friday, according to news agency ANSA.

World.title: Putin’s potential G20 comeback risks normalizing Russian war crimes, says Kallas
World.content:
Putin hasn’t yet confirmed whether he would attend the December summit hosted in the U.S. His last in-person attendance at a G20 meeting was in 2019 — three years before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kallas’ remarks come amid growing frustration among EU countries over Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov’s attendance at a G20 ministerial gathering in Atlanta.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was hosting the meeting, called off the traditional family photo after European officials refused to stand beside Lavrov.

Kallas said in the interview that “we don’t want to stand next to him [Lavrov] in this fora,” because he’s been placed under international sanctions.

However, she added that Lavrov’s presence meant “we can also immediately fight back on these lies” from Russia.

Kallas hailed the U.S. decision on Friday to sell 500 Patriot missile interceptors to Ukraine as a “very positive development” and called on allies to toughen sanctions against Russia.

World.title: Merz ‘surprised’ by Asian pushback to ‘Made in Europe’ plan for car industry
World.content:
“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning from his five-day tour of East Asian countries on Friday evening.

Merz admitted the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”

The chancellor vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and to raise them at the next EU leaders' summit. The bloc's leaders are set to meet in Dublin on Nov. 13 for an informal gathering.

Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade” between so-called middle powers in speeches in Seoul and Tokyo. The EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged the international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted" — a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals or the tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

But the pushback from South Korea and Japan are a sharp reminder of how industry-specific frictions can hamper the implementation of the larger alliance proposed by Merz.

World.title: Burnham ‘open’ to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
World.content:
However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay financial reparations for the slave trade, saying that they would be the wrong solution.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” the prime minister argued.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced in June a manifesto by Caribbean leaders setting out the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations from former colonial powers.

Burnham will attend the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, which runs through Wednesday. It will be his first foreign trip with King Charles.

It will be a crucial test for the prime minister, who will try to avoid a fight over slavery reparations that marred his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit at the last summit in 2024.

World.title: Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries
World.content:
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won't pay for the Patriot interceptors. "The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies," a statement from the State Department said.

World.title: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
World.content:
Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”

The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management. Święczkowski rejected the move.

In a statement issued around 5 a.m., Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”

Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.

The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.

The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

World.title: Funding deadlock derails global effort to save nature
World.content:
But behind that grand gesture, governments are still struggling to unlock the hundreds of billions needed to meet global biodiversity protection targets. The reason? A profound and unresolved disagreement over where that money should come from.

“If we’re mutually unhappy that’s probably the closest we can get to on these very delicate compromises,” said a member of the Swiss delegation just before the text was adopted.

After two weeks of negotiations over how to speed up efforts to protect ecosystems, nearly 200 countries secured a hard-fought agreement to "accelerate the implementation" of the global biodiversity framework "including by increased ambition in addressing the gaps, challenges and barriers related to implementation," according to a draft of the text, the final version of which was not immediately available.

Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who presided over the summit, said negotiators had "achieved more than we could have expected."

But in the end, governments could not agree on how to increase the number of countries currently contributing to biodiversity finance, instead only stating the obvious: that more funds would be better.

The summit exposed a growing chasm between nations over who should be held financially responsible for funding conservation measures worldwide: historically wealthy countries whose economies have caused immense damage to the environment, or newly rich states whose economies have grown exponentially in the last three decades.

World.title: FBI blames North Korea for $6.3 billion Binance crypto hack
World.content:
The US' Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has accused North Korea of being behind a major hack targeting the Binance cryptocurrency exchange earlier this week.

 

Binance suffered what its co-CEO Richard Teng described as a "complex attack" that saw hackers gain access to its hot wallets and steal $6.3 billion in digital assets.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the FBI said in a statement on Saturday.

"The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as 'TraderTraitor,'" it continued, adding that it had observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets into Ethereum and that it expected these to be "further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services."

According to the US' Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), TraderTraitor is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group that has been associated with cryptocurrency thefts and cyberattack tactics since at least 2020.

It is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which the CISA says has carried out attacks against a variety of blockchain and cryptocurrency industry targets using spearphishing campaigns and malware.

Following the Binance attack, the exchange announced that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals as its team carried out security checks, froze funds and worked with law enforcement operatives to investigate the incident.

The company said that it has now covered around 90% of the impacted amount stolen in the hack and that withdrawals were resuming "in phases."

Binance said the remaining 10% of tokens were "less liquid," meaning they could take longer to buy.

In a video statement posted on social media, Teng said the company was "committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds."

"Your assets are safe," he added.

World.title: The world according to Ellen von Unwerth: Glamour, sensuality and photography
World.content:
If you have ever seen a fashion photo where the woman looks like she is getting away with something — running in heels, laughing in lingerie, stealing a car in a ballgown — you have very probably seen an Ellen von Unwerth picture. You just might not have known it was her.

 

For more than four decades, the German photographer has made her name with portraits that are sensual, provocative and playful.

From luxury brand commercials to fashion magazines, she's been immeasurably influential over the years, having perfected a shooting style that's often been imitated. In short, von Unwerth hasn't just captured fashion, she's created it.

She's developed what's widely recognised as the 'female gaze' and changed who gets to be sexy, and crucially, who gets to decide.

Perhaps, it's because of the ten years she spent as a fashion model herself, and knowing all too well what it felt like to be told to "stand still and look pretty".

In this edition of European Lens, von Unwerth talks about her life and times, when she first picked up a camera, getting laughs on set and slipping into something comfortable with celebrities.

We also took the opportunity to have a sneak a peek at her one of her latest projects, a collaboration with Toiletpaper, the contemporary arts magazine set up by Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari.

You’re a former model, and you made your name through your particular eye and, most notably, the gaze through which you photographed women and the power you gave them in your pictures. How did you come up with that?

Ellen von Unwerth: Well, I think the biggest inspiration was actually being a model for ten years and being quite frustrated, because I always wanted to express myself in front of the camera, move, be silly and show my personality. Photographers were always saying, “No, no, no, don’t move. Look to the left, to the right, and just pose.”

I never felt really great about it. I always saw my model friends living their lives and being so beautiful. After ten years of modelling, my boyfriend at the time gave me a camera and said, “There’s a plus, a circle and a minus. When the circle lights up, you push the button.” It was my crash course.

Then I started to photograph my model friends. I dressed them up in my clothes. I always had fun clothes, like vintage pieces from the flea market. I dressed them up and did their makeup. Quickly, I noticed that we had a great connection, and they behaved differently. They felt free and were playful. I became very passionate about it very quickly. We had a darkroom in our tiny apartment, and my boyfriend taught me how to print pictures. I started printing my pictures and got obsessed. I worked all night and stuck them to the walls in my little bathroom. That’s how I started.

Peaches, Rouilly-le-Bas, 2002 Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

Do you still surprise yourself? How has your approach has changed over the years?

It hasn’t really changed. Of course, I’ve had an amazing career since then, and I’ve been very, very lucky. I’ve met so many wonderful people. But I still love capturing life and those moments that are real and spontaneous. It’s such a great connection that I reach with people in that way.

The recent story about Sydney Sweeney's ad campaign came to my mind as you spoke. In terms of objectifying women, do you think things have improved, or have they regressed?

Well, I never objectified women. That was my subject. I think Sydney Sweeney decides what she wants to do, and that’s what she wants to do. She doesn’t care, and I kind of think that's great. Of course, not everybody is happy about it, but she lives her life, and that’s how it should be.

Sydney Sweeney for syrn Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

I wanted to ask you about the techniques involved, especially technology and how that has evolved in photography. How do you use modern tools now? So many people now have high-powered cameras in their pockets. Does that affect your vision?

Well, mostly, everybody has a phone. People don’t even have cameras. It's actually rare to see people with cameras. Yes, of course, it has affected things enormously. I was maybe one of the last people to switch to digital because I loved film. I still love it, and I’m actually shooting more and more with film again.

With film, you have a certain grain and a certain quality. You can’t really change that afterwards, but with digital you have the RAW files and all the possibilities in the world to do what you want with them. It’s great, but it’s also more difficult to find your style. I had my style from before, and I’ve kept it, but there are lots of possibilities.

As I say, it’s more difficult to find your style. And, of course, there’s the iPhone. I love the iPhone, too. It’s incredible, with all the possibilities and options. You can film, edit and do so many things, and then you have Instagram as a direct outlet. But at the same time, there are so many images. There’s an overload of images, and people just scroll, scroll, scroll. Sometimes you spend so much time creating an image with a big team, and you think, "Wow, now it’s out," and two seconds later it’s gone.

Rihanna Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

Do you feel that this has affected your process when you take pictures? Do you think, "Okay, this may be thrown away tomorrow"? Do you spend the same amount of time trying to compose and get the right shot?

Yes, because what I love about photography, first of all, is the teamwork. I love choosing the team: the people for the hair, makeup, styling and set design. I love it. I always say that if I wasn't a photographer, I’d be a circus director. It’s a little bit like that: you choose the team. You want them to be creative, but you also want to have a good time with them. For me, the fun is in creating. It’s not about thinking what’s going to happen tomorrow.

Then there’s the talent, of course. There has to be a connection with the person, whether it’s a model, a singer or an actress. I love the process, so I don’t think of it as throwaway, because fortunately I can make books and exhibitions. You think, "Oh, maybe one day that’s going to be on a wall and somebody will buy it" or whatever.

Let's talk about your relationship with the "talent", because so many of your photos are iconic. It always makes me think: how did you get them to do that?

That’s what I mentioned at the beginning. I think there’s something about me and my camera that makes people feel free in front of it. I don’t know; there's something special about the lens. Even animals start to behave weirdly.

Of course, I have my tricks. I always have music. I love disco music, something everybody can relax to. I see all my teams having fun and dancing in the background. Before I go on a shoot, I have to know that I can connect with those people. With some people, I know I won’t take great pictures. It’s something in their eyes, something in the way they are. It's more about their personality, really.

Claudia Schiffer for Guess, Nashville, 1991 Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

Looking back at your career, who stands out in your portfolio? Are there any pictures where you think, "Yeah, if I had to choose my top five, these are the ones I’m most proud of," or where there’s a backstory that makes you think, "I never thought we’d achieve that, considering how we started"?

Of course, at the beginning of my career, Claudia Schiffer was one of my favourites. Not just the picture, but, of course, that one picture of her wearing the corset. It’s very famous and maybe the most famous picture I’ve done. It was such a fun time, actually meeting this girl and saying, "Hey, look, she looks like Brigitte Bardot. Let’s give her the hair and makeup to make her look like Brigitte Bardot."

Then I started working for Guess, and I said to Paul Marciano, “Look at this girl,” because he always loved that cinematic ’50s and ’60s vibe, the French and Italian cinema. He said, "Yeah, let’s try it." We photographed her overnight, and when the pictures came out, everybody was talking about them. There was no Instagram at the time, of course. So this was really the beginning of my career, and it's very important to me.

Then there are so many others. I did Naomi Campbell, and I took so many pictures with Naomi, including the ones with Coke cans in her hair. I worked with David Bowie, Sophia Loren and Drew Barrymore too. Drew Barrymore was one of my favourites. I remember being at an awards after-party and seeing this girl, with a huge queue of people lining up in front of the toilet. I thought, "Who’s this little girl, looking so ’20s and so charming?" I went up to her and asked her, and we did a lot of shoots together.

And, of course, some of my favourite pictures are of my daughter.

David Bowie and Kate Moss Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

I also wanted to ask you about something we touched on earlier: artificial intelligence. Are you tempted by it? Do you see it as a help or a hindrance to what you do?

Well, it definitely helps sometimes with retouching. The other day, we had a picture by the river, and there was this really ugly boat that was very distracting. I said to my retoucher, "Can we do something?". He circled it, and it was gone. I was like, "Amazing!". Of course, it helps with things like that. Sometimes we also animate my pictures, and it’s crazy how easy it is. It takes a little bit of skill, and I have fun with it.

Måneskin frontman Damiano David Credit: Ellen von Unwerth

I always get a lot of very bad comments: "Ellen, you’re an artist. Why do you use artificial intelligence?". And I’m like, "Yeah, it’s there. It’s a tool. You have to jump on the bandwagon or you’re going to be left behind."

That said, I really love the process of taking pictures, the connection with people, the creative process, having ideas and sitting in my room thinking. That’s my thing, not just sitting in my room and doing everything with AI. And, of course, you know what it's doing: it’s getting a lot of people out of jobs. Even models are now creating their own AI versions. I think it’s like a big monster coming towards humanity, and I find it quite scary, actually.

You’re not alone in that. Tell me something now about Toiletpaper. How did this collaboration begin?

Well, I was in Berlin, and I had an event at Fotografiska, where they (co-founders Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari) had an exhibition. It was a really fun exhibition, with a big pool - you know, those pools filled with plastic bananas. You could roll around in it, and the pictures were sliced open so you could walk through them. It was a super-fun experience.

Toiletpaper Calendar December 2027 Credit: Ellen von Unwerth/ToiletEllen Paper vonUnwerth Calendar 2027

ToiletPaper Courtesy of Ellen von Unwerth/ToiletEllen PapervonUnwerth Calendar 2027

I posted lots of pictures from it on Instagram, and they contacted me. They were like, "Hey, Ellen, I hope you had fun at our exhibition." I said, "My God, I loved it!".

From there, we started a collaboration. I love that very pop, loud, flamboyant style, and part of my work is also very loud, flamboyant and pop. We talked, and I was very proud that they approached me, because I’m a big admirer of what they do. I was very proud, and we started the collaboration.

It was very hard to choose, because there are only six pictures each. We had so many, and narrowing them down to six was very hard.

I can see how there was a meeting of minds there. But how did the collaboration actually work? Did you have complete free rein? I’m interested in how it went.

Yeah, I had complete free rein. But after so many years of working, you know the style of each publication or brand. When you work for Vogue it’s one thing, when you work for i-D it’s another, when you work for Dior, it’s something else. You learn their style.

Then you get to know people's styles, too. My team and I looked through my archive and chose pictures that fitted the style, because they said we'd do an opposition: one picture would be mine and one would be theirs. We chose pictures that had something in similarity, so we could make a game of asking people what the similarities were.

It was fun. It was a very fun project, and I’m super proud and happy that it’s just come out.

Looking forward, Ellen, what else are you preparing at the moment? You spoke to me about the show in St Tropez. How often are you exhibiting now? How are you filling your days?

Well, I'm having a big exhibition in Maastricht. It's called My Circus because, before I was even a model, I was working in the circus in Germany. I saw the circus and it was so magical. After the show, I asked the director if I could work in the circus.

He said, "Oh, you look like a circus girl. You can start tomorrow." I wasn't a juggler or anything, but I was an assistant to the juggler. It was a very, very fun period, which actually inspired me a lot. In my pictures, there's always glitter, dishevelled glamour and magic. So, at the museum in Maastricht, the theme is My Circus. There are around 130 pictures inspired by the circus, featuring actors and actresses, as well as my fashion stories for Italian Vogue and American Vogue.

Then I have a little exhibition in St Tropez called Not Your Angel. Obviously, beautiful women look like angels, but don't get them wrong.

I'm also working on new books. I have a couple of new book projects. I'm planning to make a movie based on one of my books. It's called Revenge. We were already talking about it years ago, but then COVID came along. We were also supposed to film in Ukraine, which unfortunately fell through. Now we're starting to talk about it again, and I'm also creating a perfume. That's my big, big project this year.

ToiletEllen von PaperUnwerth Calendar 2027 is published by Damiani Books and is available now.

World.title: Russia says 'massive' drone attack targeted 'industrial enterprise' amid reports oil refinery hit
World.content:
Russian authorities said a major drone attack had targeted an "industrial enterprise" in the Nizhny Novgorod Oblast overnight, amid reports that a key oil refinery had been struck in the region.

 

In a post on Telegram, regional governor Gleb Nikitin said a "massive UAV attack" had resulted in "significant damage" to an industrial facility in the Kstovsky district.

"More than 100 drones have been destroyed," he wrote, adding that early information suggested there had been no casualties and that emergency crews were working at the scene.

"Whilst restoration work is underway, there may be temporary power cuts, as well as reduced hot water and heating supplies in certain sections of the utility networks serving residential buildings," Nikitin said.

Telegram war monitoring channels said an attack had targeted the Kstovo oil refinery - also known as the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery, thought to be one of Russia's largest such facilities.

According to Lukoil, the site is involved in the production of diesel and aviation fuel, among other things.

Earlier this week, a major fire reportedly broke out at another oil refinery in Russia's Samara region following a drone attack, with dramatic images and video footage posted on social media showing multiple towering columns of black smoke filling the skyline.

That incident followed reports that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refineries amid pressure from Washington, which has blamed the attacks on rising global diesel prices as it has sought to shift blame from its war in Iran.

Ukraine had been ramping up attacks on Russian energy infrastructure this year, particularly targeting facilities such as oil refineries, terminals and depots, in a bid to hit a critical Russian economic driver and grind down the Kremlin's war machine.

The latest reported attack comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said around 280,000 Ukrainian households had been left without power after Russian strikes on Ukraine on Friday night.

"Russian strikes have created a difficult situation with electricity supplies across our regions," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X on Saturday, saying that around 200,000 households in Dnipro and the wider region were without electricity while a further 80,000 or more in the Kyiv region were also without power.

The Ukrainian leader said Russian forces had hit a "combined heat and power plant" in Kyiv as well as four electrical substations in the eastern Dnipro region, among other targets.

World.title: Hooray for Houdini: Budapest celebrates 100th anniversary of escape artist's death
World.content:
As part of the Houdini 100 series of events, a four-day programme has begun in Budapest to mark the 100th anniversary of Harry Houdini's death. In tribute to the Hungarian-born American illusionist and escape artist, a relief is being unveiled and, among other things, a film festival and circus performances await visitors.

 

At the opening of the programme series, the deputy mayor of District I, Csilla Fazekas, said they are proud that the Houdini House operates in Buda Castle, preserving in a unique way in Europe the legacy of a world-famous Hungarian, Harry Houdini.

According to David Merlini, a magician and founder of the Houdini House in Budapest, many guests from around the world have arrived in the city for the celebrations. They include George Hardeen, the only living descendant of Harry Houdini, the grandson of his brother; television producer Gay Blackstone, from the legendary family of magicians and former president of the Academy of Magical Arts, which runs Hollywood's Magic Castle; and also Péter Gloviczki, a world champion magician and vascular surgeon.

Magician David Merlini, founder of the Houdini House (left), and George Hardeen, the grandson of Harry Houdini's brother, in front of Houdini's bust in Budapest on 29 October 2026 Lakatos Peter/MTI - MTI

Merlini added that the programme also includes the unveiling of a memorial plaque, a magic auction, and a night-time show at Houdini's birthplace in Csengery Street.

Houdini's eventful life

Harry Houdini was born on 24 March 1874 under the name Erik Weisz in Budapest, the son of a rabbi with many children. Four years later the family emigrated to the United States, lived for a time in Appleton, Wisconsin, then moved to New York in 1882.

Erik sold newspapers and shined shoes, and at the age of nine he made his stage debut as the "prince of the trapeze". At 12, he ran away from home and joined a travelling circus, but later returned to help his parents. During his youth he trained himself, running, swimming and boxing.

His career as a magician began when he was 17, with card tricks, but he was already experimenting with escape acts. After his father's early death, he devoted his time exclusively to magic.

He adopted the stage name Houdini in honour of the Frenchman Jean-Eugene Robert-Houdin, the first modern magician. In 1893 he met Wilhelmina Rahner, who became his wife and, under the name Bess Houdini, his stage assistant.

How did he become an escape artist?

In 1899 Houdini met impresario Martin Beck, who advised him to focus his show on escape acts.

He gained fame as the Handcuff King. For freeing himself from the handcuffs of Scotland Yard he received a six-month contract and a weekly fee of £300.

He toured Europe, with the local police assisting his acts with locks, handcuffs and prison cells, and he was often stripped naked and searched, yet he always managed to work his way free.

In 1904 he returned to New York a wealthy man. His acts attracted audiences in America as well and, from 1908, because of the large number of imitators, he built his productions not on chain and straitjacket escapes but on breaking out of locked spaces.

His first attraction of this kind was escaping from a giant milk churn filled with water and hermetically sealed from the outside. He lured audiences to this spine-chilling act with the slogan "Failure means death by drowning".

Houdini broke free from tanks filled with water, ranging in size from a coffin to a prison cell, from pits filled in with earth and even from the stomach of a beached whale. He owed his success to his vivid imagination, his tremendous physical strength, flexibility and suppleness, and his exceptional skill in opening locks, knots and other mechanisms.

He could hold his breath for up to four minutes, yet even so his life often hung by a thread, and he frequently fainted after freeing himself.

With a few exceptions he devised his own tricks, and he revealed the solutions of the most difficult only to his four assistants. Because of his secrecy, the mystery of most of his escapes has never been solved.

FILE: David Copperfield beside a display case containing items from his personal collection related to Harry Houdini on 21 November 1996 at the Martin Beck Theatre in New York Kathy Willens/AP

Audiences flocked to the shows bearing the name of the best-paid American illusionist. In addition to preparing for his tricks, he still found time to write books, try flying and make films (in March 2015, his first film, long thought to be lost, The Grim Game, resurfaced).

Houdini used his powers of persuasion and did not spare his fortune to promote the self-organisation of magicians, and from 1917 he was president of the Society of American Magicians.

As an illusionist he did not believe in "supernatural" powers. He campaigned against credulity and charlatanism, attended spiritualist séances in disguise and exposed fraudsters on the spot. He wrote books on the subject entitled "Miracle Mongers and Their Methods" and "A Magician Among the Spirits".

Yet together with his wife he undertook a spiritualist experiment: they agreed that whoever died first would try to contact the partner who remained alive. His widow's attempt was unsuccessful.

His mysterious death

In the autumn of 1926 Houdini was preparing a new show, but it never premiered. On Halloween, 31 October 1926, he died in Detroit. Officially his death was caused by peritonitis brought on by a ruptured appendix.

It is alleged that on 22 October, before his last performance, two students visited him in his dressing room in Montreal and, when Houdini boasted that he could withstand any blow, one of them punched him hard in the stomach twice without warning. The magician, who had no time to brace himself, later performed his show in excruciating pain, was taken to hospital, but they were unable to save him.

FILE: James Starrs, professor of forensic medicine, photographs Houdini's grave on Thursday 22 March 2007 in the Queens borough of New York Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

Others blame Houdini's demise on the spiritualists who had previously threatened him with death, believing they poisoned him.

His body, which was transported home in the coffin prepared for his new show, was buried without an autopsy in New York, where he lies in Machpelah Cemetery in Glendale.

In 2007 the idea of exhumation was raised, but this has not happened to this day.

Houdini's legacy

In 1975 Houdini was posthumously awarded a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and his figure has been evoked in novels, for example in Doctorow's work 'Ragtime', and in films.

In the 2014 American-Canadian film about him, shot in Hungary and entitled "Houdini" (source in Hungarian), the title role was played by his great admirer, Adrien Brody, who also has Hungarian roots.

His legacy is jealously guarded at his magic centre in Las Vegas by the world-famous illusionist David Copperfield.

World.title: EU Commission: Polish Parliament has right to appoint judges to the Constitutional Court
World.content:
The European Commission said on Saturday it was closely monitoring the crisis surrounding Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, following a confrontation outside the court building on Friday night that was broadcast live on television. The incident has brought renewed attention to a dispute that has been ongoing for more than a decade.

 

“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union,” a Commission spokesperson told Euronews on Saturday.

“The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm, Poland’s parliament,” the spokesperson added.

The Commission spokesperson also pointed to a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights, which on 5 May 2026 issued interim measures requiring the competent Polish authorities “to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm in March 2026”.

Tusk: “Restoring calm does not mean accepting lawlessness”

Prime Minister Donald Tusk addressed Poles in a televised speech on Saturday evening, in his first major response to the crisis. He described Friday’s events as “scandalous incidents” and said he hoped such scenes would never be repeated in Poland.

Restoring calm could not mean accepting lawlessness or violence, Tusk said, as he vowed to restore conditions for independent justice and rule of law.

“A democratic state has to be strong and capable of enforcing justice,” he added, vowing that the rule of law would prevail over violence.

The crisis escalated on Friday night when President Karol Nawrocki attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over the appointment of new judges.

Police surrounded the building as the confrontation unfolded live on television, highlighting the growing stand-off between the president and the government over the composition of the country’s top court.

The Tusk government says it is pushing ahead with long-needed reforms to restore the rule of law after years of what it describes as interference in the judiciary by the Law and Justice (PiS) party. The opposition accuses Tusk’s government of attempting a coup.

European conservatives accuse EU of silence

The co-chairs of the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group on Saturday condemned the Polish government’s actions, describing them as a violation of the rule of law, and backed President Nawrocki.

“The Tusk government’s actions constitute a clear and grave violation of the rule of law. We condemn this attack on judicial independence and Poland’s constitutional safeguards. No government stands above the law,” ECR co-chair Nicola Procaccini said.

He added that European institutions “must not avert their eyes” and said respect for national sovereignty and judicial independence must remain a matter of principle, “unaffected by political alliances”.

The Tribunal’s legitimacy has been contested for more than a decade. The dispute dates back to 2015, when the then-governing Civic Platform and the opposition Law and Justice party clashed over the appointment of five judges.

It has since developed into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.

World.title: Europe’s crumbling coastlines face a €800 billion crisis. Is it time to move inland?
World.content:
Nearly one in two Europeans live near a coastline, but their future remains uncertain.

 

Rising sea levels, largely caused by human-induced global warming, are gnawing away at vital infrastructure, family homes and heritage around the world.

Across 28 European countries, economic losses due to coastal erosion exceed €1 billion per year and could escalate to €800 billion annually by the end of the century if effective action is not taken.

It’s why a new report urges Europe to prepare to relocate homes, businesses and infrastructure from coastlines before it’s too late.

Should Europe’s crumbling coastlines be relocated?

The report by The Council of Europe argues that many of Europe’s coasts should urgently move towards “planned retreat”.

This means new development would be banned or restricted and homes, businesses and assets – including road and rail – would be moved to more climate resilient places inland.

For example, France estimates that around 900 kilometres of mainland coastline are receding, with more than 500 municipalities affected.

In Quiberville-sur-Mer in the Normandy region, a €9 million investment moved a public campsite inland. Municipal revenue subsequently increased by 25 per cent.

A seagull flies over high water in St. Mark's Square as strong winds pushed the Adriatic Sea into the Venice lagoon, submerging part of the city, Friday, Dec.12, 2008. Copyright 2008 AP. All rights reserved.

Of course, moving a campsite is a much easier feat than relocating entire residential villages or heritage structures. However, relocating coastal communities may be the only resort if alternative solutions fail.

In Venice, for example, experts predict that engineered banks called dikes may be necessary beyond 0.5 metres of sea level rise, which may occur by 2100 even if emissions are kept low. This would cost up to €4.5 billion, but would not be a permanent solution.

Closing the lagoon with a super levee (a wide reinforced embankment) could also be viable beyond 0.5 metres of sea-level rise, and could protect the city against sea level rise of up to 10 metres. However, the initial cost for this could exceed €30 billion.

Relocating the city, its residents and historic landmarks may be necessary beyond 4.5 metres of sea-level rise – which is projected to occur after 2300 – at a cost of up to €100 billion.

More than a quarter of Europe’s coastline is eroding

The report, titled ‘How can we cope with coastal erosion?’, also calls for authorities to update risk maps, introduce and periodically review no-build and buffer zones, and make adaptation plans that assess the legal, social and financial consequences of different choices.

This planning needs to be done in conjunction with those most directly affected: transparent consultation, public information and sustained political support are essential, alongside measures to protect livelihoods, coastal heritage and vulnerable communities, the report states.

40 per cent of Europe’s GDP comes from coastal regions and 80 per cent of low-elevation coast is at risk of future erosion. Better planning and relocation now, therefore, would save significant money later.

“Europe’s coastlines are among our most valuable assets,” says Greek politician and co-author of the report, Fanis Spanos. “They host major infrastructure, support vital economic activity and are centres of cultural and natural heritage.”

More than a quarter of Europe’s coastline is eroding, and the continued occupation of “high-risk zones” puts livelihoods at risk, Spanos adds.

Anthony Buchanan, co-author of the report, argues that defending Europe’s coasts with traditional methods such as building sea walls is becoming less sustainable due to the drastic rise in sea levels.

“Sea level rise has doubled in recent years and is on course to rise by another 44 cm by 2100, while storms are becoming more intense and frequent and extreme storm surges are likely to occur 20-to-30 times more often by 2050,” he explains.
