World.title: Doha stopover travel guide: What to see and do on a city break in Qatar's capital
World.content:
If you have an upcoming stopover in Doha, take it from me, you’re in for a treat.

 

Qatar etched its name in the history books as the first Arab nation to host a FIFA World Cup, which ushered in a wave of transformations. In the run-up to the 2022 tournament, the Gulf state introduced a raft of new hotels and infrastructure projects, such as Doha Metro.

The Qatari capital is the hub for Qatar Airways, which currently flies to more than 170 destinations around the world, including various direct links to Europe.

Arguably, Doha's Hamad International Airport is a destination in its own right. It features plenty of spots to eat and stunning public art, including Urs Fischer’s iconic Lamp Bear. There are even free 20-minute guided wellness sessions on offer at the massive 6,000 square metre ORCHARD space to keep travellers occupied.

A stopover leg of your journey, however, makes exploring the country beyond the airport doors and turning one holiday into two, very easy.

When you arrive, even if just for a few days, Doha is a destination of iconic landmarks, culture, desert adventures and great dining.

Landmarks and attractions

With its quaint cobble-stoned streets and pastel coloured buildings, Doha's Mina District and old port area is great for stretching your legs after a long-haul flight.

The popular Box Park features repurposed shipping containers that have been given a coating of technicolour paint and turned into shopping and food outlets that are perfect for taking that Instagrammable shot. During the winters, you can also see cruise ships docking at the Grand Terminal building.

For more waterfront views, you should head to the Doha Corniche. The seven kilometre stretch of promenade is one of the best places for views of the city’s skyline.

Here you can watch as traditional dhow vessels glide across the water, or even set sail on one, where each turn of the wooden boat reveals a new panoramic view.

A dhow sails along the waterfront in front of the city's skyline Fakhriya M. Suleiman/Euronews Travel

Shopaholics have no shortage of high street stores and luxury labels to find souvenirs to take back home. At Place Vendôme Mall in Lusail, be sure to bring comfortable shoes to this huge retail centre which is inspired by classical French architecture. Across four floors, there are 580 high-end and mid-range stores to choose from.

Described as the “Arabian Riviera”, the Pearl Island’s Mediterranean-style and yacht-lined marina is also a scenic location for a late night stroll, where a restaurant or café is always a stone’s throw away.

While in neighbouring Gewan Island, the shopping and dining space is home to as many as 100 outlets. Its Crystal Walk also features around 180 illuminated panels embedded into the ground, studded with works of art created with crystals. Visitors can spot motifs such as caravans, desert and forest landscapes alongside a panel with a penguin colony.

In the summer, temperatures in this part of the world can also get… well, hot. But what if I told you there are outdoor spaces in Doha to explore that have air conditioning?

Gewan Island’s open-air promenade is a record holder, having earned the Guinness World Record titles for the longest outdoor air-conditioned mall and the largest outdoor interactive light canopy.

While parks such as Rawdat Al Hamama Park, Umm al Seneem Park, Al Gharrafa Park and Oxygen Park all have air conditioning placed in walkways for visitors to keep cool as they explore the greenery.

Souq Waqif Visit Qatar

Souq Waqif and Katara: Doha’s cultural epicentres

Can you really say you’ve been to Doha if you’ve not paid Souq Waqif a visit? Nestled in the capital’s old town, the open-air market place of winding alleyways carries a centuries’ old history.

While it can be visited at any time of the day, the souq comes alive as evening falls. Here, the sounds of shoppers haggling with vendors, the smells of aromatics like saffron, zaatar and dried flowers as well as conversations held over coffee, known locally as “gahwa”, fill the air.

You can also meet some of the country’s most beloved animals. At the Falcon Souq, shopkeepers are more than happy to have tourists pose with the majestic bird perched on their arm.

The Katara Cultural Village's Amphitheatre Visit Qatar

Another stop to add to your Doha itinerary is the Katara Cultural Village. The waterfront destination is replete with galleries, performance spaces and architectural landmarks. Its amphitheatre blends classic Greek style with arched entrances as a nod to Islamic architectural influences. It can seat up to 5,000 spectators and has sweeping waterfront views.

Katara Cultural Village also has various public art installations, including the striking "Force of Nature II" by Italian contemporary artist, Lorenzo Quinn.

Doha is also home to an array of galleries, like Doha Fire Station, and museums, including the architectural marvel of the National Museum of Qatar. The exterior is inspired by the desert rose, while inside holds an immersive story back in time to Qatar's history that moulded the nation's identity and its modern achievements.

Other museums in Doha worth visiting include 3-2-1 Qatar Olympic and Sports Museum, Lawh wa Qalam: M. F. Husain Museum, and Msheireb Museums. Art Mill Museum, Lusail Museum and Qatar Auto Museum are set to be added to Doha's portfolio in the future.

Also part of the city’s cultural landscape is the Qatar National Library. This treasure trove is filled with books and periodicals in various European languages, alongside Arabic manuscripts, maps and globes. There are even printed materials that date back to the 15th century, when printing was first introduced in Europe.

Shams Al-Qassabi (pictured left) is Souq Waqif's first businesswoman Visit Qatar

Dining in Doha

Choosing where to eat is always a struggle – simply because I’m so spoiled for choice. Doha has more than 3,000 restaurants, serving up everything from traditional Qatari and Gulf cuisine, to Latin American, African, Asian and European flavours.

For traditional bites, visit Kamachi after a stroll at the Katara Cultural Village. Its must-try menu items include balaleet, a popular local dish made with saffron and cardamon spiced vermicelli noodles, slightly sweetened and topped with a fried egg.

Another no-brainer dining destination is Souq Waqif. If you have a craving for local street food, try the karak, a sweet and spicy tea, alongside any of the varieties of "khobz regag", a very thin and crispy flatbread, at the rustic Shay al Shamoos – established by the Souq’s first businesswoman, Shams Al-Qassabi.

When it comes to fine dining, Doha's food scene has attracted the attention of the Michelin Guide, which debuted in the country in 2024. As many as 41 restaurants are listed in the Michelin Guide Doha, including three that earned a Michelin star and eight with a Bib Gourmand.

IDAM by Alain Ducasse is located in the city’s Museum of Islamic Art, which overlooks the Doha Corniche. The Michelin-starred fine dining restaurant serves contemporary French cuisine paired with Qatari ingredients.

Alba, which serves Italian cuisine, and Jamavar, which serves Indian cuisine, are Doha's other one-Michelin starred establishments.

Sheraton Grand Doha Resort & Convention Hotel Visit Qatar

Where to stay

From luxury hotels to wallet-friendly accommodation, there are plenty of options for places to stay during a stopover.

Mandarin Oriental, Doha is a five-star property located in Msheireb, which is about a 20-minute drive from the airport. Offering 117 rooms, 41 suites and 91 apartments and villas, this luxury hotel also features two rooftop pools and a spa to unwind. This travel journalist cannot recommend the buffet breakfast at Mosaic enough, alongside the hotel’s other dining concepts, including IZU and Liang.

Doha’s luxury hotel portfolio also includes the Sheraton Grand Doha Resort & Convention Hotel, right on Corniche Street. Its distinctive pyramid shape has been a part of the Doha skyline since the early 1980s and today offers 371 rooms and suites where guests can choose between a sea or city view. Indoors, the hotel offers nine dining options, a 24-hour fitness centre and a spa. While outdoors, a pool and a 400-metre stretch of private beach awaits.

Inland Sea, Khor Al Adaid Visit Qatar

Day trips and desert adventures

About an hour and a half from Doha by road is the Inland Sea: Khor Al Adaid. Currently on the tentative list to be included as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it’s one of Qatar’s most striking natural wonders as a landlocked lagoon surrounded by sand dunes of up to 40 metres high. It also features rocky ridges and cliffs.

Here, the water is calm and warm, making it perfect for swimming. The best time of year to visit is anywhere from November through to April, when the weather’s just right.

Stopover visitors can also venture to Al Khor, one of the oldest cities in Qatar. The sleepy city is about 45 minutes from Doha by car and is bursting with coastal charm. Visit Al Khor Towers, which date back to the early 20th-century. The cylindrical structures were first built to have watchmen defend the harbour after the discovery of a water source, once thought to possess medical properties.

My top tip for a day trip from Doha? Go kayaking through the mangroves. On my days off and on weekends, you can always find me kayaking through the mangroves and lush greenery at Al Khor’s Purple Island. The island is about an hour away from the capital and is my favourite escape away from the city (and dry land). If the season is right, you can spot flamingos and herons alongside fish and crabs.

East-West/West-East by the late Richard Serra Visit Qatar

On the west coast of Qatar, at the Brouq Nature Reserve near Zekreet, the late Richard Serra’s East-West/West-East permanent installation spans more than a kilometre and stands tall amid the desert landscape. Ras Brouq is also home to a unique area with white cliffs and geological forms like mushroom-shaped hills. Just remember to bring a cap, sunscreen and plenty of water.

Got a little longer for your Doha stopover? Swap the city skyline for the country’s desert with a stay at Regency Sealine Camp. Located an hour’s drive from the capital, on offer are tents, rooms and suites where the desert and sea are at your doorstep. Here, guests can go quad biking, dune bashing, camel riding and even enjoy a falconry show. After a day in the desert working up an appetite, guests can dine at the camp’s communal table over a selection of Arabic, Asian and international dishes.

Key info for travellers

All EU member-state passport holders, and non-EU European nationals, including travellers from the UK, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Azerbaijan and Switzerland, can benefit from visa-free travel if they have a confirmed hotel booking.

In terms of getting around Doha, visitors can rent a car, book a taxi – including Uber – or use public transport, such as the metro, Karwa bus or the country’s three tram lines from Lusail, Msheireb and Education City.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by counsel for Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.

The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.

But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.

In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.

Trump ally and former president Aleksandar Vucic was defeated in Serbia's parliamentary election on October 25 Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."

Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"

Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."

How secure are the US midterm elections? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Good relations with Putin ally Vucic

Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.

The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.

Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.

Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.

Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israel: Outcome still unclear

There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.

Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.

Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.

Israeli's right-wing leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, highlighted his closeness to Trump in his election campaign Image: Oded Balilty/AP Photo/picture alliance

No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms

With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."

But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany's search for a nuclear waste site
World.content:
Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.

Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved, despite the fact that the first large-scale nuclear power plant went online in the Soviet Union in 1954.

Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.

Germany's search underway for ten years

Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.

Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.

Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.

The toll of nuclear power on generations to come To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Only 5% of Germany's territory remains under consideration

Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.

And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."

This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.

Nuclear waste in Germany is currently being stored at interim sites near nuclear power stations, such as this one in Gorleben Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

Germany has phased out nuclear power

Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.

In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.

"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."

400 meters underground, protected by a rock barrier

The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.

As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.

Nuclear power has been a controversial issue in Germany since the 1970s Image: Dieter Klar/picture alliance

Dehmer: 'Finland has great trust in government action'

Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.

Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."

The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.

Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion Binance crypto theft
World.content:
The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The FBI said Saturday that North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion (€5.36 billion) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.

The theft, which happened within a matter of minutes, is believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.

The stolen assets included bitcoin, ethereum and stablecoins such as tether and USD Coin, whose values are pegged to traditional currencies.

News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to slump on Friday.

On Sunday, Binance resumed withdrawals, saying the process would be completed in phases, with the first covering 15 cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin.

The company had suspended withdrawals after the hack.

Cryptocurrency giant Binance hit by $6.3 billion hack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the FBI say?

The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The agency said it had "observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets" primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum.

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi [decentralized finance] and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," it added.

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to ensure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

Crypto boosts Trump family fortune since White House return To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Binance say about the heist?

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.

The exchange said on Saturday it was using company funds worth over $6.34 billion to buy tokens to replenish about 90% of the assets stolen in the attack.

The remaining 10% consisted of tokens that were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy back, the company said.

"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

The heist came amid growing worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

World.title: Bulgarians vote in highly polarized presidential runoff overshadowed by Ukraine war
World.content:
Voters in Bulgaria are choosing between two candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and ties with Russia. The runoff comes after a record-low turnout in the first round.

Bulgarians on Sunday began voting in a highly contested presidential runoff following a tight race between the two main contenders last weekend.

The November 1 runoff pits two competing visions of Bulgaria against each other. Moscow-friendly incumbent Iliana Yotova opposes military aid to Ukraine, while former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov is backed by the pro-Western opposition.

In last Sunday's first round, which saw voter turnout fall to a historic low, Yotova won with 34.76% of the vote, less than three percentage points ahead of Gyurov with 31.95%.

Iliana Yotova (left) beat Andrey Gyurov (right) by a narrow margin in the first round on October 25, 2026 Image: BGNES

Although Bulgaria's presidency has largely ceremonial duties, the president can appoint interim governments during political crises, serve as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and veto legislation.

Ukraine war divides Bulgaria

The war in Ukraine has become a central issue in the election, with voters heading to the polls amid growing security concerns in the Black Sea, which borders Bulgaria, following a rise in drone attacks targeting commercial vessels.

How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yotova has presented herself as a "president of peace" who favors dialogue with Moscow.

In a TV debate before the runoff, Gyurov accused Yotova of avoiding direct criticism of Russia over the Black Sea attacks.

"Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken. Let us name the country from which the threats are coming," he said.

In response, Yotova argued that "peace can come only through negotiations," and maintained that continued aid for Ukraine "leads only to more destruction and the deaths of many people on both sides."

Yotova vs Gyurov: Between Russia and the West

If elected, Yotova is expected to pursue a similar approach to Prime Minister Rumen Radev — keeping Bulgaria on its European path while seeking closer ties with Russia and advocating the lifting of sanctions.

A victory would make Yotova the first woman to be elected president of Bulgaria [FILE: October 25, 2026] Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

Her opponent Gyurov previously served as deputy governor of Bulgaria's central bank and as caretaker prime minister, leading the country in early 2026.

He has repeatedly voiced strong support for Ukraine and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.

After the first round of voting, Gyurov said that Bulgaria faced a choice "between two personalities, two directions, and two ways of exercising presidential powers."

World.title: Bolivia declares emergency as El Nino intensifies, threatens severe weather
World.content:
President Rodrigo Paz warned of severe droughts and flooding as El Nino intensifies, with at least 78,000 families already affected by drought.

Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz has declared a national state of emergency to mobilize resources and strengthen disaster response as the country braces for severe droughts and flooding linked to the El Nino weather phenomenon.

"This will be a phenomenon that will have very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods, and we need the cooperation of all institutions," Paz said.

Bolivia braces for extreme weather

The president's decree allows the deployment of additional rescue teams and calls for coordination between national and regional authorities, the armed forces and police.

According to a Bolivian government report, drought has:

affected at least 78,000 families across seven of Bolivia's nine departments

led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle

Authorities have also warned of potential floods, flash floods, and landslides as the rainy season begins.

What is El Nino?

El Nino is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific that disrupts global weather patterns, often bringing drought to some regions and heavy rainfall to others.

The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.

Researchers have estimated that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.

The United Nations has described the current El Nino, which is expected to peak in December, as "heading off the charts." Its impact could last years, with the UN urging nations in the Pacific to prepare for the worst.

World.title: India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions
World.content:
11/01/2026 November 1, 2026 INDIA bloc holds big rally against electoral irregularities, election chief

India's political opposition is carrying out a major march in New Delhi to protest the nationwide revision of electoral rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

They are also seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The 'Chalo Dilli' march, heralded by the main opposition Congress party, will begin from Central Delhi's Connaught Place Minto Road Junction to reach Ramlila Maidan.

Top faces of the opposition alliance — called the INDIA bloc — are among those expected to participate. These include Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav and Rashtriya Janata Dal's Tejashwi Yadav.

India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which carried out its own demonstrations against Kumar last month, has also backed the opposition rally.

What is India's electoral roll controversy?

Under a contentious nationwide voter-verification exercise, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), around 130 million names have been purged from electoral rolls.

The opposition and critics say that those struck off the voter lists include a large number of minority voters and accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. BJP denied the allegations.

The outcry against election chief Kumar began in September after an investigative report by an Indian daily said that there were divisions ​in the country's poll body — the Election Commission of India (ECI) — over the revision of voter lists, which it oversees.

Concerns emerged over the ECI's independence.

The ECI has maintained the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

India: Protesters jailed amid election row To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Opposition stages symbolic impeachment of election chief

On Saturday evening, the INDIA bloc staged a mock impeachment of the chief election commissioner. The symbolic proceedings saw opposition members reenacting a parliamentary session in a garden at Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.

"I don't think anything like this has ever happened in history. The entire opposition sitting in a garden to discuss the impeachment of the CEC, it is absurd," leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said.

He added that the opposition lawmakers had to hold the mock exercise — which even featured furniture, seating arrangements and carpeting resembling the Lok Sabha (lower house of the Indian parliament) — because they "have nowhere else to go."

"We have no other option. Every single institution ... is closed for us," Gandhi said.

Meanwhile on Sunday, the opposition expects thousands of supporters to descend upon Ramlila Maidan.

It is the first major demonstration to be held at the famous ground, located between Old and New Delhi, since it was labeled as one of the three designated protest sites in the capital last month.

Early visuals showed supporters beginning to gather at Ramlila Maidan and posters of the 'Chalo Dilli' march propped up in the capital.

The Delhi Police said that around 200 to 250 CCTV cameras have been set up at the site as part of the security arrangements.

News agency ANI reported that around 4,000 security personnel have been deployed at Ramlila Maidan.

"The organizers have set up various enclosures, and we have police personnel stationed within them. There are also pathways between these enclosures, where our police personnel are deployed to ensure the area remains secure,” deputy commissioner of police (Central District) Rohit Rajbir Singh told ANI.

The capital's traffic police announced curbs and diversions in Central Delhi ahead of the rally.

World.title: Trump grants visa to mother of Ghanaian boy killed in NYC — Mamdani
World.content:
Javits Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot in a neighborhood in the Bronx. He was 15 years old.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday that US President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old boy who was killed in a Bronx neighborhood earlier this week.

Javits Frimpong moved to New York from Ghana last year to be with his father and begin a new life in the US, according to Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.

Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning on his way to school and later died in the hospital, according to New York City police.

There have been no arrests in the case so far, with police investigating the shooting.

Mamdani says he spoke to Trump

"I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," Mamdani posted on X.

"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," he wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person."

The killing led to an outpouring of grief in New York, with Torres writing, "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him."

The White House is yet to comment on the Trump-Mamdani phone call.

Teen was bullied in school, father says

Thomas Frimpong remembered his son as a quiet boy and said he was bullied in school by two boys.

Ghana's foreign minister, Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa, thanked Mamdani and Trump in a post on X.

He said Ghanaian officials were coordinating with Javits Frimpong's mother to assist her with the visa application process.

World.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
World.content:
After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

Old accusations against Vucic

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in the parliamentary elections on October 25 Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

How much damage can the old government do to the new one?

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia , an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

Against all odds: How Serbia's students took on Vucic To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

No change in foreign policy

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Las vidas truncadas en el tren: “Gracias por quererme, por entenderme, por ser el mejor padre del mundo”
World.content:
El goteo de identificación de fallecidos y desaparecidos en el accidente de Urda desvela las historias detrás de las 69 víctimas y el dolor de sus familias

La mañana del miércoles España despertó con un soleado día de otoño que, en cuestión de minutos, quedaría ensombrecido por una gigantesca tragedia. Poco después del amanecer, 147 personas se apresuraban en la estación madrileña de Atocha para coger un tren Iryo que salía a las 7.54 horas hacia Sevilla. La joven atleta Julieta Gallego, que había llegado desde Berlín para disfrutar de unos días de vacaciones en Córdoba con sus abuelos; la podóloga argentina de 32 años, Ana María Conte, que regresaba a su lugar de residencia junto a su hermano Zacarías; el revisor portugués de 49 años Nelson Bernardino, que atendía con su uniforme a los pasajeros; o la exministra Fátima Báñez, de 59 años y actual presidenta de la Fundación CEOE, que acudía a los actos por el Día de la Empresa en Andalucía.

Solo unos minutos más tarde, otros 397 pasajeros se arremolinaban en torno al andén de entrada del AVE 2080, que tenía prevista su salida a las 8.03, y que pilotaban el maquinista Antonio Acedo de 36 años y su compañero en prácticas Daniel Cabañas, de 32, dos apasionados de los trenes. Tras ellos, en sus primeros vagones, se montaron la arquitecta y exvocal del Colegio Oficial de Arquitectos de Madrid (COAM), Patricia Fernández Häring, de 58 años, cargada con sus planos y proyectos; el guardia civil José Manuel Chacón, de 31 años, originario de Dos Hermanas y destinado en la unidad técnica de policía judicial en Madrid, que iba a reunirse unos días con su familia; el joven cordobés Francisco José Barbero, que trabajaba en Madrid cuidando a una persona mayor y que llamó a su madre esa misma mañana, desde su asiento 18B en el coche 7, minutos antes del desastre, sobre las 08.15, para avisarle de que ya iba de camino a Córdoba.

También iba en esos primeros vagones del AVE el inspector de Hacienda Antonio Montero, junto a otro compañero de profesión, que fue quien avisó de lo sucedido a los suyos; y la bióloga molecular Marta Shahbazi Alonso, de 41 años, que iba a recoger el Premio José Luis Gómez-Skarmeta a la Excelencia Científica y a pronunciar una conferencia en un congreso de Huelva. También se montó en el convoy la compositora y pianista, galardonada con el Premio Nacional de Música en 2024, Marisa Manchado, de 70 años, que ese mismo día iba a participar en la Facultad de Ciencias de la Educación de Sevilla en un simposio sobre su propia obra...

A las 8.53 horas el AVE de Renfe, a una velocidad de entre 160 a 200 kilómetros por hora, alcanzó por detrás al tren Iryo, parado en la vía a la altura de la estación de Urda (Toledo), y un total de 69 vidas se pararon para siempre en esas vías. A medida que avanzan las labores forenses, se van conociendo las historias de quienes han visto truncados sus proyectos, sueños e ilusiones tras la brutal colisión. El último balance, de la noche de este sábado, recoge que ya ha terminado la identificación de 56 cadáveres, de las que 51 ya han sido notificadas a los familiares.

De izquierda a derecha, Cristina Chao, Antonio Chao, Sheila Chao, Álex, pareja de Sheila, y Toñi Barba.

Se desvela en ese proceso de identificación de víctimas, por ejemplo, el gran amor que unía a los padres de Sheila, Toñi Barba Soler y Antonio, y que el mortífero accidente segó al llevarse por delante la vida de ella y dejarle a él malherido en una UCI, cuando pretendían disfrutar de un pequeño viaje regalado por sus hijas. Se descubren incipientes carreras, como la de la ingeniera alicantina Adriana Marroquín, de 27 años, que acudía a Sevilla a una reunión de trabajo de su empresa Engie, especializada en energías renovables. O la de la joven emprendedora de Inca (Mallorca), Maricarmen García, de 26 años, que ya lideraba su propia empresa de comunicación y viajaba con otros tres compañeros; una de ellas sigue en la UCI. O la de la escaparatista de Mango Andrea Olmo, natural de Figueres (Girona) y que también viajaba por trabajo.

Se conoce que Ana Avilés Uruñuela había salido temprano para llegar a Sevilla cuanto antes y ayudar a su hija Ana con los preparativos de su boda, que iba a celebrarse el sábado. O que Trece, el perro de Pepe (José Ángel Sanemeterio), se salvó milagrosamente en su transportín, dejando atrás a su dueño. Se identifican rostros conocidos como el del periodista de Telecinco, Raúl Triguero, de 43 años, del programa De Viernes y, antes, habitual de Sálvame, que iba a Sevilla a entrevistar al hermano de Rocío Jurado, Amador Mohedano, para el programa de este viernes, 30 de octubre.

Día tras día, hora tras hora, mientras sus familiares buscan y esperan angustiados y ansiosos noticias en el peor peregrinaje imaginable, las redes sociales se pueblan de imágenes de todos ellos, sonrientes, felices en sus vidas. Al principio, con llamamientos desesperados de localización. Después, tras la confirmación de los peores presagios, con textos de resignación y despedida. En X o Instagram, algunas familias urgen a los medios a que no publiquen que sus allegados ya están muertos, sino desaparecidos y que no difundan imágenes de las víctimas sin consentimiento.

Otros ya han publicado pequeños obituarios que reflejan que el número de fallecidos esconde vidas rotas: “Detrás de un taurino serio había un hombre extremadamente sensible que lloraba desconsolado cuando veía a sus toreros cuajar un toro en la plaza o una becerra en el campo”, escribía el torero Pablo Aguado a su apoderado Antonio Vázquez, cuando confirmó su muerte en el accidente. “Dormía soñando con el número tal que había embarcado y que no podía fallar, y se cruzaba España entera para ir a ver un sobrero”, añadía. Precisamente, Vázquez (Linares, Jaén, 1951), iba a visitar ganaderías y ver algunos toros en el campo.

“No sé qué hacer con todos los días que nos quedaban juntas ni cómo se vuelve a casa cuando el mundo se ha terminado y fuera sigue viviendo la gente como si nada, pero papá, joder mamá, papá… “, escribía Sheila para despedirse de su madre, Toñi Barba. “Porque nosotros hemos perdido a nuestra madre, pero papá ha perdido su vida entera, su casa, su compañera, su niña… Y hasta en aquel tren mamá, hasta cuando todo se venía abajo, él solo pensaba en ti”, añadía.

“Gracias por haber estado a mi lado en mis momentos de duda, y duras decisiones. Por quererme, por entenderme, por dejarme ser como soy, por ser el mejor padre del mundo”, le dedicaba unas palabras el actor César Vicente, a su padre, César Vicente Sanz, un profesor del instituto Hispalis de Sevilla recién jubilado que viajaba en el vagón 8 del AVE, con su maletín y su gato.

Los tres días de luto oficial se han cumplido, pero el duelo y el dolor seguirán por mucho tiempo. Todavía las familias están recogiendo a los suyos en la morgue de Toledo para despedirles en la intimidad y darles sepultura. Después aún tendrán que asumir la titánica tarea de seguir la vida sin ellos.

World.title: Feijóo gira la campaña hacia el perfil gestor del PP
World.content:
La escenografía de este viernes en el PP no dejaba lugar a dudas. Alberto Núñez Feijóo reunió en la sede del PP a una quincena de expertos en la red ferroviaria de dentro y fuera del partido para estudiar las causas del devastador accidente de Urda. A su espalda, en la pantalla a toda pared de la segunda planta de Génova, se leía en grandes letras: “Gestión. Rigor. Experiencia”. Esas tres palabras definen el mensaje hacia el que el PP reenfoca ahora su estrategia de precampaña, que ha saltado por los aires, como la de todos los partidos, por el cisne negro de Urda. Los populares, que suspendieron los actos electorales por la catástrofe, estudian ahora cómo retomarlos, pero con la idea de proyectar su perfil gestor, que sirve además para tratar de conjurar el riesgo de otro repunte de Vox por una reacción emocional de la sociedad española ante el desastre ferroviario.

Feijóo reunirá este lunes al Comité Ejecutivo Nacional del PP, con la presencia de los barones populares pese a que es festivo en nueve comunidades autónomas, para estudiar con la plana mayor del partido los próximos pasos. Será un acto recogido, apuntan en Génova, sin banderas ni himnos, con el que el líder del PP arrancará la semana, una vez superado el luto oficial de tres días, tratando de reforzar su perfil presidenciable.

A un mes de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, el trágico choque de dos trenes en el que han muerto 69 personas y decenas han resultado heridas es un mazazo para el Gobierno, responsable último de la red ferroviaria, y en el PP son conscientes de que, en consecuencia, les abre una nueva oportunidad electoral. Las encuestas ya apuntaban a una mayoría absoluta de PP y Vox antes del accidente, pero los socialistas habían conseguido instalar un marco de remontada con un tono de optimismo y positividad que ahora se ha acabado de un plumazo. “No acierto a ver cómo pueden levantar su campaña, porque ¿qué temas plantean? El España va bien se les ha terminado, no pueden hablar de vivienda, ni de transportes, ni pueden hablar de alegría”, analiza un miembro de la dirección, que cree que “todo ha cambiado”, aunque se resiste a dar las elecciones por sentenciadas. “Hay que ver cómo evoluciona todo”, medita. Porque el PP, que se beneficia de los problemas de su principal adversario, el PSOE, también afronta riesgos en este nuevo escenario: el de un avance de Vox.

Ese temor a un empuje de la extrema derecha recorre a la dirección del PP tras la catástrofe de Urda. “Es imposible que la gente interprete esto desde la racionalidad. La gente quiere un ajuste de cuentas, venganza”, alerta un colaborador de Feijóo. Ese riesgo de una reacción emocional que impulsa al partido de Santiago Abascal se ha visto antes, en otras crisis graves, como la de Ceuta o la dana de Valencia, y de momento había escalado a los ultras, según los sondeos anteriores a la tragedia ferroviaria, siete puntos por encima de su resultado de 2023, a un 19% de los votos. Ahora, con la incógnita de cómo moverá el voto el siniestro ferroviario, el PP trata de contener ese posible avance de Vox con el mensaje de que en este momento lo que el país necesita son esas tres palabras, “gestión, rigor y experiencia”, que solo puede representar Feijóo frente a Abascal.

Este sábado, el PP siguió esa estela y reunió a todos los consejeros de infraestructuras de sus Gobiernos autonómicos con el vicesecretario de Hacienda, Juan Bravo, para seguir analizando la crisis y volver a proyectar al PP como un partido gestor. El comité de campaña tendrá que reunirse y “rehacer todo el plan electoral”, apuntan en Génova, porque “hay que reanalizar todo, con los escaños fluctuantes” para saber dónde celebrar los siguientes actos.

Abascal ha optado en cambio por otro camino. El líder de Vox ha sido el único que no ha suspendido sus mítines y se ha lanzado a acusar desde el primer minuto al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez de cometer “un crimen” en Urda. “No es un error humano ni técnico, es un crimen”, proclamó el líder de Vox en un acto de partido en Ávila vestido con corbata de luto un día después del accidente, en el que también llamó al ministro de Transportes “Óscar Muerte”.

Feijóo, después de dos días en un perfil más institucional, también subió el tono el viernes. Y culpó al Gobierno de los dos accidentes mortales en la alta velocidad en menos de un año. “Han muerto 46 personas por un mantenimiento deficiente por parte del Gobierno en Adamuz, y al menos 69 en Toledo porque no renovó un sistema de seguridad obsoleto cuando debería haberlo hecho”, afirmó en su comparecencia en la sede del PP tras la reunión con expertos en el sistema ferroviario. El líder del PP consideró “cobarde e inmoral” que se señale a una sola persona, el operario del centro de control de Atocha que dio las órdenes equivocadas, “cuando hay fallos en cadena” y emplazó a la sociedad a dar una respuesta a lo sucedido en las elecciones. “Si no dimiten ellos”, reflexionó Feijóo, “les dimitiremos en las urnas”, dijo para tratar de convertir el 29-N en un juicio a la gestión del Gobierno.

World.title: Mägo de Oz, muy grandes, muy conflictivos: demandas, disputas por el poder y una película que reabre las heridas del grupo heavy
World.content:
Mägo de Oz es la banda más grande del heavy metal español. También la más conflictiva. Algunos pensarán: ¿y Barón Rojo, qué? Otros: ¿y Obús? Pero los números avalan a Mägo de Oz: los miles de asistentes a sus conciertos en España y Latinoamérica durante tres décadas son imbatibles. También en ventas de discos supera a cualquier otro grupo del género duro. Este año, por ejemplo, su nuevo álbum, Malicia: la noche de las brujas (2025), compite en los Grammy Latinos como mejor disco de rock. El juicio resulta menos concluyente cuando se atiende a la calidad musical y al peso histórico del repertorio. Incluso los propios integrantes de Mägo de Oz reconocerían, acaso en privado, el impacto y la trascendencia de las canciones de Barón Rojo, claramente superior al suyo.

A todo esto, a Txus di Fellatio (alias de Jesús María Hernández), líder supremo de Mägo de Oz, no le gusta el término “heavy metal”. “Yo soy un rockero, porque los rockeros somos más macarras que los heavies”, cuenta con su habitual bravuconería en una entrevista con EL PAÍS. Txus acaba de llegar a su chalet, a unos 60 kilómetros de Madrid. Son las ocho de la tarde de un miércoles. Ha ensayado la mayor parte del día. Se ha duchado, se ha vestido con un chándal, ha sacado a pasear a sus perros y, en un rato, preparará la cena para su hija Leia, de siete años. “Algunos se creerán que estoy ahora en una orgía poniéndome hasta arriba de cocaína, pero siento decepcionarles. Así es mi vida actual”. Txus tiene 56 años, ha pasado por tres divorcios y ha despedido —o alentado a que dejasen la banda— a una treintena de músicos de “su grupo”, como él considera a Mägo de Oz. “Tengo un socio [Carlos Prieto Moha, violinista del grupo], pero el dueño soy yo”, enfatiza. Recientemente, Txus asegura que presentó una demanda contra los productores de Fiesta pagana, la película sobre Mägo de Oz, su banda, que se estrena el cines el viernes 6 de noviembre. Una disputa más en la turbulenta carrera de la banda.

Mägo de Oz posa en la gala de los Premios de la Academia de la Música, el 26 de mayo de 2026 en Madrid. Desde la izquierda: Jorge Salán (guitarra), Rafa Blas (voz), Txus di Fellatio (batería) e Ix Valieri (guitarra). Carlos Alvarez (Getty Images)

Esta historia comienza un día de hace tres años, cuando Txus recibe una llamada de Moha: una productora había contactado con el violinista porque quería rodar una película sobre el grupo. “Así que nos reunimos en un Vips, nos lo plantean y yo digo: sí, Mägo es muy grande, pero no es Miguel Bosé ni Rocío Jurado, yo me siento más cómodo con un documental. Pero ellos estaban empeñados en una película. En fin, que les pedí el guion”, explica el músico. Cuando lo leyó, no le cuadraron ciertas cosas, “porque no ocurrieron así”. La productora argumentó que se trataba de “licencias cinematográficas”.

“Luego llegó el anuncio de la película”, continúa Txus, “donde la vendían de forma muy sensacionalista, como un enfrentamiento entre José Andrea [cantante de los años de éxito del grupo, de 1996 a 2011] y yo. No me gustó, porque Mägo ha hecho grandes cosas y solo se centraban en las peleas. Evidentemente ha habido polémicas, como en todas las bandas, pero no lo puedes centrar todo en eso. Tampoco me cuadraban los muchos clichés del heavy que incluían. Aquello parecía la película de Flo y Santiago Segura, Isi/Disi [comedia de trazo grueso llena de lugares comunes del heavy]. Y yo odio todas esas cosas”, explica. La siguiente reunión se produjo en su casa: “Yo les dije: ‘Vale, os voy a documentar, voy a sacar fotos antiguas, me voy a encargar de proporcionar parte de la escenografía, la ropa de la época… Todo, ¿a cambio de qué? Y me hablan de que vamos a cobrar un millón y medio de euros cada uno de los cinco miembros de la primera formación. Entonces terminé la reunión. Nos estaban tomando claramente el pelo: no podían pagarnos ese dinero, porque hablamos de cine español. Que sí, que hacemos muy bien los dramas y tal, pero no una película como la que querían rodar”.

Desde la izquierda, Juan Carlos Marín 'Carlitos' (guitarra), José Andrea (voz) y Pedro Díaz 'Peri' (bajo), en el festival Vive Latino de Ciudad de México, el 24 de abril de 2010. Jam Media (LatinContent via Getty Images)

La negociación quedó así: “Les di permiso para utilizar el nombre del grupo y el mío por 300.000 pavos, pero les dije que no quería saber nada de la película. Llegamos a ese acuerdo”, explica el músico.

El director de Fiesta pagana, Álvaro Brechner, ganador de un Goya al mejor guion adaptado por La noche de 12 años, ofrece su opinión en conversación telefónica con este periódico: “Yo creo que la película es un homenaje a la figura de Txus. Mägo de Oz es una banda que se animó a hacer cosas que sonaban disparatadas, como mezclar heavy con violines. Es como cuando ves los ingredientes de una receta gastronómica y dices: ‘Esto va a ser un desastre’. Y, sin embargo, lo de Mägo no solo fue magnífico, sino que fue único”. El director uruguayo llegó al filme por encargo. Él y Txus nunca hablaron. “Me nutrí de conversaciones con miembros actuales y con excomponentes”, señala, “y esos recuerdos estaban llenos de conflictos, así que me limité a hacer una película que debía contener energía, actitud y descaro”. Brechner cuenta que algunos de sus filmes musicales preferidas son This Is Spinal Tap (parodia sobre grupos heavies), Anvil: el sueño de una banda de rock (sobre la peculiar banda canadiense de heavy Anvil) y Metallica: Some Kind Of Monster.

Y aquí comienzan verdaderamente los choques. Txus, quien afirma que no quiere ver la película, asegura haber demandado a la productora, El Sueño Eterno, por algo para lo que no les dio permiso en el pacto que sellaron: “Registrar sin permiso y unilateralmente un nombre (Fiesta pagana —título de la película y de la canción más popular de la banda—) que por derecho, historia y justicia es un bien que pertenece a Mägo de Oz y que incumple la ley de propiedad intelectual (artículo 10.2 del Real Decreto Legislativo 1/1996)”. En conversación con EL PAÍS, Patricia González, directora de El Sueño Eterno, sostiene: “Es incierto que nos haya demandado. Al menos, todavía no hemos recibido ninguna demanda de él. La realidad es que llevamos tres años intentando levantar la película y este señor está continuamente entorpeciendo el proceso. Y es una pena, porque todo el mundo está encantado: exmiembros de Mägo, componentes actuales, el público que la ha visto en los pases…”.

El actor Adrián Lastra en la piel de Txus di Fellatio en la película 'Fiesta pagana'. Rubén Chavero / Cedida

González confirma que el único miembro del grupo que ha cobrado hasta el momento es Txus, “pero, como se debe aburrir, está todo el día medrando”. Sobre los argumentos del músico para demandarlos, señala: “Consultamos a la Oficina Española de Patentes y Marcas del Ministerio de Industria si Fiesta pagana estaba registrado, y nos dijeron que no. Así que solicitamos ese nombre en tres epígrafes audiovisuales y nos lo concedieron”. En este ambiente de fuego cruzado, la responsable de la productora anuncia una demanda contra Txus “por injurias, mentiras y difamaciones” basándose en los comunicados que el músico publica en las redes sociales.

¿Fue siempre tan desagradable la convivencia en el grupo madrileño? Hubo un tiempo en el que Mägo de Oz era el asidero al que se aferraban unos chavales de barrios madrileños para escapar de una vida enfocada a trabajos precarios. Txus, ideólogo del grupo, funcionaba como un cabecilla atípico desde la batería: ni cantaba ni tocaba la guitarra, lugares donde habitualmente se ejerce el liderato. Fantaseaban con convertirse en estrellas del rock mientras viajaban hacinados en una furgoneta maloliente rumbo a un concierto en el que solo les pagarían con cervezas. “Éramos un grupo de amigos unidos por un sueño. Lo hacíamos todo juntos y lo pasábamos muy bien”, recuerda para este reportaje Juan Carlos Marín Carlitos, 61 años, parte fundamental de la historia de la banda como guitarrista y compositor durante 27 años.

Los actores que interpretan en 'Fiesta pagana' a los componentes de la etapa más exitosa de Mägo de Oz. Rubén Chavero / Cedida

Mägo de Oz logró triunfar a finales de los noventa, cuando el heavy metal atravesaba uno de sus momentos más bajos. El especialista en rock duro Fernando Galicia, autor del libro Conversaciones con Mägo de Oz, ofrece algunas claves: “Su acierto fue proponer una música bastante exótica: heavy metal con violín y flauta. Ni siquiera vienen de la tradición de Ñu o Jethro Tull. Tampoco de la música celta. En ese aspecto son muy originales. La otra clave es que consiguieron que el heavy metal sonara popular, que llegara a gente que no era aficionada al género. Cuando suena Fiesta pagana en un bar o en unas fiestas, la gente se la sabe de memoria. Ellos lograron trascender el heavy para llegar al gran público”. Galicia destaca también las letras, que define como “rompedoras”: “Txus escribe muy bien, con su obsesión antiiglesia, con su implicación ecologista o al abordar el tema de la homosexualidad, nada habitual en el rock duro, en canciones como El que quiera entender que entienda”.

Pero con el éxito también afloraron las disputas entre los componentes. “Esto ocurre porque alguien cambió las reglas por el ego y la avaricia”, apunta Carlitos. Txus se defiende: “Puedo ser autoritario, pero no un dictador, como se ha dicho”. Existen dos periodos especialmente críticos en las agitadas tres décadas y media del grupo. Cuando comienzan a acumular popularidad, con discos como La leyenda de La Mancha (1998), Finisterra (2000) y Gaia (2003), colisionan los dos temperamentos más fuertes: el cantante, José Andrea, un espíritu libre y bohemio con alma de hippy; y Txus, dominante, obsesivo y ambicioso. En la película se retrata a un vocalista con problemas con la bebida. Txus ofrece su versión: “Tuvimos que suspender muchos conciertos. Yo le decía: ‘José, pero si es que hay tiempo para todo. En cuanto termine el concierto, yo soy el primero que me pongo lo que haga falta y nos vamos de juerga, pero antes del concierto, no, tío’. Además, yo me puedo comprar otro instrumento, una batería mejor, pero él no puede comprarse una voz mejor”. Andrea fue perdiendo facultades vocales progresivamente, hasta su salida del grupo en 2011.

La otra crisis se produjo en 2017. Carlitos la detalla: “Txus, a nuestras espaldas, registró la marca del grupo a su nombre. No estaba registrada porque no se podía ya que coincidía con el título de la película El Mago de Oz. Pero el sistema legal sobre patentes y marcas cambió. Alguien que sabía del tema ayudó a Txus a registrarlo a su nombre. Fue injusto. Todos pusimos dinero de nuestros bolsillos al principio, cuando no se ganaba nada. Habíamos participado todos del proyecto, éramos un grupo. Pero cuando por fin consiguió registrar la marca, el grupo ya era suyo”. A partir de entonces, el ya precario contrapeso al poder omnímodo de Txus desapareció por completo. Según el guitarrista, Txus les propuso contratarlos por un “sueldo de mierda”. La situación se enconó y los dos guitarristas, Carlitos y Frank, abandonaron la banda en 2020, “después de una situación de maltrato psicológico”, afirma el músico. Ambos reclamaron una cantidad de dinero, ya que también eran copropietarios de la empresa, y ganaron el pleito: 33.000 euros para cada uno. Txus recurrió la sentencia y el proceso sigue pendiente de la resolución final.

Los personajes de Txus (a la izquierda, encarnado por Adrián Lastra) y José Andrea (el actor Adrià Mondaray) discutiendo en una escena de 'Fiesta pagana'. En el centro, Moha, interpretado por Guillermo Furiase.

Otra demostración de la buena salud del cancionero de Mägo de Oz es la ramificación encarnada por Kabrönes, una banda compuesta por cuatro de los miembros de la formación más exitosa del grupo. O sea, están todos, menos Txus y Moha: José Andrea (voz), Carlitos (guitarra), Frank (guitarra) y Salva (bajo). Kabrönes emprende una gira en breve por Latinoamérica y en diciembre por España. “Es como en los buenos tiempos, y ahora se agradece tocar con un batería que llega a tiempo a los ensayos y lleva bien el tempo en los conciertos”, señala con sorna Carlitos. A Txus no le ha gustado que en algunos carteles Kabrönes se anuncie como “exmiembros de Mägo de Oz”, así que amenaza con volver a dar trabajo a sus abogados.

El último enredo de esta agria y rocambolesca historia nos devuelve a la película, Fiesta pagana, un filme, por otra parte, divertido, que cuenta con interpretaciones logradas de Adrián Lastra (como Txus), Adrià Mondaray (como José Andrea), Guillermo Furiase (como Moha) y, sobre todo, con la antológica presencia de Antonio Dechent en el papel de Goyo Esteban, director de la primera discográfica del grupo, Locomotive Records. Para la banda sonora, integrada por temas emblemáticos de Mägo de Oz, se ha grabado una canción nueva, indudablemente del estilo de los homenajeados, Brinda con nosotros.
