World.title: Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019166/Reel to Real: The ‘Voy Boys’ and the Movie That Never Was
World.content:
It’s late 2024, and Bilali Yasen barrels toward goal, the football skipping at his feet as he narrowly passes his opposition. In the pitch darkness, he hears only the sound of his heartbeat and the faint calls of his teammates.

He shoots and hits the back of the net, capping a 5-1 rout.

Having lost their first four games at China’s 2024 National Blind Football Championship, the win marks a major milestone for the 16-year-old striker and the rest of the “Voy Boys,” a newly formed team of visually impaired players from China’s northwestern Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

Born with glaucoma and cataracts, Bilali had never expected to play football again after his sight began fading at age 7. But at the final whistle, he is brimming with confidence and even envisioning a call-up to the national squad.

China has had a national men’s blind football team since 2006, winning eight Asian titles as well as silver at the 2008 Beijing Paralympic Games.

Yet the sport remains largely unknown in the country. For this young Xinjiang team, the struggle to secure sufficient long-term funding, along with professional coaching and management, is just beginning.

Even more improbably, the Voy Boys wouldn’t exist if not for a movie that was never made.

Cameras, action!

Su Yiyan, a dancer turned movie producer in Beijing, had been toying with a story about blind football for a while before starting production in 2021. The idea centered on a disillusioned big-city football coach who takes over a small-town team of visually impaired children, with both sides finding healing in each other.

Initially, she planned to base the movie in the southwestern Yunnan province, which already had a relatively strong tradition in the sport, but was encouraged instead to head north by Shanghai’s Xinjiang aid office, part of a national paired-assistance program in which wealthier cities coordinate economic, educational, and infrastructure projects in underdeveloped areas.

In the spring of 2021, Su and her crew arrived in Xinjiang to find local boys who could appear in the movie. The only real criteria were that they needed to be visually impaired and in good physical condition.

After visiting schools in several towns and cities, they traveled to Shache County, on the southern rim of the Taklimakan Desert in Xinjiang’s Kashgar prefecture, where they invited 13 students aged 13 to 14 from its Special Education School to take part in a basic running test.

“I was stunned. Every one of them had the bravery to run,” recalled Su, highlighting the fact that it takes immense courage to do that when you can’t see clearly.

The following summer, two physical education teachers from Kashgar were drafted in to begin training the children in skills and tactics at the school.

Blind football uses a modified ball with bells inside, allowing players to locate it by sound, and is played on an enclosed 40-by-20-meter pitch. Each team fields four visually impaired outfield players, all in blackout eye masks, and one sighted or partially sighted goalkeeper. Teams can also use a sighted off-field guide to call and direct players toward the goal.

Much of the initial training focuses on building the players’ courage to run and prepare for the inevitable collisions.

Abudumijiti Memet, a 19-year-old defender with congenital cataracts, said he was frightened at first, and would always lean backward when moving at pace. “The coach told me that the more afraid you are, the more likely you are to get hurt when someone runs into you,” he said. “Players who keep moving forward are less likely to be injured.”

Zhang Jian, head coach for the Shanghai Blind Football Team, provided remote support in 2021 and briefly led on-site training in 2023. He was surprised by how quickly the team took shape and impressed by their boldness, coordination, stamina, and general enthusiasm. Zhang took special note of Bilali, whose performances were “beyond everyone’s expectations.”

“It’s rare for someone of his height to perform as well as he does,” he said, referring to Bilali, who stands at a relatively short 1.65 meters. “He wasn’t good at dribbling at first, and his coordination could be poor … but he was certainly the bravest and the most determined in matches.”

For Bilali, it was a joy to be playing the “beautiful game” again. “Once I started running, I felt I’d rediscovered a familiar feeling,” he said, explaining that football was his favorite pastime before his eyesight faded. “The wind was blowing past my ears — it made me happy. Only on the pitch can we run without fear.”

Missing the target

Although things looked good on the field, by 2022 the movie project was stalling. The pandemic had caused scheduling issues, and some promised production financing never materialized. The money the crew did have — mainly from Su’s friends and connections — was vanishing fast.

Attempts to drum up further investment had all failed.

“To film my original idea required tens of millions of yuan, but we had no backers,” said Su, explaining that she had initially hoped to cast a big-name actor in the coach role. “One director suggested I change the focus of the movie to the children, which would only cost about 5 million yuan ($740,000). But we still couldn’t raise the money.”

With the project still in its early stages, she decided to shut it down. That summer, she flew to Xinjiang to break the news to the cast and their coaches.

Without a movie, there was no one to organize coaching or matches. “We’d just discovered blind football, and with it found hope,” said Bilali. “We all feared that the opportunity would disappear and we’d feel lost again.”

After returning to Beijing, Su couldn’t stop thinking about the children. “You can’t give people something and then take it away, especially a group of visually impaired kids so eager to play football,” she recalled thinking.

A year later, Su quit her job and teamed up with filmmaker Li Zhiwei to continue the project as a documentary about Xinjiang’s first blind football team. They used their own money, a bank loan, and about 260,000 yuan borrowed from friends to rent recording equipment and buy supplies including balls, goals, eye masks, and pitchside barriers.

“To save money, we sometimes took three connecting flights in a single day, getting up at 3 a.m. to reach the airport and arriving in Shache at nearly 11 p.m.,” Su once told domestic media. “Our crew spent no more than 100 yuan a night on accommodation. When we ran out of money, we went back out to raise more funds.”

In the summer of 2023, Zhang invited four boys from the Xinjiang team, including Bilali, to his annual training camp at the Shanghai School for the Blind, where they could learn from veteran players.

In addition to football practice, the trip included visits to the Shanghai Zoo, Shanghai Tower, and a café staffed by visually impaired workers. For Bilali, it was a glimpse into another world.

His elder sister, Maierwanimu Yasen, said her brother was different upon his return. After losing his sight, he’d become withdrawn and less talkative, and physically weaker, “but now he told us much more. He’d realized that visually impaired people could do all kinds of things — not just massage, but run cafés and pursue other careers,” referring to the default vocation for blind people in China.

He also now felt that if the team trained hard enough, it could play in more major cities, taking on China’s 10 or so provincial teams.

Taking another shot

In October 2023, Su’s crew arranged an exhibition match between the Xinjiang youth squad and the Shanghai Blind Football Team. The game was played on the pitch at Shache’s special education school, with relatives and local officials watching on.

“That’s when I first saw them play,” said Maierwanimu. “I felt then that they could really do it. I realized this wasn’t just a game they were playing for fun.”

The Xinjiang team won 2-0.

Almost a year later, the Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation announced the official establishment of the region’s first men’s blind football team, comprising 11 members, and the opening of a dedicated arena and training facility in Korla, almost 1,ooo kilometers by road from Shache.

The team — nicknamed the Voy Boys for the players’ shout of “voy” (Spanish for “I go”) to warn others they are moving — immediately began preparing for the 2024 National Blind Football Championship in Fuzhou, capital of the eastern Fujian province.

Bilali’s five-goal display in the team’s final match of the tournament provided the climax to Su’s documentary, “Voy Boys,” which went on limited release nationwide in July 2026. So far, it has grossed just over 340,000 yuan, far less than the 3 million yuan it cost to make.

Final whistle?

When the cameras stopped rolling in 2024, life carried on for the team.

Xinjiang finished in ninth place in Fuzhou. However, to encourage them and other newly formed squads to keep competing, all participating teams received automatic qualification for the combined National Games for Persons with Disabilities and the National Special Olympic Games, co-hosted in December 2025 by the southern Guangdong province along with the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions.

The team went on to finish seventh in that competition and then fourth at the 2026 national championship, held in Korla.

Luo Chengmian, a 28-year-old former blind football player from the eastern Zhejiang province, took over as head coach in 2024. He was assisted by Mahemuti Rozi, vice principal of the Shache’s special education school, who’d followed the team’s progress from the beginning.

“At first, I thought playing football was unnecessary, so I didn’t pay much attention,” said Mahemuti. “But in every match I saw how they gave everything they had. They fought with everything, always pushing to play out the entire match. It really moved me.”

However, the team has struggled to recruit for certain positions, including goalkeepers and off-field guides. Often, candidates are found just a day or two before a match and lack experience.

The players being separated by large distances is another challenge. Because the Shache school launched its high school program only in 2025, Bilali, Abudumijiti, and five other players had earlier transferred to a special education school in the Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, about 1,700 kilometers away, to continue their studies.

After Luo quit in late 2025 over disputes related to his salary and the players’ subsidies, it was up to Mahemuti to keep the team going. He juggled the job alongside his responsibilities overseeing the school’s logistics and cafeteria, and connected with coaches in Yunnan for remote guidance and training plans. This December, he aims to help the players in Changji arrange internships in Shache so they can restart training with the rest of the team.

Without a regular coach, those in Changji had to organize their own training sessions before morning reading and in the hour between classes and evening study.

“If we get the chance, we just want time to train, a better pitch, medicine, and a coach,” Abudumijiti said. “At least we chose this path ourselves. We want to keep walking it until we can’t go any farther.”

By contrast, Luo now coaches the Sichuan Blind Football Team’s women’s squad, based in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, where players train six hours a day, receive daily allowances, and enjoy full medical insurance and access to traditional Chinese medicine massage services.

Su told Sixth Tone that the Xinjiang players receive a few hundred yuan a month in food subsidies, and hope for further support, including for medical supplies. The Xinjiang Disabled Persons’ Federation did not respond to Sixth Tone’s request for comment.

At least four of the Voy Boys are expected to graduate high school next June, creating a dilemma over what to do next.

For visually impaired people in China, massage therapy remains one of the most accessible careers. Bilali and Abudumijiti both chose massage courses after transferring to Changji, yet the school didn’t even have textbooks for visually impaired students. They had to take photographs of the materials with their phones and use text-to-speech apps to understand the content.

“And I feel this kind of work often means staying indoors. You can’t feel the sunshine,” Abudumijiti said. “That made me reluctant to pursue it, even though many people told me it was the most suitable profession for someone like me.”

Without that option, though, he’s unsure about the future. The son of a police officer and gas station worker, he’s now thinking about working with his older brother, who plans to open an auto repair shop.

“If we have to rely on our families’ money to continue training outside school, honestly, that’d be too much of a burden,” Abudumijiti added. “A dream is a dream, but we also need to plan. What happens when we get too old to play and haven’t earned enough money? We can’t live on dreams.”

Su, now 51, has quit show business and is paying off her debts working as a bungee fitness instructor in Beijing. She argued that, like anyone, disabled people need opportunities: “It’s us, as able-bodied people, who imagine that they can’t do this or that. We assume they don’t need to create social value, and that as long as they are safe, that’s enough. But they don’t want to live that way. They still want to find their own worth.”

After an accident during training earlier this year involving a Xinjiang player, Su proposed the China Blind Football Players’ Sports Injury Protection Fund, aiming to provide medical insurance coverage to registered players. The idea is still awaiting approval from authorities.

In March 2025, Bilali was selected for the national team’s reserve squad, based in Fuzhou. For the first time, he encountered professional gym equipment, a dedicated medical team, and an individualized training plan. “The intensity was high. I’d never experienced such demanding training in Xinjiang,” he said.

Later, he joined a national team training camp ahead of the recent 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, but wasn’t selected. China took gold on Oct. 23 after defeating the hosts 1-0 in the final.

“I’m looking forward to eventually going back to Xinjiang to see my family and teammates, but I’m also afraid that I won’t be able to train anymore,” he said. “I worry that my skills will fall behind.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A poster for “Voy Boys.” Courtesy of Su)

World.title: Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019172/Rack and Ruin: How China’s Trillion-Yuan Womenswear Market Lost Its Color
World.content:
Editor’s note: According to Syntu Data, e-commerce platforms made a combined 1.6 trillion yuan ($239 billion) in sales last year during “Double Eleven,” China’s annual online shopping event in November. Clothing accounted for 14%, driven largely by womenswear.

Zhou Keke used to get excited when she ordered clothes online. Not anymore. Now she returns about 70% of what she buys, either because of poor quality or because the dimensions don’t match what was listed.

Browsing the Chinese e-commerce platform Taobao recently, she stumbled across a store clearing out unsold stock from a decade ago. She says it was like stepping into another world. Compared with the “simple and vanilla” skirts, scarves, and tops on sale today, she found designs that were bold, irregular, thoughtful, even avant-garde and ingenious.

“So this is what fashion looked like when the economy was booming?” thought Zhou, who lives in China’s eastern Zhejiang province. She bought seven pieces for less than 1,000 yuan ($150) and posted a review on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, receiving nearly 10,000 likes and 1,000 comments.

The womenswear market in the Chinese mainland exceeded 1.23 trillion yuan in 2025, up from 619.7 billion yuan in 2011, according to iiMedia Research. Still, social media is today awash with complaints from female consumers over the blandness of modern clothing. As one netizen put it, “Beauty used to come in 100 forms; now even ugliness is mass-produced.”

However, industry insiders argue that this isn’t a one-sided problem but rather a feedback loop. They say that, as China’s economy slows, most online shoppers are tightening their belts and are less willing to spend on distinctive or niche designs, so brands have no option but to follow what’s selling.

Meanwhile, in the physical space, more consumers can only choose between fast-fashion outlets and luxury brands, as mid-range and boutique stores continue to disappear from malls nationwide.

How’s it looking?

Li Li, a 19-year-old university student from Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, recently found a matching top and miniskirt — vivid red with huge black embroidered flower buds — at a vintage clothes market.

“You could tell at a glance it was meant to stand out. A lot of womenswear now comes in muted Morandi colors, or other pale shades,” she says, adding that clothes in the 2000s were “much brighter.”

Li notes that when a piece sells well on Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, there’s immediately a rush of near-identical versions.

Zhou says clothes today feel cut-and-paste, with only the logos changing. “If everyone’s designing like that, honestly, what am I supposed to choose? All I can do is compare the price and the fabric. It’s so boring,” she adds.

Gu Hawen, a fashion designer at Unreal World, a clothing company based in the eastern Jiangsu province, recalls that when she entered the industry in 2019, designs in the domestic womenswear market were flourishing. She began noticing a slide in 2023.

“Whether you look at high-end luxury, affordable luxury, or ordinary brands, it’s the same story now,” she says. “Everything is more alike. Some clothing has been stripped back so far that there isn’t a single decorative detail.”

She explains that an unspoken chain of imitation runs through the Chinese womenswear industry: mass-market and fast-fashion brands follow designer and luxury brands in terms of color, silhouette, and other details, and online shops follow mass-market brands.

“The public is more receptive to designs from big-name brands. If companies want to sell, we have to keep up with international tastes and aesthetics,” says Gu, although she stresses that “we only take inspiration; we don’t copy outright. Online sellers copy brands wholesale. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Chen Chen launched her own online clothing brand this year, selling products that stick closely to the design concepts of major labels. The first item she listed, inspired by the British fashion house Vivienne Westwood, sold more than 100 pieces — no easy feat. Within six months, several items promoted on her page had become modest hits on Xiaohongshu, approaching 1,000 sales.

Chen feels modern Chinese consumers tend to follow the crowd, and tastes are becoming increasingly uniform as e-commerce platforms grow.

“Instead of discovering things for yourself, you end up in an algorithm bubble,” she says. “Maybe the first time you see an item of clothing, you don’t even like the style. But the platform keeps pushing it, and then it’s all you see. Eventually, everyone gets conditioned into the same very narrow idea of what looks good.”

She argues that not all consumers recognize or value original design. “You can be selling in exactly the same category, but someone else slaps ‘same style as Chanel’ on their listing and wipes the floor with you.”

In Chen’s view, online womenswear brands that invest in developing unique designs are being squeezed out. Spending six months refining a collection no longer works, as everyone is chasing the next viral hit, and keeping up is the only way to make money.

“Trends change way too fast now,” she adds. “A brand might plan its collection for months, but by the time it hits the rails, everything looks dated. Then a new bestseller suddenly appears, and they have no choice but to follow. … Copying a bestseller means lower costs, less risk, and higher profit margins.”

Imitation game

Zhou feels China’s womenswear market is not only becoming more conservative and homogeneous but also that brands are cutting corners on materials compared with a decade ago, creating a false economy. “Brands are becoming less responsible, so more shoppers are sending items back more often. But returns cost the sellers money. It’s a vicious cycle.”

Industry insiders argue the root of the issue lies in an underlying shift in consumer psychology, as younger consumers place greater emphasis on value for money.

“It’s become harder for people to earn money these past few years,” says Chen. “They’re expecting more from every penny.”

With consumers more price-sensitive, brands have grown cautious about what they charge, applying pressure further down the supply chain.

“Sewing workers are putting in more effort, but their pay hasn’t gone up, so the quality keeps getting worse,” Chen explains. “The pressure on workers at the bottom of the industry is intense. They have to get orders out by a fixed deadline. Companies keep squeezing them and demanding more pieces per day.”

Gu also sees the domestic market’s homogenization as a symptom of the broader economic chill. “Staying alive matters far more than being original,” she says. “After all, beyond the designer, there’s a sales team, logistics, and 50 or 60 other mouths to feed. No business owner is going to bankrupt themselves simply to underwrite a designer’s personal aesthetic.”

For clothing companies, a design’s main job is to keep the business alive, so giving the market what’s familiar is the safest survival strategy, Gu explains.

“Designers have the least say in whether a garment gets made,” with the final decision usually in the hands of marketing and store managers, she adds. This group’s preference is for more “universal garments” that match a wide range of body shapes and personal tastes. “Designed pieces are selective — they can depend on a person’s height, figure, looks, their whole bearing.”

Even when an inventive design survives internal vetting, an unusual cut or trim can increase the retail price, potentially sending consumers elsewhere. Gu recently incorporated neo-Chinese style elements including knot buttons, mandarin collars, and wide cuffs into her garments, but they sold poorly. The feedback was that shoppers deemed the items too expensive.

Copycats are also astonishingly fast. Gu says imitations of her designs have appeared for sale online within as little as 24 hours, at a fraction of the price. “It gets to the point where it feels original designs are a bit of a joke,” she says with a resigned sigh.

Market gap

According to the domestic retail industry tracker Linkshop, at least 40 well-known Chinese online womenswear stores announced they were closing or halting new product releases in 2024, while e-commerce news outlet Ebrun reports that more than a dozen more shuttered in the first half of this year.

Meanwhile, many mid-range sellers have withdrawn from city malls across China, widening the gap between high-end and cut-price clothing stores.

“Expensive clothes are just getting more expensive. In malls, items can cost 5,000 or 6,000 yuan, or even more than 10,000. At the other end, there are fast-fashion brands like Uniqlo and Zara,” says Chen. “Some of the really good mid-range brands, ones pricing items at 1,000 or 2,000 yuan, seem to have gone from the malls. Even where you find them, their designs and quality are far less appealing than they used to be.”

Like Zhou, many shoppers are now turning to secondhand and vintage clothing stores. Others are even learning to sew and making their own clothes, to ensure they get the design, fabric, and cut they want.

“I miss a time when imagination could go anywhere, when people dared to design and weren’t in such a hurry to see results,” laments Li.

Some designers have tried to resist uniformity, like Gu, who makes small adjustments while sticking to her company’s established style. Last year, she took one of its hit jackets and added seams at the collar or cuffs, and extra trim, to achieve something “slightly different.”

She hopes the market turmoil will ease within the next couple of years. “When people are doing a little better financially, and companies have some breathing room — when one bad season no longer means bankrupting the business — things should get much better.”

(For privacy reasons, Zhou Keke, Li Li, and Gu Hawen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Xiaotong.

A version of this article originally appeared in Oh Youth! (36Kr). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: Did ex-BuCor chief Bantag just evade arrest in Ifugao operation?
World.content:
ARREST. Lamut police launch an operation to arrest former BuCor chief Gerald Bantag, a fugitive wanted over the killings of broadcaster Percy Lapid and inmate Jun Villamor.

Mayor Mariano Buyagawan Jr. says police received information that former Bureau of Corrections chief Gerald Bantag was posing as a poultry worker in Lamut, Ifugao

Former Bureau of Corrections chief Gerald Bantag reportedly evaded arrest during a predawn police operation at a poultry farm in Lamut, Ifugao, on All Saints’ Day, November 1, according to Mayor Mariano Buyagawan Jr.

In a Facebook post, Buyagawan said police received confidential information that Bantag was posing as a poultry worker at Sitio Alupapan in Barangay Pugol.

The Lamut Municipal Police Station launched an operation to arrest at 5 am Bantag, who has been a fugitive since courts issued warrants against him in connection with the killings of broadcaster Percival “Percy Lapid” Mabasa and New Bilibid Prison inmate Cristito “Jun” Villamor.

But Bantag was no longer at the poultry farm when police arrived, the mayor said.

Buyagawan said he waited anxiously at home for updates, hoping police would report Bantag’s arrest. He had even prepared for a photo opportunity with the handcuffed fugitive and planned to invite Bantag to be a godfather at an upcoming event.

“Wala na si General (The General is gone),” Buyagawan wrote, expressing his disappointment after police failed to find the former official.

Despite the unsuccessful operation, the mayor praised the Lamut police for acting on the intelligence report and pursuing Bantag.

He also expressed relief that no one was hurt during the operation, which he had hoped would end peacefully on a day traditionally devoted to remembering the dead.

Buyagawan joked that Bantag’s reported presence in Lamut showed that the town was peaceful and attractive, even to a fugitive. He also joked that former Philippine National Police chief and Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa might turn up in Barangay Mabato-Bato.

The mayor’s account did not explain how Bantag left the poultry farm or say whether police had verified that he was there.

Bantag has been wanted since 2023, when courts issued arrest warrants against him and former BuCor deputy security officer Ricardo Zulueta.

World.title: A portrait puts Cainta’s sepoy heritage in the spotlight
World.content:
SEPOY. Artist Joel Rocafort’s 'Sepoy,' a portrait of Generoso 'Papay' Sumulong, is displayed on the second floor of Museo Cainta. The artwork uses charcoal and turmeric to honor Cainta’s sepoy heritage.

A large portrait of 61-year-old Generoso ‘Papay’ Sumulong now hangs at Museo Cainta, honoring the town’s sepoy heritage. But his story raises questions about how a community recognizes the people who keep its traditions alive.

CAINTA, Rizal – Ask residents of Barangay Sta. Rosa where to find “Papay, the sepoy,” and they can point you to P. Burgos Street, to an old-looking house just before an arch.

At lunchtime, 61-year-old Generoso “Papay” Sumulong carried a bowl of rice to a tiled bench across from his family’s house, one of the spots where neighbors gather to pass the time. After returning to the house, he was greeted by a little girl who wrapped her arms around his waist from behind and called him “Pappy.”

Sumulong said the nickname “Papay” was derived from Popeye the Sailor Man, the fictional sailor created by American cartoonist E.C. Segar, who first appeared in the newspaper comic strip Thimble Theatre in 1929.

Sumulong, meanwhile, has become a recognizable figure in his own community: a relative who once took his niece’s daughter to school on his bicycle, a neighbor whom people approach for directions, and a longtime performer in Cainta’s senakulo (Passion play).

A living face

Sumulong’s face now has another kind of public presence. A large portrait of Sumulong hangs on the second floor of Museo Cainta, where it forms part of the town’s effort to preserve its sepoy heritage.

Created by artist Joel Rocafort, the seven-by-5.5-foot artwork, titled Sepoy, depicts Sumulong using charcoal and turmeric.

In a Facebook post on September 8, Cainta Mayor Johnielle Keith “Kit” Nieto described the portrait as “isang mukha na kumatawan sa kasaysayan ng bayan natin” (a face that represents the history of our town).

Rocafort said the charcoal used to draw Sumulong’s face and the turmeric used to color his headcloth were materials associated with Cainta’s famous suman and other traditional rice cakes. His piece went on display on the second floor of Museo ng Cainta when the space opened to the public in early October.

The portrait drew praise from residents on Facebook, with some calling Sumulong a “buhay na alamat” (living legend) and others commending Rocafort for bringing local history into public view.

MORE THAN ONE PORTRAIT. Other artworks featuring Sumulong are on display at Museo Cainta. Contributed photo

But among the congratulatory messages were calls for Sumulong to receive an award, pension, or financial assistance. Some commenters noted that he no longer had regular work and asked the local government to help with his daily expenses.

The response raises a question beyond the artwork itself: What does it mean to recognize the people who embody a town’s heritage, and what does that recognition look like beyond a museum display?

Cainta’s history

Cainta’s official history traces the town’s sepoy heritage to the British invasion of Manila in 1762, when British forces brought Indian soldiers known as sepoys.

According to the municipality’s website, some of the soldiers stayed in Cainta after the British withdrawal in 1764 and settled among the local population. Their descendants remain part of the town’s historical and cultural identity.

HONOR. An exhibit at Museo Cainta explains the significance of May 31 as Araw ng mga Sepoy sa Cainta and shows a collage of residents descended from sepoys. Photo by Dominique Astucia/Rappler

The town has also formalized its recognition of this heritage. Museum exhibits cite Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 2025-51, which designates May 31 as Araw ng mga Sepoy sa Cainta (Day of the Sepoys in Cainta), in recognition of the community’s contributions to local culture and tradition.

For Barangay Sta. Rosa Chairman Richard dela Cruz, who said his own family traces its sepoy ancestry through his grandmother, Sumulong is a recognizable representative of that history.

“Sakto talaga ‘yung mukha niya (His face is absolutely perfect for it),” Dela Cruz said.

Older residents with similar features had died, he added, leaving Sumulong among the people who remain recognizable to the community.

Dela Cruz clarified, however, that Sumulong is not Cainta’s oldest living sepoy descendant. Other families in the municipality have older members, including people in their 80s and beyond.

THE SEPOYS OF TODAY. The exhibit mentions Dela Cruz as one of the public servants with sepoy lineage. Photo by Dominique Astucia/Rappler

Sumulong said his grandmother told him about their family’s sepoy ancestry when he was a child. He could no longer recall many details about the family’s origins, explaining that older relatives knew more of the story.

For him, the connection to Cainta’s history is also expressed through performance.

He said he began participating in the senakulo in 1976 and helped establish Kabataang Walang Sindak (KWS), his first group, before joining The Romans Club. He described the performances as a panata (religious vow).

In her book Semana Santa: Senakulo at Penitensya sa Bayan ng Cainta, former Cainta mayor Atty. Maria Elenita “Elen” Nieto traces the town’s senakulo tradition to 1904, when residents of Barrio Dayap began staging the Passion play. Over time, the tradition developed into larger productions involving actors, musicians, artisans and production teams.

Dela Cruz said Sumulong was known for portraying the high priest Annas and the biblical figure Samuel. Photographs he shared with Rappler show the two men during a 2009 Lenten observance. Dela Cruz said Sumulong had been performing since his younger years.

IN CHARACTER. Sumulong portrays Annas, a high priest involved in the biblical account of Jesus’ trial, during a senakulo performance. Photo courtesy of Richard dela Cruz

The barangay chairman and Sumulong became friends through The Romans Club, which also participates in Cainta’s Lenten religious observances.

Dela Cruz described their relationship as close, saying Sumulong supported him even before he became barangay chairman.

Outside the frame

Despite his longstanding involvement in local traditions, Sumulong has no regular source of income. He previously took welding jobs, but said illness and health limitations have reduced the work he can do.

“Wala. Minsan, natatawag, nagwe-welding sa araw,” he said when asked about his livelihood.

(Nothing regular. Sometimes someone calls me to do welding work during the day.)

His niece, Evangeline Sumulong Jambalos, said he still accepts occasional jobs and helps the family when needed. She operates a small street food business in front of their house.

STAGE ACTORS. A younger Sumulong and Dela Cruz pose with fellow members of The Romans Club in 2009. Photos courtesy of Richard dela Cruz

Jambalos recalled that Sumulong helped raise her daughter, taking her to and from school on his bicycle. He also helps with errands and arranging goods for the family’s business.

“Malaki rin naman ang naitulong niyan (He has also helped us a lot),” she said.

Jambalos said Sumulong sometimes receives money and food from relatives. A distant relative living abroad previously paid him to tend plants, and family members have contributed to his expenses when needed.

Jambalos recalled that she and her cousins pooled money to prepare a small celebration for Sumulong’s 60th birthday.

“Nung nalaman naming senior na [si Papay], sabi ko, ‘Sige, lalakad kaming magpipinsan.’ [Kasama] ‘yung mga pinsan namin sa Cogeo, pinag-ambagan namin,” she said.

(When we found out that Papay would be a senior citizen, I said, ‘Alright, us cousins ​​will take care of it.’ Together with our cousins ​​from Cogeo, we all chipped in.)

Sumulong lives in the family home with relatives from several generations. He never married, but remains part of a household where family members continue to rely on and look after one another.

The family was surprised when they learned that Sumulong’s image would be displayed at Museo Cainta. Jambalos said they had not known the municipality intended to exhibit the artwork until other people began telling them about it.

“Hindi naman niya kasi inakala [na] lalabas siya sa mga gano’n,” she said.

(He never expected to appear in something like that.)

She acknowledged the public calls for assistance, but said the family was not asking others to solicit help on Sumulong’s behalf. Any assistance, she said, should come from the initiative of those willing to provide it.

Sumulong was similarly noncommittal when asked whether he wanted particular assistance from the local government.

“Kung ano ang ibibigay nila. Wala na akong magagawa. Kung anong gusto nilang ibigay,” he said.

(Whatever they give. There is nothing I can do about it; whatever they choose to give.)

He added that he would accept whatever help was offered rather than demand a specific amount or form of support.

What recognition means

The calls for financial assistance have also raised questions about what benefits Sumulong may qualify for.

Sumulong said he had completed paperwork for assistance but was told he could receive benefits only at age 65. His niece, meanwhile, said the family understood that he was too young for the Expanded Centenarians Act cash gift, which is reserved for Filipinos reaching the milestone ages of 80, 85, 90, 95 and 100.

These are distinct from the broader benefits available to senior citizens. Republic Act No. 9994 defines a senior citizen as a resident Filipino aged 60 or older, although eligibility for particular forms of financial assistance depends on the program’s requirements.

For Sumulong’s family, recognition is not only about what the local government might provide. It is also reflected in the everyday ways Sumulong has contributed to their lives and the neighborhood he has called home since childhood.

For the municipality, his portrait offers a visible way to preserve a part of Cainta’s past. His decades in the senakulo also place him within a tradition sustained not only by museum displays but by people who continue to perform, organize, and pass their practices on to younger generations.

The portrait gives Cainta’s sepoy heritage a recognizable face. But as residents’ comments suggest, honoring a person’s place in history and supporting the person behind that history are separate questions. – Rappler.com

Dominique Astucia is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

World.title: Unbeaten Martin clinches world crown with stunner over Picasso
World.content:
HIT. Filipino boxer Carl Jammes Martin throws a punch against Mexican David Picasso during their WBC Silver featherweight bout in Saudi Arabia on October 31.

MANILA, Philippines – Call Carl Jammes Martin “Wonderboy” no more. He is now a legit talent set to conquer the world stage.

Martin stunned touted Mexican David Picasso to clinch the WBC (World Boxing Council) Silver featherweight crown via split decision (96-93 and 95-94 for Martin, and 95-94 for Picasso) at the King’s Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Saturday, October 31 (Sunday, November 1, Philippine time).

Defying pre-fight predictions and a 2-inch height and 5-inch reach disadvantage, Martin dictated the tempo of the 10-rounder, was the busier fighter, and landed the clearer power punches to beat Picasso despite incurring a flash knockdown, when his gloves touched the canvas after getting hit by a stiff jab in the seventh round.

Already the No. 1 contender by the WBO (World Boxing Organization) and the No. 7 by the IBF (International Boxing Federation) at super bantamweight, Martin is expected to enter the super featherweight top contenders after his successful foray in the 126-pound division.

Oddsmakers tagged Martin as the huge underdog because of the higher quality of opposition Picasso has faced, with one betting site assessing the Mexican’s chances of winning at 87% and Martin’s upset hopes at 13%.

Little did they know that Martin, true to his Lagawe, Ifugao, heritage, relishes the odds and thrives on challenges.

For three months, he trained hard with his father and coach, Abel Martin, before seeking help from United States-based trainer Marvin Somodio for the latter part of his preparation, starting at the Knucklehead Boxing Gym in Las Vegas, Nevada, owned by MP Promotions president Sean Gibbons.

Reaping the benefits, Martin dictated the tempo from the opening bell and outworked Picasso, leaving the Mexican no time to launch his vaunted body shots.

During the post-fight interview, Martin thanked the fans and said, “So much I appreciate this one (crown).”

According to Martin, he “learned a lot in the US, trained so much, and sparred with great fighters,” paving the way for the victory that left boxing pundits in awe and fight promoters on notice.

While Martin’s purse for the Picasso fight was reportedly at least $150,000 (P9.58 million), the big bucks would come on his next fight, wherever it may be. – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump says Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in US as long as he wants
World.content:
FLORIDA, USA – President Donald Trump said on Saturday evening, October 31, that defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in the United States indefinitely.

The comments, made to reporters during a Halloween party at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, suggest that relations between the Western Hemisphere’s two largest democracies may remain strained for some time, even as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Brazil’s top diplomat earlier in the day.

“He can stay here as long as he wants,” Trump said of Bolsonaro, who left Brazil after losing the election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, despite leading in most opinion polls. “In my opinion, the election was a disgrace.”

The Brazilian embassy in Washington did not immediately return a request for comment.

Outside observers described the election as free and fair. Bolsonaro’s decision to go to the US followed a ruling by a Brazilian Supreme Court justice to revoke his passport shortly after his loss, as the candidate faces a pair of federal money-laundering probes in Brazil and police there considered him a flight risk.

He was admitted to the US under humanitarian parole, Reuters has previously reported, a status that typically only lasts for one year.

Rubio had said earlier on Saturday that he spoke with Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira at a Group of 20 meeting in Atlanta, and that they would see each other again in a few weeks.

In comments that had pointed to a potential rapprochement, Rubio told journalists that he and Vieira were expected to see each other again in France at a G7 foreign ministers’ summit that will take place next month. Brazil is expected to attend the meeting as an observer, he noted.

A US official and a person familiar with the matter have told Reuters that Trump has no current plans to support the political ambitions of Bolsonaro — who has described himself as Brazil’s rightful leader — despite allowing the Brazilian politician into the US. Trump on Saturday said he has no plans to meet with Bolsonaro.

Rubio said on Saturday that the US government “was not involved directly in any of the moves” that led to Bolsonaro’s departure from Brazil earlier this week. However, Reuters and several other media outlets have reported that Jason Miller, a White House official, helped arrange Bolsonaro’s journey.

Bolsonaro’s father, far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, is imprisoned in ​Brazil for plotting a coup after losing his own re-election bid in 2022. Lula himself spent 17 months in jail in 2018 and 2019 on corruption charges that were later annulled. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dead pets dumped in Bulacan: What we know so far
World.content:
REMAINS. Local officers exhume remains of pets buried in Bulacan allegedly by a pet crematorium based in Cavite.

Animal rescue groups are helping pet owners file complaints against a Bacoor crematorium following allegations that it dumped their pets' remains in Bulacan

MANILA, Philippines – Bacoor City Mayor Strike Revilla on Saturday, October 31, ordered the closure of a local pet crematorium after the remains of dogs and cats that were supposed to be cremated were found dumped in a vacant lot in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan.

Revilla said the closure order against Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium had been implemented following a meeting with the crematorium’s owner, Jonathan Legaspi, and more than 30 pet owners who had entrusted their deceased animals to the business.

The San Jose del Monte City Police Station (SJDM CPS) earlier reported finding 25 dogs and cats inside seven large sacks near Barangay Minuyan Proper.

Residents reported a foul odor on October 31, while witnesses told police they had seen a white van and unidentified individuals unloading the sacks early on October 29.

Crematorium owner unable to prove pets were cremated

Revilla said the crematorium had a valid business permit to provide cremation services in Bacoor. It operated two cremation machines, one in Bacoor and another reportedly in Caloocan.

Legaspi acknowledged that some pets had been taken to Caloocan for cremation. However, he could not provide sufficient documents or other evidence to establish that the cremations had actually taken place.

The owner also could not confirm if the animals found in the viral posts were among those entrusted to the business.

According to Revilla, the establishment had no CCTV footage or sufficient documentation to prove that the pets had been cremated or that the ashes returned to customers came from their animals.

The mayor said he had directed the city’s legal office, Business Permits and Licensing Department, Environment Service Department, and City Veterinary Office to investigate the establishment.

Police exhumes 18 animal remains

In a separate update on Saturday, the SJDM CPS said authorities had exhumed previously buried animal remains after pet owners sought to identify and retrieve their deceased pets. The operation recovered 16 dogs and two cats.

Police said unclaimed remains would be reburied at the Citrus Public Cemetery in San Jose del Monte because of decomposition and possible health risks. It was also coordinating with the city veterinary office and the City Environment and Natural Resources Office to investigate the disposal of the animals.

Rescue group Luna And Furry Siblings said all the recovered animals had been claimed by their owners.

It also called on the public to help gather CCTV footage, provide USB drives, and fund the printing of evidence as it prepares to file complaints.

Pet owners prepare complaints

The Bacoor City Police Station and Barangay Kaingin-Digman assisted pet owners in documenting their complaints, Revilla said. Some were seeking compensation and damages, while others planned to pursue cases with the police.

The Bacoor City Police Station is handling complaints for estafa and civil damages, while the San Jose del Monte police is handling complaints involving alleged violations of local sanitation and solid waste ordinances, according to the SJDM CPS.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) condemned what it described as the alleged deception of pet owners who paid for cremation services, only to find that their animals’ remains had reportedly been dumped instead.

PAWS said the alleged acts may constitute estafa under the Revised Penal Code. It urged affected pet owners to preserve receipts, certificates, communications, photographs, and other records related to the service, and to seek legal assistance.

“The bond between a person and a companion animal does not end with death,” it said. “PAWS stands with affected pet parents in seeking truth, accountability, and justice.”

The Animal Kingdom Foundation also condemned the incident, saying the dogs and cats were not garbage but family members whose owners had paid to give them a dignified farewell.

The foundation described the disposal of the animals’ remains as an act of betrayal and a failure to value the trust placed in those entrusted with their care.

“Lahat sila ay inilaban ng kanilang mga pamilya hanggang sa huling hininga,” the group said. “At ng matalo sa laban ay ginastusan upang mabigyan ng maganda at marangal na pamamaalam.“

(Their families fought for them until their very last breath. And when the battle was lost, their families spared no expense to give them a beautiful and dignified farewell.) – Rappler.com

World.title: On Bangladesh’s temporary islands, Runa Khan helps families stand with dignity
World.content:
Along the Brahmaputra River in Bangladesh, some communities live on land that is constantly shifting. They are situated on sandbar islands called char, formed by sediment deposition from major river systems.

These areas, which are continuously reshaped by erosion and flooding, are home to up to 20 million people, according to some estimates.

Runa Khan was introduced to char communities in 1997 while doing her work in preserving traditional boat-building skills.

During her visits, one moment stayed with her: a woman feeding her sick child with only two meals to save money for lamp oil. The second meal, rice and onions, was the child’s early dinner, given in hopes that he would forget his fever and sleep throughout the night.

Khan, who came from a privileged, wealthy family, said she saw the injustice and poverty that had become the reality for those living on these temporary, shifting river islands. Residents there are at risk of displacement as river erosion threatens to wash away their villages. Families have to constantly relocate even with their unstable income, trapping them in extreme poverty.

Her sadness turned to anger — and it might have been anger that pushed Khan to search for answers to help these communities.

“Realization, as I keep saying, leads to a responsibility. The fact that you can do something, then it becomes your responsibility,” she said in a virtual roundtable discussion last September.

In 2002, Khan founded the social purpose organization Friendship and established a hospital ship along the Jamuna River, a branch of the Brahmaputra River, in northern Bangladesh.

HOSPITAL SHIP. The Lifebuoy Friendship Hospital, the organization’s first floating hospital. Photo courtesy of Friendship/Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation

Over two decades later, Friendship has expanded its services to include education and livelihood, as well as programs for climate resilience, for 7.5 million people annually.

“I started the work because I just couldn’t leave or not be responsible for what was staring at me in the face, which was incredible poverty. Twenty-five years ago, these areas were totally untouched,” the 67-year-old humanitarian told journalists.

Khan earned the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award, considered Asia’s Nobel Prize, for her “profound empathy for the poorest of the poor in her country, and her courage, vision, and tenacity in building and leading Friendship to accomplish her mission.”

Her work is not over yet, however, as char communities become more vulnerable because of the worsening climate crisis.

INITIAL REACTION. Runa Khan thanks the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation for naming her a 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardee on August 31, 2026. Photo by Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler

Better access to health care

Char dwellers find it difficult to access healthcare services and be properly diagnosed with their diseases. Their communities are low-lying, flood-prone areas as they sit across rivers.

Residents frequently suffer from common infectious and water-borne diseases amid floods triggered by the monsoon season from June to October. Mothers and children could also have elevated health risks. If they get sick, they have to cross rivers to reach hospitals on the mainland — or rely on alternative medicine.

This did not sit well with Khan, who believes the first thing a person needs is good health. So, through Friendship, she converted a river barge into a hospital ship for these temporary river islands.

“Without access to health, you can’t provide…any kind of empowerment to a person or any kind of hope to a person, nor give them dignity,” Khan said.

“Impossible” was a comment she would hear about the floating hospitals. But those hospital ships now provide surgeries to treat cataracts, clubfoot, and other common but debilitating conditions; give pediatric, gynecological, dental, and eye care; and supply free or cheap consultations and medicines.

It’s part of Friendship’s three-tier health care system. The organization trained local women to become medic aides, who handle door-to-door check-ups, provide maternal care, and gather patient data through a mobile app.

Meanwhile, roving medical teams give primary healthcare services in mobile and satellite clinics. If patients need major interventions and specialized care, they are referred to the hospitals.

Today, the organization has seven hospital ships and two land-based hospitals, 550 mobile clinics, and 700 medic aides.

World.title: [Two Pronged] A cross-dressing husband seeks a chance to reply
World.content:
A cross-dressing husband — who may be the subject of an earlier Two Pronged column — responds to 'half-truths' raised in that earlier column

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr Holmes and Mr Baer:

I refer to your column of Oct 10, 2026.

I do not intend to sue you for publishing the half-truths of my wife, but I insist on (the) right of reply. This column allows that, I presume?

I have every reason to believe my wife (or former wife, as she insists although divorce is yet to be legal in our country) wrote the letter you published the 10th of October, 2026.

All the details she mentions are accurate, although there are other facts she forgets to mention:

Yes, I used to cross dress and it is my eternal regret that instead of sharing this voluntarily with her, she discovered this on her own. I immediately promised never to do it again. She said it explained many things that did not seem right in a marriage between two people who loved each other. I love her — and still do, despite the years we have been separated. I gave her many books and research articles to read unequivocally stating that my being a cross dresser did not translate to being gay and/or being transgender. After a while she stopped reading them. I cannot understand such denial of logic. How could she refuse such undisputed data? My wife is also an attorney, but working for a non profit. She has a good heart but no business sense. Her final decisions are guided by heart, not a hard core mind. Each time she discovered I broke my promise never to cross dress again, I could feel her love for me diminish. I will never forgive myself for this, but each time I failed, there was a very good reason that I did. When she finally left me, I stopped cross dressing for the next few years in an effort to win her back. She has always refused my attempts at reconciliation, so can you blame me for going back to cross dressing every now and then? I am not gay, I do not hate women, and I don’t think I am a woman trapped in a man’s body. I just enjoy doing so. It provides much needed relief from a job that is full of pressure.

Any thoughts?

– Andrew

Dear Andrew,

Thank you for your email. This column welcomes all responses of whatever nature, positive or negative. In this case, there is just one caveat – we will answer your letter without treating your wife as a party to this exchange since we have not verified any connection between you.

Your letter states that you regret that rather than hearing about it from you, your wife discovered your cross-dressing for herself. You also acknowledge that your broken promises diminished her love for you and eroded the trust between you. However, regarding the broken promises, you claim that there were ‘very good reasons’ for them, unfortunately without revealing what these were and thus forestalling any analysis of your reasoning.

It seems clear that despite your concealment of your cross-dressing, it was not the cross dressing per se, but the continuous breaches of promise that drove your wife from the marriage.

This was no doubt exacerbated by your decision to conceal the supposedly ‘very good reasons’ from her, since how was she to be expected to understand you if you consistently failed to explain yourself?

Perhaps it is also significant that you have done exactly the same in your letter to us — claimed that there were ‘very good reasons’ without any further explanation. How are we then expected to evaluate this situation, much less your wife?

Your refusal to explain yourself, together with your efforts to deflect by deluging your wife with information to prove that cross-dressing did not mean you were gay or trans, suggesting that reason alone should convince her, are thus what drove her away and you seem to make it clear that you never altered these tactics, despite claiming you wanted to win her back.

So, to answer your question, no one can blame you for going back to cross-dressing now that you have alienated the only person whose opinion you actually wanted. As for further thoughts, perhaps it is time to recognize that your marriage is over for good, regardless of the law.

Further efforts to win her back will simply confirm what she already believes, namely that your promises are hollow.

All the best

– JAF Baer

Dear Andrew,

Thank you very much for your letter. There are two points Mr Baer brings up in his answer above that I would like to expound on.

First, it was not your cross dressing per se that caused your wife to leave you. If it were, she would have left you the first time she discovered it… or the second… or, at the very most, perhaps the third or fourth. It was how you promised repeatedly that you would stop doing so and never did.

How exhausting that must have been for her! And yet… AND yet… I see no attempt on your part to understand how she must be feeling. Instead, I read rationalization after rationalization about why you behaved the way you did, and why you have gone back to cross dressing. And even then, you rationalize why you went back and manage to blame her for it!

Besides, for a lawyer who seems to place logic above all else, is it not ironic that you “immediately promised” never to do it again. This belies your statement that you find nothing wrong with cross dressing. I feel it is only when you finally reach point #8, your last point, that you seem to give the actual reasons you cross dress: “I just enjoy doing so. It provides much needed relief from a job that is full of pressure.”

Why in God’s name did you not share this with her? Why did you not open your heart to her, trusting her to believe you (or, at the very least, hoping she would believe you)?

There seems every reason to think she would have. After all, she believed your promise to stop cross dressing (even if you felt there was nothing wrong with it, as all the research articles and books you insisted she read confirmed).

I realize that, with the quick razor-sharp mind you pride yourself on having, you will accuse me of merely projecting my own feelings when I share another reason for your wife’s refusal to believe you. But clinical experience says otherwise.

Many — though admittedly not all — people who pride themselves on, and convince themselves that, their intellect is what makes them who they are; that it is their formidable mind that makes them not just admirable, but also lovable.

Not so. I have yet to hear a wife say the major reason she loved her partner was their IQ. Many — and admittedly not all — women who love their partner do so for inner qualities that usually cannot be measured by simple metrics. Most women love their partners basically for how their partners make them feel: cherished but also safe.

I can’t help feeling it was your behavior and your arrogance, both during your marriage and after it ended, that was the nail that finally ended your marriage.

Here’s hoping you find the courage to discover some truths — and not mere data — about yourself

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: How chefs Kevin Uy and Gabriel Ong steered FLOW to one Michelin star
World.content:
For Filipino chefs Kevin Uy and Gabriel Ong, returning home isn't just a culinary homecoming — it’s a humbling, emotional rediscovery of the country they thought they knew

The hardest thing chef Kevin Uy had to unlearn after returning to the Philippines was not a cooking technique. It was how to speak.

Abroad, Uy said, he could communicate directly with colleagues and express his thoughts without much hesitation. But after becoming a boss at FLOW, the Makati restaurant he co-leads with fellow chef Gabriel Ong, he realized that straightforwardness alone was not enough.

“What I had to unlearn was being more diplomatic, because I’m not a very diplomatic person,” Uy told Rappler.

The adjustment revealed an unexpected lesson from his years in international kitchens: Professional experience does not automatically translate into knowing how to lead in a different environment.

The 32-year-old chef spent years training and working in Barcelona and Peru before returning to the Philippines. His experiences abroad helped shape his culinary perspective, but building a restaurant at home required him to reconsider how he worked with people and dealt with constraints he had not encountered in quite the same way overseas.

For Filipino chefs who leave to learn, the journey home is not simply about bringing back recipes or techniques. It can also mean discovering how much they still need to understand about the country where they grew up.

A different kind of culture shock

Uy graduated from Enderun Colleges in 2016 with a degree in International Hospitality Management, specializing in Culinary Arts. He completed an internship at Hotel Arts Barcelona in Spain, later studied at the Basque Culinary Center, and spent years working with the group behind Peruvian restaurants Central and Mil and research initiative Mater Iniciativa.

His five years in Peru, much of them spent working under chefs Virgilio Martínez and Pía León, helped him approach food through the environments, ingredients, and people behind each dish.

But returning to the Philippines presented challenges beyond the kitchen.

One was sourcing. Uy said he had worked in prestigious restaurants abroad where obtaining supplies seemed relatively easy. Starting out in the Philippines made him realize that getting ingredients was not always as straightforward as he had expected.

Although he said his own suppliers had been accommodating, he had heard from other chefs who struggled to obtain particular ingredients.

Ong, who also worked abroad before returning to the Philippines, said logistics can affect the quality of produce by the time it reaches a restaurant.

“Some of the produce being so nice, the raw materials being so nice, gets through a three-hour traffic,” Ong said. “[Of] course, at the end, it ends up in your restaurant, it’s not the same quality.”

For chefs accustomed to working in established international kitchens, the challenge is not simply finding ingredients. It is learning to work with the quality, availability, and consistency of what reaches their kitchens locally.

Ong sees this contrast as both a limitation and an opportunity. International exposure gives returning chefs a reference point for the standards they want to achieve, while working in the Philippines shows them how much room there is to improve sourcing and distribution.

“The learning is the contrast,” he said.

Managing people posed another steep learning curve for Uy. Despite prior experience in Europe and Latin America, this was his first time leading a local team as an employer — not to mention his first job in the Philippines.

FLOW’s staff of about 18 came from different parts of the country, including Leyte, Bacolod, Antipolo, and Laguna. Uy said working with people from different backgrounds taught him that communication involves more than giving instructions.

“It’s not just all about saying things and people follow,” he said. “It’s making sure that they understand it and that they respect you for it.”

The road to a Michelin star

It was the same group of people that helped push FLOW to the periphery of the Michelin Guide’s anonymous inspectors, who felt that the fine dining concept deserved to receive its own highly coveted Michelin star.

WORTH A STOP. One Michelin star is awarded to restaurants that are ‘worth a stop.’ Photo courtesy of Michelin Guide

During the 2027 Michelin Guide ceremony, FLOW became the latest addition to the Philippines’ mighty roster of one-star restaurants. Uy and Ong were present to receive the glass trophy on stage, while their 18 staff members were at FLOW preparing for the upcoming dinner service.

While the recognition had come as a shock to the two chefs, they knew it had all been made possible by their hardworking team.

“I think just working hard every day,” Uy told Rappler just after the ceremony when asked what they think FLOW was doing right to have earned a star.

Play Video

“And the team is behind us. So they understand, and they work just as hard, and it’s because they care as much as we do. So that’s something that I think that they recognize as well.”

“It’s our team who deserves all of this award. We could not have done it without them,” Ong added.

The accolade had clearly come as a surprise to the two chefs. Anytime a member of the press would ask how they were feeling about it, they would answer that they were still processing the fact that they had received a Michelin star, but were nonetheless grateful for it all.

Perhaps one of the first things you would notice about Uy and Ong is that they are of Filipino-Chinese descent. Culinary is not a common path for the people in their community to take, but it was something both chefs were willing to gamble on — all the more now that FLOW finally has a Michelin star to its name.

“I think more than anything, for Filipino-Chinese in particular, [we have] perseverance, perseverance in the fact that we are able to push and prove to our families who really are skeptical about this entire industry, that we can manage to make it. And that’s something very important to us,” Uy told Rappler.

Uy and Ong take perseverance seriously in their work. Evolution is expected in the world of gastronomy, and the two know that by heart. A chef’s original vision must be tested against sourcing, preparation, consistency, and the experiences of the people expected to bring it to life.

For Uy and Ong, adapting also means learning from one another. Uy contributes much of FLOW’s creative direction, while Ong helps translate those ideas into a working kitchen.

Ong said chefs returning from abroad have a responsibility to use their experience to help improve the industry around them. Rather than demanding that local colleagues adopt the same standards or methods they encountered elsewhere, they must find ways to communicate what they learned.

“For me, I think it’s about being the bridge,” Ong said.

Coming home with humility

Asked to compare his years abroad to a television show or film, Uy settled on Emily in Paris. The comparison, he explained, was not about glamour but about a person finding her way in an unfamiliar place and building a life in an industry she wanted to join.

It is a fitting description of the experience he and Ong now encourage other Filipino chefs to embrace: being willing to learn even after gaining experience in prestigious kitchens.

Uy said chefs returning home should be flexible enough to absorb lessons from the people around them, rather than assuming their overseas experience has prepared them for everything.

“The only difference is what they were doing is where they were doing it,” he said, referring to Filipino chefs who built their careers locally while others trained abroad.

Uy said working overseas does not mean that a chef knows more than everyone who stayed, nor does growing up in the Philippines guarantee that returning professionals understand the local industry.

“Just because you grew up here doesn’t mean you know everything, and just because you worked there doesn’t mean no one else knows everything,” Uy said.

His advice is simple: “Be humble.”

The value of going abroad, for Filipino chefs, may lie not only in what they learn elsewhere, but in how they use those lessons when they return. The work at home is not simply to recreate an international kitchen; it is to understand the people, ingredients, and constraints around them, then find ways to build something that belongs here. – Rappler.com

Dominique Astucia is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers.
