World.title: Driver charged after pedestrian's death in Adelaide's north
World.content:
A pedestrian has died, while another was seriously injured, after a crash in Adelaide's northern suburbs on Sunday morning.

SA Police say emergency services were called to the intersection of Waterloo Corner Road and Whites Road in Salisbury North just after 10am when a vehicle collided with a traffic light pole and two pedestrians.

"Sadly, one of the pedestrians died at the scene and the second pedestrian was taken to hospital with serious injuries," a spokesperson said.

The driver was arrested at 11:20am and charged with causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious harm by dangerous driving.

"He was granted bail and will appear in the Elizabeth Magistrates Court on 14 December," they said.

The 19-year-old driver, who was uninjured, was issued with an instant loss of licence until further order.

Police said the crash occurred after 10am on Sunday. (ABC News)

Road closures were in place, and the intersection was closed.

Major crash investigators attended the scene and are examining the surrounding circumstances, while anyone who witnessed or has dashcam footage has been asked to contact police.

The pedestrian's life is the 90th lost on SA roads this year.

World.title: Australia's latest World Cup smash-up helps nobody
World.content:
Gallows humour was the order of the day for Australia's World Cup match against Wales, which was only fitting given it trudged towards its inevitable conclusion like the condemned to the executioner's block.

The Jillaroos ran out 124-6 winners in a game where the only element of contest was whether the reigning world champions could bring up the century.

They did it easily in the end, smashing their own record for biggest World Cup win, with Jamie Chapman's sixth try in the shadows of the full-time siren eclipsing France's 116-0 victory over Serbia in 2023 in the most lopsided result in women's international rugby league history.

Wales was helpless in the face of the Australian onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the first half, as they ran up a 60-0 lead, Australia scored 10 tries and Wales played the ball just 15 times. Five-eighth Jesse Southwell finished with 44 points on her own.

The Jillaroos did not make a tackle from the fifth minute until after the half-time siren and Australian halfback Tarryn Aiken did not make a tackle until 10 minutes before full-time.

After Australia scored its 15th try of the match it started getting booed by the sparse Parramatta Stadium crowd, who reserved their biggest cheer of the day for Welsh second rower Paige Travis's score that narrowed the gap to 100-6.

It was the sole bright spot of the match but the punters soon returned to an idle stupor as Australia added four more tries in the final seven minutes.

All World Cups are going to have their blowouts and rugby league's more than most. But they must serve a wider purpose and this one did not.

It benefited nobody and served to damage the tournament's credibility and its only legacy can be like Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in the men's 2000 World Cup, which is to say as a historical oddity for the trainspotters.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

As the women's World Cup reckons with what has been an uneven tournament at best, marred by the same enormous scorelines of the men's edition but with few of the strong crowds, questions must be asked as to why a game like this could happen at all.

The uninterested and meagre turn-out for this match was proof it did not maximise the product, which very much felt like a curtain-raiser to the two men's matches that followed. Nor does it aid development.

It stuffed some stat sheets and gave ammunition to the bad-faith actors who are always on the hunt for an opportunity to take a shot at women's sport.

The Jillaroos are the best team in the world by an order of magnitude and have been for years. They gain nothing by putting the cleaners through Wales, who exist in a different universe.

That's why the Welsh should be spared any blame for how this went down. When the criticism comes it should not fall on them.

They qualified fair and square but they did not ask for this and there's no way to say it without sounding patronising but they did their best in the face of impossible odds.

While they have Canterbury halfback Tayla Preston and North Queensland winger Sian Williams as well as a smattering of Super League talent in Bethan Daiton, Carys Marsh and Agnes Wood, most of their players ply their trade in the women's second division in England.

It's a competition that can still have the draw disrupted by forfeits and a far cry from the semi-professional existence most of the Australians lead.

Cardiff plays the same sport as the Sydney Roosters, but the two teams live in different worlds.

Some of the Welsh players had only played a handful of rugby league games before this tour and their entire coaching staff is filled by volunteers.

As Australia moves on to the semi-finals, Wales heads home with a few bumps and bruises and perhaps a few stories to tell.

It is part of the developing arm of a developing sport and while it has its place on the international scene it is not across from an Australia side who are so dominant it's starting to become a problem.

They are overwhelming against everyone they play, let alone a team from the sport's frontiers packed with players who have never taken on athletes like Chapman, Tamika Upton or Jess Sergis in their lives.

Even so, lopsided results are not an issue on their own, so long as they serve a wider purpose.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

The progress of Samoa, Fiji and Papua New Guinea through this World Cup would not have happened if they were not exposed to teams like Australia and New Zealand, even if there were growing pains.

Hours later, in the same stadium, Tonga and Samoa played out the most eagerly anticipated clash of the men's World Cup, one which could have sold out the ground twice over.

None of that happens without some blow-outs along the way.

But there are limits to what can be found amid the wreckage when a team who shouldn't be there are thrown into the fast lane.

Total obliteration leaves nothing behind. This was not a building block; this was a massacre that left no survivors.

World.title: Epstein survivor thinks serial sex offender would be 'proud'
World.content:
Every time Lisa Phillips is on her phone, she knows she will see a picture of the man who abused her, Jeffrey Epstein.

"I'm on Instagram, TikTok, his face always pops up," she says.

"It makes me really, really angry.

"I just click off it now.

"I do what I need to do but I don't want to look at his face."

Loading...

More than a year after Ms Phillips joined dozens of other Epstein survivors on Capitol Hill, sharing their experiences publicly for the first time and demanding the release of the Epstein files, the podcast host is reflecting on the "interesting" turn her life has taken.

"I'm feeling a lot better now than I was about a year ago," she tells triple j hack.

"I have a lot of answered questions, things that I was really curious about since my early 20s.

"I don't regret it because it's actually where I found myself again and got my power back."

'It was pretty dirty'

Lisa Phillips is one of hundreds of Epstein survivors.

She first met the disgraced businessman on his private island in 2000, when she was working as a model.

Like many others, she describes a cycle of grooming and abuse that continued for years, until she was finally able to get away from the sex offender in 2004.

An email chain printout illustrates the amount of redactions of personally identifiable information the DOJ was required to do before releasing the Epstein files. (AP Photo: Jon Elswick)

Now, seven years after Epstein's death, and months after millions of documents, images and videos related to the financier were made public, she's relieved.

"Everything that I had known was in those files, so it validated it all for me," she says.

"But many of my survivor sisters' names weren't redacted — their addresses, their emails, pictures.

"It was pretty dirty what they did to them."

While the US Department of Justice maintains it has published all significant records under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, there is ongoing debate about what has not been released.

"There's a lot that people don't know," Ms Phillips tells hack.

"I think the Department of Justice just doesn't know what to do because there's so much to go through.

"But there's a lot more to look into, that's for sure."

Questions over Epstein's death

Conspiracy theories around the death of Jeffrey Epstein in his New York jail cell in August 2019 continue to captivate the world.

Whether or not his death was self-inflicted, as determined by the New York City medical examiner and federal investigations, sparks furious discussions online.

The Epstein files: Why the sex offender's brother and lawyer do not believe he took his own life The US Department of Justice, the FBI and New York City forensic experts might have moved on from the possibility Jeffrey Epstein did not take his own life, but many have not, and now suspicions around his death have gone mainstream.

Many, including Epstein's brother and lawyer, have publicly stated they do not believe the sex offender took his own life.

Lisa Phillips agrees.

"Absolutely not. No way," she tells hack.

"I don't believe he killed himself because I just felt like he always knew that he would get away with it.

"I think he had too many people behind him to help him get away.

"So no, I don't believe that for a second."

'He would be proud of us'

When asked what she believes Jeffrey Epstein would say if he was alive today, Ms Phillips pauses, knowing that her answer will not only surprise but confuse a lot of people.

"When I was with my survivor sisters last … we thought of that … if Jeffrey was alive and he walked in the room right now, what would he say?

"We thought that he would be proud of us."

Survivors of Jeffrey Epstein have continued campaigning for more transparency, including at a congressional hearing with Pam Bondi in February. (AP: Tom Brenner)

Ms Phillips says that reaction is indicative of the power of grooming.

"He groomed us to think of him … as a mentor type," she says.

"It's almost like we think he would say, 'Wow, you didn't just stay silent, you're standing up for yourselves.'

"I know it's kind of ironic, but I think that's actually what he would say.

" I do think people, men, weren't expecting that … because they like you to live in your shame and live in your silence. "

'Use your voice'

After a break from advocacy to protect her mental health, Lisa Phillips is throwing herself into her podcast, From Now On, where she speaks with other survivors, experts and changemakers.

Loading Instagram content

"We have a big problem all around the world, in Australia too … with sexual abuse in our society," she says.

"We have to figure out what's going on.

"How do we fix this?"

Ms Phillips says she has been overwhelmed with the response from other survivors flooding her inbox with their own experiences.

Many of them are men, speaking about abuse that happened to them as children.

She says it's a good reminder for young people to "use their voice" to protect themselves.

" If something happens to you … immediately go tell somebody. I just stayed silent and kept that shame and didn't want to say anything. "

"But your mental health, it will destroy you if you keep things inside."

Always an Epstein survivor

After a year of public campaigning, travel and advocacy, Lisa Phillips says she is looking forward to getting on with the rest of her life.

"It's kind of hard because now I wear a hat … I'm just like, 'Oh great, I am the Epstein survivor.'

"That's not really what I wanted to be in life."

But she admits speaking out has given her a self-belief she never knew existed.

"When people say, 'I am proud of you' or, 'You're so brave because you spoke up,' that's really nice."

Ms Phillips says she's now in a "good place" and is looking forward to finding purpose by supporting other survivors.

"It makes me feel really good changing lives, seeing them getting into a healthy relationship and having a beautiful life," she says.

"That's what we all want, right?"

World.title: Suns miss top four by a whisker despite win over Giants
World.content:
Gold Coast won its final game of the home and away season, but left the field shattered after letting slip the double chance in the finals.

The Suns needed a solid win to boost their percentage sufficiently to replace Carlton in fourth spot after the Blues' win over Brisbane on Saturday.

But instead their 9.8 (62) to 7.11 (53) victory at Henson Park left them just 0.2 percentage points behind Carlton.

GWS could be proud of its efforts, having fought hard before a home crowd to send off the retiring Alicia Eva and Isabel Huntington at their final game.

Eva was an inaugural AFLW player 10 years ago with Collingwood and served as the Giants' captain for five years.

Huntington was a number one draft pick and All-Australian, though three separate ACL injuries plagued her six-year career.

It seemed it was going to be a walk in the park for the Suns, who dominated the first half around the stoppage and in midfield and led the clearances 16-10 thanks to Charlie Rowbottom and Lucy Single, who had five each.

But the Giants came out with a bang in the third quarter.

They led disposals 68–46 and converted from eight of their 10 entries inside-50, kept the Suns scoreless and took an 11-point lead before the final term.

Rowbottom did everything she could in the fourth quarter to claw back the lead and kicked a goal in the dying minutes to put the Suns back in front.

She ended with 33 disposals, two goals and 12 clearances, but didn't have much to celebrate after the Suns' ninth win of the season.

"Obviously we're happy to get away with the four points, but I wanted to finish fourth," Rowbottom said post-game.

"We'll take the long way home."

Meanwhile, Essendon's 4.14 (38) to 4.7 (31) win over Collingwood handed outgoing Bombers coach Natalie Wood one last win and Pies boss Sam Wright one final loss.

In Adelaide, Melbourne franked its premiership credentials with a 6.11 (47) to 3.11 (29) victory over the Crows. The win confirmed a third-place finish for the Demons and a qualifying final date with Geelong.

In the final game of the season, Sydney held on for a thrilling one-point away win over Fremantle.

Though the Swans were already guaranteed of an elimination final against the Western Bulldogs, the 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36) win over the Dockers will provide a timely boost on the eve of the post-season.

The Dockers even attempted to implement "Wharfie Time" during the game's final minutes, but it proved as successful as it did in the men's grand final as Chloe Molloy took a critical intercept mark to ice the game for the Swans.

Molloy kicked four of Sydney's five goals, in the process winning the league's goalkicking award.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Queensland's 28th governor sworn in at parliament house
World.content:
Justice Thomas Bradley has been sworn in as Queensland's 28th governor in the state's parliament.

In his first address as governor, Justice Bradley said he and his partner, Dr Matthew Yoong, looked forward to engaging with people across Queensland.

"We aim to spend as much time out of Brisbane as we spend in it," he said.

"To help harness the wisdom, the skill and the goodwill that is in every community as we all answer the call of the Olympic motto, which is to go faster, higher and stronger, together."

Premier David Crisafulli said the appointment marked a "significant moment" for Queensland.

Justice Bradley served on the Supreme Court from 2018 and moved to the Court of Appeal in 2025.

Justice Thomas Bradley was appointed to the Supreme Court in 2018. (ABC News: Stephen Cavenagh)

Mr Crisafulli said Justice Bradley's experience in the law had given him "strong preparation" for the office.

" You have encountered people at some of the most difficult moments of their lives. You have listened to them, weighed decision of profound consequence and helped bring resolution. "

Outside of his career in the courts, Justice Bradley has carried out roles including as chair of the Brisbane Festival Giving Committee, ambassador for the Pinnacle Foundation, and on the Gallery of Modern Art Foundation Committee.

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the state was stronger when people in public roles reflected the community.

"That is the Queensland we are all proud of and the Queensland His Excellency represents."

Governor role a 'privilege'

Outgoing governor Dr Jeanette Young said she departed the role with a "profound sense of gratitude and pride".

"Serving the people of Queensland as governor has been one of the greatest honours and privileges of my life," she said.

Prior to her role as governor, Dr Young served as Queensland's chief health officer during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During her time as governor, Dr Young said she had travelled to all 77 local government areas in Queensland and visited each of the state's public hospitals.

Dr Jeanette Young departed her role as Queensland's 27th governor on Sunday. (ABC News)

She granted royal assent to 168 pieces of legislation, attended 257 consecutive council meetings and welcomed more than 114 diplomatic representatives from overseas.

Dr Young said Queensland's government house had welcomed more than 100,000 visitors during her time in the role.

"As I leave here today I have every confidence that government house will continue to evolve, serve and reflect the very best of Queensland," Dr Young said.

World.title: Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven
World.content:
Opal Miela Sowah has etched her name in Australian women's basketball history books as her Golden State Valkyries overcame Izzy Borlase's Atlanta Dream 68-63 to win the WNBA championship.

The 26-year-old entered the league's first-ever game seven at San Francisco's Chase Centre on Saturday (Sunday AEDT) looking to join the 11 previous Australian winners of the top women's basketball competition in the world.

That list includes some of the country's biggest basketball names such as Lauren Jackson and Penny Taylor, while Sowah was also aiming to become the first Australian winner since Cayla George in 2023.

The Opal didn't take the court as she is on a player development contract, making her ineligible to feature in the playoffs.

But Sowah was an avid supporter from the sidelines, as she helped spur on Gabby Williams to a masterclass as the forward posted 30 points and four blocks.

Of those, 28 were in the second half — a WNBA finals record for most points by a player in a half.

Izzy Borlase had some big moments as her Dream went down in game seven. (Getty Images: Matthew Huang)

Ex-Bendigo Spirit star Veronica Burton was also busy, registering 10 points, 11 rebounds and five assists to help Golden State claim a maiden championship in the franchise's second season.

While Sowah will bask in title glory, her Opals teammate Borlase will not after her team missed a golden opportunity to claim a historic first championship.

The 22-year-old played another important role off the bench as she recorded eight points and two rebounds in 14 minutes of game time.

Her best moment came in the third quarter when she coolly sank a three to end the Valkyries' 6-0 run before she later drove to the basket and earned a three-point play in the fourth period.

A title would have capped off a remarkable year for Borlase, who became the WNBL's youngest MVP in 15 years, made her Women's World Cup debut with the Opals and played her first minutes in the American league.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Suspended Powerhouse CEO denies wrongdoing as 14 disclosures revealed
World.content:
The curtain is about to be raised on Sydney's so-called 'Opera House of the west' with the new Powerhouse Parramatta due to open on November 7.

But the $915 million project remains under a cloud with a Minns government investigation into alleged misconduct by unnamed executives, a whistleblower report, and a referral of undisclosed allegations to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

While supporters of the suspended CEO, Lisa Havilah, have launched a petition for her immediate reinstatement, questions persist over how millions of dollars in public money has been managed.

On the eve of the grand opening, Ms Havilah is fighting back against the government, saying that she acted with integrity.

7.30 can reveal Ms Havilah made 14 declarations of perceived conflicts of interest and matters that may give rise to a conflict of interest during her tenure, according to internal documents released under state freedom of information laws.

The declarations, since 2019, include entries about former work associates of Ms Havilah's hired to consult for the Powerhouse, and a $1.9 million marketing contract awarded to a company founded by former Powerhouse trustee, Mark Hassell.

In all 14 cases, there were "actions proposed to mitigate the real or perceived conflict", according to the documents.

Ms Havilah was suspended in August amid a governance and procurement investigation.

The Powerhouse Parramatta is due to open on November 7. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Ms Havilah is not authorised to speak publicly but her spokesperson told 7.30 in a statement that the records show she acted properly.

"No findings have been made against Ms Havilah, who denies any wrongdoing and at all times has maintained the highest standards of integrity," the statement said.

"The disclosures in question were made out of an abundance of caution to ensure transparency regarding her legitimate professional relationships. The disclosures were made for the purpose of perceived conflicts of interest and did not give rise to any actual conflict of interest."

Declarations of conflicts of interest, real or perceived, are widely used by public institutions to ensure integrity of processes, particularly in the awarding of public contracts.

The Museum's own declaration form states that: "Conflicts of interest are not wrong in themselves. It is how they are managed that is important."

Ms Havilah's spokesperson said that none of the disclosures resulted in any personal gain for her.

It took four years for the Powerhouse Parramatta to be built. (Supplied: Powerhouse Museum)

Millions of dollars in contracts

In 2019, Ms Havilah declared "a perceived conflict of interest" over the hiring of three former work associates as consultants for the Powerhouse Museum, Lisa Ffrench, Amanda Burgess and Cass O'Connor.

The documents state that "the perceived conflict has been disclosed, and the procurement was undertaken by the Executive Officer, who has noted this conflict. The contract will also be managed by the Executive Officer".

7.30 understands the Executive Officer referred to was not Ms Havilah.

Prior to becoming Powerhouse CEO in 2018, Ms Havilah was director of arts and performance venue, Carriageworks in Sydney's Eveleigh.

Some of her previous links to Carriageworks were declared in the documents.

An entry in May 2021 declared that during her time at Carriageworks, "Felix Media were a resident company".

Lisa Havilah was the CEO of Carriageworks from 2011 until 2018. (Supplied: Museum of Arts and Applied Sciences)

Felix Media was awarded a $2.5 million contract (before rebates) over two other applicants to deliver a documentary film about the setting up of Powerhouse Parramatta.

In January this year, Ms Havilah noted "I have two conflicts to declare" as she had previously worked with public relations companies Articulate PR and Original Spin.

The documents reveal a "perceived conflict of interest" was identified in November 2025 over a $1.9m marketing contract awarded to a "creativity-driven investment company" called Ki Community, founded by former Powerhouse trustee, Mark Hassell.

The 12-month contract was part of a selective request for tender and was to deliver an "integrated marketing, communications, and engagement plan" for Powerhouse Parramatta.

"The perceived risk relates to potential public or stakeholder perception of preferential treatment or informational advantage", the documents state.

This risk was mitigated "to ensure transparency and fairness".

"With these measures, the residual risk is assessed as low-moderate, noting that transparency and equal access to information substantially mitigate the risk of any actual advantage," the document said.

"All respondents received equal access to the scoping information."

The Powerhouse Parramatta project is being investigated over alleged misconduct and has been referred to the ICAC. (ABC News: Anton Rose, Monish Nand)

In July, the Museum's Chief Operating Officer, Mark Wilsdon, also stepped aside.

In a disclosure of conflict of interest form signed by him in May 2025, he wrote "I have work (sic) with Mark in my capacity as COO through FARM (Finance Audit and Risk Management Committee) and (Powerhouse) Trust".

"This perceived conflict will be managed through the procurement process. Other senior Powerhouse staff will also be involved. Mark Hassell will not be part of the team working with Powerhouse on this engagement. This perceived conflict will be appropriately mitigated by these actions."

A separate letter from Ki Community in November 2025 released to 7.30 declares that "Mark Hassell has not participated in, contributed to, or provided any input — directly or indirectly — into the preparation or submission of our tender response".

"He has not been involved in any way regarding the strategy, pricing, technical content, or supporting documentation for this tender."

7.30 contacted Ki Community but did not receive a reply.

Alleged misconduct probe continues

The Minns government had concerns about Powerhouse management as far back as March 2025 when Arts Minister John Graham asked his department to launch a fact-finding assessment.

A referral to the ICAC was also made at the time. The ICAC would not tell 7.30 whether the referral was still active.

The $915 million Powerhouse Parramatta project has been referred to ICAC. (ABC News)

7.30 requested the report of the government's assessment under freedom of information laws but was refused access because of secrecy provisions under the ICAC Act.

In December 2025, Mr Graham escalated the matter to a formal misconduct investigation.

By mid-2026, "a range of allegations were put to a number of Powerhouse executives," Mr Graham told a state parliamentary committee in August.

In response to the release of the disclosure documents, Mr Graham told 7.30:

"After seven years of hard work, from hundreds of people, the government and team at the Powerhouse Parramatta are focused on making sure when the doors swing open next week, everyone can enjoy a truly great museum experience.

"All public servants, including senior executives, have an obligation to declare and manage any actual, potential, or perceived conflicts of interests appropriately.

"An investigation into allegations relating to procurement and governance practices at the Powerhouse is progressing. It is not appropriate to comment on matters that are under investigation."

The Powerhouse declined to comment.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: BioWare studio shuttered by EA after more than 30 years of video games
World.content:
In 1995 three Canadian doctors, joined by a love of video games, pooled their money to launch a studio which would provide countless hours of entertainment, joy and magical storytelling to people all over the world.

Thirty-one years later, on October 22, 2026, that dream died.

BioWare, the studio which created Mass Effect, Dragon Age and the first two Baldur's Gate games, released a statement on social media announcing the closure and the cancellation of development of Mass Effect 5, which had loosely been slated for release in 2028.

Loading Instagram content

"There is nothing easy about writing these words," it said.

"Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition."

Fan farewells flowed in.

Facebook user Melantha Justice wrote: "I would not be me without Dragon Age. Dragon Age: Originsmeans more to me than anyone could ever know. I salute you BioWare."

In Mass Effect, players destroyed Reapers, travelled through the galaxy to different worlds and forged alliances with various alien races. (Supplied: EA)

On Reddit, users expressed dismay at the closure and the uncertain future of the studio's intellectual property, however some said the writing had been on the wall.

"After Dragon Age: The Veilguard I'm surprised this didn't happen sooner," commenter Matt Pierce wrote.

Some commenters blamed the poor sales performance of recent games and called the closure predictable, many also blamed Electronic Arts (EA), which bought BioWare in 2007.

Regardless of its recent titles, BioWare's impact on gaming and the role-playing genre is indisputable.

From Doctors to Dungeon Masters

Founders Greg Zeschuk, Ray Muzyka, and Augustine Yip, met in medical school at the University of Alberta and in 1995 they started BioWare, releasing their first commercially successful game by 1996.

But the first feather in their cap came in 1998 in the form of Baldur's Gate, which cost an estimated $CAD1 million to make and sold more than 2 million copies on release.

The isometric RPG Baldur's Gate was one of BioWare's first big successes. (Supplied: Bioware)

Set in the world of Dungeons and Dragons, Baldur's Gatelet players create their own characters and have a say in its outcome.

Writer David Gaider says Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic was a big hit and "made BioWare a well-known studio". (Supplied: Bioware)

In 2000 Baldur's Gate 2 was released, matching the first game's success.

It was followed by Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic in 2003, which also received critical acclaim.

Founder of Melbourne-based Summerfall Studios game company, David Gaider, was brought on as a writer for Baldur's Gate 2.

David Gaider joined BioWare after learning he would have to reapply for his job at an Edmonton hotel following a buyout. (Supplied: Summerfall Studios)

He said he joined the company at a time it had just 50 employees, including two of the founders, and the game would help BioWare flourish.

"Baldur's Gate 2 kinda put BioWare on the map," Gaider said.

These successes were just a prelude for what came next.

The golden era

In 2004 BioWare began work on its first new intellectual properties.

"The bosses were tired of having a third-party IP owner always on the line," Gaider said.

"So we're gonna start our own fantasy IP and sci-fi IP."

Mass Effect, set in a future Milky Way Galaxy, let players step into the role of Commander Shepard, an interstellar special forces operative on a mission to save the galaxy from obliteration.

Mass Effect 2 is widely regarded by players and critics as the best in the series and received almost universal acclaim. (Supplied: EA)

It took a team of 130 people three years of work to deliver the game.

The game featured multiple-choice, fully-voiced conversations and had more than 20,000 lines of spoken dialogue which, according to lead writer Drew Karpyshyn, was equivalent to 20 movies or four to five novels.

Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 sold millions of copies with the latter widely regarded as one of the best games ever created.

Mass Effect 2 was Good Game Spawn Squad presenter Gemma Driscoll's first BioWare game.

"It kind of just dazzled me," Driscoll said.

"It was my first choose your own adventure kind of game.

"I'm on my 30th or 40th full play through of the series now."

The games also featured romance, with players being able to pursue a relationship with different companions.

Mass Effect character Thane Krios, also known as the love of Gemma Driscoll's life. (Supplied)

These relationships were a hallmark of BioWare's title and fans remain invested in them to this day, including Driscoll who described Mass Effect character, Thane Krios, as "the love of my life".

"There was something kind of revolutionary in the idea that companionship could be found in such an interactive way that could still hit you emotionally even if it isn't real," she said.

Between the two releases, and a surprise success, was the fantasy Dragon Age: Origins, whose world was created by Gaider.

"I had no idea what I was doing," he said.

"It was sort of like I was a dungeon master for a DND game run amok."

Gaider created the world in which Dragon Age was set and has written three novels for the series. (Supplied: Bioware)

With three hits between 2007 and 2010, BioWare was enjoying a golden age and Gaider said there was "a lot of skill and imagination under one roof".

Great expectations

Dragon Age 2 in 2011 didn't receive the same high praise as the first and the highly anticipated Mass Effect 3, while received well by critics, did not meet up to some fans' expectations.

Gaider said the romances in BioWare games were a "hallmark" and fans became deeply invested in them. (Supplied: EA)

On the other hand, Dragon Age: Inquisition launched in 2014 and sold more than 12 million copies, becoming the best-selling BioWare game to date.

Gaider felt Dragon Age was his baby.

"I created the world. There were other writers, but I was the first one with my toe in the water and I was the one who kicked it off," he said.

Although not all of his ideas were realised over the three-game run, he never begrudged the changes or cuts made.

After the release of Inquisition, Gaider felt he'd "written all the mage, templar and demon stories" he could and transitioned to a new title, Anthem.

EA's influence

Electronic Arts (EA), the publishers behind the FIFA, Dead Space and The Sims series, bought Bioware in 2007 for roughly $US1.2 billion.

Gaider said initially very little changed, but by the time he started work on Anthem its influence was being felt.

Despite the success of titles like Dragon Age: Inquisition and BioWare's overall profitability, Gaider feels they were not successful by EA's standards. (Supplied: EA)

"When you have a corporation looming over you … their comparison for a game that sells well is their sports titles," he said.

He said the thought process at EA was: "If a BioWare game doesn't sell 10 million copies why are we doing it?"

"And BioWare games never sold 10 million copies," he said.

"We were the red-headed stepchild."

He said the focus went from making a good game to maximising sales and profit.

Anthem was developed as an online, multiplayer, action, role-playing game and released in 2019 to a mixed reception.

Gaider left Anthem's development midway through production.

It did not meet EA's commercial expectations and in January 2026 all servers supporting Anthem were shut and the game is now unplayable.

End of an age

Anthem's failure was preceded by the poor reception of the anticipated fourth Mass Effect game, Mass Effect Andromeda.

The last major release from BioWare, and a common fan scapegoat for its ultimate closure, was 2024s Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which had been in development since 2014 and had been intended as a monetised, live service, multiplayer game, similar to Anthem.

Long-time Dragon Age creative director Mike Laidlaw left BioWare along with other veteran staff after development on Dragon Age's fourth title was cancelled in 2017, only to be rebooted in 2018. (Supplied: EA)

The failure of Anthem led to it being rebooted, more than once, and developers were pressed for time.

Gaider attributed its failure to the symptomatic issues plaguing BioWare.

"It's just changed too much, I suppose, internally," he said.

"The golden days are over.

"Whatever sort of mentality had taken hold which EA had put in there it was clear for Veilguard that Electronic Arts had set them up to fail."

Driscoll said she was empathetic to BioWare "being under the thumb of a publisher that demands insane numbers (of sales) again and again and again".

"We are seeing more and more, especially in the last five years, that it does not matter if you make a good game or a bad game; studios are getting axed left and right," she said.

"You are numbers on spreadsheets, and it doesn't matter if it means it can save some money."

On October 22 EA announced it was closing BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect game.

"BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly," the publisher said.

A lasting legacy

Driscoll said BioWare's closure left her gutted, but the stories it created will "always remain very dear to my heart".

"The outpouring of support and emotion and for lack of a better term of grief is indicative of the impacts these games had," she said.

"For people out there, this meant a lot to them.

"That defies numbers on a spreadsheet."

Gaider said BioWare's impact on the gaming world was unmistakable.

"You can see (its) influence everywhere.

"The way a cinematic game is shot that everyone for quite a while … if a game had story they wanted to present it in the way BioWare did."

Larian Studios developed Baldur's Gate 3, but the influence of BioWare remains evident in its design. (Supplied: Larian)

BioWare's intellectual properties are held by EA, but Gaider believes it's unlikely fans will see a new Mass Effect or Dragon Age game any time soon.

He also believes BioWare's games "represented a progressive view of the world" which doesn't match with EA's investors, which includes Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

However fans have hope in the future and a petition to #SaveMassEffect has garnered more than 275,000 signatures.

Gaider said he feels sad about BioWare's fate.

"In an era where we're considering AI as a possible replacement for writing … this was a company that valued good story from humans," he said.

"Especially a little company out in the middle of Canada in Edmonton Alberta, where there's not exactly a hub of game development, here rose a world class studio that for a time made games the entire world paid attention to."

World.title: From homework to big kids: What keeps primary school students up at night
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWMental health From homework to big kids: What keeps primary school students up at night Rachel Rasker and Emily Kowal November 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Children kick a Texta-covered ball around a field. The students from Tempe Public School have written their anxieties on the ball’s surface: Homework. Big kids. High school. With every bounce, those worries rub off. As schools across the country battle a rise in childhood anxiety, activities such as the scribbled-on soccer ball have become crucial parts of the school day – as important as maths or spelling. Year 5 students (L-R) Georgie, Eva, Stevie and Mina, who participated in the Mentally Fit program at Tempe Public School, write their anxiety words on a ball in Sydney. Janie Barrett The average age for first anxiety diagnosis has fallen to 11 years old, according to the National Mental Health Commission, while a 2020 survey of 700 primary school principals found 81 per cent thought children’s anxiety was a significant issue within their school.



To address the escalating challenge, the NSW government announced a $450,000 investment for the Gotcha4Life Mentally Fit Schools program last week, enabling the charity to expand its reach to a further 20 schools in the state’s central west and south coast. Related Article Education In selective schools, parental pressure is driving students to the psychologist’s office At Tempe, Gotcha4Life participants invented a strategy to make their school a more “mentally fit” environment. As part of their student voice project, year five students Georgie, Eva, Stevie and Mina created the “forget about it ball” on which they wrote all their anxieties. “You kick it back and forth to a friend, and you’re basically just forgetting about your bad emotions,” Georgie said. “Gradually [the writing] will come off, symbolising letting go of your worries.” The girls said they worried about getting enough sleep, making new friends, balancing school and hobbies, forgetting tasks, and public speaking.



Stevie said the ball concept was also about being physical and socialising with a friend: “You’d talk to someone in your village about how you feel, and as you talk to them, then you should feel … calmer, and let go of your worries.” Founded by media personality Gus Worland, with Karl Stefanovic also a board member, Gotcha4Life’s ethos is grounded in the preventative skill of so-called mental fitness, built around the organisation’s three protective factors: emotional adaptability, help-seeking behaviour and social connectedness. The year five students created the “forget about it ball” as part of the Gotcha4Life program. Janie Barrett Gotcha4Life’s chief executive, Belinda Elworthy, said the program upskilled teachers to recognise when students were struggling, including how they could escalate their concerns: “Part of what the Gotcha4Life program does [is] build that village of support.” But the Australian Association of Psychologists’ Policy Coordinator Carly Dober said that teachers shouldn’t be expected to manage their students mental distress on top of their daily workload, and warned that while well-intentioned, universal mental health programs can do more harm than good, particularly for vulnerable children.



“There might be kids or young people who already have existing mental health conditions, and the programs don’t actually fit their need at all,” she said. Related Article Education Skipping camp, public speaking: How schools have it wrong on kids’ anxiety She said if a child’s distress stemmed from bullying or hate speech, and the school hadn’t addressed the root of the problem, mental wellbeing programs could exacerbate the situation: “It can actually increase their distress if nothing tangibly different is going to occur at school … it’s just hot air, essentially.” The mental health system remains under-resourced and unreachable for many families, Dober said, which can place added pressure on a student. “[If they’ve] reached out ... they need psychological intervention, and they can’t afford it, where does that trickle down to?” she said. “If you’ve got stressed parents, you’re going to have stressed kids.”



Elworthy said Gotcha4Life’s three-year program was comprehensive and tailored to each school, supporting teachers, students and parents. “The work that we are doing is prevention, it’s skill-building, it’s capacity-building,” Elworthy said. Year six students at Tempe Public are apprehensive about the transition to high school. Janie Barrett The latest Kids Helpline impact report found NSW had the highest overall contact volume in the country – although it is also the state with the greatest population – and recorded a 41.6 per cent increase in contacts over two years, from 29,083 in 2023 to 41,170 in 2025. NSW Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said there was more work to be done when it came to supporting the mental health of children.

World.title: Aussie rugby players launch legal action amid pay war impasse with RA
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Aussie rugby players launch legal action amid pay war impasse with RA Iain Payten November 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wallabies stars will kick off the spring tour in London this week amid an escalating pay dispute with Rugby Australia, with the players’ union confirming it plans to take legal action after failing to strike a deal with RA for a new collective bargaining agreement. But in a hint of potential turbulence to come, RA responded by saying it made a strong offer which also protects the whole game, and fired a shot at Rugby Union Players Association officials for blocking them from talking directly to players. Australian rugby players (from left) James Turner, Piper Duck, Max Jorgensen and Maddi Levi. James Brickwood As the Wallabies jetted out of Sydney for the start of a month-long tour of the UK, the current CBA between the RUPA, RA and the Super Rugby clubs expired on Saturday. Months of tense negotiations between RUPA and RA reps failed to agree to terms for a new deal by deadline, after RUPA pushed strongly for a significant increase in pay for all men’s and women’s professional players, and for improved conditions in areas such as insurance, as well.



The parties started out tens of millions of dollars apart, in terms of the minimum spend on player wages over a five-year term, and despite coming closer together, the final positions RUPA and RA were still significantly apart, according to sources unable to comment publicly due to the confidential nature of talks. The funding arrangements for players’ career-ending insurance policies and private health premiums were also a sticking point, according to sources. Wallabies players are among the RUPA members fighting for a better deal. Getty Images The deadlock means players are now not bound by the conditions of the previous CBA, opening a door for potential industrial action. The Wallabies are on tour and play England next weekend; the Australian sevens sides begin the World Series later this month, and Super Rugby men’s squads start pre-season training this week. In a statement on Sunday, RUPA boss Adrian Turner appeared to rule out strike action by saying “the players remain focused on their playing commitments”, but with no CBA in place, he indicated the players are looking to block Rugby Australia from using the players, and their images, for commercial purposes.



“Unfortunately, we haven’t reached agreement, despite making every effort to find a reasonable compromise. We put forward revised proposals and positions this week in an effort to bridge the remaining differences, but RA has confirmed the Rugby Bodies aren’t prepared to improve their financial offer,” Turner said. RUPA boss Adrian Turner (middle) and new COO Tom Symonds (front left) with the Wallabies in camp recently. RUPA “The players have every interest in seeing the game grow financially, and we’ve approached these negotiations with that firmly in mind. Equally, we have a responsibility to our members, and there are some fundamental conditions we can’t compromise on. Any agreement needs to properly recognise the players’ contribution to the game and provide the conditions and protections they should expect as professional athletes. “The ball is in RA’s court now, and we’ll wait to hear from them on whether there’s a way forward. In the meantime, we’ve formally notified RA of our intention to commence legal proceedings concerning the commercial use of player rights following the expiry of the CBA. “The players remain focused on their playing commitments. It’s our job as their association to work through these issues with RA, and that’s what we’ll continue to do.”



Turner and fellow RUPA official Tom Symonds, who both used to work for the RLPA, met with Wallabies players in camp in Sydney last week. Wallabies players may be able to refuse to engage in commercial activities with RA sponsors and partners. It is unclear if all players are in the same boat, however, with informed sources saying some players have individual arrangements in their contracts. Having negotiated the last two CBAs under the financial peril brought by COVID, RUPA has been more bullish and argued for RA to invest far more in players in the next cycle, using the significant windfalls from the Lions and the Rugby World Cup. RA boss Phil Waugh hugs Wallabies captain Harry Wilson after the team’s win over South Africa in Perth. Getty Images



RUPA said last month it was “unacceptable” players would not get a cut of the $100m fee paid to RA for hosting the 2027 World Cup. RA has argued its focus is to provide an uplift for players but to also ensure that cash reserves aren’t exhausted within the next few years. “Rugby Australia and Australia’s Super Rugby Clubs have engaged in good faith and proposed to RUPA a position that rewards today’s players while protecting the communities, pathways and high-performance systems that will produce all the generations to come,” Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh said in a statement. Related Article Analysis

Australian rugby Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms “Rugby Australia has transparently and consistently provided RUPA’s leadership with the game’s current and future financials, which form the basis of the position put forward by RA and the SRCs.



“In addition, RA has requested on several occasions to speak directly with the players to convey its position. These requests have been rejected by RUPA.“ Talks between RUPA and RA are set to continue this week.

World.title: Coach admits he’s out of ‘ideas’ as Magpies end season with defeat; AFLW finals locked in
World.content:
Departing Collingwood coach Sam Wright conceded he has “no energy left” and had “run out of suggestions” as the Pies finished their dismal 2026 season with just one win and independent review of the struggling women’s program looming.

The Pies faced Essendon on Sunday, who, like them, entered the game with just win to their name and preparing to farewell their senior coach.

Mia Busch celebrates a goal for the Bombers. AFL Photos via Getty Images

But it was the Bombers who got their second win of the year to claim 16th spot on the ladder, overcoming a late scare from the Pies to win by seven points in front of a roaring Windy Hill home crowd and sen coach Natalie Wood off in style.

Collingwood finished the season with a slightly better percentage than St Kilda (also one win), meaning they avoided the wooden spoon 17th. But finishing 17th was little comfort for Wright, who leaves the coaching job with the women’s program at Collingwood mired in uncertainty and mediocrity.

“I just really honest with the girls [pre-match], I’ve got no energy left,” he said after the game.

“I think I’ve given everything that I can to the club and the girls over the last three years. The win, loss [ratio] takes its toll.

“But what I’m really proud of is that I have given it everything.”

Collingwood president Barry Carp and CEO Craig Kelly watch Sunday’s final-round AFLW fixture. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Wright said he’d spent a lot of time on his long drives home wondering what he could do to help the team.

“I probably ran out of suggestions, to be honest, and I think whenever you hit that space … you’ve got to look at the priorities in your life. My priority is family at the moment, but the club’s been nothing but supportive, and it [leaving] comes with it some guilt with where the club’s at.

“But I think the girls understand that I’ve given everything that I have.”

A fortnight after CEO Craig Kelly declared the club did not need an independent review of its women’s program, the Pies announced last week announced an “independent external expert” would be involved in a review of the program.

A source familiar with the Collingwood situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Collingwood’s executive and board, following a meeting on Tuesday, decided it was important for an external figure to work with the club on improving its AFLW program.

Collingwood AFLW coach Sam Wright bowed out on Sunday. AFL Photos via Getty Images

The Magpies did not offer a timeframe for the review, but are facing pressure following the departure of captain Ruby Schleicher, with several senior players voicing concerns about a lack of improvement and direction in the program.

When asked if he had advocated for there to be a review into the program, Wright said he wasn’t able to get into specifics, but emphasised that he trusted Collingwood’s leadership.

“I think we all know we need to improve,” he said.

In contrast, departing Bombers coach Wood, said she had not run out of energy, despite not being offered a contract.

“Yes, I do definitely [have more to give], and that’s OK,” she said post match.

“The club’s made the decision that it’s time for a fresh start, and I fully respect that.

“I’m still full of energy, but yeah, I’ll rest and recuperate, and you know, see if there’s any opportunities that lie ahead.”

Essendon have not announced an independent external review of their women’s program, but will expand the scope of its annual internal AFLW review.

Wood said she hoped the review would be an opportunity to “zoom out and look at everything”.

Ultimately, Wood hoped to leave the playing group with the knowledge that a coach could develop good relationships with their players while also challenging them.

“My job as a coach, we see the game from a different perspective, my job’s to stand alongside you and walk with you ... you do your role, and I’ll do mine,” she said.

“But we’ll push each other, but we’ll do it together.”

Collingwood had a goalless first quarter, trailing in contested possessions, failing to stop Emily Gough and Mia Busch, who piled on the goals for the Bombers.

For a while, it looked like Collingwood might be staring down a goalless game again, but majors to Tarni White and Ash Centra, with a heavily taped nose, saved the Pies.

A soaring goal from captain Bonnie Toogood in the third quarter pushed the Bombers ahead, but Collingwood came back hard in the fourth.

A brilliant pass from captain Lucy Cronin to Irish debutant Ellie Brady followed by a goal cut the margin to nine points with 10 minutes left to play.

Busch countered with a goal, but Imogen Trengove scored a free kick and a 50-metre penalty with five minutes to go. Undeterred by the chorus of boos and jeers from the crowd, Trengove booted converted to cut the margin again.

But after crucial intercepts and tackles, the Bombers held on to win 4.14 (38) to 4.7(31).

“It’s been a tough year, it’s been a bit of a slog, and it has felt like it has gone forever, but I’m proud of us for coming out here today,” Bomber Madison Prespakis told Seven.

“Woody [Natalie Wood] has been my only coach at Essendon,” she added.

“Five years. There was no one here and she said ‘we want you here’. I’ve got a lot of love and respect for Woody and what she has done with the program.

“Set aside the coach and she is a beautiful human. We did this for her, and it has been an honour to be coached by her, and I know she will be in the stands watching us for sure.”

When the siren blared, Essendon players rushed to embrace each other and also farewell veteran Sophie Alexander, who announced her retirement from the AFLW after an 85-game career.

The 33-year-old told teammates ahead of their final game of the season, coincidentally against her former club, Collingwood.

Pies players comforted each other and gathered for a guard of honour for retiring ruck Sabrina Frederick.

World.title: This horse is barred from running in Cup week after failing a drug test – that its trainer requested
World.content:
Blinkers On SportRacingVictorian racing This horse is barred from running in Cup week after failing a drug test – that its trainer requested Danny Russell and Angelica Snowden November 1, 2026 — 7:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Blinkers On is a weekly column covering the biggest issues of the spring racing carnival. It is the last thing racing needed on the eve of Melbourne Cup week – another group of unsuspecting victims caught up in racing’s breast cancer drug saga. But, here we are again. Major Share had a win at Flemington early last year, but has spent the past year on the sidelines. Racing Photos via Getty Images This time around, up to 50 owners have had their Cup week dreams ruined because their horse Major Share has produced a left-field positive to formestane – a mysterious substance that popped out of nowhere almost four years ago and which has baffled the racing industry ever since. It is the second time Major Share has thrown a positive swab in 12 months and as a result, their talented gelding can’t run on Oaks Day.



To say the large cohort of country-based owners are gutted is an understatement. One minute they are booking their tickets to Flemington, the next they are packing away their suits. “I’ve been involved in horses in one form or another for 50 years, and this is the best horse I’ve ever been involved in, by a considerable margin,” retired school teacher Greg May told this masthead. Trainer Adam Chambers. Racing Photos via Getty Images “To not be able to see him race because of something, which all the evidence points to occurs naturally and in minute doses, so it has no impact on his physical performance whatsoever, is incredibly frustrating. “We’ve got another six or eight weeks of bills to pay with no possible chance of getting any prizemoney back, and it’s not [trainer] Adam Chambers’ fault.



“If anything, I think Adam is more of a victim in this than the owners because his reputation has been impinged.” Major Share was due to return this week after 12 months out. It first tested positive at Moonee Valley on Cox Plate day last year. No one has ever been able to explain why. Tom Madden rides Major Share to victory in the VRC Super Saturday in March, 2025. Racing Photos via Getty Images There are two trains of thought. The substance is produced naturally by horses as it is in humans, or it is a performance-enhancing supplement. As a drug, formestane is not available in Australia. In this case, as in all the mystery cases, owners have backed their trainers. They all circle back to UK research that points to the substance being exogenous – naturally occurring. Sadly for them, the research is still yet to be peer-reviewed and published, so cannot be used in evidence.



But here’s what sets this latest case apart: it was a voluntary test. Warrnambool-based Chambers organised for the swab to be taken so that Major Share could be cleared to return to racing. He drove the horse to Hamilton races seven weeks ago to provide the urine sample. It is hard to believe a trainer would set himself up to fail. A bitter pill to swallow When it comes to formestane, which is used in some countries to treat breast cancer, Racing Victoria continues to hide behind the rules. RV says a horse must be banned for 12 months if it throws up a positive at a race meeting, trial or jumpouts.



The organisation says it is bound by the Australian rules of racing, and cannot make state-based exceptions. Related Article Racing integrity Another six racing stables to face the heat over breast cancer drug charges It is a bitter pill for connections to swallow. “I can tell you that there are owners of Major Share who won’t be investing again in horses because of the way we’ve been treated,” May said. So far, 13 Victorian stables have had horses disqualified since February 2023. All have protested their innocence.



“It is something that we have no control over, no trainer has any control over, and Racing Victoria has dropped the ball in terms of amending the rules to say, ‘well, we accept that trainers aren’t doing it. It occurs naturally’,” May said. “Surely, it’s within their powers to say, ‘we’ll either stop swabbing for it or put any penalties on hold until the scientific evidence from their research is finalised’.” At least in this latest case, Major Share will not be rubbed out because Chambers requested the sample outside a race, trial or jumpout. Meanwhile, we have to wait. Racing Victoria told this masthead it has commissioned its own research.



Racing Analytical Services Laboratory, which is part-owned by Racing Victoria, will conduct a global study of more than 15 target compounds including formestane, 4-hydroxytestosterone, 6a-hydroxyandrostenedione and DHEA. The study will take 12 months. By then, Major Share might be cleared to run on Oaks Day. More than 88,000 people flocked to Flemington for Derby Day. Penny Stephens Unhappy punters at Derby Day On face value, Derby Day was a roaring success. More than 88,000 people flocked to Flemington and largely avoided the forecast rain.



But not everyone was happy. Those who spent the day in the precinct’s nursery carpark were left feeling unloved. They said drivers had to wait more than an hour to enter that section of the course to set up their catering for the day; those on foot had to wait more than an hour to pass through the limited number of turnstiles; and there were not near enough toilet facilities. Interestingly, these issues might have ramifications at the coming Victoria Racing Club elections. Loading Melbourne Cup week is run by a members-based club, unlike, say, the Australian Open or Formula 1 Grand Prix.



The board can be held accountable, and members will be asked to cast votes on four VRC boardroom seats at the end of this month. A large chunk of those members were in the nursery carpark on Saturday, many of them busting to use the loo. Shadow over Tabcorp? Racegoers might continue to live it up at Flemington this week amid a sea of TAB-sponsored green, but it is not all fun and frivolity for the gambling giant. Gillon McLachlan at the races on Saturday. Louis Trerise



Tabcorp boss Gill McLachlan fronted investors last week and revealed his company was still being probed by the financial crimes cop (Austrac) about their ability to manage money laundering risks. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep “Our growth plans will not come at the expense of keeping our customers safe,” McLachlan told those tuning in to Tabcorp’s annual general meeting. “[We have a] dedicated team fully co-operating with Austrac. [We will] inform the market when there is a material update. Financial crime and risk transformation programs are an absolute priority.” Tabcorp, which booked a net profit of $46.3 million from $2.63 billion in revenue for the 2026 financial year, said the investigation was at an early stage despite kicking off in May.



But, in its annual report, McLachlan’s mob acknowledged that any breaches of anti-money laundering and counterterrorism financing laws could lead to “significant” penalties. Related Article Melbourne Cup Briefing

Melbourne Cup Horror fall on Saturday, procedure on Sunday … Melbourne Cup on Tuesday? Jockey’s bid for miracle ride For its part, the watchdog said it “had a number of serious concerns with Tabcorp’s ability to effectively identify, mitigate and manage its ML/TF [money laundering and terrorism financing] risks”. McLachlan hired ex-Austrac chief executive Paul Jevtovic as its chief financial crime officer, after news emerged about the regulator’s concerns in May. Read more from our racing coverage

World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government Queensland’s 28th governor Thomas Bradley sworn in Courtney Kruk November 1, 2026 — 7:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Justice Thomas Bradley KC has been sworn in as Queensland’s 28th governor in a ceremony at Government House on Sunday. The Court of Appeal judge will replace Dr Jeannette Young, who has held the role since 2021. In an address to attendees on Sunday, Bradley described the appointment as a “tremendous honour” and said he looked forward to engaging with people across the state “to help harness the wisdom, the skill, and the goodwill that is in every community”. Court of Appeal judge Thomas Bradley has been sworn in as Queensland’s 28th governor. Renae Droop/RDW Photography He continued with an extensive list of Queensland towns and cities visited by he and partner Matthew Young this year, and said they aimed “to spend as much time out of Brisbane as we spend in it” while fulfilling his new role as governor.



“Over the next few years, we will meet people, and we will honour achievements in those and in many other communities across the state, large and small,” Bradley said. Related Article Queensland government Senior judge appointed as Queensland’s next governor The governor appointment does not have a fixed term, but representatives typically spend about five years in the role. Bradley noted that his term will capture the lead up to the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, and described an opportunity to showcase Queensland to the world. “In the coming years, we will understand more of the best that the world has to offer in sport, in thought, culture and in values.



“In the same conversation, the world will learn that in each of those fields, some of the best is already here in Queensland. “Using our imagination, we will share with the world some secrets about living in this special place, and fresh eyes from around the world will notice more of the detail and perhaps the beauty that is here.” Premier David Crisafulli, Thomas Bradley and his partner Matthew Yoong at Government House. Renae Droop/RDW Photography Premier David Crisafulli acknowledged Bradley’s lifelong commitment to public service, and said his career achievements would bring value to the role. “These duties call for sound judgment, integrity, and an instinct for treating people with respect,” he said.



“Your career gives Queenslanders every reason to look forward to your service with great confidence.” Related Article Queensland government Meet Thomas Bradley: Arts patron, youth mentor, and Qld’s first openly gay governor Bradley was born in Cairns and attended school at Clairvaux College in Brisbane. He graduated from the University of Queensland with a law degree in 1987 and was admitted as a barrister in 2000. Three years after becoming a barrister, he was appointed Queen’s Counsel, a title held by senior, highly experienced barristers. He had been a sitting judge of the Supreme Court since 2018, and served on the Supreme Court Library Legal Heritage Subcommittee.



Opposition leader Steven Miles highlighted Bradley’s cultural accolades, including his role as the first state-based ambassador for the Pinnacle foundation, an LGBTQIA+ education charity, his work on the Brisbane Festival Giving Committee, and as the chair of the Brisbane Writers Festival. “I think there is one thing all of us can agree on: is that representation matters,” Miles said. “Queensland is stronger when the people in public roles are a reflection of its citizens.” The Crisafulli government appointed Bradley to the Court of Appeal in March last year. He was announced as Queensland’s next government in August. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Psychosis linked to ADHD medication on the rise, doctors warn
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare Psychosis linked to ADHD medication on the rise, doctors warn Henrietta Cook November 1, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A growing number of patients are developing psychosis, including paranoia and hallucinations, after taking medication to treat ADHD, psychiatrists have warned. While the drugs can be transformative for people with ADHD, psychiatrists say stimulant medication can, in rare cases, trigger psychosis. In rare cases ADHD medication can cause psychosis. Getty Images It is estimated that between 2 and 6 per cent of Australian adults have ADHD. Rates of diagnosis have skyrocketed due to increased awareness of the disorder, and the number of Australians using stimulant medication to treat the neurodevelopmental condition is surging.



Stimulant-induced psychosis was rare 10 years ago, Australian Society of Psychiatrists executive director Dr Pramudie Gunaratne said. “This is more of a regular presentation now,” Dr Gunaratne said. “If you’ve increased the number of people being prescribed this medication, there’s going to be a certain proportion of those people that will develop psychosis,” she said. “If you take more than prescribed, if you take it without medical supervision, if people are accessing stimulants from friends, that can put them at particularly high risk.” The number of adults being treated for ADHD has increased more than sixfold since 2017, research by the University of NSW found. Gunaratne said stimulant medications could alter brain chemistry.



“Like all medications, they carry significant risks,” she said. “Even when stimulants are taken exactly as prescribed in people without known risk factors, there is a rare but real risk of psychosis.” Symptoms of psychosis can include paranoia, hallucinations or delusional beliefs. Australian Society of Psychiatrists executive director Dr Pramudie Gunaratne. Wolter Peters “Sometimes the person themselves might not have insight or recognise that this is happening, and it will be the people around them that notice that their behaviour or thinking is out of character,” Gunaratne said. Sydney psychiatrist Dr Matthew Large, a conjoint professor at UNSW, is treating an increasing number of patients for psychosis linked to ADHD medication.



Large has seen four cases in the past year, including a young patient who experienced psychosis after she was prescribed stimulant medication to treat her inattention. He said the patient’s inattention was linked to trauma. “The patient instead needed treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder,” he said. In another case, a high-achieving student feigned ADHD symptoms to secure medication to improve their academic performance. This patient experienced psychosis after increasing the dose. Too few patients were informed of the risk of psychosis before starting treatment, Large said. He said that while safety studies of stimulants in children indicated only a small proportion developed psychosis, it was unclear whether the drugs carried the same low risk in adults.



“The practice has outstripped safety evidence, in my view,” he said. Psychosis is thought to be caused by excessive dopamine transmission in the brain. Psychiatrist Dr Matthew Large. Audrey Richardson Large said this dopamine transmission is increased by stimulant medication. People experiencing psychosis are usually admitted to hospital, where they receive anti-psychotic medication, therapy and social support.



“Even treatment of one psychotic episode is a very significant event in a person’s life,” Large said. “They lose contact with reality. They often do things that are deeply embarrassing to themselves, and they can get in trouble with the law.” Associate Professor Mark Putland, Victoria branch chair of the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine, said misuse of ADHD medication was triggering psychosis in some patients, but some people using the medication as directed had developed psychosis. “It is a real health problem from an addiction and mental health point of view,” he said. “Psychosis is the pointy end of that.” He said combining ADHD medication with other substances was also fuelling psychosis. “They might be abusing prescribed stimulants and also using some amphetamines they bought on the street, and they might also have some mental health conditions. It’s often messy.”



ADHD Australia chief executive Melissa Webster, who was diagnosed with ADHD while at university, knows at least four people who have experienced psychosis while using stimulant medication. She said these people also had pre-existing mental health conditions, so it was difficult to determine what led to the psychosis. Related Article Review Rage, depression, despair: This book explains why PMDD is still so misunderstood Better communication of side effects was needed, she said. Some psychiatrists relied on patients reading the paperwork tucked into their boxes of medication, she said, while others outlined potential side effects in great detail. But serious side effects were rare and many people found the medication life changing for the better.



More states are allowing GPs to diagnose, treat and prescribe ADHD medication. Last week, 150 Victorian GPs started diagnosing and prescribing the medication, following NSW, South Australia and Queensland. The change is designed to reduce the costs of obtaining a diagnosis, which previously required people to seek a referral from a GP to see a specialist.
